meta.note: Pipeline record for Little Lexicon content. Word ids are permanent: saved progress refers to them. Edit content here, then run `npx tsx src/run.ts --only=export`.

words.etymology: From Old French abatre ("to knock down"), from Late Latin abbattere, built from ab ("away") and battuere ("to beat"), the verb that also gives debate.
From Latin aberrare ("to go astray"), from ab ("away") and errare ("to wander"), the verb that also gives err.
From Latin abscondere ("to hide"), perhaps by way of Middle French, from abs ("away") and condere ("to put away, store"), the verb also behind recondite.
Latin joined abs ("away") and tenere ("to hold") into abstinere, to keep yourself away from something; English took the word over through Old French.
From Latin admonere ("to remind, warn"), built on monere ("to warn"), the verb that also gives monitor.
From Latin adulterare ("to commit adultery", and also "to falsify, corrupt"), built from ad ("to") and alter ("the other"); adultery comes from the same family.

From Ancient Greek aisthetikos ("of sense perception"), akin to aisthesis ("sensation"). The link to beauty is German: 1700s thinkers named the study of taste after the senses, and English followed in the 1800s.
From French agrandir ("to enlarge"), from a and grand ("big"), which goes back to Latin grandis ("great"), as in grandiloquent.
From Latin alacritas, from alacer ("brisk, lively"), which through French and Italian also gave the music term allegro.
From Late Latin alleviare ("to lighten"), from ad and levis ("light"), the adjective behind levity: to alleviate pain is to make it lighter.
From Medieval Latin amalgamare, from amalgama ("mercury alloy"), from Arabic, from Greek malagma ("softening ointment"); mixing metals with mercury led to the general sense of blending into one.
From Latin ambiguus ("shifting, doubtful"), from ambigere ("to go around, be in doubt"), built from ambi ("on both sides") and agere ("to drive").
words.watch_out: Ambiguous describes words or situations open to more than one reading; a person torn between feelings is ambivalent.

words.etymology: The psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler coined German Ambivalenz in 1910 for conflicting feelings held at once, from Latin ambi ("both") and valere ("to be strong"); English took ambivalence, then ambivalent.
words.watch_out: Ambivalent means torn between opposing feelings, not indifferent or uninterested.

words.etymology: Reshaped from the older English meliorate after French améliorer; meliorate comes from Late Latin meliorare ("to improve"), from melior ("better").
From Ancient Greek anachronismos, from anachronizomai ("to refer to the wrong time"), built from ana ("up, against") and chronos ("time").
From Latin analogus, from Ancient Greek analogos ("proportionate"), built on logos ("reckoning"); Greek analogia, formed from analogos, gave English analogy.
With the prefix an ("not"), Greek turned homalos ("level") into anomalos ("uneven"), whose noun anomalia came into English through Latin.
Through French and Latin from Ancient Greek antipatheia, from anti ("against") and pathos ("feeling, suffering").
words.watch_out: Antipathy is strong dislike, not a lack of feeling; a lack of interest or feeling is apathy.

words.etymology: Through French and Latin from Ancient Greek apatheia ("freedom from emotion"), from a ("without") and pathos ("feeling, suffering").
From Old French apeser ("to bring to peace"), built on pais ("peace"), which comes from Latin pax.
From Latin arduus ("steep, high, hard to reach"): an arduous task is an uphill climb.
From Latin articulare ("to divide into joints", and so "to speak distinctly"), from articulus ("small joint"), which also gave article.
From Ancient Greek asketikos, from asketes ("monk, hermit"), from askeo ("to exercise, train"): ascetics trained themselves to go without comforts.
words.watch_out: Ascetic is easily confused with aesthetic, but it has nothing to do with beauty: it means giving up comforts on purpose.

words.etymology: From Old French asuagier ("to calm"), from a Vulgar Latin verb built on Latin suavis ("sweet"), the source of suave.
Latin audere ("to dare") gave the adjective audax ("bold") and the noun audacia, which English turned into audacious.
Goes back to Ancient Greek austeros, harsh or bitter, a word first used of fruit and wine sharp enough to leave the mouth dry.
From Old French averer, from a Medieval Latin verb built on Latin verus, true: to aver something is to declare it true.
From French banal, built on ban, a feudal lord's authority: it first described things the lord owned and all his tenants shared, and so came to mean commonplace.
From Old English beleogan, to deceive with lies, made of be- and lie, to tell an untruth; an outward look that belies something gives a false picture of it.
words.watch_out: Belie means to hide or contradict something, not to reveal it; using it for reveal or show is a common mistake.

words.etymology: Built from Latin bene, well, and a form of facere, to do or make: a beneficent person is one who does good.
From Old English bolster, a pillow or cushion: to bolster something is to prop it up, as a pillow props up someone in bed.
From bombast, cotton stuffing once used to pad clothes, which came through Old French from Late Latin bombax, cotton. The word moved from padded clothes to padded speech.
words.watch_out: Bombastic comes from cotton padding and means puffed up with grand words; its colloquial use for loud or aggressive is common but disputed.

words.etymology: From boor, which English borrowed from Dutch boer, a peasant; boor shifted from meaning a country person to anyone with crude manners.
From Old French borjoner, a verb related to burjon, a bud: something that burgeons grows fast, like a plant putting out new shoots.
From Old French ars bouterez, supporting arches, from a Germanic verb meaning to push: a buttress pushes back against a wall to keep it standing.
From French cacophonie, from Ancient Greek kakophonia, made of kakos, bad, and phone, sound.
From French cajoler, probably a blend of two older French verbs, one for a jay's chattering and one for luring into a cage, which together suggest coaxing talk.
From Latin callosus, hard-skinned, from callum, hardened skin: a callous person's feelings have grown a tough, numb layer.
words.watch_out: The noun for a patch of thick, hard skin is usually spelled callus; callous is the adjective, as in a callous remark.

words.etymology: From Latin candor, a bright whiteness, from candere, to shine, a word Latin also used for an open, honest character. English took the whiteness sense first and the frank sense by about 1600.

Through French from Italian capriccio, a whim. Capriccio grew from caporiccio, which sources explain either as curly head, curls being taken as a sign of an unruly nature, or as a fright or sudden start.
From Latin castigare, to correct or punish, formed on a stem meaning purity that is related to castus, chaste. Chastise and chasten come from the same Latin verb.

From catalysis, a chemistry word for speeding up a reaction, from Ancient Greek katalysis, a dissolving, made of kata, down, and lyein, to loosen. The sense of setting off any change grew from the chemical one.
From Latin causticus, from Ancient Greek kaustikos, burning, from kaustos, burnt: caustic words sting the way a burn does.
From French chicanerie, trickery, from the verb chicaner, to quibble or squabble over small points.
From Latin coagulare, to curdle, from coagulum, rennet, which comes from cogere, to bring together, itself made of co- and agere, to drive.
Latin coalescere joined co-, together, with alescere, to grow or increase: parts that coalesce grow into a single whole. Adolescent is built on the same verb.
Through French from Latin cogens, a form of cogere, to drive together or compel, made of co- and agere, to drive: a cogent case forces agreement.
From Late Latin commensuratus, measured together, from com-, with, and mensurare, to measure, which comes from mensura, a measure.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: Goes back to Latin conciliare, to bring together or win over, from concilium, a council or meeting; reconcile comes from the same verb.
From Latin condonare, to give up or forgive, made of con- and donare, to give: to condone a wrong is to let it go.
From Latin conflagratio, a great burning, from conflagrare, to burn up, built on flagrare, to burn or blaze.
Borrowed from French in the early 1700s: a connoisseur was literally a knower, from the verb connaître, to know, which goes back to Latin cognoscere.
From Latin contritus, crushed, the past participle of conterere, to grind, built on terere, to rub: a contrite person is ground down by guilt.
Of unknown origin. One etymologist's best guess ties it to 16th-century Jesuit commentaries on Aristotle from Coimbra, whose arguments played on double meanings.
From convolute, taken from Latin convolutus, rolled together, the past participle of convolvere, built on volvere, to roll, as in revolve and involve.
From Latin copiosus, plentiful, from copia, abundance, itself built from ops, wealth. Copia also gave cornucopia, the horn of plenty.
From Latin corroborare, to strengthen, built on robur, hard oak wood and so strength, the same word that gave robust.
words.watch_out: Corroborate is not collaborate: it means to back up a claim with further evidence, not to work together.

words.etymology: From Latin credulus, quick to believe, from credere, to believe, the verb behind credit, creed and credible.
words.watch_out: Credulous describes a person who believes too easily; a claim that deserves belief is credible, not credulous.

words.etymology: From Latin cursorius, of running, from cursor, a runner, from currere, to run: a cursory look runs over the surface.
From Middle English derthe, made up of dear and the noun ending -th, as warmth is made from warm. Its Germanic source meant costliness: when goods run short, they grow dear.
From French débâcle, the breakup of ice on a river, from débâcler, to unbar or set loose. In both languages it came to mean any sudden, disastrous collapse.
Formed in 1923 from de- and bunk, nonsense, short for bunkum. Bunkum goes back to a long, empty 1820 speech in Congress that its speaker said was meant for Buncombe County, North Carolina.
From Latin decorum, that which is fitting, a form of decorus, proper or seemly, from decor, grace.
From French déférence, linked to defer in its sense of yielding to someone else's judgment. Both go back to Latin deferre, to carry down or hand over, built on ferre, to carry.
From Greek deleterios, harmful, from deleter, a destroyer, from a verb meaning to hurt or spoil. Despite the look, it is not related to delete.
From Latin deridere, to laugh at or mock, from de-, down, and ridere, to laugh, which also gives ridicule.
From French dérivatif, from Latin derivare, to draw off, a verb built on rivus, a brook or channel: derivative work is drawn off from an earlier source.
From Latin desiccare, to dry up completely, built on siccus, dry.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Medieval Latin diaphanus, from Greek diaphanes, see-through, from dia-, through, and phainein, to show or to shine.
From Greek diatribe, built on tribein, to rub or wear away: a way of wearing away time, so a pastime, and also a lecture. Latin used it for a learned discourse.
From Greek didaktikos, apt at teaching, from didaskein, to teach, by way of French didactique.
From Latin diffidere, to distrust, from dis-, not, and fidere, to trust, the verb behind confident. It once meant distrustful of others; now it means unsure of oneself.
words.watch_out: Diffident does not mean indifferent: a diffident person may care a great deal but lacks the confidence to push forward.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Latin dirige, steer or guide, the first word of a chant in the church's service for the dead; it came to mean any song of mourning.
Built from dis-, reversing, and abuse in an old sense, to deceive: to disabuse someone is to undo a deception. French has the matching verb désabuser.
words.watch_out: Disabuse does not mean to stop abusing someone; it means to free them from a false belief.

words.etymology: From Old French discordant, from Latin discordare, to disagree, from discors, at odds, made of dis-, apart, and cor, heart.
From Latin discrepantia, from discrepare ("to differ, disagree"), which joins dis- ("apart") and crepare ("to rattle, creak").
From Old French desparagier, from des- ("dis-") and parage ("rank"), built on pair ("equal"), from Latin par. English once also used it to mean to match unequally or to degrade, senses now obsolete.
From Latin disparatus ("divided"), perhaps by way of Middle French, from disparare ("to divide"), made of dis- ("apart") and parare ("to arrange"), the verb that is also inside separate.

From Old French dessembler, a reshaping of Latin dissimulare ("to hide, disguise") under the influence of sembler ("to seem"). The Latin verb comes from dissimilis ("unlike"), built on similis ("like").
words.watch_out: Dissemble does not mean disassemble (take apart); it means to hide your real feelings or plans behind a pretense.

words.etymology: From Latin disseminare ("to scatter, broadcast"), made of dis- ("in all directions") and seminare ("to sow"), from semen ("seed").
From Middle French dissonance, from Latin dissonantia, from dissonare ("to clash in sound, disagree"), made of dis- ("apart") and sonare ("to sound").
From Latin distendere ("to stretch out, swell"), made of dis- ("apart") and tendere ("to stretch").
From Greek dogmatikos ("didactic"), from dogma ("an opinion, belief or decree"), by way of Late Latin dogmaticus and Middle French dogmatique.
From Latin dubius ("wavering, doubtful"), a relative of doubt. Its deeper origin is uncertain, but it probably goes back to a root meaning "two", as in a mind torn between two choices.
From Latin ebulliens, a form of ebullire ("to boil or bubble up"), from ex- ("out") and bullire ("to bubble"), the source of English boil.
From French éclectique, from Greek eklektikos ("selective"), from eklegein ("to pick out"), made of ek ("out") and legein ("to choose"). It is a distant relative of elect.
From Late Latin efficacia, from efficax ("effective"), from efficere ("to bring about"), made of ex- ("out") and facere ("to do, make"); it came into English through Old French efficace.
words.watch_out: Efficacy is not efficiency (doing a job with little waste); it is whether something produces the result it is meant to.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Greek elegeia, short for a phrase meaning "elegiac song", from elegos ("a song of lament"), which may come from Phrygian. It reached English through Latin elegia and Middle French elegie.
words.watch_out: An elegy is not a speech praising the dead (that is a eulogy); it is a poem or song of mourning.

words.etymology: From Latin eloquens ("speaking"), a form of eloqui ("to speak out"), from e- ("out") and loqui ("to speak"), by way of Old French.
From Old French embellir ("to make beautiful"), made of em- and bel ("beautiful"), which comes from Latin bellus.

Formed from empiric, which goes back through Latin empiricus to Greek empeiria ("experience"), built on peira ("a trial"): knowledge won by trying things. The look-alike empire has a separate history.
From Latin aemulatus, a form of aemulari ("to try to equal or outdo, to rival"), from aemulus ("a rival").

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerare ("to implant"), made of in- ("in") and generare ("to beget, produce"), which comes from genus ("birth, descent").
From Greek ephemeros ("lasting only a day"), made of epi ("on") and hemera ("day"), by way of New Latin ephemerus.
From Greek epigramma ("an inscription"), from epigraphein ("to write on, inscribe"), made of epi ("on") and graphein ("to write"). Latin and Middle French passed it to English.
words.watch_out: An epigram is not an epigraph (a quotation that opens a book) or an epitaph (words on a tomb); it is a short, witty saying.

words.etymology: From Medieval Latin aequivocare ("to share a name"), based on Late Latin aequivocus ("ambiguous"), made of aequus ("equal") and vocare ("to call, name"), a verb built on vox ("voice").
From Latin eruditus, a form of erudire ("to educate, train"), made of e- ("out of") and rudis ("rough, raw, unskilled"): training brings a person out of a raw state.
From Greek esoterikos ("for insiders"), built on esotero ("more inward"), a form of eso ("within"). Its opposite, exoteric, described teaching open to the public.
From Medieval Latin eulogium, which seems to blend Greek eulogia ("praise, good words") with Latin elogium ("an epitaph"). The Greek word is built on eu ("well") and logos ("word, reason").
words.watch_out: A eulogy is not a mournful poem (that is an elegy); it is a tribute praising someone, most often given at a funeral.

words.etymology: From Ancient Greek euphemismos, from eu, "well", and pheme, "speech". The Greek root word described speech that avoided words of ill omen.
Via French from Latin evanescere, "to vanish, fade away", built on vanus, "empty". Vanish and vain come from the same Latin source.
From Latin exacerbare, "to provoke", from ex-, "thoroughly", and acerbare, "to make bitter", which comes from acerbus, "harsh, bitter". Acerbic shares the root.
words.watch_out: Exacerbate is not exasperate: you exacerbate a problem by making it worse, but you exasperate a person by annoying them.

words.etymology: From Medieval Latin exculpare, from ex-, "out of", and culpa, "blame": to exculpate someone is to free them from blame. Culpable comes from culpa too.
From Latin exigere, "to demand", formed from ex-, "out", and agere, "to drive". Exact and exigency come from the same verb.
From Latin exonerare, "to unload", from ex-, "off", and onus, "a burden": to exonerate someone is to lift a burden of blame. Onerous shares the root.
From Latin expedire, "to free the feet from a snare", from ex, "out", and pes, "foot". It came to mean to help along, and so to be useful or advantageous.
words.watch_out: Expedient is not a synonym for expeditious (fast and efficient); it means convenient for getting a result, often at the cost of what is right.

words.etymology: From Latin expungere, "to strike out", from ex-, "out", and pungere, "to prick". Pungent and puncture come from the same verb.
From Latin extollere, "to raise up", from ex-, "up, out", and tollere, "to lift": to extol someone is to lift them up with praise.
From Latin extraneus, "from outside, foreign", built on extra, "outside". Through Old French, the same Latin word also gave English strange and estrange.
From French facétieux, from Latin facetia, "a jest", which comes from facetus, "witty".
Via Old French from Latin fallacia, "deceit", from fallax, "deceptive", from fallere, "to deceive". False and fallacy come from the same verb.
From Latin fatuus, "foolish". Infatuate shares the root: the Latin verb infatuare meant to make a fool of someone.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Old English ficol, "changeable, crafty, deceitful", related to an old verb meaning to flatter or deceive.
Of uncertain origin, perhaps from Middle English flouten, "to play the flute". An older meaning, now rare, is to mock or jeer at someone.
words.watch_out: Flout is not flaunt: you flout a rule by openly ignoring it, but you flaunt something by showing it off.

words.etymology: From Latin fomentum, "a warm compress", from fovere, "to keep warm". In Middle English it meant to treat the body with warm liquids; the sense of stirring up trouble came later.
From Old English foresteall, "an ambush", from fore, "in front", and steall, "a standing place". In Middle English it meant to waylay someone on the road; now it means to head off trouble.
From Latin fortuitus, "happening by chance", which is thought to be built on fors, "chance". Fortune comes from the same Latin family.
words.watch_out: Fortuitous traditionally means happening by chance; its use to mean simply lucky is now common, though some careful writers object.

words.etymology: From fraction in an old sense, "discord", plus -ous. Fraction goes back to Latin frangere, "to break", which is also the source of fracture.
Via French from Latin frugalis, from frux, "produce, crops". A related Latin word, frugi, "fit for food", came to mean useful, honest and thrifty.
From Latin garrulus, "talkative", from garrire, "to chatter", a verb of imitative origin.
From Old English gad, a pointed stick for driving cattle. The Lombards, an early Germanic people, had a related word for a spear.
From Latin gregarius, "of the flock", from grex, "flock, herd". Congregate, aggregate and egregious come from the same root.
From Old French guile, "deceit", from a Frankish word for a ruse. English wile, as in wily, comes from the same Germanic word.

From hackney, a horse often hired out, a name probably taken from Hackney, then a village near London. Hired horses and carriages were used by everyone, which most likely gave the sense of stale from overuse.

Through French from Old Italian aringa, tied to aringare, to speak in public, and aringo, a public assembly. These probably come from a Germanic word for ring, making harangue a relative of ring and rank.
Made in English from Ancient Greek hedone, pleasure, with the ending -ist; hedonism is built the same way.
From Ancient Greek hegemonia, leadership or supreme command, from hegemon, a leader, which comes from a verb meaning to lead. Its use in the early 1800s owed something to German Hegemonie.
From Ancient Greek hairesis, a choosing, and so a set of principles someone adopts, from a verb meaning to take for oneself. It reached English through Latin and Old French.
From Byzantine Greek eikonoklastes, image breaker, from eikon, image, and a verb meaning to break, by way of French and Medieval Latin. It first named people who destroyed religious images.
From Greek eidololatreia, worship of idols, which joins eidolon, an image or idol, to a word for worship. It came into English through Latin and Old French.
From Latin immutabilis, unchangeable: in-, not, plus mutabilis, changeable, which comes from mutare, to change, as in mutation.
Made in English from im-, not, and passive in its old sense of able to suffer or feel. Passive comes from Latin pati, to suffer, which also gave English passion and patient.
words.watch_out: It does not mean impassioned: an impassive face shows no feeling, while an impassioned speech is full of it.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Latin imperiosus, mighty or commanding, from imperium, command or the power to rule, the word that also gave English empire.
From Latin impertinens, from in-, not, and pertinere, to concern, which is built on tenere, to hold. It first meant irrelevant and later came to mean rude.
words.watch_out: It now usually means rude rather than irrelevant, though the older sense, not pertinent, still turns up in old books and legal writing.

words.etymology: From Latin impervius, impassable, from in-, not, and pervius, having a way through, which joins per, through, and via, way.
From Latin implacabilis, unappeasable: in-, not, plus placabilis, easy to calm, from placare, to appease, the source of placate.
From Latin imputare, to enter into the account or charge to someone, from in-, in, and putare, to reckon or think. It came to English through French imputer.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Latin incipiens, beginning, a form of incipere, to begin, which joins in-, in or on, and capere, to take hold of.
From Latin indigens, a form of indigere, to need, which joins indu, within, and egere, to lack. It came to English through Old French.
words.watch_out: It is easily mixed up with indigenous (born in or belonging to a region) and indignant (feeling wronged), but an indigent person has next to no money.

words.etymology: Built on Latin dolere, to hurt: Late Latin indolens meant painless, and English took it directly or by way of French. Perhaps in French, the word moved from painless to easygoing and lazy.
Through French from Latin ineffabilis, unutterable: in-, not, plus effabilis, utterable, from effari, to speak out, which is built on fari, to speak.
From Latin inexorabilis, unmoved by pleading: in-, not, plus exorabilis, from exorare, to win over by begging, which is built on orare, to plead or pray.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Late Latin inimicalis, hostile, from inimicus, an enemy, which joins in-, not, and amicus, friend, as in amicable.
words.watch_out: It does not mean inimitable (impossible to copy); inimical means harmful or unfriendly.

words.etymology: From Latin iniquitas, unfairness, from iniquus, unequal or unjust: in-, not, plus aequus, equal or fair, as in equal and equanimity.
words.watch_out: It is not the same as inequity, which means unfairness or unequal shares; iniquity means wickedness, a far graver charge.

words.etymology: From Latin innocuus, harmless: in-, not, plus nocuus, harmful, from nocere, to harm, the verb behind noxious and innocent.
Through French from Latin insipidus, tasteless: in-, not, plus sapidus, tasty, from sapere, to taste, the source of savor.
From Latin insularis, of an island, from insula, island, as in peninsula. The sense of narrow and inward-looking pictures a group cut off as if on an island.
Formed from in- ("not") and tractable, which goes back through Latin tractabilis to tractare ("to handle"), itself from trahere ("to pull"): an intractable problem refuses to be managed.
Reached English through French intransigeant and Spanish intransigente, from Latin in- ("not") and transigere ("to come to terms"), built from trans ("across") and agere ("to do").
From Latin inundare ("to flood, overflow"), built on unda ("wave"), the noun behind undulate too: an inundated office gets hit by wave after wave.
From Latin inveteratus ("long-standing"), from veterare ("to grow old"), from vetus ("old"), the source of veteran. Here in- means "in", not "not".
From Late Latin irascibilis, by way of Old French, from irasci ("to become angry"), from ira ("anger"), which also gives irate.
From Late Latin itinerari ("to travel"), from iter ("journey, road"), whose stem itiner- also gives itinerary.
Spartans were famous for answering in very few words; their region, Laconia, gave Greek Lakonikos, which reached English through Latin Laconicus.
words.watch_out: Strictly, laconic means using few words; it is also often used to mean laid-back or languid, a use some usage guides reject.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Latin laudare ("to praise"), from laus ("praise, glory"), by way of Old French and Middle English; laudable has the same source.
From Greek lethargikos, from lethargos ("forgetful"), joining lethe ("forgetting") and argos ("idle"). The Greek noun lethargia already meant drowsiness, the heavy, sluggish state the word names now.
From Latin levitas ("lightness"), from levis ("light in weight"), the root of lever, elevate and alleviate: levity treats a heavy moment lightly.
From Latin loquax ("talkative"), from loqui ("to speak"), the verb behind eloquent and soliloquy.
From Latin lucidus, from lucere ("to shine"); elucidate is built on lucidus too. A lucid account lets light into its subject.
From Latin luminosus ("full of light"), from lumen ("light"), through Middle French; illuminate comes from the same noun.
From Latin magnanimus ("great-souled"), joining magnus ("great") with animus ("mind, spirit"), the noun also behind equanimity.
Apparently from French malingre ("frail, puny"): a malingerer plays the weakling to dodge work.
words.watch_out: Despite the linger inside it, malinger does not mean to hang about; it means to fake or play up an illness to avoid work.

words.etymology: From Late Latin malleabilis, through Middle French, from malleare ("to hammer"), from malleus ("hammer"), which is also the source of mallet.
From Maudelen, a Middle English spelling of Magdalene. Artists usually showed Mary Magdalene weeping, so her name came to mean tearfully sentimental.
From Latin mendax ("lying"), through mendacium ("a lie") and Middle French. Mendax first meant "faulty" and is related to mendum ("flaw"), behind amend and mend.
From Latin mercurialis ("of Mercury"), from Mercurius, the Roman messenger god. In astrology, people under the influence of Mercury were thought quick and changeable.
From Latin meticulosus ("fearful, timid"), from metus ("fear"). The sense of great care over details came later, from French méticuleux.
From Latin mitigare ("to soften, tame"), from mitis ("mild, gentle"): to mitigate a harm is to make it milder.
words.watch_out: Mitigate means to lessen; to work against is militate, so most usage guides count "mitigate against" as an error.

words.etymology: From Late Latin mollificare, built on Latin mollis ("soft"), which also gives emollient: to mollify people is to soften their anger.
From Latin morosus ("fussy, peevish, self-willed"), from mos ("custom; self-will"), the root of moral and mores, by way of French.
Through Old French mondain from Late Latin mundanus, from mundus ("world"): mundane things belong to the ordinary world of every day.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Medieval Latin, from Arabic naẓīr as-samt, "counterpart of the zenith": the nadir is the point of the sky straight below, opposite the zenith overhead, so it came to mean the lowest point.
From Latin nascens, "being born", a form of nasci ("to be born"), the verb behind natal and native: a nascent thing has only just come into being.
From Latin nebulosus, "misty, cloudy", from nebula ("mist, cloud"), by way of French: a nebulous plan is one you can only make out as if through fog.
From Latin nefarius, from nefas ("a wrong against divine law"), which joins ne- ("not") to fas ("what divine law allows").
From Ancient Greek neophytos, "newly planted", from neos ("new") and phyton ("plant"), through Latin neophytus: a neophyte has only just taken root in a field.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Late Latin obfuscatus, "darkened", from obfuscare, built on fuscare ("to darken"), perhaps by way of French: to obfuscate a point is to throw shadow over it.
From Latin obsequiosus, from obsequium ("compliance"), from obsequi ("to yield to"), which joins ob ("toward") and sequi ("to follow"), the verb behind sequel and sequence.
From Latin obstinatus, "resolved", from obstinare ("to set one's mind firmly on"), built on stare ("to stand"): an obstinate person stands firm and will not shift.
From Latin obtusus, "blunted, dull", from obtundere ("to beat against, to blunt"): an obtuse mind, like an obtuse angle, has lost its sharp point.
words.watch_out: Using obtuse to mean hard to understand, as if it were abstruse, is common but disputed; its core sense is slow to catch on.

words.etymology: From Latin officiosus, "obliging, kind", from officium ("service, duty"), the source of office: an officious person is too eager to be of service.
words.watch_out: Officious does not mean official: it describes someone who takes over matters that are not theirs to manage.

words.etymology: Through Old French from Latin onerosus, built on onus ("burden"), stem oner-, which also gives English onus and exonerate.
From Latin opacus, "shaded, dark", a word of unknown source, later influenced by French opaque: what is opaque lets no light, or no understanding, through.
From Latin opprobrium, "reproach, disgrace", from opprobrare ("to taunt"), which joins ob- ("toward") to probrum ("shame, insult").
From Latin ostentatus, a form of ostentare ("to show off, to display"), which repeats the action of ostendere ("to show"), also the source of ostensible.
From Latin palliatus, "cloaked", from pallium ("cloak"), either directly or through French: to palliate a fault or a pain is to cover it without removing it.
From Ancient Greek panakeia, through Latin, from panakes ("all-healing"), made of pan ("all") and akos ("cure").
Through French from Old Italian paragone, from paragonare ("to test on a touchstone"), perhaps from a Greek verb meaning "to sharpen": a paragon is the standard others are tested against.
From Latin parsimonia, "thrift", formed from parcere ("to spare, to save"), a verb whose own source is uncertain.
From Latin paucitas, "fewness", partly by way of French, built on paucus ("few"), which is related to English few.
From pedant, which came through French from Italian pedante, "schoolmaster": in English a pedant was once simply a teacher, before the word came to mean a stickler for petty rules.
From French penchant, "leaning", from pencher ("to tilt, to lean"), which goes back to Latin pendere ("to hang"), as in pendulum: a penchant is a leaning toward something.
From Latin penuria, "want, scarcity". Where the Latin word came from is uncertain; it may be linked to paene ("almost").
From Latin perfidiosus, from perfidia ("treachery"), from perfidus ("faithless"), built on fides ("faith"), the root of fidelity: a perfidious person breaks faith.
From Late Latin perfunctorius, "careless", from perfungi ("to carry through, to fulfill"), built on fungi ("to perform"), as in function: a perfunctory act is aimed only at getting the duty over.
From Latin perniciosus ("destructive"), by way of Old French. Its base, pernicies ("ruin"), goes back to per ("through") and nex ("violent death").
From Latin perspicax ("keen-eyed"), from perspicere ("to see through"), which joins per ("through") and specere ("to look"), the verb behind perspective.
words.watch_out: Easily mixed up with perspicuous, which means clearly expressed; perspicacious describes a sharp mind, not clear writing.

words.etymology: From the Latin verb pervadere ("to spread through"), made of per ("through") and vadere ("to go"); vadere also gives English invade.
From Latin petulans ("saucy, impudent"), by way of Middle French; the Latin word is traced to petere ("to aim at, ask for").

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From pith, the spongy core of a plant stem and so the heart of a matter, plus -y. Pith goes back to Old English; where it came from before that is unknown.
From Latin placare ("to calm, appease"), which is related to placere ("to please"), the source of please and placid.
Borrowed from French platitude, which means flatness and also dullness, from plat ("flat").
Borrowed through Late Latin from Greek plethora ("fullness"), from plethein ("to be full"). The Greek verb shares an ancient root with Latin plenus, the source of plenty.
words.watch_out: Traditionally it means an excess, more than is needed, but it is now widely used for simply a large amount, which some editors dislike.

words.etymology: From French polémique, which goes back to Greek polemos ("war") through the adjective polemikos ("warlike"): a polemic wages a war of words.
From Latin ponderosus ("heavy, weighty"), from pondus ("weight"), the noun that also gave English ponder and pound.
From Greek pragmatikos ("versed in affairs"), via Late Latin and French, from pragma ("a deed"), from prassein ("to do"), which also lies behind practical.
Formed from prate ("to chatter") with -le, an ending that marks repeated action; prate came into Middle English either from Old English or from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German.
From Latin praecipitare ("to fling down headfirst"), built on praeceps ("headlong"): prae ("before") plus -ceps, a form related to caput ("head").
From Latin praecludere ("to close off, block"), from prae ("before") and claudere ("to shut"), the verb that also gave English close.
From Latin praecox ("ripened early"), from prae ("before") and coquere ("to cook, ripen"). Apricot, a fruit that ripens early, comes from a form of the same Latin word.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin praedilectio, from praediligere ("to prefer"), made of prae ("before") and diligere ("to love, single out"), the verb behind diligent.
From Latin praesciens ("knowing beforehand"), from praescire, made of prae ("before") and scire ("to know"), the verb behind science.
From Latin praevaricari ("to walk crookedly"), from prae and varicare ("to straddle"). The Latin verb also meant to play a double part, as a lawyer secretly working for the other side.
words.watch_out: Easily confused with procrastinate, which means to put things off; to prevaricate is to speak evasively so as to avoid the truth.

words.etymology: From Latin pristinus ("former, original"), by way of Middle French: something pristine is still in its first, unspoiled state.
From Latin probitas ("honesty"), by way of Middle French, from probus ("good, upright"), the adjective that also lies behind prove and probe.
From Latin proclivitas, from proclivis ("sloping downward, prone to"), made of pro ("forward") and clivus ("slope"): a proclivity is a leaning you slide into.
Goes back to Latin prodigus ("lavish, wasteful") and the verb prodigere, "to squander", which literally meant to drive forth, from agere ("to drive").
words.watch_out: From the parable, many take it to mean returning home after an absence, but the son was called prodigal for wasting his inheritance.

words.etymology: From Latin profligatus, which meant "depraved" and comes from profligare ("to strike down, overthrow"), built on fligere ("to strike"), the verb also found in inflict.
Through French prolifique from Latin prolificus, made of proles ("offspring") and facere ("to make"): a prolific writer keeps producing new work.
From New Latin propensitas, from Latin propensus, "inclined", the past participle of propendere, "to hang forward", which is built on pendere, "to hang".

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Latin prosa, "prose", through Medieval Latin prosaicus, "in prose", and Middle French. Prose lacks the rhythm of verse, so the word came to mean plain and dull.
Named after Proteus, a sea god of Greek myth who could turn himself into any shape he liked.
From Latin prudens, a shortened form of providens, "foreseeing", from providere, made of pro- ("ahead") and videre ("to see"). Prude is an unrelated word.
From Latin puerilis, "childish", from puer, "boy" or "child".
From Latin pugnax, "combative", from pugnare, "to fight", a verb formed from pugnus, "fist".

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Latin pungens, "pricking", the present participle of pungere, "to prick or sting". Puncture comes from the same verb.
From Latin quiescens, "resting", the present participle of quiescere, "to rest or keep still", which is formed from quies, "rest".
From Don Quixote, the hero of Miguel de Cervantes's novel, who sets off as a knight to right the world's wrongs and charges at windmills he takes for giants.
From Latin quotidianus, "daily", partly by way of French. Its base, quotidie, "every day", was formed from quot ("how many") and a form of dies ("day").
Formed from rancor, "a long-held grudge", plus -ous. Rancor came into English through Old French from Latin rancor, which could mean a grudge.
From Latin rarefacere, "to make rare or thin", through Old French. Its parts are rarus ("thin, loose"), in its adverb form rārē, and facere ("to make").
From French récalcitrant, from Latin recalcitrare, "to kick back with the heels", as a balky horse does, from calx, "heel".

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).
Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Latin refractarius, "obstinate", from refringere, "to break up", a compound of frangere, "to break".
From Latin refutare, "to check or push back", a verb that also meant "to disprove".
words.watch_out: Strictly, refute means to prove a claim false; using it to mean simply deny is common but disputed.

words.etymology: From Latin relegare, "to send away, banish", built from re- ("back") and legare ("to send"), as in delegate. Even in Latin it could mean to set something aside.
From Late Latin remonstrare, formed from re- and monstrare, "to show". The sense moved from pointing something out to protesting against it.

From Latin reprobatus, "condemned", from reprobare, formed from re- and probare ("to approve"), which is based on probus ("good"). In Middle English it meant damned; now it means a person of low morals.
From Latin repudiare, "to cast off, reject", from repudium, which meant a rejection and also a divorce.
From Latin rescindere, which meant "to cut off" and also "to annul", from re- ("back") and scindere ("to cut").
From Latin reticens, the present participle of reticere, "to keep silent", formed from re- and tacere, "to be silent", the verb behind tacit and taciturn.
words.watch_out: Reticent means unwilling to talk about yourself; using it to mean reluctant, as in "reticent to act", is common but disputed.

words.etymology: From Latin reverens, "respectful", the present participle of revereri, "to stand in awe of", partly by way of French. Revere comes from the same Latin verb.
words.watch_out: Reverent means full of respect and awe; do not confuse it with Reverend, the title given to members of the clergy.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).
Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Latin sanctio, a decree or the penalty for breaking one, from sancire, "to make sacred" or "to confirm": a sanction can approve a rule or punish a breach of it.
words.watch_out: Sanction can mean approval (the sanction of the court) or a penalty (trade sanctions), so check which sense is meant.

words.etymology: From sanctimony, from Latin sanctimonia, "holiness", based on sanctus ("holy"), the past participle of sancire. Sanctimony once meant real holiness and later a show of it.

From French sardonique, by way of Latin, from Ancient Greek sardonios, used of bitter, scornful laughter. The Greek is often linked to a Sardinian plant said to kill those who ate it, leaving a scornful-looking grin.
From Latin satiare ("to fill up, satisfy"), from satis ("enough"), the word that also gives satisfy.
From Old French saturnin or straight from Medieval Latin Saturninus, "of Saturn". Astrologers held that people born under that planet were cold and gloomy.

From French savant ("knowing"), once the present participle of savoir ("to know"), which goes back to Latin sapere ("to be wise, to taste"). The sense of a person with one rare gift is short for idiot savant.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Latin servilis ("of a slave"), from servus ("slave"), the word that also gives serve.
From French soporifique, made from Latin sopor ("deep sleep") and the suffix -ficus ("making"), which is related to facere ("to make").
From Latin spurius, said of a child born outside marriage and later of anything false. Where spurius itself comes from is uncertain.
Of unknown origin. It first appears in the late 1500s, when it could also mean to scatter, and may be a blend of scatter and wander.
From the verb stay: its past participle stayed was once also spelled staid, and that spelling lived on as a word for settled, sober people.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From French strident, from Latin stridere ("to creak, screech, hiss"), a verb whose sound imitates the noise it names.
First a golf term for a ball lying between another ball and the hole. Its source is uncertain, perhaps a Scots word for someone who can barely see.
From Latin sublimis ("lifted up, lofty"), partly through Middle French: something sublime stands far above the ordinary.
From Medieval Latin substantiare ("to give substance to"), from Latin substantia ("substance"), built from sub ("under") and stare ("to stand").
From Latin superfluus ("overflowing"), from super ("over") and fluere ("to flow"), the verb also behind fluid.
From Old French surfait, "overdone", formed from sur ("over") and faire ("to do"), which goes back to Latin facere.
From Latin surrepticius ("stolen, secret"), usually traced to surripere ("to snatch away"), from sub ("under") and rapere ("to seize"). Some trace it instead to surrepere ("to creep under").

From Ancient Greek sykophantes ("informer"), literally "fig-shower", from sykon ("fig") and phainein ("to show"), for reasons now unclear. In English it first meant an informer, later a flatterer of the powerful.
Borrowed from French taciturne, or made by shortening taciturnity; either way it goes back to Latin tacitus ("silent"), from tacere ("to be silent"), the verb that also gives tacit.
From tangent, from Latin linea tangens, "touching line", a line that meets a curve at one point. Tangens comes from tangere ("to touch").
From Latin tenuis ("thin, fine") plus the English ending -ous. The same Latin adjective lies behind attenuate.
From Latin tersus ("wiped off, tidy"), from tergere ("to wipe"), the verb also behind detergent. In English it first meant polished or neat, and later brief and spare.

words.retired: Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).
Rare in modern text and used less than in the early 1900s (frequency audit, 2026-10-12).

words.etymology: From Latin tortuosus ("full of twists"), from tortus ("a twisting"), from torquere ("to twist"), the verb that also gives torque and contort.
words.watch_out: Tortuous is about twists and needless complications, not suffering; for something painful to endure, the word is torturous.

words.etymology: From Latin tractabilis ("easy to handle"), from tractare ("to handle"), a form of trahere ("to draw, pull") that stresses repeated action.
From Old French trenchier ("to cut"), whose present participle trenchant meant "cutting". The noun trench comes from the same verb.
