words.etymology: From French accolade, an embrace, which goes back to Latin ad, to, and collum, neck, the root of collar. The hug that once welcomed a new knight became a word for any honor.
From Latin acerbus, a word for the sour taste of unripe fruit that Romans also applied to harsh, bitter people. English uses it for words with that sour sting.
Latin acumen meant a sharpened point, from acuere, to sharpen. English borrowed it for a mind sharp enough to see quickly what matters.
From French adroit, made of à, to, and droit, right, which goes back to Latin directus, straight. An adroit person handles things the right way.
Latin affabilis, built on affari, to address, from ad, to, and fari, to speak, described someone you could readily approach and speak with. It reached English through French.

Through Late Latin from Ancient Greek anathema, a thing set up as an offering to a god. Church writers, influenced by Hebrew herem, used it for a person cursed and cast out, and so for anything detested.
Ancient Greek anodynos, painless, was made of an-, without, and odyne, pain, so the word first named painkillers. Its sense of bland probably came through French anodin, harmless.
From apocrypha, Late Latin for books of doubtful source kept out of church use, from Ancient Greek apokryphos, hidden, built on kryptein, to hide. By 1590 it also meant of doubtful truth.
Latin approbare, to approve, built on probare, to find worthy, from probus, good, gave the noun approbatio, which came into English through Old French.
Latin arcere, to shut in, a verb related to arca, a chest, gave arcanus, secret, the source of arcane: such knowledge is kept shut away from most people.
From Latin assiduus, built on assidere, to sit by or settle at, from ad- and sedere, to sit: an assiduous person stays seated at a task until it is done.
Latin avarus, greedy, built on the same root as avere, to yearn for, gave avaritia, which reached English through Old French.
Latin bellum, war, also behind belligerent, gave bellicus, of war, and then bellicosus, warlike, the source of bellicose.
Old English blithe meant happy or gentle, and Dutch blij, glad, is a cousin. Today the word usually describes good cheer where some worry would be wiser.
Through French from Italian brusco, which could describe sour wine as well as a sudden, abrupt manner. Where the Italian word came from is uncertain.
Ancient Greek boukolos, a cowherd, gave boukolikos, rustic or pastoral, which reached English through Latin: a bucolic scene is the herdsman's countryside of fields and cattle.
From Latin censura, the post and rulings of a Roman censor, from censere, to assess or judge. In English it once meant any judgment before narrowing to a harsh one.
words.watch_out: Censure does not mean cutting or banning material, which is censoring; it means strong, often official criticism of someone's conduct.

words.etymology: Old English cearig could mean careful, anxious or sad, and was formed on the Germanic word that became care, so a chary person is full of care.
Latin circum, around, and specere, to look, formed circumspicere, to look all around, from which this word comes: a circumspect person checks every side before acting.
From Latin clandestinus, 'secret, hidden', which was formed from the Latin adverb clam, 'secretly'.
From Latin conflare, 'to blow together', used for kindling a fire and fusing metal, from flare, 'to blow'. Conflated ideas are melted into one.
From French consternation, from Latin consternatio, a noun formed from consternare, 'to alarm, to throw into confusion'.
Through Old French from Latin culpabilis, built on culpa, 'fault', the same root as in exculpate: someone culpable is at fault.
Through French from Latin cupiditas, 'strong desire', from cupidus, 'eager', and in turn cupere, 'to long for', the verb behind the name Cupid. In English it names greed, mostly for money.
words.watch_out: Despite the link to Cupid, cupidity means greed for wealth and goods, not love or romantic desire.

words.etymology: From French decrier, earlier descrier, 'to shout', with de- probably taken as 'down': to cry something down. In French it could also mean to proclaim a coin devalued.
From Old French demorer, 'to stay, linger', from Latin demorari, 'to delay', built on morari, 'to delay'. Someone who demurs holds back from agreeing.
words.watch_out: Demur, a verb meaning to object or hold back, is easily confused with demure, an adjective meaning modest and reserved.

words.etymology: From Latin denigrare, 'to blacken', built on nigrare, 'to make black'. To denigrate people is to blacken their reputation.
From Latin deprecari, from de- and precari, 'to pray': to pray for a danger to be kept away. From there it came to mean openly disapproving of something.
words.watch_out: Deprecate means to disapprove of; some usage guides object to its common use for 'belittle', as in self-deprecating, as a mix-up with depreciate.

words.etymology: From Italian dilettante, 'delighting', a form of dilettare, which goes back to Latin delectare, the source of delectable: someone who dabbles for the pleasure of it.
From Old French desconfire, 'to undo, destroy', from Latin conficere, built on facere, 'to make'. It meant 'defeat'; the sense 'unsettle' came through confusion with discomfort.
words.watch_out: Discomfit is a verb, not a form of discomfort; most dictionaries accept its sense 'unsettle', though some usage guides still limit it to 'defeat'.

words.etymology: Formed in English from dis- and ingenuous, 'innocent and frank', from Latin ingenuus, which meant both 'freeborn' and 'noble, candid'.
From Latin dissolutus, 'loose, lax', a form of dissolvere, 'to unfasten', which is built on solvere, 'to loosen'. A dissolute life has slipped its moral ties.
Built on Latin duplex, 'double, twofold', the source of duplicate as well: a double game, with one face shown and another hidden.
From Latin egregius, from e-, 'out of', and grex, 'flock': picked out from the herd. It began as praise; the bad sense appeared in the late 1500s, probably through irony.
From Anglo-Norman eschiver, from a Frankish verb meaning to dread or shun. Skew comes from a northern French form of the same verb, and shy is a Germanic relative.
Through Old French from Latin exhortari, 'to encourage', from ex- and hortari, 'to urge on', the verb also behind hortatory.
From Latin expiare, 'to atone for', from ex- and piare, 'to appease, purify', a verb formed from pius, 'devout', the source of pious.
Latin fastidium meant loathing, and also a choosy, dainty taste; its adjective fastidiosus gave English the word. Someone easily put off is hard to please.
From Scots, a shortened form of effectless, with feck standing for effect: a feckless person gets nothing done.
Through French from Latin fecundus, 'fertile', a relative of the Latin words that gave English fetus and feminine.
From Latin floridus, 'flowery, in bloom', from flos, 'flower'. Florid prose is flowery in the same way, and a florid face has a blooming color.
From an older spelling of French faible, 'weak', which makes it a twin of English feeble. A foible is a slight flaw in a person's makeup.
From Middle English gainsayen, made of gain-, an old prefix meaning against, and say: to gainsay a claim is to speak against it.
Of unknown origin; it may come from gawren, a Middle English verb meaning to stare, but that link is not proven.
A form of the old word german, closely related, which goes back to Latin germanus, having the same parents. Writers quoting a line from Shakespeare's Hamlet gave it today's sense of relevant.
From Latin grandiloquus, by way of Middle French, built from grandis, great, and loqui, to speak; eloquent and loquacious come from the same Latin verb.
From Latin gratuitus, freely given, from the root of gratia, favor. Something given for nothing came to mean something done for no good reason.
From Old French herbergeor, one who provides lodging, from herbergier, to shelter. A harbinger once went ahead of a traveling court to find rooms, so seeing one meant others were coming.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek hubris, insolence or outrage; in Greek myth it was the pride of mortals who set themselves against the gods.
From Ancient Greek idiosynkrasia, a person's own temperament, made of idios, one's own, syn, together, and krasis, a mixing: each person's own blend of traits.
words.watch_out: The usual spelling ends in -crasy, from Greek krasis, a mixing; the spelling with -cracy, as in democracy, is widely treated as a mistake.

words.etymology: From Latin ignominiosus, from ignominia, disgrace, which joins in-, not, to nomen, name or good name: something ignominious costs you your reputation.
From Late Latin impetuosus, violent, from Latin impetus, an attack, which comes from impetere, to rush at, made of in- and petere, to seek or attack.
From French importuner, from Latin importunus, built from in-, not, and portus, harbor. The Latin word first meant having no harbor, then unsuitable or troublesome.
Latin incorrigibilis joins in-, not, to a form of corrigere, to correct: an incorrigible habit is one that nothing can correct.
Latin indefatigabilis meant unable to be worn out; it adds in-, not, to defatigare, to exhaust, a form of fatigare, which also gave English fatigue.
French insouciant joins in-, not, to souciant, a form of soucier, to worry or care; English took the word from French in the 1820s.
From Middle English inuren, from in and ure, an old word for use or practice heard in phrases like in ure: what you are inured to has become a matter of habit.
Latin invehere, to carry into, was used in the passive for attacking someone with words, and Medieval Latin made invectiva, a tirade, from it. Its base is vehere, to carry, as in vehicle.
Latin jocus, a joke, is the source of English joke; its diminutive joculus, a little joke, gave the adjective jocularis, which became jocular.
Latin judicare, to judge, gave judicium, judgment, and French built judicieux on it; judicial and adjudicate belong to the same family of Latin words.
words.watch_out: Judicious is not judicial: a judicial matter concerns courts and judges, while a judicious choice shows good sense.

words.etymology: From Latin lacrimosus, tearful, from lacrima, a tear, a word that shares a distant ancestor with English tear.
First recorded in the 1630s, probably made from two verbs that both meant to beat, lam and baste; to lambaste someone now usually means to beat them with words.
From Latin languidus, faint or weak, from languere, to be weak or listless, the verb behind languish and languor too.
From Old French largesce, generosity, from large, generous or wide, which goes back to Latin largus, plentiful or free-handed; English large has the same source.
From lion and -ize, using lion in the sense of a famous person whom everyone is curious to see: to lionize someone is to treat them as that kind of star.
From Latin lugubris, mournful, from the root of lugere, to mourn, with the English ending -ious; today it often suggests a gloom that seems overdone.
From Latin malevolens, made of male ("badly") and volens ("wishing"), from velle ("to wish"), the verb also behind volition.
From mawk, an old dialect word for a maggot that came from Old Norse, plus -ish. It once meant queasy or sickly in taste; now it means sickly in sentiment.
From Ancient Greek, joining misein ("to hate") and anthropos ("human being"): a misanthrope dislikes people as a whole.
From Latin modicum ("a little"), a noun use of modicus ("moderate"), from modus ("measure"): a modicum is a small, measured amount.
From French mordant ("biting"), from Latin mordere ("to bite"), the verb also behind remorse: mordant humor leaves a sting.
From Latin obviare ("to meet, to prevent"), from obvius ("in the way"), built on via ("way") just as obvious is: to obviate a need is to meet it early.
From Latin odiosus, through Old French, from odium ("hatred"), a word English also took over for the loathing that odious acts earn.
From French panégyrique, from Ancient Greek panegyrikos ("for a festival assembly"), from panegyris, a gathering of all the people. In Greek it could also mean flattering.
From Tamil paraiyar, "drummers" (from parai, "drum"), a caste of southern India held low and shunned by others. Another account traces it to Sanskrit para, "outsider".
From Late Latin peiorare ("to make worse"), from Latin peior ("worse"): a pejorative word makes its subject sound worse.
From Ancient Greek peripatetikos ("given to walking about"), via Latin and French. Aristotle's followers were named for the walkways of his school, or for his reputed habit of teaching on foot.
Shortened from plaudite, Latin for "applaud!", a command form of plaudere ("to clap"), the verb also behind applaud and plausible.
From Latin proscribere, "to publish in writing", from scribere ("to write"). Romans used it for posting the names of people declared outlaws, and it came to mean to ban.
words.watch_out: Do not confuse it with prescribe, which means to order or recommend; proscribe means to forbid.

words.etymology: From Late Latin querulosus, through Old French, from Latin queri ("to complain"), the verb that also gave English quarrel.
Ultimately from Latin rapax ("grasping, greedy"), from rapere ("to snatch, carry off"), perhaps by way of English rapacity: the rapacious grab all they can.
From Latin recantare, from re- ("back") and cantare ("to sing"); the Latin word already meant to revoke as well as to sing back.
From Latin sanguineus ("of blood"), from sanguis ("blood"), via Old French. Old medicine held that people with more blood than the other humors were cheerful and hopeful.
words.watch_out: It means hopeful and confident; do not confuse it with sanguinary, which means bloody or bloodthirsty.

words.etymology: From Latin speciosus ("good-looking"), from species ("appearance"), from specere ("to look"). In English it once meant beautiful, then fair-seeming but false.
From Latin superciliosus ("haughty"), from supercilium ("eyebrow"), which in Latin also meant pride: a raised eyebrow is the look of someone who feels superior.
From Latin tacitus ("unspoken"), directly or through French tacite, from tacere ("to be silent"), the verb also behind taciturn.
From Latin temeritas ("rashness"), through Old French, from temere ("rashly, at random"), which goes back to an older word meaning "blindly, in the dark".
From French coterie, which first meant a community of peasants under a feudal lord and later any exclusive circle. Through Medieval Latin coteria it goes back to Old English cot ("cottage").
From Old French contenance, which goes back to Latin continere ("to hold together"), built on tenere ("to hold"). The English noun meant a face and also favor or support, the sense the verb keeps.
Of uncertain origin: Middle English cravant came either from Old French cravanté ("defeated") or from creaunt ("defeated") reshaped to look like crave. A craven person gives in without a fight.
Through Old French from Latin dignare ("to judge worthy"), built on dignus ("worthy"), the root of dignity. To deign is to judge a task worthy of you, though only just.
Through French from Ancient Greek demagogos, a popular leader or a mob leader, made of demos ("people") and agogos ("guide, leader"). In English it mostly keeps the darker sense.
From Old French denzein, formed from deinz ("within"), which goes back to Late Latin de intus ("from within"): a denizen is one of those inside a place.
Formed in English from dis- ("not") and interested in its sense of "having a stake", or from the verb disinterest ("to make impartial"). Either way it describes someone with nothing to gain.
words.watch_out: Using it to mean "not interested" is common but disputed; many editors keep it for "impartial, with nothing to gain."

words.etymology: From French drôle ("funny, odd"), earlier a noun for a clown or a likable rogue. The French word goes back to Middle Dutch drol, a stout little man or a goblin.
Formed in English from erst, an old word meaning "first" or "formerly", and while.
Through Middle French from Latin evincere ("to conquer completely", and also "to prove beyond doubt"), built on vincere ("to conquer"). From proving a thing, it came to mean showing it plainly.
From Latin extans, from extare ("to stand out, to exist"), made of ex- ("out") and stare ("to stand"): what is extant still stands when others of its kind have gone.
Through French from Latin facilis ("easy"), built on facere ("to do"). It first meant simply easy; the sense of too simple and shallow appeared in the 1800s.
From Anglo-Norman feauté, from Latin fidelitas ("faithfulness"), which in the Middle Ages also meant a vassal's sworn loyalty. It goes back to fides ("faith"), as fidelity does.
Through French from Latin furtivus ("stolen, hidden"), from furtum ("theft"), which comes from fur ("thief"): a furtive glance is a thief's glance.
From French gauche ("awkward, clumsy"), from gauchir ("to bend, warp"). The French word took on its other meaning, "left", only in the 1500s, replacing an older word.
Coined in 1812 by the Boston Gazette, joining the name of Massachusetts governor Elbridge Gerry with salamander, after a district on a map he signed that looked like one.
Shortened from glibbery, an old English word for slippery, or from its Low German or Dutch source, glibberig: glib talk slides smoothly past what matters.
Formed in English around 1400 from hap ("luck"), an old word still heard in happen and mishap, and -less.
From Latin impingere ("to push or dash against"), the verb that also gave impact. It first meant to strike a surface, and figuratively came to mean to press in on rights or time.
Through Middle French from Latin impugnare ("to fight against"), built on pugnare ("to fight"), from pugnus ("fist"). To impugn a claim is to attack it with words.
From Medieval Latin incisivus, from Latin incidere ("to cut into"), built on caedere ("to cut"), the verb also behind incision and incisor. An incisive mind cuts to the point.
From Latin incongruus, made of in- ("not") and congruus ("fitting, in agreement"), from congruere ("to come together, agree"): what is incongruous does not agree with its setting.
From Latin inculcare ("to press in by treading"), from in- ("in") and calcare ("to trample"), from calx ("heel"): a lesson that is inculcated is stamped into the mind by repetition.
From Italian ingraziare or a Medieval Latin verb, both built on the Latin phrase in gratiam ("into favor"), from gratia ("favor, thanks"): you ingratiate yourself by working your way into favor.
From Late Latin inscrutabilis, from in- ("not") and scrutari ("to search, examine"), the verb behind scrutiny: what is inscrutable cannot be searched into and understood.
From Medieval Latin interlocutor, a noun formed from Latin interloqui, from inter- ("between") and loqui ("to speak"): someone who talks with another, back and forth.
From French lampon ("satire"), probably from lampons ("let us drink"), a refrain of rowdy mocking songs, from lamper ("to gulp down"). Such songs jeered at public figures.
From Ancient Greek litaneia ("prayer, supplication"), through Latin and Old French. A church litany runs through a long series of petitions, and the word spread to any tiresome list.
From Middle English loth, from Old English lath ("hateful, hostile") or a related Old Norse word; the verb loathe comes from the same source. Being unwilling grew out of finding a thing hateful.
words.watch_out: Do not confuse loath, an adjective meaning unwilling ("loath to leave"), with the verb loathe, meaning to hate.

words.etymology: Through French from Italian pasticcio, a pie with a mixed filling, from Late Latin pasta ("dough, paste"): a pastiche mixes or copies borrowed styles as such a pie mixes ingredients.
From Ancient Greek pathos ("suffering," also "strong feeling"), the root of sympathy, empathy and pathetic: pathos is what makes an audience feel for someone who suffers.

Of uncertain origin: either Anglo-Norman peruser ("to use up") or a Medieval Latin verb for "wear out," in form per- ("thoroughly") and use. The using-up sense died out; going through a thing with care remained.
words.watch_out: Peruse traditionally means to read with care; using it to mean skim or browse is common but disputed.

words.etymology: From the Philistines, foes of Israel in the Bible, through German Philister, a student word for townspeople outside the university and then for anyone without culture. Thomas Carlyle brought it into English.
From French pique ("resentment, a quarrel"), from the verb piquer ("to prick, sting"): pique is the sting a person feels when their pride is pricked.
words.watch_out: The verb meaning to stir interest is spelled pique ("piqued my curiosity"), not peak or peek, which sound the same.

words.etymology: From Latin plebeius ("of the common people"), from plebs, the ordinary citizens of Rome as opposed to the patrician families. It came to mean common in a way that snobs look down on.

From Medieval Latin pontificare, from pontifex, a Roman high priest and later the pope, a word made of pons ("bridge") and facere ("to make"): to pontificate is to talk with a pope's air of authority.
From Latin portendere ("to foretell"), from por- ("forward") and tendere ("to stretch"): an omen that portends something reaches forward to what is coming.
From Latin positus ("placed"), a form of ponere ("to put, place"), which also gave position and deposit: to posit a claim is to set it down as a starting point.
From Latin praeceptum ("a rule, an instruction"), from praecipere, from prae ("before") and capere ("to take"): praecipere meant to take beforehand and also to instruct.
From Latin promulgare ("to make known, publish"), whose own source is uncertain: either pro- ("forth") with vulgare ("to make public") or mulgere ("to milk," and so "to bring out").
From Middle French putatif, from Latin putativus ("supposed"), from putare ("to think, reckon"), also the root of reputation and compute: a putative fact is one that people reckon true.
Of uncertain origin, perhaps Old English cwealm ("death, plague") or a Dutch or German word for vapor or daze. It meant a fit of faintness before it meant a pang of doubt or conscience.
From French régaler ("to entertain, to feast"), from Old French gale ("merriment, fun"), probably of Germanic origin: to regale people is to fill them with enjoyment.
From Latin remissus ("slack, careless"), from remittere ("to send back, let go, relax"), from mittere ("to send"): a remiss person has let their attention to a duty go slack.
From Medieval Latin renegare, to deny, built on Latin negare, to deny; renegade comes from the same verb. To renege on a deal is to deny a promise already given.
From Latin repletus, filled up, a form of replere, made of re-, again, and plere, to fill. The same plere is in complete and deplete.
From Latin resplendere, to shine out or glitter, built on splendere, to shine, which also gave splendid and splendor.
From Old English rife, plentiful or frequent, a Germanic word with relatives in Dutch and Icelandic. Today it is used mostly of bad things that are spreading, such as disease or rumor.
Of uncertain origin, perhaps from French rouiller, to make muddy or rusty. In English it can still mean to stir up the mud in water, which shows the link to churning.
From Latin ruminari, which meant both to chew the cud and to mull something over, from rumen, the throat or gullet. The word ruminant, for cud-chewing animals, has the same root.

From Latin saliens, leaping, a form of salire, to leap. The sense most noticeable came through the phrase salient point, Latin punctum saliens, the throbbing speck of heart Aristotle described in an egg.
From French, from Medieval Latin subterfugium, from Latin subterfugere, to escape in secret, made of subter, beneath, and fugere, to flee, the root of fugitive and refuge.
From Old French surmis, a form of surmettre, to accuse, made of sur, upon, and mettre, to put, from Latin mittere. In English it first meant to allege, and later to suppose without proof.
First recorded in English in the 1600s, from Anglo-French tant amunter or from Italian tanto montare, both meaning to amount to as much; the sources do not agree on which.
words.watch_out: Tantamount means equal in effect and comes before to; it does not mean most important, which is paramount.

words.etymology: From Old English thræl, a slave, which came from Old Norse thræll. Being in thrall is being held as if enslaved, and enthrall is built on the same word.
From Latin tropus, from Ancient Greek tropos, a turn or manner, which was also used for a figure of speech. The sense of a stock theme in stories is much newer.
From un- and tenable, which came from French tenir, to hold, going back to Latin tenere. An untenable position or idea is one that cannot be held against attack.
From un- and toward, an old adjective for willing, easy to teach or promising. Something untoward is the reverse: unruly, unlucky or out of place.
From French vestige, from Latin vestigium, a footprint or track. A footprint stays after the walker has gone, so the word came to mean any trace that is left.
From French volition and Medieval Latin volitio, built on Latin velle, to wish, the verb behind voluntary and benevolent.
From Middle English wantowen, undisciplined, made of wan-, not, and towen, brought up or trained. Lack of restraint led to its sense of doing harm with no reason or limit.
From Middle English welteren, to roll about or wallow, a Germanic verb related to wallow itself. The noun went from a tossing, tumbling motion to a tumbled heap of things.
From Middle English wrien, to turn or twist, from Old English wrigian; awry is a relative. Wry first meant twisted, as of a face pulled to one side, and then dryly mocking.
From Latin adjudicare, from ad, to, and judicare, to judge, a verb built on judex, a judge; judicial and judicious share the root.
Taken straight from Latin animus, the mind or spirit, a word Romans also used for strong feeling and anger. Animosity comes from the same root.
Through Latin from Ancient Greek antithesis, a setting against, made of anti, against, and thesis, a placing, the word also behind hypothesis and synthesis.
From French feinte, from feindre, to pretend, which goes back to Latin fingere, to shape or to make up. Feign, fiction and figment come from the same Latin verb.
Probably from an old Dutch verb vuisten, to hold in the hand, from vuist, fist. In English it first meant palming a die to sneak it into a game, which led to pushing unwanted things on people.
From forbear, to hold back, plus -ance. Forbear comes from Old English forberan, to refrain or to endure, built on beran, to bear: forbearance is bearing a wrong instead of striking back.
From Middle English fraught, loaded, the past participle of a verb for loading a ship, from Middle Dutch vracht, cargo, which also gave English freight. A plan fraught with risk is loaded with it.
From Greek phrenetikos, delirious, through Latin and Old French, built on phren, mind; frantic and frenzy share the root. Once used of the insane, it now means wildly busy.
From the verb gall, to wear skin raw by rubbing, as a saddle can do to a horse. The verb later came to mean to vex, so something galling chafes at your pride.
From Old French glener, from Late Latin glennare, to gather, whose source is uncertain, perhaps Celtic. It first meant gathering the grain left by reapers, then gathering facts bit by bit.
From Latin imbuere, to wet or to stain. A mind imbued with an idea has soaked it up the way cloth soaks up dye.
From Latin impellere, to drive on, made of in-, against or toward, and pellere, to drive or push. Compel, propel and repel come from the same verb.
From Latin impunitas, freedom from punishment, from impunis, unpunished, which joins in-, not, to poena, penalty. Penal and punish come from the same noun.
From Latin indelebilis, that cannot be destroyed, made of in-, not, and delebilis, able to be wiped out, from delere, to blot out, the source of delete.
From Late Latin indomitabilis, untamable, made of in-, not, and domitare, to tame, a form of domare. A spirit that nothing can tame is one that nothing can beat.
From Latin inimitabilis, through Middle French: in-, not, plus imitabilis, imitable, from imitari, to imitate.
From Latin inordinatus, disordered, from in-, not, and ordinare, to set in order. What is inordinate breaks the bounds that order would keep, so it means far too much.
From Latin insinuare, to creep or wind one's way in, from in- and sinus, a bend or fold, as in sinuous. A hint that is insinuated works its way in sideways instead of being said outright.
From Late Latin interminabilis, endless, made of in-, not, and terminare, to set a limit or end, from terminus, a boundary. Terminate comes from the same verb.
From Latin irrevocabilis, through Middle French: ir-, not, plus revocare, to call back, from re- and vocare, to call. Revoke comes from the same verb.
From Anglo-Norman getteson, the throwing of cargo overboard, from Old French jeter, to throw, which comes from Latin iactare, a form of iacere, to throw, as in eject. It now means dumping any burden.
From Latin luridus, pale yellow or wan. In English it first described a sickly, ghastly color, and it now describes both harsh, glaring colors and stories that dwell on gruesome detail.
From French malaise, made of mal, badly, and aise, ease or comfort: the state of being ill at ease, in body or in spirit.
From Old French malfaisance, from malfaire, to do evil, which goes back to Latin male, badly, and facere, to do. In English it is mainly a legal word for wrongdoing in office.
From Old English metan, to measure, related to German messen. To mete out punishment is to measure out the share each person has earned.
First a variant spelling of metal; the word was applied to a person's spirit or temper from the 1500s, and in the 1700s the mettle spelling settled on that sense.

senses.definition: Ease off from a fierce or troubling level, or bring something down from such a level.
senses.plain_language_definition: To calm down after being at its worst.

senses.definition: Markedly different from an accepted norm.
senses.plain_language_definition: Wandering off from what is normal or expected.

senses.definition: Disappear on the quiet to dodge arrest or repayment, often with someone else's cash.
senses.plain_language_definition: To run off in secret, often with stolen money, so you will not get caught.

senses.definition: Go without a pleasure on purpose, for a while or for good.
senses.plain_language_definition: To say no to a treat or habit by your own choice.

senses.definition: Call out someone's misbehavior and caution them against doing it again, usually without anger.
senses.plain_language_definition: To give someone a serious talking-to about what they did wrong.

senses.definition: Cut a food, drink or drug with a lesser ingredient and pass the result off as pure.
senses.plain_language_definition: To sneak a cheap or bad ingredient into food, drink or medicine.

senses.definition: Bearing on the beauty or artistic quality of something, as judged by taste.
senses.plain_language_definition: Having to do with beauty and how good something looks.

senses.definition: Make a person or group mightier, or puff up their image beyond what is true.
senses.plain_language_definition: To build up how powerful or famous someone is, or to make them seem bigger than they are.

senses.definition: A brisk, willing response to a task or request, with no hint of holding back.
senses.plain_language_definition: Being quick and happy to do something as soon as you are asked.

senses.definition: Take some of the weight off a pain or hardship without removing its cause.
senses.plain_language_definition: To take some of the sting out of pain or hardship.

senses.definition: Fuse separate organizations or substances into a single unit.
senses.plain_language_definition: To merge separate groups or things into one.

senses.definition: Leaving a reader or listener unsure which of several possible senses the speaker had in mind.
senses.plain_language_definition: Leaving you guessing, because it could mean one thing or another.

senses.definition: Divided in one's attitude toward something, because parts of it appeal and parts of it repel.
senses.plain_language_definition: Part of you likes something and part of you does not, so you cannot make up your mind.

senses.definition: Bring a poor or painful state of affairs up to a better one.
senses.plain_language_definition: To make a hard situation less bad for the people in it.

senses.definition: Something located at a time when it could not have existed or occurred.
senses.plain_language_definition: Something that appears in the wrong historical era.

senses.definition: Parallel to another thing in structure or role, even where the two differ in other respects.
senses.plain_language_definition: Like something else in some ways, though different in others.

senses.definition: A case that does not match what the rest of its group or the usual rules would predict.
senses.plain_language_definition: One thing that is out of step with all the others.

senses.definition: A strong and settled aversion that sets one against a certain person or thing.
senses.plain_language_definition: A deep dislike of someone or something that makes you want to stay away.

senses.definition: Emotional flatness that leaves a person unmoved and unwilling to get involved.
senses.plain_language_definition: Not caring about something, and so not bothering to do anything about it.

senses.definition: Buy calm from an angry or threatening party by handing over part of what it wants.
senses.plain_language_definition: To say yes to some demands so an angry person will back off.

senses.definition: So hard and long that finishing it calls for stamina and grit.
senses.plain_language_definition: Needing so much effort that it wears you out.

senses.definition: Express an idea or emotion in exact and orderly language.
senses.plain_language_definition: To put an idea into words so plainly that others get it.

senses.definition: Refusing ease and pleasure as a discipline, in the belief that hardship trains the spirit.
senses.plain_language_definition: Living very simply and refusing comforts and pleasures on purpose.

senses.definition: Ease a painful or unwelcome feeling, such as guilt, fear or grief, so that it troubles someone less.
senses.plain_language_definition: To ease a bad feeling, such as worry or guilt.

senses.definition: Daring enough to try something risky that most people would not attempt.
senses.plain_language_definition: Very bold and ready to take big chances.

senses.definition: Unrestrained by convention or propriety.
senses.plain_language_definition: Disrespectfully bold and showing no regard for normal rules or manners.

senses.definition: Spare to the point of harshness, with nothing added to please the eye or ease the body.
senses.plain_language_definition: Bare and simple in a strict, almost harsh way.

senses.definition: Put something on record as true and stand behind it.
senses.plain_language_definition: To put your word behind a statement and stick to it.

senses.definition: Repeated too often; overfamiliar through overuse.
senses.plain_language_definition: Boring because everyone has heard or seen it many times before.

senses.definition: Cover up the true nature of something with an outward appearance that suggests otherwise.
senses.plain_language_definition: To make something seem different from how it really is.

senses.definition: Using one's wealth or power to do good for other people.
senses.plain_language_definition: Doing good for others, often by giving them money, time or care.

senses.definition: Add backing to something weak or under strain so that it holds up better.
senses.plain_language_definition: To prop up something weak so it stands firmer.

senses.definition: Padded with grand, showy wording that hides how little is actually being said.
senses.plain_language_definition: Puffed up with fancy words that say very little.

senses.definition: Crude in conduct, with the manners of someone who never learned how to behave in company.
senses.plain_language_definition: Rude and loud, with bad manners.

senses.definition: Swell rapidly in size, number or reach, with a lively burst of new growth.
senses.plain_language_definition: To grow fast and spread out, like new leaves in spring.

senses.definition: Give a claim or stance extra backing so that it stands up to challenge.
senses.plain_language_definition: To back up an idea or plan so it is harder to knock down.

senses.definition: A din of loud, clashing sounds with no harmony between them.
senses.plain_language_definition: A harsh racket where no sound fits with any other.

senses.definition: Wear down someone's reluctance with sweet words and flattery until they agree.
senses.plain_language_definition: To keep sweet-talking someone until they give in.

senses.definition: Grown so hard and unfeeling that other people's pain or misfortune stirs no pity.
senses.plain_language_definition: Unmoved when others are suffering, as though the heart has gone hard.

senses.definition: The quality of speaking one's mind plainly, without hedging or softening the truth.
senses.plain_language_definition: Telling people straight out what you really think.

senses.definition: Given to abrupt reversals of mood or course that nobody can see coming.
senses.plain_language_definition: Quick to flip on a whim, so others never know what to expect next.

senses.definition: Determined by chance or impulse or whim rather than by necessity or reason.
senses.plain_language_definition: Decided on a whim rather than for a good reason.

senses.definition: Attack someone's conduct with fierce words of blame.
senses.plain_language_definition: To tear into someone with angry words about what they did wrong.

senses.definition: Inflict severe punishment on.
senses.plain_language_definition: To punish someone harshly.

senses.definition: Anything that sets off a shift in people or events, or hurries along one already under way.
senses.plain_language_definition: The spark that gets things moving, or moving faster.

senses.definition: Mocking or critical with a deliberate edge that is meant to wound.
senses.plain_language_definition: Saying harsh, mocking things that are meant to hurt.

senses.definition: Sly maneuvering with rules, words or paperwork to win by deceit rather than merit.
senses.plain_language_definition: Sneaky tricks with rules or words that let someone cheat while seeming to play fair.

senses.definition: Lose the ability to flow and set into a jelly or curd, as blood does in a clot.
senses.plain_language_definition: To thicken until it stops running and holds its shape.

senses.definition: Draw together from scattered pieces until they form one united thing.
senses.plain_language_definition: To slowly blend from many separate bits into one.

senses.definition: Convincing because the reasoning behind it is sound, clear and to the point.
senses.plain_language_definition: So clear and sensible that people find it convincing.

senses.definition: Scaled to fit something else, so that the two stand in balance.
senses.plain_language_definition: Fairly sized to match something else, the way a reward should match the effort.

senses.definition: Showing a cheerful willingness to do favors for others.
senses.plain_language_definition: Eager to please others and quick to go along with their wishes.

senses.definition: Offered in a spirit of peacemaking, to soothe an opponent and mend a rift.
senses.plain_language_definition: Meant to cool tempers and patch things up after a fight.

senses.definition: Look past a wrong in a way that amounts to accepting it.
senses.plain_language_definition: To let bad behavior slide without punishing it.

senses.definition: A fire grown to enormous size, consuming whole streets or hillsides.
senses.plain_language_definition: A huge fire that keeps spreading and burns down everything near it.

senses.definition: A person whose eye, ear or palate has been trained to rank fine things within one field of taste.
senses.plain_language_definition: Someone with such practiced taste, say in cheese or painting, that they can tell great from merely good.

senses.definition: Humbled by remorse over a fault of one's own and openly owning the harm it caused.
senses.plain_language_definition: Ashamed of a wrong you did and ready to say so.

senses.definition: A puzzle or problem that resists every attempt to work it out.
senses.plain_language_definition: A question that keeps you stuck no matter how you turn it over.

senses.definition: Tangled in structure, with turns and side branches that make the main line hard to trace.
senses.plain_language_definition: Full of loops and detours, so you keep losing your place.

senses.definition: Flowing or piling up in a large, generous supply.
senses.plain_language_definition: Very large in amount, with lots of it to go around.

senses.definition: Confirm a statement independently, so that it no longer rests on one source alone.
senses.plain_language_definition: To back up what someone has said with proof from a second, separate source.

senses.definition: Disposed to believe on little evidence.
senses.plain_language_definition: Quick to believe things without needing much proof.

senses.definition: Carried out at speed and only on the surface, with the finer points left unchecked.
senses.plain_language_definition: Quick and shallow, giving something only a passing look.

senses.definition: A supply of something so thin that people looking for it mostly come up empty.
senses.plain_language_definition: A thin supply, with far less on hand than people want.

senses.definition: Something meant to go well that falls apart badly and in plain sight.
senses.plain_language_definition: A huge, public failure that people remember with a wince.

senses.definition: Flooding caused by a tumultuous breakup of ice in a river during the spring or summer.
senses.plain_language_definition: Flooding caused by broken ice rushing down a river.

senses.definition: Pull apart a myth or a puffed-up claim until people see it has nothing behind it.
senses.plain_language_definition: To show that a common belief or bold claim does not hold up.

senses.definition: Dignified, restrained behavior that keeps to what a solemn or formal setting expects.
senses.plain_language_definition: Proper, dignified conduct suited to a serious or formal place.

senses.definition: Yielding one's own views or wishes to another person whose standing one honors.
senses.plain_language_definition: Stepping back and letting someone you look up to have the final say.

senses.definition: Courteous regard for people's feelings.
senses.plain_language_definition: Being thoughtful and polite about other people's feelings.

senses.definition: Damaging to health, to living things or to the proper working of something.
senses.plain_language_definition: Bad for something, harming its health or how well it works.

Twain's mordant jabs at preachers and politicians drew laughs from his readers and furious letters from his targets.
Her mordant account of family Christmas dinners, where every toast hid an insult, made readers wince with laughter.
Installing a dehumidifier in the basement would obviate the yearly job of scrubbing mold off the walls.
Writing a clear contract at the start can obviate months of argument later on.
The new bridge obviated the long ferry ride that commuters had made for decades.
She packed snacks and games for the children to obviate any meltdowns on the long drive.
Charging grieving families double for funeral flowers struck everyone as an odious way to make money.
The regime's odious policy of jailing children along with their parents drew protests around the world.
Most voters found the candidate's jokes about wounded veterans odious and punished him at the polls.
Forging a dead soldier's signature to keep collecting his pension was the most odious fraud the investigators had seen.
Without new members, the club's traditions ossified, and every meeting followed the same script for thirty years.
Critics warned that the party had ossified into a circle of aging leaders who no longer listened to voters.
Some novelists ossify after an early success and write the same book again and again.
The judge warned that the law would ossify if courts refused to apply old statutes to new technology.
At the ship's launch, the owner gave a long panegyric hailing its builders as the finest craftsmen alive.
State radio broadcast a panegyric on the dictator's birthday, crediting him with every good harvest in the nation's history.
Pliny the Younger's panegyric to the emperor Trajan praised him at great length for his modesty and justice.
The best man's toast turned into such a gushing panegyric to the groom that guests began to wonder what he was hiding.
Once the rumor spread that she had lice, the new girl became a pariah on the school bus and sat alone every morning.
In the medieval village, the leper lived as a pariah in a hut beyond the fields, where food was left for him at the gate.
Smokers have gone from cool rebels to pariahs, sent outside to huddle by the office bins.
In the novel, the villagers treat the orphan as a pariah and cross the road to avoid him.
The peripatetic poet never kept an address for long, dating each letter from whatever town he happened to be sleeping in.
Because of his father's army postings, he had a peripatetic childhood, moving between eight schools in ten years.
The band's peripatetic schedule took it to a new city almost every night of the tour.
After retiring, the couple sold their house and took up a peripatetic life in a camper van.
The real estate listing was grandiloquent, calling a cramped one-bedroom flat 'an intimate urban sanctuary of refined proportions'.
The grandiloquent waiter announced a plain bowl of carrot soup as 'a symphony of autumn's harvest', and the whole table burst out laughing.
In a grandiloquent toast, the best man compared the couple's first date at a bowling alley to the meeting of two mighty rivers.
Her editor circled the grandiloquent opening line, 'Since the dawn of time, humankind has pondered the lawnmower', and wrote in the margin: just start.
Nobody had asked about his salary, and his gratuitous mention of it at dinner struck everyone as bragging.
The referee had already sent him off, so the gratuitous shove he gave a defender on the way out only earned him a longer ban.
Readers complained that the recipe blog buried its three-line method under twenty gratuitous photos of the author's dog.
The flashlight app asks for gratuitous permissions, such as access to your contacts and location, though all it does is turn on a light.
The flickering office lights turned out to be a harbinger of the blackout that shut down the whole block an hour later.
For the little bookshop, the giant chain store opening across the street was a harbinger of hard years ahead.
The new coach's first act, banning phones at practice, was a harbinger of the strict season to come.
Her phone's first sluggish week was a harbinger; within a month it would barely hold a charge.
It was pure hubris to plan the victory party before a single vote had been counted.
The builders' hubris showed when they called the ship unsinkable and fitted lifeboats for only about half the people on board.
In the myth, Icarus's hubris carries him so close to the sun that the wax in his wings melts.
Having climbed two easy peaks, he set off up the mountain in sneakers and without a map, an act of hubris that ended with a rescue helicopter.
One of the professor's harmless idiosyncrasies was humming a few bars of Bach before each new topic.
Hanging every picture slightly crooked was an idiosyncrasy of the painter, who claimed straight frames made a room feel tense.
The biographer listed the poet's idiosyncrasies: green ink, no chairs in the study and a tortoise named Horace.
A good actor studies the small idiosyncrasies of a real person, such as how he blinks or holds a cup.
After promising a landslide, the senator suffered an ignominious defeat, losing even his home county.
The champion was knocked out in the first round by an unranked amateur, an ignominious exit she still refuses to discuss.
The army made an ignominious retreat, leaving its flags and supplies behind in the mud.
The famous restaurant was closed in ignominious fashion, its doors padlocked by health inspectors after a rat was filmed in the kitchen.
On an impetuous whim, she dyed her hair bright green the night before her job interview.
He made the impetuous choice to sell all his furniture and move abroad after a single holiday in Lisbon.
The goalkeeper's impetuous dash off his line left the net empty, and the striker simply lobbed the ball in.
Within a minute of reading the review she had fired off an impetuous reply, and by breakfast she wished she had waited.
For a whole season, the young pianist importuned the famous teacher to hear her play, writing a letter every week.
She had importuned the city council for months to repair the broken streetlight, and at last a crew arrived.
Too proud to importune his wealthy uncle for a loan, he took a second job instead.
Fans importuned the actor for autographs all the way from the stage door to his car.
My incorrigible uncle still tells the same awful jokes at every family dinner, however often my aunt kicks him under the table.
The chef was an incorrigible tinkerer who could not send out a dish without changing the recipe once more, even on opening night.
Her incorrigible lateness became a family joke, so we told her dinner was at six when it was really at seven.
Fines did nothing to stop the incorrigible litterbug, who simply paid them and kept tossing cans from his car.
The indefatigable toddler ran laps around the living room long after every adult had collapsed on the sofa.
An indefatigable letter writer, the old sailor answered every one of the thousands of notes children sent him about his voyage.
The ants were indefatigable, rebuilding their hill grain by grain each time the rain washed it away.
The baker seemed indefatigable, kneading dough from midnight until dawn and then cheerfully serving the morning queue.
With the final boarding call already sounding, he strolled to the gate sipping a coffee, as insouciant as if he had all the time in the world.
Ten minutes before the guests arrived, with the kitchen in chaos, Dad sat in the garden with a book, perfectly insouciant.
When the stage lights failed mid-joke, the comedian kept talking in the dark, so insouciant that the crowd assumed it was part of the act.
Investors stayed strangely insouciant about the rising debt, buying more shares as the warnings piled up.
The phlegmatic chess champion sat motionless for twenty minutes, his face giving no hint of whether he was winning or losing.
Her phlegmatic husband showed no sign of joy at his surprise party, nodding to the guests as if it were an ordinary Tuesday.
When the toddler tipped the birthday cake onto the floor, her phlegmatic grandfather did not so much as raise his eyebrows.
Lottery officials were surprised by the phlegmatic winner, who showed no more excitement than if he had found a coin on the sidewalk.
The young surgeon won plaudits from senior staff for staying calm through a twelve-hour operation.
The mayor took the plaudits for the new park, though volunteers had done most of the work.
The rookie firefighter shrugged off the plaudits, saying anyone would have carried the child out of the smoke.
The town's recycling scheme has drawn plaudits from environmental groups as far away as Japan.
After two wildfires last summer, the city's new code proscribes fireworks within a mile of the forest.
Medical boards proscribe romantic relationships between doctors and their patients.
Building codes in earthquake zones proscribe unreinforced brick walls.
The league's new rules proscribe any contact with a referee, and a player who so much as taps one is suspended.
By the third hour of the drive, the querulous passenger had complained about the music, the heat and every stop.
The querulous patient pressed the call button every ten minutes to report that the soup was cold, the room too bright or the nurse too slow.
Help desk staff learn to stay patient with querulous callers who find fault with everything.
The restaurant's online reviews were mostly querulous, griping about portion sizes that no one else seemed to mind.
The rapacious executor quietly sold the old woman's paintings and jewelry and kept the money for himself.
Rapacious traders stripped the island of its sandalwood within a decade, leaving the hills bare.
Critics accused the firm of rapacious tactics: it loaded each company it bought with debt and sold off the pieces.
The invading army was rapacious, seizing grain, livestock and anything else the soldiers could carry.
Facing a heresy trial, the astronomer chose to recant rather than risk being burned at the stake.
Once no other lab could repeat his results, the chemist publicly recanted his claim of a cold-fusion breakthrough and apologized to his colleagues.
Even under torture, the poet refused to recant a single line of his attacks on the regime.
Years later the senator recanted her support for the war, telling reporters she no longer believed a word of her old speeches.
The novel's first chapters are redolent of Dickens, full of orphans, fog and cruel schoolmasters.
The prime minister's crackdown on newspapers is redolent of the dark years of military rule.
The CEO's stiff, carefully worded apology was redolent of a hostage reading from a script.
With its onion domes and painted shutters, the little Ohio church is redolent of a village in Ukraine.
She was sanguine about the surgery, joking with the nurses and planning a hiking trip for the spring.
Though the forecast called for storms, the bride's sanguine mother refused to rent a tent for the garden wedding.
The coach was sanguine about the rookie quarterback, predicting he would be starting by midseason.
Asked whether the old stone bridge would survive another flood, the engineer stayed sanguine, pointing out that it had already survived forty.
It is specious to claim that the new law cut crime just because crime fell the year after it passed.
The ad sounded scientific, but its specious logic, that thin people take vitamins and so vitamins make people thin, would not survive a first-year statistics class.
Her brother's specious claim that the cookies were already broken, so eating them did not count, did not fool their mother.
The salesman's specious math made the lease look cheaper by leaving out the fees due at signing.
His mother eyed my clothes with a supercilious air, as if I had shown up in pajamas.
At the reunion, the supercilious banker asked each old classmate what they earned, then smirked at every answer.
The art dealer looked over the couple's flea-market painting and said with a supercilious sniff that she did not handle that sort of thing.
Some critics take a supercilious tone toward popular novels, as if anyone who enjoys them must be a little dim.
The burglar had the temerity to leave a thank-you note in the empty safe.
After losing every match this season, he had the temerity to demand a raise.
One reporter had the temerity to interrupt the general mid-sentence and call his answer a lie.
She was stunned by the temerity of a stranger who walked into her kitchen and helped himself to the fridge.
Three winters on a fishing boat had inured her to the cold, and she now works the dock bare-handed in January.
After a decade of covering city hall, the reporter was inured to politicians' broken promises; they no longer even made her angry.
Some worry that a steady stream of violent news inures viewers to real suffering.
The coach held winter practices outdoors to inure the team to playing in the snow.
When the neighbor's dog dug up his roses for the third time, the old gardener's invective could be heard three houses away.
Her resignation letter began politely but ended in invective, calling her manager a petty tyrant and a liar.
The captain's invective, shouted over the wind, left the new deckhand red-faced and shaking.
Years later he regretted the invective in his old letters, which called his brother greedy, spineless and cruel.
The editor made a few judicious cuts, removing the weakest scenes and leaving the story tighter.
A judicious host seats feuding relatives at opposite ends of the table.
A judicious coach knows when to rest an injured star rather than risk losing her for the whole season.
With only enough water for three days, the hikers had to be judicious about when and how much they drank.
My lachrymose uncle wept through his nephew's piano recital, though the boy only played scales.
She was a lachrymose bride, sobbing through her vows and again through the first dance.
Reporters expected a defiant speech, but the lachrymose senator had to stop twice to wipe his eyes.
Colleagues learned to give even gentle criticism carefully to the lachrymose intern, who teared up at the slightest correction.
In her memoir the former actress lambastes the studio bosses who, she says, cut her pay and buried her best films.
The surgeon lambasted the junior doctor in front of the whole ward for skipping the patient's allergy check.
A group of retired generals lambasted the minister's war plan as reckless, vague and doomed to fail.
The editor lambasted my first draft in red ink, crossing out whole pages and writing 'lazy' in the margins.
The cat stretched one languid paw toward the string but could not be bothered to chase it.
The waiter took our order with languid indifference, strolling back to the kitchen as though his shift would never end.
On Sunday mornings the old dog padded around the garden at a languid pace, stopping often to lie down.
On the last day of the cruise, the passengers lay about the deck, too languid to join the dance class.
Each December the factory owner showed his largesse by handing every worker a turkey and a hundred-dollar bill.
Voters grew wary of the governor's sudden largesse, which arrived as tax rebates just weeks before the election.
Medieval kings bought loyalty with largesse, showering their nobles with land, horses and gold.
Tired of living on her uncle's largesse, she took a second job so she could pay her own rent.
The young chef was lionized by food critics for a year, then forgotten when the next new restaurant opened.
The tenor was lionized in Vienna, where crowds waited outside the opera house just to watch him leave.
After her novel topped the charts, the shy librarian found herself lionized by talk-show hosts who had ignored her first three books.
Critics argue that we lionize tech founders while ignoring the engineers who actually build the products.
Our basset hound slumps beside the dinner table, looking so lugubrious that guests assume he has never been fed.
My brother's lugubrious text about losing his umbrella read like an obituary.
Grandpa reads out the weather forecast in such a lugubrious drone that a little drizzle sounds like a disaster.
Fans groaned through the coach's lugubrious press conference, where he sighed before every answer as if the season were already lost.
Iago is a malevolent schemer who poisons Othello's mind for the pleasure of watching him suffer.
Out of malevolent envy, he hid his teammate's running shoes on the morning of the final.
The outage was no accident but the work of a malevolent former employee who deleted every backup on his way out.
The dictator took malevolent pleasure in making prisoners beg for food they would never receive.

mnemonics.text: Efficacy sounds like effect, so it measures how well something achieves its effect.
Extra means outside, so extraneous things are extra and out of place.
Penury sounds like penniless, meaning having no money at all.
Prattle sounds like rattle, as in a baby's rattle making endless meaningless noise.
The word aberrant contains err, reminding you of behavior that errs from the standard path.
Anomaly comes from the Greek an- (not) and homalos (even or regular), meaning it does not follow the normal pattern.
Bene means well and -ficent comes from facere (to do), so a beneficent act is literally doing good.
Cacophony comes from Greek roots kakos (bad) and phone (sound), making it a harsh noise.
A capricious person acts on a sudden caprice, shifting their mood or mind without any warning.
Commensurate shares a root with 'measure'; things that are commensurate have matching measures.
Castigate comes from the Latin castigare, "to correct or punish": to castigate is to correct someone with harsh words.
Caustic comes from the Greek kaustikos, "burning": caustic words burn like acid.
Precipitate comes from the Latin praeceps, "headlong": to precipitate an event is to send it rushing forward headfirst.
Prolific shares the Latin root proles, "offspring", with proliferate: both are about producing a lot.
Propitiate shares a root with propitious, "favorable": you propitiate people to make them favorable toward you.
Reticent comes from the Latin reticere, "to keep silent", built on tacere, the same root as tacit.
Derivative work is derived from someone else's: it repeats rather than creates.
Catalyst comes from the Greek katalysis, "dissolving": a catalyst breaks a fixed situation apart so that change can happen.
Deride comes from Latin ridere, to laugh, the root of ridicule: to deride people is to laugh them down.
Desiccate comes from Latin siccus, dry: to desiccate something is to dry it out thoroughly.
Desultory comes from Latin desultor, a circus rider who leapt from horse to horse, just as desultory work jumps from one thing to another.
Diaphanous comes from Greek dia, through, and phainein, to show: a diaphanous veil lets the light show through it.
Diatribe comes from a Greek verb meaning to wear away, and a long diatribe wears down everyone who has to hear it.
Didactic comes from Greek didaskein, to teach: a didactic story is written to teach a lesson.
Diffident shares Latin fidere, to trust, with confident; the dif- (from dis-, not) marks a person who does not trust their own ability.
Dilatory comes from Latin dilatus, put off, a form of the verb that also gave English defer: a dilatory person keeps deferring.
Dirge comes from dirige, the opening Latin word of a chant in the church's service for the dead, which is why a dirge is a song of mourning.
Disabuse joins dis-, undo, with an old sense of abuse, to deceive: to disabuse someone is to undo a deception.
Discordant comes from Latin dis-, apart, and cor, heart: discordant views come from hearts set apart.
Impassive joins im-, not, to the Latin root of passion (pati, to suffer or feel): an impassive face shows no passion.
Reverent and revere share a Latin root, revereri, to stand in awe: a reverent person reveres what is before them.
Sagacious comes from Latin sagax, keen-scented, a word Romans used for good hunting dogs: a sagacious person sniffs out the truth.
Salubrious comes from Latin salus, health, also the root of salute: Romans greeted each other by wishing good health.
Abscond comes from Latin abscondere, to hide away: someone who absconds slips off and hides, often with the money.
Abstain comes from Latin abs-, away, and tenere, to hold: to abstain is to hold yourself away from something.
Admonish shares a Latin root with monitor: monere, to warn. To admonish someone is to warn them about their conduct.
Adulterate comes from Latin adulterare, to corrupt, a close relative of adultery: both spoil something that should stay pure.
Aggrandize contains grand, from Latin grandis, large: to aggrandize someone is to make them grander in power or in show.
Alacrity comes from Latin alacer, lively and eager, the same root as allegro, the music term for a quick, bright pace.
Disparage contains par, from the Latin for "equal": to disparage someone is to talk as if they are below par.
Disparate shares a Latin root, parare, with separate: disparate things are so unlike that they seem to belong in separate worlds.
Dissemble comes from the same Latin root as simulate: to dissemble is to simulate a feeling so the real one stays hidden.
Disseminate comes from the Latin for "seed," the root of seminal and seminar: to disseminate ideas is to scatter them like seed.
Dissonance comes from Latin dis-, "apart," and sonare, "to sound": ideas in dissonance sound wrong together, like clashing notes.
Distend shares the Latin tendere, "to stretch," with extend and tension: a distended belly is stretched out from inside.
Dogmatic comes from dogma, a belief that an authority says must not be questioned: a dogmatic person treats their own opinions that way.
Dubious shares its Latin root with doubt: a dubious claim is one you have good reason to doubt.
Eclectic comes from the Greek eklegein, "to pick out": an eclectic person picks out the best from many sources.
Effrontery contains front, from the Latin frons, "forehead" or "face": effrontery is showing a bold face when you should feel shame.
Candor shares a root with candid and candle, Latin candere, to shine: candor lets the plain truth shine through.
Chicanery comes from the French chicaner, to quibble: it means winning by sly tricks and hair-splitting arguments rather than fair means.
Coagulate comes from Latin coagulum, rennet, the stuff cheesemakers use to curdle milk: to coagulate is to clot or curdle.
Coalesce comes from Latin co-, together, and alescere, to grow: separate parts grow together into one.
Cogent comes from Latin cogere, to drive together or compel: a cogent argument compels you to agree.
Complaisant comes from French complaire, to please: a complaisant person goes out of the way to please others. Do not confuse it with complacent, meaning smug.
Conciliatory comes from Latin conciliare, to bring together or win over, the root of reconcile: conciliatory words aim to reconcile.
Condone shares a root with donate, Latin donare, to give: when you condone a wrong, you give it a free pass.
Conflagration comes from Latin conflagrare, to burn up, from flagrare, to blaze: a conflagration is a blaze out of control.
Connoisseur comes from an old French word meaning to know, related to recognize: a connoisseur knows quality when they see or taste it.
Contrite comes from Latin contritus, ground down or crushed: a contrite person feels crushed by guilt over a wrong.
Conundrum ends in drum: a hard puzzle keeps drumming in your head until you work it out.
Convoluted comes from the Latin convolvere, 'to roll together': a convoluted story is rolled up in so many loops that it is hard to unwind.
Corroborate and robust share the Latin robur, 'strength': to corroborate a story is to make it stronger with evidence.
Credulous comes from the Latin credere, 'to believe', like credit and creed: a credulous person believes too easily.
Cursory comes from the Latin cursor, 'runner', like the cursor that races across a screen: a cursory look runs past the details.
Dearth is built from dear plus -th, like warmth from warm: when food is scarce, it grows dear, meaning costly.
Debacle comes from a French word for river ice breaking up: picture a frozen plan cracking apart all at once.
Decorum comes from the Latin decorus, 'fitting' or 'proper': decorum is behavior that fits the occasion.
Deference comes from defer, 'to yield': showing deference means you defer to someone else's wishes.
Elegy comes from the Greek elegos, a song of grief, and an elegy is still a poem that grieves for the dead.
Eloquent comes from the Latin e-, out, and loqui, to speak: an eloquent person speaks out with skill.
Embellish contains the French bel, beautiful (as in belle): to embellish a story is to make it prettier than the truth.
Empirical comes from the Greek empeiria, experience: empirical knowledge is learned by experience and testing, not by theory.
Emulate comes from the Latin aemulus, a rival: you emulate people when you try to match or even beat them.
Enervate comes from the Latin e-, out, and nervus, sinew: picture the sinews pulled out, leaving you limp. It is the opposite of energize.
Engender shares its Latin root with generate (generare, to beget): to engender trust or anger is to generate it.
Ephemeral comes from the Greek epi, on, and hemera, day: something ephemeral lasts about a day.
Epigram and telegram both end in gram, Greek for something written. Think of an epigram as a telegram of wit: short, because every word counts.
Erudite comes from the Latin e-, out of, and rudis, rough or untaught (as in rude and rudimentary): an erudite person has been taught out of roughness.
Esoteric comes from the Greek eso, within: esoteric knowledge stays inside a small circle, while exoteric knowledge is for outsiders.
Assuage goes back to Latin suavis, sweet, the root of suave: to assuage a bitter feeling is to sweeten it.
Audacious comes from Latin audere, to dare (not audire, to hear): an audacious person dares to do what others will not.
Austere goes back to a Greek word for a dry, harsh taste; an austere room is dry in the same way, with nothing sweet or soft added.
Aver comes from Latin verus, true, the root of verify and veracity: to aver something is to declare it true.
Belie contains lie, and comes from an old English word for deceiving: a calm face that belies your nerves tells a lie about how you feel.
Bombastic comes from bombast, cotton stuffing once used to pad out clothes: bombastic speech is padded out with grand words.
Burgeon comes from an old French word for a bud: picture buds bursting open all over a tree in spring, and you have something that burgeons.
Buttress comes from an old French word meaning to push against: a stone buttress pushes back against a wall, and evidence can buttress an argument the same way.
Cajole rhymes with goal: you cajole someone with sweet talk until you reach your goal.
Alleviate comes from the Latin levis, meaning light, as in levity: to alleviate a pain is to make it lighter to carry.
Ambivalent joins the Latin ambi-, 'both', with valere, 'to be strong': two opposite feelings pull with equal strength.
Ameliorate contains the Latin melior, meaning better: to ameliorate a bad situation is to make it better.
Anachronism contains the Greek chronos, 'time', as in chronology: an anachronism is something placed in the wrong time.
Apathy is the Greek a-, 'without', plus pathos, 'feeling': apathy is a state without feeling or interest.
Appease has peace inside it, from the Old French pais, 'peace': you appease an angry person to restore the peace.
Arduous comes from the Latin arduus, 'steep': an arduous task feels like a long climb up a steep hill.
Articulate comes from the Latin articulus, 'small joint': to articulate a thought is to lay it out in clear, separate parts, like the segments of a finger.
Eulogy joins Greek eu (good) and logos (word): good words spoken about someone, usually at a funeral.
Euphemism comes from Greek eu (good) and pheme (speech): speaking of a bad thing in good-sounding words.
Evanescent comes from Latin evanescere, to vanish; the English word vanish grew from the same root.
Exacerbate shares a root with acerbic (Latin acerbus, bitter): to exacerbate a bad thing is to make it more bitter.
Exculpate is Latin ex (out of) plus culpa (blame), the root of culpable: it takes someone out of blame.
Exigent comes from Latin exigere, to demand, the same root as exact: an exigent problem demands action now.
Exonerate comes from Latin ex (off) and onus, oneris (a burden): to exonerate someone is to lift the burden of blame off them.
Expedient comes from Latin expedire, to free the feet: an expedient choice frees you to move toward what you want, right or not.
Extol comes from Latin extollere, to lift up: when you extol someone, you lift them up with praise.
Fallacious comes from Latin fallere, to deceive, the same root as false: a fallacious argument leads you to a false conclusion.
Officious comes from Latin officium, "duty", the root of office: an officious person treats every matter as their duty to manage.
Onerous comes from Latin onus, "burden", the same onus as in "the onus is on you".
Opaque comes from Latin opacus, "shaded": an opaque explanation leaves its meaning in the shade.
Opprobrium comes from Latin probrum, "a shameful act": opprobrium is the scorn heaped on someone who commits one.
Ostentatious comes from Latin ostentare, "to keep showing": an ostentatious person keeps showing off what they own.
Palliate comes from Latin pallium, "cloak": to palliate a fault is to throw a cloak over it so it looks less bad.
Panacea comes from Greek pan, "all", and akos, "cure": a panacea is a cure for all.
Paragon comes from Italian paragone, a touchstone used to test gold: a paragon is the standard others are tested against.
Parsimony comes from Latin parcere, "to spare": a person known for parsimony spares every coin.
Paucity comes from Latin paucus, "few": a paucity of anything means there are too few of them.
Pedantic comes from pedant, which came into English through French from Italian pedante, a schoolmaster: a pedantic person corrects everyone like a fussy teacher.
Penchant comes from French pencher, "to lean": a penchant is a natural leaning toward something.
Intractable comes from Latin tractare, to handle: an intractable problem is one nobody can get a handle on.
Intransigent comes via Spanish from Latin transigere, to settle a deal. Add in- (not) and you get someone who will not settle.
Inundate comes from Latin unda, a wave: to inundate is to send wave after wave over something.
Inveterate shares the Latin root veter-, old, with veteran: an inveterate habit is a veteran habit that has grown old with you.
Irascible and irate both come from Latin ira, anger: an irascible person turns irate at the smallest thing.
Itinerant shares the Latin root iter, a journey, with itinerary: an itinerant worker's whole life is an itinerary.
Laconic comes from Laconia, home of the Spartans, who were famous for short replies. To a king's threat beginning 'If I invade,' they answered only 'If.'
Lassitude comes from Latin lassus, weary: lassitude is a weariness so deep that it drains the will to act.
Laud comes from Latin laus, praise, as does laudable. Applaud has a different root, but it still helps: to laud someone is to applaud them with words.
Levity comes from Latin levis, light, the same root behind elevate and lever: levity is a light touch where weight is expected.
Loquacious comes from Latin loqui, to speak, also found in eloquent and soliloquy: a loquacious person speaks and speaks.
Lucid comes from Latin lucere, to shine: a lucid explanation lets light into a murky subject.
Luminous comes from Latin lumen, light, the same root as illuminate: something luminous gives off light.
Magnanimous joins Latin magnus, great, and animus, spirit: a great-spirited person rises above grudges.
Malinger comes from French malingre, sickly: a malingerer acts sickly to dodge work.
Malleable comes from Latin malleus, hammer: a malleable metal, or a malleable mind, can be hammered into a new shape.
Maudlin comes from Magdalene, once pronounced maudlin, because Mary Magdalene was often painted weeping.
Meticulous comes from Latin metus, fear: a meticulous worker is almost afraid of making even one small mistake.
Mitigate comes from Latin mitis, mild: to mitigate damage is to make it milder.
Mollify comes from Latin mollis, soft: you mollify an angry person by softening their mood.
Morose comes from Latin morosus, peevish or hard to please: a morose person sulks and will not be cheered.
Impute shares a root with compute: Latin putare, 'to reckon'. To impute is to reckon a fault into someone's account.
Inchoate comes from Latin incohare, 'to begin': an inchoate plan has only just been started and has no shape yet.
Incipient comes from Latin incipere, 'to begin' (in- 'on' + capere 'to take'): something incipient is just taking hold.
Indigent comes from Latin indigere, 'to be in need': indigent people need help just to get by.
Indolent comes from Latin in- 'not' + dolere 'to feel pain': the indolent avoid the pain of hard work. Doctors still call a slow, painless tumor indolent.
Ineffable comes from Latin in- 'not' + effari 'to speak out': something ineffable cannot be spoken.
Inexorable comes from Latin in- 'not' + exorare 'to win over by pleading' (orare, 'to pray'): no prayer can stop it.
Ingenuous comes from Latin ingenuus, 'freeborn' and so 'frank'. Hear genuine inside it: an ingenuous person is genuine, with nothing hidden.
Inimical comes from Latin inimicus, 'enemy' (in- 'not' + amicus 'friend'): something inimical acts like an enemy.
Iniquity comes from Latin iniquus, 'unjust' (in- 'not' + aequus 'equal, fair'): iniquity treats people in a cruelly unfair way.
Innocuous comes from Latin in- 'not' + nocuus 'harmful', from nocere 'to harm' (as in noxious): innocuous things do no harm.
Insipid comes from Latin in- 'not' + sapidus 'tasty' (from sapere 'to taste', the root of savor): insipid things have no savor.
Insular comes from Latin insula, 'island' (as in peninsula): insular people live as if on an island, cut off from everyone else.
Hackneyed comes from the hackney, a horse kept for hire; ridden by everyone, it ended up worn out, like an overused phrase.
Hedonist comes from Greek hedone, "pleasure": a hedonist lives to chase it.
Hegemony comes from Greek hegemon, "leader": a nation with hegemony leads and the rest follow.
Heresy comes from Greek hairesis, "a choosing": a heretic chooses a belief of his own over the official one.
Iconoclast joins Greek eikon, "image", and klastes, "breaker": first a smasher of holy images, now a smasher of sacred ideas.
Idolatry joins idol with Greek latreia, "worship": it is the worship of an idol.
Immutable holds Latin mutare, "to change", as in mutation; the im- means not, so it cannot change.
Impecunious holds Latin pecunia, "money", as in pecuniary; the im- means without, so it means without money.
Imperious comes from Latin imperium, "command", the root of empire: an imperious person gives orders like an emperor.
Impertinent is in- (not) plus pertinent, relevant: an impertinent remark was first one that did not belong, and the word came to mean cheeky.
Impervious comes from Latin per, "through", and via, "way"; with im- in front, nothing finds a way through.
Fatuous shares a root with infatuated, from Latin fatuus, 'foolish': people who are infatuated often say fatuous things.
Fervid comes from Latin fervere, 'to boil', the same root as fervent: fervid feelings are boiling hot.
Flout rhymes with out: people who flout a rule step out of it in plain sight, as if daring anyone to stop them.
Foment comes from Latin fovere, 'to keep warm': to foment a revolt is to keep feeding its heat until it boils over.
Forestall comes from Old English foresteall, an ambush, literally a standing in front of someone on the road: to forestall something is to get in its way before it arrives.
Fortuitous comes from Latin fors, 'chance', the same root as fortune: a fortuitous event is left to chance.
Fractious shares a root with fracture, Latin frangere, 'to break': a fractious group keeps breaking the rules and breaking into quarrels.
Frugal comes from Latin frux, 'fruit' or 'produce': a frugal person makes every bit of the harvest last.
Garrulous comes from Latin garrire, 'to chatter': a garrulous seatmate chatters for the whole flight.
A goad was first a pointed stick for driving cattle; to goad someone is to keep poking at them until they move.
