Gregarious comes from Latin grex, 'flock', also found in congregate: a gregarious person likes to be part of the flock.
Guile is the root of beguile: someone with guile can beguile you into trusting them.
Mundane comes from Latin mundus, world: mundane things belong to the ordinary everyday world.
Munificent comes from Latin munus, gift, and facere, to make: a munificent person makes many gifts.
Nadir comes from Arabic nazir, opposite: the nadir is the point opposite the zenith, the very bottom.
Nascent comes from Latin nasci, to be born, the root of natal and renaissance: a nascent thing has just been born.
Nebulous comes from Latin nebula, mist: a nebulous idea is misty, with no clear outline.
Obdurate comes from Latin obdurare, to harden, from durus, hard: an obdurate heart has hardened and will not bend.
Obfuscate comes from Latin fuscus, dark: to obfuscate is to darken a point until no one can see it clearly.
Obstinate comes from Latin obstinare, to persist, a relative of stare, to stand: the obstinate stand their ground and will not budge.
Obtuse comes from Latin obtusus, blunted: an obtuse mind is dull rather than sharp, like an angle too wide to come to a point.
Rarefy comes from Latin rarus, thin or scattered, plus facere, to make: to rarefy air is to make it thin.
Recondite comes from Latin recondere, to put away or hide: recondite knowledge is tucked away where few people find it.
Redoubtable comes from Old French redouter, to dread; douter once meant fear as well as doubt, so a redoubtable foe is one you dread.
Relegate comes from Latin relegare, to send away: when you relegate something, you send it away to a lesser place.
Repudiate comes from Latin repudium, a formal divorce: to repudiate a belief is to divorce yourself from it.
Sanction comes from Latin sancire, to make sacred or decree: a sanction is a decree, which can approve an act or punish one.
Perfunctory comes from Latin perfungi, to get through a duty: a perfunctory job is done just to be finished with it.
Pernicious comes from Latin pernicies, ruin, built on nex, violent death, the same root found in internecine.
Perspicacious comes from Latin perspicere, to see through, the same root as perspective: a perspicacious person sees through to the truth.
Pervasive comes from Latin per (through) and vadere (to go), as in invade: something pervasive goes through everything.
Petulant starts with pet: picture a spoiled pet that sulks and snaps whenever it does not get its treat.
A pillory was a wooden frame in the town square where offenders were locked and jeered at; to pillory someone now is to put them in that frame with words.
Pithy comes from pith, the soft core of a plant stem; a pithy remark gets straight to the core of the matter.
Placate comes from Latin placare, to calm, a cousin of placid: you placate someone to make them placid again.
Platitude comes from French plat, flat: a platitude is a flat remark with nothing fresh in it.
Plethora comes from Greek plethein, to be full, a distant cousin of plenty: a plethora is plenty and then some.
Sanctimonious comes from Latin sanctus, 'holy', as in saint and sanctuary: a sanctimonious person puts on a show of holiness.
Sardonic goes back to a Greek tale of a Sardinian plant whose poison twisted the face into a grim grin: a sardonic smile is bitter, not merry.
Satiate comes from Latin satis, 'enough', the same root as satisfy: once you are satiated, you have had enough.
Saturnine comes from Saturn: astrologers held that people born under that slow, distant planet were gloomy and sullen.
Savant comes from French savoir, 'to know': a savant is someone who knows a great deal.
Sedulous sounds a bit like schedule: a sedulous student keeps to a study schedule every day without fail.
Servile shares its Latin root with servant and serve: a servile person serves anyone in power too eagerly.
Soporific comes from Latin sopor, 'deep sleep', plus -fic, 'making': something soporific makes you sleep.
Spurious comes from Latin spurius, 'illegitimate child': like a false heir, a spurious claim has no true right to what it claims.
Squander ends in a sound like wander: squandered money wanders off and never comes home.
Staid began as an old spelling of stayed: a staid person has stayed in the same sober habits for years.
Stolid comes from Latin stolidus, 'slow and dull': a stolid person is slow to show any feeling.
Prodigal comes from Latin prodigere, to drive away or squander. The prodigal son in the parable squandered his whole inheritance.
Profligate comes from Latin profligare, to strike down or ruin: profligate spending ruins a fortune.
Protean comes from Proteus, a Greek sea god who kept changing his shape so that no one could hold him.
Prudent is a shortened form of Latin providens, foreseeing. A prudent person sees trouble coming and plans for it.
Puerile comes from Latin puer, boy: puerile humor is the kind a schoolboy finds hilarious.
Pugnacious comes from Latin pugnare, to fight, from pugnus, fist. Picture a pugnacious person with fists always raised.
Punctilious comes from Latin punctum, a point, through Italian puntiglio, a fine point. A punctilious person minds every little point.
Pungent comes from Latin pungere, to prick, the root of puncture: a pungent smell seems to prick your nose.
Quixotic comes from Don Quixote, the hero of Cervantes's novel, who charged at windmills he believed were giants.
Quotidian comes from Latin quotidie, every day, built from dies, day. Something quotidian turns up every day.
Polemic comes from Greek polemos, war: a polemic wages war on someone's ideas with words.
Ponderous comes from Latin pondus, weight, the same root as pound and ponder (to weigh in the mind): a ponderous thing moves under its own weight.
Pragmatic comes from Greek pragma, a deed or thing done: a pragmatic person cares about what can actually be done.
Precocious comes from Latin praecox, ripened early (prae, before, and coquere, to cook or ripen): a precocious child is ready before the usual time.
Prescient comes from Latin prae, before, and scire, to know, the root of science: knowing what will happen before it does.
Prevaricate comes from Latin praevaricari, to walk crookedly: someone who prevaricates will not walk a straight line to the truth.
Pristine comes from Latin pristinus, former or original: a pristine thing is still as it first was.
Probity comes from Latin probus, upright or honest, which also gave us prove: a person of probity proves honest every time.
Proclivity comes from Latin pro, forward, and clivus, a slope: a proclivity tilts you toward a habit, like ground that leans downhill.
Unctuous comes from Latin unguere, to anoint with oil, the same root as ointment: an unctuous person is greasy with flattery.
Undulate comes from Latin unda, a wave: things that undulate move or curve the way waves do.
Vacillate comes from Latin vacillare, to sway or totter: a person who vacillates sways between choices like a wobbly table.
Venerate shares its Latin root with Venus, the goddess: to venerate is to honor something almost as people honored a god.
Veracity comes from Latin verus, true, the same root as verify and verdict: veracity is truthfulness.
Verbose comes from Latin verbum, word, as in verbal: a verbose speaker hands out words by the bucketful.
Vilify contains vile, from Latin vilis, cheap or worthless: to vilify someone is to paint them as vile.
Timorous comes from Latin timor, 'fear', the same root as timid: a timorous person is ruled by fear.
Torpid shares a Latin root, torpere, 'to be numb', with torpedo, first the name of a fish whose shock numbs its prey.
Tortuous comes from Latin torquere, 'to twist', the root of contort and torque: a tortuous path keeps twisting back on itself.
Tractable comes from Latin tractare, 'to handle': a tractable horse is easy to handle.
Trenchant comes from Old French trenchier, 'to cut', the same source as trench: trenchant remarks cut deep.
Truculent comes from Latin trux, 'fierce': a truculent person is fierce and ready for a fight.
Turgid comes from Latin turgere, 'to swell': turgid writing is swollen with more words than it needs.
Turpitude comes from Latin turpis, 'shameful' or 'ugly': turpitude is shamefully ugly conduct.
Ubiquitous comes from Latin ubique, 'everywhere': ubiquitous things turn up everywhere you look.
Vindicate comes from Latin vindex, a champion who stepped forward to defend a claim: when the facts vindicate you, they step forward on your side.
Virulent comes from Latin virus, which meant poison or venom: a virulent attack is written to poison its target.
Viscous comes from Latin viscum, mistletoe, whose berries were boiled into a sticky paste for trapping birds.
Vituperate comes from Latin vitium, fault, and parare, to prepare: to vituperate is to lay out every fault you can find in someone, loudly.
Volatile comes from Latin volare, to fly: a volatile mood or market can fly off in any direction at any moment.
Wily is wile plus -y: a wile is a trick or lure, so a wily person is full of tricks.
Zenith comes from Arabic samt ar-ra's, the path over the head: the zenith is the point straight above you, so anything at its zenith can climb no higher.
Insidious comes from Latin insidiae, an ambush, from sitting in wait: an insidious threat lies hidden until it strikes.
Strident comes from Latin stridere, to creak or screech: a strident voice screeches at you.
Stymie began as a golf word: your putt was stymied when another ball lay between yours and the hole.
Sublime comes from Latin sublimis, raised high: sublime things lift you up.
Substantiate contains substance: you give a claim substance by backing it with proof.
Superfluous comes from Latin super, over, and fluere, to flow: what is superfluous overflows what is needed.
Surfeit comes from Old French surfait, overdone: sur, over, plus fait, done. A surfeit is too much.
Sycophant comes from Greek sykophantes, literally fig-shower. Picture a fawning courtier forever showing the king a basket of figs.
Taciturn comes from Latin tacere, to be silent, the same root as tacit.
Tangential comes from tangent, a line that touches a circle at one point and heads off; a tangential remark touches the topic and drifts away.
Tenuous comes from Latin tenuis, thin: a tenuous link is a thin thread that could snap.
Terse comes from Latin tersus, wiped clean: a terse reply has every extra word wiped away.
Vex comes from Latin vexare, 'to shake or harass': a vexing habit shakes your calm.
Waver is wave with an r added. Like a flag waving in shifting wind, a wavering mind swings one way and then the other.
Zealous means full of zeal, from Greek zelos, ardor. Jealous comes from the same Greek word, which is why the two look so alike.
Abjure comes from Latin ab, away, and jurare, to swear: to abjure a belief is to swear it away.
Accolade comes from French accoler, to hug around the neck (Latin ad, to, and collum, neck), from the embrace once given to a new knight.
Acerbic comes from Latin acerbus, harsh or sour, related to acer, sharp: an acerbic remark has a sharp, sour bite.
Acumen is a Latin word for a point, from acuere, to sharpen: a person with acumen has a sharp mind.
Adroit comes from French à droit, properly, from droit, right. Droit also names the right side, the hand long tied to skill, as in dexterous.
Affable comes from Latin affabilis, easy to speak to, from ad, to, and fari, to speak.
In Greek, anathema meant an offering set apart for a god; the early church used it for a person cursed and cut off, so an anathema is something cast out.
Anodyne comes from Greek an, without, and odyne, pain: first a painkiller, and now anything so mild it could not hurt anyone.
Apocryphal comes from Greek apokryphos, hidden away, the name given to books kept out of the Bible because their origin was in doubt.
Arcane comes from Latin arcanus, secret, related to arca, a chest: arcane knowledge is locked away where few can reach it.
Avarice comes from Latin avarus, greedy, from avere, to crave: avarice is a craving for wealth that is never satisfied.
Bellicose comes from Latin bellum, 'war', which also gives belligerent and antebellum: a bellicose person is always ready for war.
Blithe meant simply 'joyful' in Old English. A blithe attitude stays happy-go-lucky even when something deserves worry.
Brusque came into English through French from Italian brusco, 'rough' or 'tart': a brusque reply leaves a tart taste.
Bucolic comes from Greek boukolos, 'herdsman', built on bous, 'ox': a bucolic scene is the herdsman's world of fields and grazing cattle.
Canard is French for 'duck'. Picture a duck quacking a made-up story until the whole pond believes it.
Capitulate comes from Medieval Latin capitulare, 'to draw up under headings' (caput means 'head'). It first meant to set out the terms of an agreement and later narrowed to agreeing to surrender.
Chary grew from the same Old English root as care: a chary person takes great care before trusting or acting.
In Greek myth the Chimera was a monster made from a lion, a goat and a snake. A hope as impossible as that beast is a chimera.
Circumspect joins Latin circum, 'around' (as in circle), and specere, 'to look' (as in inspect): a circumspect person looks all around before acting.
Clandestine comes from Latin clam, 'secretly': a clandestine plan is one that is kept out of sight.
Conflate comes from Latin conflare, 'to blow together', which was used for fusing metals in a fire: to conflate two ideas is to fuse them into one lump.
Consternation has stern in the middle: picture a stern boss's sudden frown throwing the whole office into alarmed confusion.
Culpable comes from Latin culpa, fault, as in mea culpa (my fault): a culpable person is the one at fault.
Cupidity comes from Latin cupere, to desire, the root of Cupid's name, but this desire is for money rather than love.
Decry comes through French from crier, to cry out: to decry something is to cry it down in public.
Denigrate comes from Latin denigrare, to blacken: to denigrate people is to try to blacken their name.
Deprecate comes from Latin deprecari, to pray against: you deprecate what you would like to see go away.
Dilettante comes from Italian dilettare, to delight: a dilettante studies a subject for the delight of it, not to master it.
Discomfit sounds like discomfort, though the roots differ: to discomfit someone is to leave them flustered and ill at ease.
Disingenuous is dis- (not) plus ingenuous (innocent and open): a disingenuous person only plays at being innocent.
Dissolute comes from Latin dissolutus, loosened: a dissolute person's morals have come loose.
Duplicity comes from Latin duplex, double: a person of duplicity wears a double face, one honest and one false.
Egregious comes from Latin e- (out of) and grex (flock): an egregious error stands out from the herd.
Equanimity joins Latin aequus, 'even' (as in equal), and animus, 'mind': an even mind that stays level under pressure.
Eschew comes from an Old French word related to English shy: when you eschew something, you shy away from it on purpose.
Exhort comes from Latin hortari, 'to urge', the root also found in hortatory: to exhort is to urge someone hard.
Fastidious comes from Latin fastidium, 'disgust': a fastidious person is put off by the smallest smudge or mistake.
Feckless comes from Scots feck, a shortened form of effect: a feckless person is without effect and gets nothing done.
Fecund shares its Latin start, fe-, with fetus: fecund herds and fields keep bringing forth new life.
Foible comes from an old French word for weak, the same word that gave us feeble: a foible is a small weak spot in someone's character.
Gainsay is built from an old prefix gain-, 'against' (as in against), plus say: to gainsay is to say against.
Garish sounds a bit like glare: garish colors glare at you, bright and cheap.
Germane comes from Latin germanus, 'having the same parents': a germane point is closely related to the topic, like a brother or sister.
Gratuitous shares its Latin root with gratis, 'free': a gratuitous remark is thrown in for free, though nobody wanted it.
Ignominious holds Latin nomen, 'name' (as in nominate): an ignominious act costs you your good name.
Impetuous comes from Latin impetus, 'a rush or attack': an impetuous person rushes ahead before thinking.
Incorrigible is in-, 'not', plus Latin corrigere, 'to correct': an incorrigible person cannot be corrected.
Insouciant is French: in-, 'not', plus soucier, 'to worry'. An insouciant person has no souci, no worry at all.
Inure comes from the old phrase in ure, 'in use': whatever you are inured to has been put to use on you so often that you stop feeling it.
Jocular comes from Latin joculus, a little joke, from jocus, the same root that gave English the word joke.
Lachrymose comes from Latin lacrima, a tear: a lachrymose person always seems close to tears.
Lionize comes from an old use of lion for a celebrity whom everyone wanted to see; to lionize someone is to make them that kind of lion.
Lugubrious comes from Latin lugere, to mourn: a lugubrious voice sounds as if it belongs at a funeral.
Malevolent joins Latin male, badly, and volens, wishing: a malevolent person wishes others harm, while a benevolent one wishes them well.
Misanthrope joins Greek misein, to hate, and anthropos, human being: a misanthrope hates humankind.
Obviate shares Latin via, "way," with obvious: you meet a problem in the road ahead and clear it, so no fix is needed later.
Odious comes from Latin odium, "hatred," which English also uses for strong public dislike. Odious things earn odium.
Ossify comes from Latin os, "bone": an ossified mind has gone as stiff as bone.
Panegyric comes from Greek panegyris, a gathering of all the people (pan, "all"): it was praise spoken before the whole crowd.
Pariah comes from Tamil paraiyar, "drummers," a caste in southern India that others long treated as outcasts.
Pejorative comes from Latin pejor, "worse": a pejorative word makes something sound worse than it is.
Phlegmatic comes from phlegm, one of the four body fluids that old doctors thought shaped a person's temper. Too much phlegm was said to make a person slow and calm.
Proscribe comes from Latin proscribere, "to post publicly": Roman leaders posted the names of people they declared outlaws. Link PROscribe with PROhibit.
Querulous comes from Latin queri, "to complain," which also gave English the word quarrel. A querulous person always has a complaint ready.
Rapacious comes from Latin rapere, "to seize": a rapacious person seizes whatever they can get.
Recant comes from Latin re-, "back", and cantare, "to sing": to recant is to sing your old words back, taking them back.
Redolent comes from Latin olere, "to smell", also found in olfactory: a redolent scene smells of another time and brings it to mind.
Sanguine comes from Latin sanguis, "blood": medieval doctors believed people ruled by blood were cheerful and hopeful.
Specious comes from Latin species, "appearance": a specious argument has the look of truth and nothing more.
Supercilious comes from Latin supercilium, "eyebrow": a supercilious person looks down on others with one eyebrow raised.
Tacit comes from Latin tacere, "to be silent": a tacit agreement is one made in silence.
Temerity comes from Latin temere, "blindly" or "rashly": temerity is boldness that charges ahead without looking.
Vicarious shares a Latin root with vicar and vice president, people who stand in for someone else: a vicarious thrill is felt in someone else's place.
Vitriolic comes from vitriol, an old name for sulfuric acid: vitriolic words burn like acid.
Vociferous comes from Latin vox, "voice", and ferre, "to carry": vociferous people make their voices carry.
Venal comes from Latin venum, "sale", the root of vendor: a venal official is up for sale.
Gerrymander joins Gerry, the Massachusetts governor who signed an 1812 voting map, with salamander, the shape one twisted district on that map seemed to have.
Impinge comes from Latin impingere, to drive or push into: whatever impinges on your rights pushes into them.
Acolyte comes from Greek akolouthos, meaning a follower or attendant: an acolyte follows a leader around.
Acquiesce comes from Latin acquiescere, to rest or be at peace (quies, rest, as in quiet): when you acquiesce, you stay quiet instead of objecting.
Adulation comes from Latin adulari, to fawn or flatter: adulation is the fawning praise a crowd heaps on its hero.
In Greek myth the aegis was a protective shield carried by Zeus and Athena, so working under someone's aegis means working under their shield.
Amenable comes from French amener, to lead or bring: an amenable person can be led to agree.
Apostate comes from Greek apostasis, a standing away (apo, away, and stasis, standing): an apostate stands away from a faith.
Apropos comes from the French phrase à propos, meaning to the purpose: an apropos remark is to the point. The phrase apropos of means speaking of.
Arbiter is a Latin word for a judge, and it shares a root with arbitrate: an arbiter settles the question.
Ascendancy comes from Latin ascendere, to climb up: a group in the ascendancy has climbed to the top.
Attenuate comes from Latin tenuis, thin, the root of tenuous: to attenuate something is to thin it out.
Beguile contains guile, meaning sly cunning: to beguile someone is to work your guile on them.
Demagogue comes from Greek demos, the people, and agogos, leader: a demagogue leads the people by playing on their fears.
Denizen comes from Old French deinz, inside: a denizen is someone inside a place and at home there, never just a visitor.
Disinterested is dis-, meaning not, plus interest in its old sense of a stake, as in conflict of interest: a disinterested umpire has nothing riding on the game.
Dour probably comes from Latin durus, hard: picture a dour face as hard as stone, never softening into a smile.
Droll comes from French drôle, funny or odd: a droll remark is funny in an odd, quiet way.
Elucidate comes from Latin lucidus, bright, the root of lucid: to elucidate an idea is to make it bright and clear.
Erstwhile joins erst, an old word for formerly, with while: your erstwhile friend was your friend a while ago.
Evince comes from Latin evincere, to prove: when your face evinces surprise, it proves to everyone that you are surprised.
Extant comes from Latin exstare, to stand out or exist: extant species are still standing, unlike extinct ones.
Facile comes from Latin facilis, easy, as in facility: a facile answer came too easily to be any good.
Fealty comes through Old French from Latin fidelitas, the root of fidelity: fealty is faithfulness sworn to a lord.
Furtive comes from Latin fur, thief: a furtive glance is the quick, guilty look of a thief.
Pastiche comes through French from Italian pasticcio, a pie filled with a mix of ingredients: a pastiche bakes borrowed styles into one dish.
Pathos is Greek for suffering or feeling, the root of sympathy and pathetic: pathos makes you feel for someone who suffers.
Patina comes through Italian from Latin patina, a shallow dish: picture an old bronze dish dug up green with age.
Peruse is probably built from per-, thoroughly, and use: it first meant to use something up, and now means to go through a text thoroughly.
Pique comes from French piquer, to prick or sting: a fit of pique is the sting of hurt pride.
Plebeian comes from Latin plebs, the mass of ordinary Roman citizens outside the noble patrician families: plebeian tastes are those of the crowd.
Pontificate comes from pontifex, the Latin title of Rome's high priests and later of the pope: to pontificate is to speak as if issuing a papal decree.
Portend comes from Latin portendere, to stretch forward (por-, forward, and tendere, to stretch): a portent points ahead to what is coming.
Posit comes from Latin positus, placed, the root of position: to posit an idea is to place it down as the base of an argument.
Precept comes from Latin praeceptum, a teaching, built from prae-, before, and capere, to take: precepts are lessons you take in before life tests you.
Promulgate comes from Latin promulgare, to make publicly known, which Roman officials did with new laws: to promulgate is to get word out to the public.
Putative comes from Latin putare, to think or suppose, also the root of reputation. A putative fact is one that people suppose is true.
Qualm rhymes with calm: a qualm is the small doubt that keeps your conscience from feeling calm.
Regale contains gale, as in a gale of laughter: a good storyteller regales a table until it roars.
Remiss contains miss: someone who is remiss misses a duty they were supposed to carry out.
Renege shares its root with renegade: both come from Latin negare, to deny. To renege is to deny a promise you once made.
Replete comes from Latin replere, to fill up. Its root plere, to fill, also gives us complete.
Resplendent comes from Latin resplendere, to shine brightly, from the same splendere, to shine, that gives us splendid.
Rife rhymes with strife: where strife is rife, trouble is everywhere you look.
Roil sounds like boil, and a roiling crowd or sea churns like a pot at a rolling boil.
Ruminate comes from Latin ruminari, to chew the cud. A cow chews the same mouthful again and again, and a person who ruminates chews on the same thought.
Salient comes from Latin salire, to leap: a salient fact leaps out at you.
Subsume joins Latin sub, under, and sumere, to take: to subsume is to take something in under a larger heading.
Bereft is the old past form of bereave, from an Old English verb meaning to rob: someone bereft of hope has been robbed of it.
Cabal reached English through French cabale, a word for hidden knowledge, and a cabal keeps its plans hidden from everyone outside its small circle.
Cavalier comes from Italian cavaliere, a horseman: picture a rider who looks down from the saddle and brushes off whatever happens below.
Chagrin ends in grin, but it is the stiff, forced grin you put on when you are embarrassed and annoyed.
Circumscribe comes from Latin circum, around, and scribere, to write or draw: you draw a line around something, and it may not cross it.
Concomitant comes from Latin con, with, and comes, companion: a concomitant effect travels with something as its companion.
Connive comes from Latin connivere, to shut the eyes or wink: conspirators wink at one another, or shut their eyes to the crime.
Consummate comes from Latin summa, the total, from summus, highest, the root of summit: a consummate artist has reached the top of the craft.
Contravene comes from Latin contra, against, and venire, to come: to contravene a rule is to come up against it head-on.
Countenance is also an old word for a face: to countenance a plan is to show it an approving face instead of a frown.
Craven sounds a lot like cave in, and a craven person caves in the moment courage is called for.
Deign comes from Latin dignari, to think worthy, from dignus, worthy, the root of dignity: you deign to do a task you think barely worthy of you.
Glib is related to old Dutch and German words for slippery: glib talk slides smoothly past the hard parts of a question without getting a grip on them.
Hapless is hap, an old word for luck or chance (still heard in happen and mishap), plus -less: a hapless person is without luck.
Histrionic comes from Latin histrio, an actor: a histrionic person acts out every feeling as if on a stage.
Impugn comes from Latin impugnare, to fight against (pugnare, to fight, as in pugnacious): to impugn a claim is to fight it.
Incisive comes from Latin incidere, to cut into, the root of incision and incisor: an incisive comment slices through the clutter to what matters.
Incongruous is in-, not, plus congruous, from Latin congruere, to come together or agree: incongruous things do not go together.
Inculcate comes from Latin inculcare, to press in with the heel (calx, heel): picture a lesson trodden into the mind step after step until it stays put.
Inscrutable comes from Latin in-, not, and scrutari, to search or examine, the root of scrutiny: no amount of scrutiny will tell you what an inscrutable face is thinking.
Interlocutor comes from Latin inter, between, and loqui, to speak (as in eloquent): an interlocutor is one of the people speaking back and forth in a talk.
Lampoon may come from a French cry, lampons, 'let's guzzle,' heard in rowdy songs that poked fun at people: think of a tavern mocking the mayor in verse.
Litany comes from Greek litaneia, an entreaty: a church litany is a long run of pleas repeated one after another, so any droning list of grievances became a litany too.
Loath (rhymes with both) is the adjective meaning unwilling; loathe (rhymes with clothe) is the verb meaning hate. You are loath to do what you loathe.
Subterfuge comes from Latin subterfugere, 'to escape in secret' (fugere, to flee, as in fugitive): a trick that lets you slip away unseen.
Surmise goes back to Old French surmettre, built from sur (on top of) and mettre (place): to surmise is to lay a guess on top of the few facts you have.
Thrall is the root of enthrall. To be in thrall, like a thrall (an old word for a slave), is to be held captive, whether by a master or by a gripping story.
Trope comes from Greek tropos, 'a turn': a trope is a familiar turn that stories take again and again.
Untenable contains Latin tenere, 'to hold', as in tenant: an untenable position is one that cannot be held.
Untoward is un- plus toward. Something untoward heads away from what you hoped for or from what is proper.
Vestige comes from Latin vestigium, 'footprint': a vestige is the print left behind after something has passed.
Volition comes from Latin volo, 'I wish', the same root as voluntary: acting of your own volition means doing what you yourself want.
Wanton comes from Middle English wantowen, 'badly brought up' (wan-, lacking, plus towen, trained): wanton acts are what an unruly person does for no reason.
Welter rhymes with helter-skelter, and a welter is a helter-skelter heap of things. It comes from an old verb meaning 'to roll or toss about'.
Wry once meant 'twisted', from an Old English verb for 'to turn', and a wry smile twists up at one corner, half amused and half mocking.
Parlance comes from French parler, to speak: your parlance is the way your group speaks.
Parochial shares its Latin root, parochia, with parish: a parochial view stops at the edge of your own parish.
Prodigious is related to prodigy, a person with amazing gifts: both come from Latin prodigium, a marvel or omen.
Proffer is pro-, forward, plus offer: when you proffer something, you put an offer forward.
Proselytize comes from proselyte, Greek for one who has come over: a person who proselytizes wants you to come over to their side.
Provenance comes from French provenir, to come from: an object's provenance tells you where it came from.
Purview comes from Anglo-French purveu, provided, a word that opened old laws. It also ends in view: matters within your purview are in view of your authority.
Quagmire joins quag, an old word for a bog, with mire, deep mud: step into a quagmire and you sink.
Rapprochement comes from French rapprocher, to bring back together, built on approcher, to approach: old rivals approach each other again.
Recidivism comes from Latin recidivus, falling back: recidivism is falling back into crime.
Recrimination joins re-, back, with Latin criminari, to accuse: you throw the charge back at your accuser.
Redress is re- plus dress in its old sense of set straight: redress sets a wrong straight again.
Indelible is in- (not) plus the Latin root of delete: what is indelible cannot be deleted.
Indomitable comes from Latin in- (not) and domitare, to tame: an indomitable spirit is one that nobody can tame.
Inimitable is in- (not) plus imitable, able to be imitated: whatever is inimitable, no one can imitate.
Inordinate comes from Latin in- (not) and ordinatus, set in order: an inordinate amount has gone past its proper order or limit.
Insinuate comes from Latin insinuare, to wind one's way in, from sinus, a curve: an insinuation curves in sideways instead of coming straight at you.
Interminable is in- (not) plus Latin terminare, to end, the root of terminate: an interminable speech never seems to terminate.
Irrevocable is ir- (not) plus Latin revocare, to call back, the root of revoke: an irrevocable choice cannot be called back.
Jettison comes from Old French getaison, a throwing, from Latin iactare, to throw: to jettison a plan is to throw it overboard.
Lurid comes from Latin luridus, sallow or ghastly pale: a lurid story is full of ghastly details.
Machination comes from Latin machinari, to contrive or plot, from machina, a device, the root of machine: a machination is a device built for scheming.
Malaise is French, from mal, bad, and aise, ease: it is literally a bad ease, a feeling that things are not right.
Malfeasance comes from Old French mal, badly, and faisance, doing, from faire, to do: it is literally bad doing by someone trusted to do right.
Mete comes from Old English metan, to measure: to mete out punishment is to measure out what each person is owed.
Tutelage shares a Latin root with tutor, tueri (to watch over): under someone's tutelage, a tutor watches over your learning.
Unassailable is un- plus assail, to attack: an unassailable lead or argument is one that no attack can break.
Unconscionable comes from conscience: an unconscionable act is one that no conscience could allow.
Unmitigated is un- plus mitigate, to ease or soften: an unmitigated disaster has nothing that makes it easier to bear.
Unseemly is un- plus seemly, a formal word for fitting or proper: unseemly conduct does not suit the occasion.
Unwitting keeps wit in its old sense of knowing: an unwitting helper does not know what he is helping with.
Upshot first meant the final shot of an archery match; now it means how anything finally turns out.
Usurp comes from Latin usurpare, to seize for one's own use: a usurper takes a power and uses it as if it were theirs.
Variegated comes from Latin varius, meaning varied or spotted: a variegated leaf shows varied colors.
Vaunt goes back to Latin vanus, empty, the source of vain: to vaunt is to boast in a vain, empty way.
Visceral comes from viscera, the body's internal organs: a visceral reaction is one you feel in your gut.
Wrest is related to wrestle: to wrest something away is to twist and pull it free, as a wrestler would.
Mettle began as another spelling of metal, so a person of mettle is made of tough stuff, like good steel.
Milieu is French: mi, middle, plus lieu, place. Your milieu is the place you stand in the middle of.
Miscreant comes from Old French mescreant, unbelieving: mes-, wrongly, and creant, believing. A heretic slowly became any villain.
Misnomer joins mis-, wrongly, with Old French nomer, to name: a misnomer names a thing wrongly.
Say mores as MOR-ayz. It is the Latin plural of mos, custom, the root of moral: a group's mores are its moral customs.
Moribund comes from Latin mori, to die, the same root as mortal: something moribund is on its way to dying.
Myopic comes from Greek myein, to shut, and ops, eye: a myopic planner squints at what is near and misses what lies ahead.
Nihilism comes from Latin nihil, nothing, the root of annihilate: to a nihilist, nothing has any real value.
Oblique comes from Latin obliquus, slanting: an oblique remark comes at its point on a slant instead of head-on.
Onus is Latin for a load, and it is the root of onerous: the onus is the burden someone has to carry.
Ostensible comes from Latin ostendere, to show: the ostensible reason is the one put on show, not always the true one.
Panache first meant the plume of feathers on a knight's helmet; to do something with panache is to ride in with your plume held high.
Cede comes from Latin cedere, 'to yield or go away', the root of recede and concede: to cede land is to yield it to another.
Codify contains code: to codify a set of rules is to turn them into a written code.
Cognizant shares the Latin root cognoscere, 'to get to know', with recognize: when you are cognizant of a fact, you recognize it and keep it in mind.
Corollary comes from Latin corollarium, a tip once handed over to buy a garland, and so a bonus: a corollary is the extra result you get for free once the main point is settled.
Corporeal comes from Latin corpus, 'body', as in corpse: something corporeal has a body you can touch.
Depravity shares the Latin root pravus, 'crooked', with deprave: a person sunk in depravity has a crooked moral compass.
Detritus comes from Latin deterere, 'to wear away': detritus is what is left after things are worn down, rubbed off or thrown aside.
Disaffected is dis- ('not') plus affected in its old sense of 'fond of': disaffected people have lost their fondness for those in charge.
Edify comes from Latin aedificare, 'to build', as in edifice: to edify someone is to build up their mind or character.
Efface is e- ('out') plus face: to efface something is to wipe its face away until nothing shows.
Entreat contains treat: picture a child at the door begging for a treat, because to entreat is to plead hard for something.
Espouse shares its Latin root sponsus, 'promised in marriage', with spouse: when you espouse a cause, you take it as a partner and stand by it.
Eviscerate comes from Latin e- ('out') plus viscera, 'inner organs': to eviscerate a law or plan is to rip its guts out.
Exegesis comes from Greek exegeisthai, to lead out or explain: an exegesis leads the meaning out of a text.
Expound comes from Latin exponere, to put out or set forth: to expound an idea is to set it out piece by piece.
Extenuating comes from Latin tenuis, thin, as in tenuous: extenuating circumstances thin out the blame.
Extricate and intricate share Latin tricae, perplexities: you extricate yourself by working out (ex-) of a perplexing mess.
Feint comes from French feinte, a pretense, from the same root as feign: a feint is a feigned attack.
Forbearance contains bear, as in bear with me: to show forbearance is to bear with someone instead of lashing out.
Fraught is an old cousin of freight: a ship was once fraught with cargo, and a plan can now be fraught with risk.
Frenetic shares its Greek root, phren (mind), with frenzy: a frenetic day is one long frenzy.
Galling comes from gall, a sore rubbed raw by a saddle: a galling remark rubs your pride raw.
Glean first meant picking up the grain left behind by reapers; now you glean facts the same way, one stray bit at a time.
Impel holds the Latin pellere, to drive, also found in propel and compel: what impels you drives you on.
Impunity joins Latin in-, not, with poena, penalty: to act with impunity is to act with no penalty at all.
Retinue comes from Old French retenue, a body of people kept on, from retenir, to retain: a great person retains a retinue to travel at their side.
Riposte comes from Italian risposta, an answer, a cousin of respond: a riposte is a reply that strikes back fast.
Schism comes from Greek schisma, a split or cut: a schism cuts one group into two.
Semblance comes from Old French sembler, to seem, the root of resemble: a semblance only seems to be the thing itself.
Spate first meant a river in sudden flood, so a spate of events is a flood of them arriving all at once.
Squalid comes from Latin squalere, to be caked with dirt, which also gives squalor, the state of a squalid home.
Stalwart comes from Old English stael, place, and weorth, worth: a stalwart friend is worth their place at your side.
Sunder comes from Old English sundrian, built on sundor, apart, which also gives asunder: to sunder something is to tear it asunder.
Supplant comes from Latin supplantare, to trip up, built on planta, the sole: you trip a rival and step into their place.
Tantalize comes from Tantalus, a king in Greek myth made to stand in water under fruit trees: the water sank and the fruit rose whenever he tried to drink or eat.
Titular comes from Latin titulus, a title or label: a titular leader has the title and little else.
Travel began as the same word as travail: long journeys were once such hard, painful work that one word covered both.
Debase pairs de-, down, with base in its old sense of low (as in base metal): to debase something is to push it down to a lower, cheaper level.
Imbue comes from Latin imbuere, to wet or soak: an idea that imbues you has soaked in all the way.
Whet is the old word for sharpening a blade on a whetstone: when something whets your appetite, it sharpens your hunger.
Adjudicate comes from Latin ad-, to, and judicare, to judge: you adjudicate a dispute by sitting as its judge.
Animus is Latin for mind or spirit, the same root as animosity: animus is a spirit turned against someone.
Antithesis joins Greek anti, against, and thesis, a position: it is a position set directly against another.
Bandy first meant to knock a ball to and fro in a game: a name that gets bandied about is batted from person to person.
Beholden is an old past form of behold, which once meant to hold or keep: someone you are beholden to has a hold on you.
Broach comes from Old French broche, a pointed spike used to tap a barrel: broaching a touchy subject taps it open.
Bulwark comes from Middle Dutch bolwerc, a defense made of tree trunks (bole) and work: a log wall that holds off attack.
Burnish comes from Old French burnir, to polish, related to brun, brown: to burnish a reputation is to rub it until it glows like polished brass.
Canny comes from can in its old sense of know how: a canny person knows how to come out ahead.
Careen comes from Latin carina, a ship's keel: sailors careened a ship by tipping it on its side, and a careening car tips and lurches the same way.
Deleterious goes back to Greek deleter, a destroyer: something deleterious slowly destroys health or good working order.
Analogous comes from the Greek analogos, 'in due proportion', the source of analogy too: analogous things line up well enough that you can draw an analogy between them.
Antipathy mirrors sympathy: both end in Greek pathos, 'feeling', but sympathy starts with syn-, 'together', and antipathy with anti-, 'opposed'.
Banal comes from French ban, a lord's decree: a banal oven was one the whole village had to share, so anything banal is common to everyone and has gone stale.
A bolster is a long, firm pillow that keeps you sitting up in bed; to bolster something is to give it that same steadying support.
Boorish comes from Dutch boer, a farmer: city snobs once used boor for anyone they thought had rough country manners.
Callous shares its Latin root, callum (hard skin), with callus: a callous heart has grown a thick, numb layer that pity cannot get through.
Abate comes from Old French abatre, to knock down: something that abates has been knocked down from its full strength.
Aesthetic goes back to Greek aisthanesthai, to perceive with the senses; anesthetic, from the same root, means without feeling.
Ambiguous starts with Latin ambi-, on both sides: an ambiguous remark leans both ways at once.
Copious comes from Latin copia, 'plenty', which also gives cornucopia, the overflowing horn of plenty.
Debunk is de- plus bunk, short for bunkum, meaning nonsense: to debunk a claim is to strip the nonsense out of it.
Lethargic comes from Greek lethe, forgetfulness (the river of forgetting), plus argos, idle: a lethargic person seems to have forgotten how to get moving.
Mendacious comes from Latin mendax, lying, which is related to mendum, a flaw, the source of mend and amend: a mendacious story is full of flaws that need mending.
Implacable shares Latin placare, "to calm", with placate; the im- means not, so it cannot be calmed.
Nefarious comes from Latin nefas, a crime against divine law (ne-, not, plus fas, what is right): a nefarious act is the opposite of what is right.
Facetious goes back to Latin facetia, a joke or witty remark: a facetious person turns things into a joke, even when a joke is out of place.
Fickle goes back to Old English ficol, meaning deceitful: a fickle lover's vows do not hold.
Upbraid is built from up and the Old English verb that also gave us braid. It first meant to bring up a fault against someone.
Urbane comes from Latin urbanus, of the city, like urban. City manners were thought more polished than country ones, so the word came to mean smooth and refined.
Vapid comes from Latin vapidus, used of wine that had gone flat, and is probably related to vapor. Vapid talk has lost its spirit the same way.
Propensity comes from Latin propendere, to hang or lean forward: a propensity is a lean toward some kind of behavior.
Prosaic grows from prose, the kind of writing that does not rhyme or scan: something prosaic has no poetry in it.
Umbrage comes from Latin umbra, shade, the root of umbrella. Picture someone stalking off into the shade to sulk after a slight.
Voracious comes from Latin vorare, to swallow up, the root also found in devour and carnivore.
Quiescent comes from Latin quiescere, to rest, the same root as quiet: a quiescent seed is resting quietly until conditions change.
Rancorous is built on rancor, an old grudge left to fester: rancorous words come from anger that never healed.
Recalcitrant comes from Latin recalcitrare, to kick back with the heels (calx, heel): a recalcitrant person kicks back at every order.
Refute comes from Latin refutare, to drive back: you refute a claim by driving it back with proof.
Rescind comes from Latin rescindere, to cut off: rescinding an order cuts it off so it no longer counts.
Preclude shares its root with close and closet, Latin claudere, to shut: to preclude something is to shut the door on it in advance.
Predilection holds Latin diligere, to single out and love, the root of diligent: a predilection is what you single out ahead of everything else.
Demur comes from Latin demorari, to linger or delay: someone who demurs hangs back instead of agreeing straight away.
Callow goes back to Old English calu, 'bald'. Picture a hatchling with no feathers yet: a callow newcomer has not grown the cover that experience brings.
Censure comes from Latin censere, 'to judge or assess': a censure is a judgment passed against someone's conduct.
Florid comes from Latin floridus, 'flowery', and florid writing is just what English calls flowery: heavy with ornament.
Approbation and approve come from the same Latin verb, approbare: approbation is the approval something earns.
Assiduous comes from Latin assiduus, busy and unceasing: an assiduous worker never lets up until the job is done.
Modicum comes from Latin modus, "measure": picture a measuring spoon that holds only a pinch.
Mordant comes from Latin mordere, "to bite": think of humor with teeth in it.
Grandiloquent comes from Latin grandis, 'great', and loqui, 'to speak': grandiloquent speakers talk big, in grand, puffed-up words.
In old royal courts, the harbinger was the man who reached a town first and claimed rooms for the king's party. When you saw him, you knew the king himself was coming.
Hubris comes from a Greek word for insolent, outrageous behavior. Think of the proverb 'pride goes before a fall': hubris is that pride, and the fall comes after.
Idiosyncrasy comes from Greek idios, 'one's own', and krasis, 'a blend': your idiosyncrasies are your own personal blend of odd habits.
Importune comes from Latin importunus, 'unsuitable, troublesome', the opposite of opportunus (the source of opportune): someone who importunes keeps up a troublesome stream of requests.
Hidden inside indefatigable is fatigue: an indefatigable worker never seems to feel any.
Plaudit is a clipped form of Latin plaudite, "clap your hands!", the cue that closed a Roman comedy. It shares its root with applaud.
Judicious comes from Latin judicium, judgment: a judicious choice is one made with good judgment.
Languid goes back to Latin languere, to droop or lack strength: a languid person seems too drained to hurry.
Largesse comes through French from Latin largus, which meant generous as well as abundant: largesse is generosity with an open hand.
Discrepancy comes from Latin discrepare, to differ or disagree: when two accounts do not sound the same, there is a discrepancy.
Ebullient comes from the Latin ebullire, "to boil up": an ebullient person bubbles over with joy.
Equivocate joins the Latin aequus, equal, and vocare, to call (from vox, voice): words that speak with two equal voices, so no one can tell which meaning you intend.
Expunge comes from Latin pungere, to prick, as in puncture: to expunge a name is to prick it out of a list.
Mercurial comes from Mercury, the swift messenger god, like the metal named after him, which slides and splits apart unpredictably.
Harangue came through French from Old Italian aringa, linked to a word for a public assembly. It also starts like harass, which is what a harangue does to its listeners.
Neophyte comes from Greek neos, new, and phyton, plant: a neophyte is newly planted in a field.
Obsequious comes from Latin obsequi, to comply, built on sequi, to follow: an obsequious person follows the boss's every wish.
Perfidious holds fid, from Latin fides (faith), as in fidelity: a perfidious person breaks faith.
Amalgamate is related to amalgam, the blend of mercury and other metals long used to fill teeth: to amalgamate is to blend things into one.
Ascetic comes from the Greek askeo, "to exercise": an ascetic trains the body to do without comforts.
Surreptitious is usually traced to Latin surripere, to snatch from under: a surreptitious act is done under cover.
Refractory comes from Latin refringere, to break up, the same root as fracture: a refractory person breaks every rule you set.
Remonstrate comes from Latin re- plus monstrare, to show: you remonstrate by showing someone, point by point, why they are wrong.
Reprobate comes from Latin reprobare, to reject or condemn: a reprobate is someone who failed the test of decent behavior.
Tantamount ends in amount: if one thing is tantamount to another, it amounts to the same thing. It may come from Anglo-French tant amunter, 'to amount to as much'.
Invective comes from Latin invehi, 'to attack with words', literally 'to be carried into': invective charges at its target.
Lambaste begins with lam, probably the old verb meaning to beat hard: to lambaste someone is to beat them with words.
Mawkish comes from mawk, an old word for a maggot, so it once described food that turned the stomach. Today it means sentiment laid on so thick that it does the same.
Peripatetic comes from Greek peripatein, "to walk around" (peri, "around"). Aristotle's pupils perhaps got the name from the covered walk where he taught.
Ingratiate grows out of Latin gratia, favor or thanks (related to gratitude and grace): you ingratiate yourself to get into someone's good graces.
Philistine comes from the Philistines, the Bible's foes of Israel; German students used Philister for dull townsfolk, and Matthew Arnold popularized the insult in English.
Coterie goes back to cot, an old word for a hut, kin to cottage: picture a few friends in their own little cottage with the door shut to outsiders.
Gauche is French for left and also for awkward: picture a right-handed guest fumbling with the left hand at a formal dinner.
Expiate shares a root with pious: Latin piare, 'to purify or appease', from pius. To expiate a sin is to make yourself clean of it again.
Foist probably goes back to a Dutch word for fist: cheats at dice would hide a loaded die in the hand and foist it into play.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the definition in my own words (WordNet text matches Merriam-Webster), cut six examples with two fragments to four with clear clues, and replaced look-alike-free wrong answers with sedentary, salutary, desolate, derogatory and sultry. reviews.notes: Expanded the three-word definition, varied the examples beyond speeches by politicians, and replaced wrong answers with look-alikes (dialogue, dialect, tribulation, tribunal, diadem). Definition tracks Oxford's figurative sense, 'A tension or clash resulting from the combination of two disharmonious or unsuitable elements' ('tense clash' between things that 'do not fit together'). Reworded, so 4; e.g. 'Conflict between things that ought to match but do not, such as...'. Examples: three of four use the same 'dissonance between X and Y' frame; recast one (e.g. a meeting full of dissonance). Wrong answers: sustenance, ordinance and provenance share only -nance; assonance and distance are the strong ones.

Definition is close to the stock wording shared by Oxford ('Swell or cause to swell by pressure from inside') and Cambridge ('swell and become large, especially because of pressure from inside'); reworded, so 4. Plain: 'because too much has been put inside' is inexact, since swelling usually comes from gas or fluid building up, not from something being put in; try 'To bulge and stretch because something inside is pushing outward.' Wrong answer for distill opens like Oxford's distil ('Purify (a liquid) by heating it...'); short and common, so 4.

The wrong answer for dramatic uses its theater sense, which is less tempting than the 'showy' sense, but it is accurate.

reviews.notes: Made the "questionable, not to be trusted" sense first, since the examples and test use lean that way, and kept the uncertain and unconvinced senses as other senses. reviews.checker_notes: No score under 4. Sense 4: the other sense 'Uncertain in outcome; not at all sure to happen or succeed.' opens with Merriam-Webster's gloss for doubtful ('uncertain in outcome : undecided'), and Dictionary.com has 'of uncertain outcome' for dubious. Short shared phrasing, so 4; 'Not at all sure to happen or succeed.' on its own avoids it.

reviews.notes: Expanded the two-word WordNet definition, simplified the plain one, and gave the examples stronger and more varied clues. Added look-alike wrong answers, made the hook state the ebullire root plainly, and filled out synonyms and antonyms.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition and the hook. Rewrote the plain one, which was close to Oxford, replaced the fragment and the second medicine example, added look-alike wrong answers (efficiency is the classic confusion), and replaced rare related words.

'It measures' is also slightly off, since efficacy is the power itself.
