reviews.notes: The first sense was WordNet's fairness sense; made frankness the first sense and kept fairness as the other sense. Rewrote the plain line, the fairness example, the hook and the wrong answers (dropped condor as absurd, added rancor), and removed the fairness synonyms and the spelling variant candour.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: antonyms are only two; could add 'dishonesty'. No copying found.

reviews.notes: The WordNet definition narrowed the word to getting money; rewrote the definition and plain line to cover legal and political trickery. Gave every wrong answer a look-alike (chancery, chic and others) in fresh wording, replaced the made-up "chic trickery" hook with the French root, and swapped rare synonyms (chicane, wile) for common ones.
reviews.checker_notes: Definition runs 26 words; trim the 'especially in law, politics or business' tail. Wrong answers: chivalry blends Oxford ('courteous behaviour, especially that of a man towards women') and Cambridge ('especially by men towards women'); finery swaps each word of Cambridge's 'decorative and expensive clothing and jewelry worn on a special occasion'. Not verbatim, but reword both in a different structure.

reviews.notes: Dropped the other sense, a transitive copy of the first, and made the definition name clotting and curdling so it differs from freeze or set. Replaced the fragment and two doubtful examples (starch in gravy, resin), rewrote the wrong answers with look-alikes, replaced a hook that only used the word, and added synonyms and an antonym.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: two of four examples are about blood clotting; replace one with a different setting (gravy, paint, sap). No copying found.

reviews.notes: The first sense was WordNet's generic mixing gloss; rewrote it as joining into one whole and dropped the near-duplicate other sense. Rewrote the plain line and examples, replaced wrong answers that copied Oxford (acquiesce, evanesce, convalesce) and the collude option, and swapped rare mixing synonyms (flux, immix) for merge and unite.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the definition's opener 'Of separate parts,' is stilted; 'Join together to form one mass, group or idea.' reads better. Hook root alescere is true but not memorable.

reviews.notes: Expanded the two-word definition and made the plain line less absolute. Replaced the fragment and an example that pointed to clarity rather than persuasion, rewrote the wrong answers with look-alikes (cognizant, cognate), replaced a hook that only used the word with the Latin root, and replaced the odd antonym dissuasive. Second review round 1: reworded the contingent wrong answer (Merriam-Webster Learner's) and removed the circular tail of the definition.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: new definition and contingent option are clean (no dictionary match; contingent only loosely echoes Dictionary.com's 'dependent ... on something not yet certain'). Weakest point: cognate 'Related by having the same origin, as words in sister languages often are.' follows American Heritage's structure ('Related in origin, as certain words in genetically related languages...'); reword if convenient.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the definition, which was close to a dictionary's, and the plain line, and replaced the unpunctuated example and a second pay example with other settings. Gave every wrong answer a com- look-alike, added synonyms, and replaced the antonym incommensurate, which gives the word away.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the definition's 'amount, size or degree' echoes Merriam-Webster's 'size, extent, amount, or degree' (short shared phrasing, not a copy). Related lists are thin; add 'corresponding' or 'equivalent'. Hook is plain; drop the single quotes.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition; replaced the slangy plain line and the generic or fragment examples with ones that show going along with others' wishes. Removed wrong answers that meant the word itself (complaisance, compliant, pleasant), added look-alikes such as complacent and complicit, and gave the hook its French root. Second review round 1: reworded the competent wrong answer, which followed Longman.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: new competent option is clean (no match in Longman, Cambridge or Oxford). Weakest point: the definition is WordNet's 'obliging' text (licensed) and misses the yielding-too-readily sense the plain line catches; synonym 'agreeable' is ambiguous.

reviews.notes: Made the placating meaning the first sense and kept the concessions sense as the other sense. Rewrote the examples with clearer clues, removed a wrong answer that described the word itself ("overcome distrust"), gave the rest look-alikes, and replaced the ambiguous synonyms compromising and flexible.
reviews.checker_notes: Other sense 'Making or willing to make concessions.' overlaps heavily with the first sense; consider dropping it. Synonym 'placatory' is uncommon; 'pacifying' or 'peacemaking' would serve learners better.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the WordNet definition so it says the thing allowed is wrongdoing, and replaced the unpunctuated example and three similar "refuse to condone" sentences. Rewrote the wrong answers (two were close to Oxford) with con- look-alikes, replaced the condo hook with the true root shared with donate, and added synonyms and antonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Wrong answer condescend 'Treat others as though one were better or more important than they are.' follows Oxford Learner's ('as though you are more important and more intelligent than they are') and Cambridge closely; reword, e.g. 'Talk down to people in a superior way.' Synonyms forgive and pardon lean to forgiving after the fact rather than tolerating.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition and the plain line, and added the figurative war sense as an other sense. Sharpened two examples, rewrote the wrong answers with labeled look-alikes (one copied Oxford), fixed the hook, which claimed the word contains "flagrant", and added synonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Definition is WordNet's (licensed) but 'very intense' omits size; 'A large fire that spreads out of control and destroys much property.' would be sharper. Wrong answer congregation tracks Oxford's 'a group of people regularly attending a particular place of worship'; reword. Examples 1 and 3 are generic. Hook could link flagrare to flagrant.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the fragment-style WordNet definition and the slangy plain line, and made the examples give clearer clues. Removed a wrong answer that was the word's own meaning and a duplicate conjurer option, added look-alikes such as concierge and confidant, gave the hook its French root, and added synonyms and antonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Definition's 'can judge quality' overlaps Cambridge ('can judge quality and skill in that subject'), not a copy. Plain 'a fine thing' is awkward. Wrong answer conspirator follows Cambridge's 'plans secretly with other people to do something bad, illegal'; reword. Hook should name the French verb (connaitre, to know). Synonym 'expert' is generic; 'aficionado' fits better.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the definition, which echoed a commercial dictionary, and the examples so each has a clue. Replaced wrong answers copied from Oxford (contrived, contrary) and gave all of them look-alikes, including trite; made the hook name the Latin root it hinted at; dropped the archaic synonym ruthful.
reviews.checker_notes: Wrong answers: recondite 'Known or understood only by a few specialists' is close to American Heritage's 'known or understood by relatively few'; concrete echoes Oxford's 'real or solid; not abstract'. Neither is a full copy; reword recondite.

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin WordNet definition, rewrote generic examples, and replaced unlabeled wrong answers (one was decorum's own definition) with look-alikes such as corundum, tantrum and eardrum. The hook was nonsense; it now uses the sound-alike drum, since the origin of conundrum is unknown.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: wrong answers. eardrum and tantrum share only the -rum ending and name concrete things, so they will not tempt someone who half knows the word, and eardrum is a membrane, not 'a thin layer of skin'. Hook is a sound-alike (drum), which is fine since the origin of conundrum is unknown.

reviews.notes: The first sense was the botanical "rolled lengthwise"; moved it to other senses and made "hard to follow because of many twists" the first sense, with new examples, look-alike wrong answers and related words. Dropped "byzantine", which WordNet lists only capitalized.
reviews.checker_notes: convivial wrong answer 'fond of shared meals and good company' echoes Merriam-Webster's 'fond of feasting, drinking, and good company' (partial, so 4; reword, e.g. 'Friendly and lively, the way a good dinner party is.'). Definition's 'side steps' is an odd image; 'twists, layers or side issues' reads better.

reviews.notes: Dropped the misleading "especially of discourse" from the definition and plain text, and the other sense that repeated the first. Replaced the fragment example, labeled new wrong answers in my own words (the old ones were Oxford text), and swapped rich and plenteous for abundant and profuse.
reviews.checker_notes: capricious wrong answer 'Prone to sudden, unexplained changes of mind or mood' closely paraphrases Oxford's 'given to sudden and unaccountable changes of mood or behaviour' (several words changed, so 4; reword, e.g. 'Changing plans or moods on a whim, with no warning.'). Definition is thin; 'present in great quantity' is WordNet's gloss for abundant, which is licensed. Plain's 'with lots of it to go around' implies sharing, which does not fit 'copious notes'. Hook should name the shared root: copious and cornucopia both come from Latin copia, 'plenty'.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition. Dropped two other senses that repeated the first, fixed the "suspecting alibi" error, rewrote the generic examples, and replaced the wrong answers (two meant "work jointly") with labeled look-alikes. The hook now names the shared root robur.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: definition is WordNet's and 'as with new evidence' reads stiffly. Plain's 'fresh facts' misses that the support usually comes from a second, independent source ('with evidence from another source').

reviews.notes: Definition and plain were fine. Turned the fragment example into a sentence, rewrote the wrong answers in my own words (they were Oxford text) with look-alikes credible, creditable, sedulous, tremulous and querulous, and added synonyms; dropped "sophisticated", which fits the other sense. Second review round 1: dropped an other sense that repeated the first, and replaced two generic examples with concrete ones.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: near-copy other sense removed and the new examples (street-cart Roman coin, shared airline-ticket story) are concrete with clear clues. Weakest: example 2 ('Scam artists often target credulous investors') is still generic.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition. Fixed the example where a quick glance found hidden fees, replaced the fragment, and replaced the wrong answers with labeled look-alikes in my own words; dropped curt, which is close in meaning. Hook now gives the true root cursor, "runner".
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: illusory shares only the -sory ending, so it is the least convincing look-alike. Definition is WordNet's (licensed).

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin definition, dropped the other sense that repeated it, and rewrote the examples with stronger clues. Replaced the wrong answers (one meant "scarcity", the answer itself) with labeled look-alikes in my own words. The hook now uses the true origin, dear plus -th.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: definition is wordy ('where there is far too little of something'), and 'serious' overstates mild uses such as 'a dearth of good jokes'. Something like 'A shortage of something that is needed or wanted.' is tighter.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the thin definition as a humiliating total failure, sharpened the examples, and dropped "A sound defeat" from other senses. Replaced the wrong answers (one meant "highest point", near an opposite) with de- and -acle look-alikes, replaced the nonsense hook with the true French origin, and swapped the defeat-sense synonyms for fiasco, disaster and flop. Second review round 1: dropped the synonym rout, which belongs to the military-defeat sense.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: 'rout' removed, related now fits the first sense. Weakest: barnacle (a sea creature) and debit will not tempt anyone for an abstract word; pinnacle or obstacle would.

reviews.notes: The definition and plain text centered on ridicule; they now say "show to be false". Rewrote the examples with concrete clues, replaced the wrong answers (deride overlapped the ridicule idea, defame the reputation idea) with de- look-alikes, and added synonyms and antonyms. The hook was true and stays.
reviews.checker_notes: Wrong answers: bunk defines itself ('To sleep in a bunk...') and is close to Merriam-Webster's 'to sleep in or as if in a bunk'; reword, e.g. 'To sleep somewhere for a night or two, often on a narrow or makeshift bed.' debrief opens with Cambridge's 'to question someone in detail' (short shared phrase, 4). Hook is true (de- + bunk, short for bunkum, 'nonsense'), but many learners do not know bunk means nonsense; say so in the hook.

reviews.notes: The WordNet definition leaned on the harder word "propriety", and the plain text said "polite" twice; both rewritten. New examples give clearer clues. The wrong answers were invented meanings with no look-alikes; replaced with decor, decoy, decree, quorum and forum. The hook linked decorations falsely; it now gives the Latin decorus.
reviews.checker_notes: Wrong answers paraphrase dictionary wording: decree ('A formal command ... that has the force of law') follows Dictionary.com's 'a formal and authoritative order, especially one having the force of law', and forum ('A meeting, website or other setting where people trade views on a subject') follows Oxford's 'a meeting or medium where ideas and views on a particular issue can be exchanged'. Neither is word for word, so 4, but reword both. Hook restates the definition; linking to decorate (same Latin decor, 'beauty, fitness') would give a firmer peg.

reviews.notes: The definition and plain text missed the core idea of yielding to someone; rewritten, and the "tendency to yield" other sense folded into the first. Rewrote the examples, replaced invented wrong answers (one already used by another word) with -ference look-alikes, replaced the nonsense hook with the link to defer, and trimmed rare synonyms. Second review round 1: synonyms now mean yielding (dropped esteem and regard, which mean admiration).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: related improved. 'obedience' and 'submission' are stronger than the word (deference is a respectful choice to yield, not following orders); courtesy or consideration would fit better than obedience. Other sense 'Courteous regard for people's feelings.' still overlaps the first: example 1 ('In deference to her grandmother's wishes') fits both.

reviews.notes: Widened the definition beyond living things, since the word also covers machines and systems, and made the plain text describe a quality rather than "something". Replaced the fragment and generic examples, labeled new look-alike wrong answers, rewrote the hook as a spelling link to delete (no false root), and added synonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: hook is a sound-alike only. Deleterious (Greek deleterios, 'harmful') is not related to delete (Latin delere); the hook does not claim it is, but 'wipe out' overstates the meaning, which is 'harmful', not 'destroying'.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition and plain text. Rewrote the examples so each names a poem and a death (ruling out eulogy), replaced the made-up wrong answers with real look-alikes, swapped the ledge hook for the true Greek root, and added dirge and threnody.
reviews.checker_notes: All 4s are small. Examples 1 and 3 are the same scene (a poem for a dead relative read at the funeral or memorial); move one to a different setting, such as an elegy for a lost town or era. Wrong answer liturgy ('The fixed set of words and actions that a church uses in public worship.') follows the shape of Cambridge's 'a fixed set of ceremonies, words, etc. that are used during public worship in a religion'; not a whole copy, but reword it (for example 'The order of prayers, readings and rituals in a church service.'). Hook: elegos is just Greek for the same thing, so it links to nothing the learner already knows. Definition is WordNet's text (licensed).

reviews.notes: Rewrote the choppy WordNet definition and the plain text, which echoed Oxford, and added the 'eloquent silence' sense. New examples show moving or persuasive speech, real look-alike wrong answers replace invented ones, the elephant hook became the Latin root, and facile and silver were dropped from synonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the definition describes a person ('Skilled at putting thoughts into...'), but examples 1 and 2 apply the word to a toast and a letter. Something like 'Expressing ideas in fluent, well-chosen words that move or persuade.' covers both. Other sense, wrong answers and hook (e- + loqui, true) are good.

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin definition ('Add details to.') and reworded the plain text, which was close to Oxford. Merged two near-copy decorating senses into one, rewrote the examples, added real em- look-alikes, fixed the 'flare' hook with the true French root, and replaced aggrandize and lard with common synonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Sense 4: most dictionaries put the decorating sense first, and the hook (bel, beautiful) explains that sense better than the story sense. Leading with 'add invented details' is defensible for test prep, since the other sense keeps 'decorate'. Wrong answer abolish is a weak look-alike (it shares only -lish).

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition. Dropped the dated 'medical quackery' sense, fixed the plain text (the contrast is theory, not guessing), replaced generic and fragment examples, and replaced wrong answers that were really antonyms with real look-alikes. The empire hook was false, so it now uses the Greek root; empiric (a variant) left the synonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: only two synonyms (WordNet also has 'experiential' and 'data-based'). Definition is WordNet's text (licensed). Etymology (empeiria, experience) is true. Wrong answers are all real meanings of real look-alikes.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition and the plain text. Dropped an other sense that repeated the first, reworded the computing sense, and replaced the fragment and generic examples with ones that show admiring and copying. Added real em- look-alikes, a true Latin hook, and synonyms (there were none). Second review round 1: reworded the emanate wrong answer, which another word (amalgamate) already used word for word.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. New emanate option is a real meaning and no dictionary match turned up; 'from a single point' is a little narrow (emanate means from any source), which is a nit. Weakest point is still 'rival' among the synonyms, which fits 'reach equality with' more than 'strive to match by imitating'. Definition and emigrate option are WordNet text (licensed).

reviews.notes: Rewrote the definition to the main meaning (draining strength and vigor, not only 'mentally or morally') and simplified the plain text. Examples now give clear clues, one contrasting with energize. Wrong answers that were antonyms (activate, motivate) became real look-alikes; the hook now uses the true Latin root instead of implying a link to energy; synonyms came from the 'unnerve' sense and were replaced, and antonyms added. Second review round 1: dropped the other sense "disturb the composure of", which is the very misreading the word is tested on, and reworded the enunciate (Longman) and innervate wrong answers.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. Sense fixed: the misleading 'disturb the composure' sense is gone, and the definition covers WordNet's 'weaken mentally or morally'. Copying fixed: the enunciate and innervate options are now in original wording, and searches found no dictionary match. Both are accurate. Weakest point: example 1 is long (27 words).

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin definition ('Call forth.'); kept the plain text and the offspring sense. Rewrote the examples with concrete causes, added real look-alike wrong answers, replaced a hook that only restated the meaning with the true Latin link to generate, and removed father, mother and get, which belong to the offspring sense. Second review round 1: removed "and help it grow" from the definition and gave engorge its common meaning (swell with fluid).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The definition is accurate now; its object list echoes Oxford's '(a feeling, situation, or condition)', but the verb and examples differ, so it is not a copy. The engorge option now uses the common swelling sense and is accurate. WrongAnswers 4: endanger's 'Expose ... to possible harm or loss' is close to the stock 'to expose to danger, harm, or loss' (short shared phrasing, not a whole copy); 'Put a person, animal or place at risk of being hurt or lost.' would avoid it.

reviews.notes: Expanded the short definition and made the plain text simpler, since it nearly repeated the definition. Dropped the fragment example and freshened the rest, replaced invented wrong answers (one misspelled) with real look-alikes such as ethereal and peripheral, used the true Greek root for the hook, and swapped rare fugacious for fleeting.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: funereal is only a rhyme-alike. Definition, plain, examples, wrong answers and hook (epi + hemera, true) are all accurate.

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin definition to include the short poem, reworded the plain text, and fixed examples (one described an epigraph, another had a grammar slip). Wrong answers now use the classic confusions epigraph, epitaph and epithet; the hook explains the real gram root; added witticism, bon mot and aphorism.
reviews.checker_notes: Examples 4: Franklin's 'an ounce of prevention' is a proverb or maxim, not an epigram with a witty twist; replace it with a truly witty line or an everyday setting. Small nit in wrong answers: anagram reads as a process ('Letters of one word rearranged...'); 'A word formed by rearranging the letters of another, as listen from silent.' is cleaner. Hook (gram, something written; telegram) is true.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition. The plain text said 'confusing'; it now says vague and covers dodging a side. Replaced two weak examples, gave the wrong answers real look-alikes (equate, advocate, evoke), rewrote the hook so it names the word and uses the true Latin roots, and swapped rare tergiversate and palter for hedge, fudge and sidestep.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: example 1 (a politician dodging a journalist) is the stock scene; the other three are good. 'beat around the bush' is a phrase in the synonym game. Definition is WordNet's text (licensed). Hook (aequus + vox) is true.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the definition (WordNet's was thin and close to Oxford's) to stress learning from study, and simplified the plain text. Replaced the all-academic examples and the fragment with varied ones, replaced garbled invented wrong answers with real look-alikes, swapped the false 'eradicate' hook for the true Latin root, and filled out synonyms and antonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Definition 4: it describes a person ('Deeply learned, with knowledge built up through years of study'), but examples 2 and 4 apply the word to a review and a biography. Add 'or showing' (for example 'Having or showing deep knowledge gained from long study and wide reading.'). Hook (e- + rudis, as in rude and rudimentary) is true.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition. Reworded the plain text, which was close to Oxford's, dropped the fragment example and replaced one of two humor examples. Wrong answers now use real look-alikes, including the common confusion eclectic; the hook uses the true Greek root; added synonyms (there were none).
reviews.checker_notes: Definition 4: WordNet's 'enlightened inner circle' leans to the mystical sense, while the plain and most examples use the everyday sense (specialized, known to few). Consider 'Meant for or understood by only a small group with special knowledge.' Examples 4: example 1 (a physicist's theories baffle the public) is the generic scientist sentence the rubric warns about; 'complex' fits the blank as well. Related 4: the only antonym, exoteric, is rare; add a common one such as 'accessible' or drop it.

reviews.notes: The first sense was WordNet's 'win the good will of', with examples about placating people; it is now easing a painful feeling, the main use, and the old sense stays as an other sense. New examples, wrong answers from real look-alikes, a hook that names the Latin root suavis, and related words for the easing sense.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: wrong answers. 'assume' is a loose look-alike (shares only 'ass-'). The assay option, 'Test a metal or chemical to find out what it contains', echoes Merriam-Webster's simple definition ('to test something (such as a metal or drug) to find out what it contains'); only part of it and common phrasing, so 4, but rewording it (for example 'Analyze an ore or metal to measure how pure it is.') would be safer. Etymology (Latin suavis) checked and true.

reviews.notes: Definition moved from 'invulnerable to fear' to daring risk-taking, the test meaning; dropped the other sense that repeated it. Replaced the fragment and two weak examples, gave every wrong answer a real look-alike in fresh wording, rewrote the hook around Latin audere, and swapped rare related words (unfearing, hardy, ashamed) for common ones.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the cheeky, shocking side of the word ('an audacious lie') lives only in the terse WordNet other sense; 'brave' in synonyms is broader than the risk-taking sense. Hook etymology (audere, to dare) checked and true.

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin 'Severely simple.' and reworded the plain line; replaced two near-identical room examples. New look-alike wrong answers (dropped the Austria and 'authentic' options), a hook from the Greek root for a harsh taste, and related words limited to the plain-and-bare sense.
reviews.checker_notes: Sense 4: the 'stern, strict in manner' meaning is tested about as often as the 'plain, bare' meaning and survives only as a WordNet other sense; acceptable choice. Hook 4: true (Greek austeros, harsh, making the tongue dry) but it says 'a Greek word' without naming it, and 'dry in the same way' is a strained link; name austeros and tie dryness to 'nothing sweet added'. Wrong answers 4: only 4 options; fine otherwise.

reviews.notes: Replaced the vague 'Report or maintain.' with a definition that carries the firmness, and made the other sense the legal meaning instead of a near copy. New examples with clues to certainty, real look-alike wrong answers, hook fixed (verus means true, not truth), and dropped say, allege and verify from synonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Definition 4: a little wordy ('speaking as one who has no doubt about it'); 'State firmly that something is true.' would be tighter. Hook etymology (verus, true) checked and true.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition and the ban hook; plain line reworded without 'way too'. Two examples given stronger clues, wrong answers rebuilt from rhyming look-alikes (venal, penal, renal, baleful) with bland dropped as too close, and rare synonyms (old-hat, shopworn, threadbare, stock) swapped for common ones. Second review round 1: reworded the baleful wrong answer, which was Oxford's definition reordered.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the new baleful option is original; no dictionary match found. Wrong answers 4: 'willing to take bribes' (venal) and 'kidneys' (renal) are short common phrasing. Weakest point: the WordNet definition stresses overuse and misses 'dull and unoriginal' (the plain line covers it); three examples reuse the 'heard it many times' clue; the hook is a sound-alike when the true root (the feudal ban, things common to all) would teach more.

reviews.notes: Definition rewritten for the 'give a false impression' sense the examples use, with 'show to be false' kept as the other sense. Examples now use belies and belied instead of the awkward 'would often belie'; wrong answers had Oxford wording and no look-alikes, so all were rewritten, and beguile was left out as too close.
reviews.checker_notes: Definition 4: 'Cover up ... with an outward appearance' casts the subject as someone hiding things, but in every example the subject is the appearance itself (a smile, an exterior). Try 'Of an appearance, give a false idea of what lies underneath.' Related 4: 'conceal' is a little off; fine. Hook etymology (Old English, deceive by lying) true.

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin definition and plain line; the other sense now covers the 'good effect' meaning. Old wrong answers were synonyms (benevolent, beneficial) or antonyms (malevolent, maleficent), so all were replaced with -ficent and ben- look-alikes; dropped the fragment and generic examples and the rare eleemosynary.
reviews.checker_notes: Wrong answers 4: the efficient option says 'fast and cheaply', but efficient means getting results with little waste, not speed; try 'Getting the most done with the least wasted time, effort or money.' Only 4 options.

reviews.notes: Expanded the compressed WordNet definition and moved the plain line off Collins's 'sound impressive'. Replaced a clue-less example, rebuilt wrong answers from -astic look-alikes (bombard was a verb), hook now gives the true cotton-padding origin, and related words swapped large, tumid, orotund and unrhetorical for common ones.
reviews.checker_notes: Examples 4: the first ('The politician delivered a bombastic speech that lacked any concrete policy proposals.') is the generic politician sentence the rubric warns about; the other three are good. Hook etymology (bombast, cotton padding) checked and true.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition, plain line and boar hook. Dropped the fragment, replaced a weak example, rewrote the wrong answers with look-alikes (brutish and bullish dropped: one too close, one a pair with bearish), and replaced neanderthal, neandertal and swinish with common synonyms. Second review round 1: replaced WordNet's clumsy definition, tightened the plain line, and replaced an example that gave no clue.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the new definition is original; no dictionary match found, though 'rough' overlaps Oxford and Collins ('rough and bad-mannered'), which is short shared phrasing. Plain 4: 'loud' narrows the meaning, since boorish people need not be loud; 'Rude and crude, with bad manners.' would fit better. Examples 4: the wedding example fixes the clue problem; two of four are meal scenes. Hook 4: the boar sound-alike works; Dutch boer (farmer, peasant) is the true root.

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin definition, moved the plain line off Cambridge's 'grow or develop quickly', and added the budding sense as an other sense. New examples with numbers and growth clues, wrong answers rewritten from bur- look-alikes (the old ones copied Oxford), a hook from the French word for bud, and related words added where there were none.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the hook says 'an old French word for a bud' without naming it (borjon); etymology checked and true. Everything else is strong.

reviews.notes: Changed the part of speech to verb: the test meaning is strengthening an argument, not the architectural noun; the wall-propping meaning is kept as the other sense and in the hook. All content rewritten to match, with verb look-alikes as wrong answers and verb synonyms (buttressing dropped).
reviews.checker_notes: Sense 5: the verb (strengthen an argument or case) is the meaning GRE lists teach and test, so the change from noun to verb is right; the literal verb sense is kept as the other sense. Wrong answers 4: harass and embarrass share only an -ass ending and are weak look-alikes; 'batter' (strike again and again) or 'abut' (lie next to) would tempt more. Hook etymology (Old French bouter, to push or strike) checked and true.

reviews.notes: Definition now says the sounds clash, and the plain line moved off Oxford and Cambridge's 'mixture of sounds'; the other sense, a near copy, became the literary meaning. Replaced the 'delightful' aviary example, rewrote wrong answers (symphony was Oxford's wording, polyphony too close, tautology no look-alike), and refreshed related words.
reviews.checker_notes: Wrong answers 4: the homophone option ('One of two or more words ... that sound alike but differ in meaning') follows Merriam-Webster and Britannica ('one of two or more words that sound the same but have ... different meanings'); common phrasing, but reword. The symphony option maps slot for slot onto Oxford ('elaborate musical composition for full orchestra, typically in four movements'). Examples 4: the first three are generic noise scenes; 'rush hour traffic jam' needs a hyphen ('rush-hour'). Hook 4: true (kakos + phone) but 'making it a harsh noise' dangles; try 'so a cacophony is literally a bad sound'.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the definition, which repeated itself ('urge by gentle urging') and mentioned caressing. Wrong answers copied Oxford and lacked look-alikes, so all were rewritten; the hook now names the jolly sound-alike; dropped the rare palaver and blarney. Examples and plain line kept. Second review round 1: two examples now show the flattery, the plain line no longer echoes Merriam-Webster, and the hook uses a true rhyme (the old jolly sound-alike did not match).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the new plain line and examples are good; every example now shows charm or flattery; no dictionary match found. Hook 4: the goal rhyme is a true sound-alike, but 'goal' links to any kind of persuasion, not to flattery in particular. Weakest point only.

reviews.notes: Widened the definition from physical pain to pain, worry and problems, since that is how the word is used, and wrote new examples in varied settings. Gave every wrong answer a real look-alike (elevate, allocate, alienate and others), dropped facilitate from the synonyms and the overlapping other sense "Make easier.", and added antonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest points: the definition's 'so that a person can cope with it more easily' fits pain but not the traffic or hunger examples; 'Make pain, hardship or a problem easier to bear, even if it does not go away.' covers both. The abbreviate wrong answer follows Cambridge's shape ('to make a word or phrase shorter by using only the first letters of each word'); common phrasing, but a fresh wording would be safer.

reviews.notes: Replaced the thin WordNet definition with one that says what gets joined, and replaced the odd chemistry example with varied ones (districts, a novel, villages, fillings). Wrong answers now come from real look-alikes such as ameliorate and emulate; swapped the rare commix and the loose mix and mingle for closer synonyms, and added antonyms. Second review round 1: reworded the emanate, ameliorate and amputate wrong answers (close to Oxford and Cambridge), and amalgam fillings are "long used", not "once used".
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the new emanate, ameliorate and amputate options match no dictionary text I could find, and the amalgam dates are now accurate. Weakest point: amputate 'Remove a limb by surgery' is generic wording that many sources share.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the three-part WordNet definition and the plain one, which was close to a commercial dictionary, and replaced the fragment example. Wrong answers now come from real look-alikes, including ambivalent, the word most often confused with it; the ambitious text was Oxford wording and is rewritten. Dropped a near-copy other sense, and the antonym structured, which belonged to another sense. Second review round 1: dropped the antonym unambiguous (it gives the answer away) and reworded the amphibious and contiguous wrong answers.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the new amphibious and contiguous options are original, and 'unambiguous' is gone. Weakest point: only two synonyms.

reviews.notes: The WordNet definition was about indecision and missed the core idea of mixed feelings, so both definitions are rewritten. Examples now show the two pulls in each sentence, and the fragment is gone. Wrong answers come from look-alikes (benevolent, malevolent, prevalent, equivalent, valiant), replacing an unrelated one; added synonyms and an antonym.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: related words. 'uncertain' and 'undecided' describe indecision more than mixed feelings; 'conflicted' fits the first sense better if WordNet lists it.

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin definition "To make better." to say it applies to bad conditions. New examples say what was bad and how it improved. Wrong answers come from look-alikes, including amalgamate, which learners often mix up with it; the commemorate text was Oxford wording. Dropped the near-copy other sense "Get better." and the rare meliorate, and added antonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest points: all four examples are about public services or housing, and 'ameliorate the long waits' is an odd pairing (waits get shorter, not better); swap one for a personal or historical case. 'amend' in synonyms mostly means changing a text.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition and the plain one. Replaced two examples that gave no clue (a manuscript, a translation) with ones that name the out-of-place item. Wrong answers now come from look-alikes, replacing aneurysm and chauvinism and the Oxford-like anarchism and aphorism texts. Merged the two near-copy other senses into one and dropped mistiming, which fits sports better than history. Second review round 1: dropped the rare synonym misdating, which names the act, not the thing.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: dropping 'misdating' leaves no related words, which is acceptable. Weakest points (unchanged): the WordNet definition's 'located at a time' is stiff, and all four examples are mistakes in films, novels or scripts.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition. Cut the six examples to four that show the partial likeness, dropping two fragments and the bird-wing one, which belongs to the biology sense. Wrong answers come from look-alikes; the anomalous text was Oxford with one word changed. Removed homologous and heterologous, antonyms of the biology sense, and added common synonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the hook only links the word to its own word family ('analogy'). It could add the true Greek root analogos, 'in proportion' (ana- 'according to' + logos 'ratio').

reviews.notes: Rewrote the abstract WordNet definition to describe a thing that breaks a pattern, which is how the word is used. Examples are rewritten to give clearer clues. Wrong answers come from look-alikes, replacing anemia, enormity and anomie (too close in meaning). Dropped the near-copy sense "A person who is unusual.", rewrote the astronomy sense as a sentence, and replaced the synonyms anomalousness and unusual person.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the hook is accurate (Greek an- 'not' + homalos 'even') but gives the learner nothing familiar to hold on to. homalos is related to homos, 'same', as in homogeneous: an anomaly is not the same as the rest.

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin definition and made the plain one less overstated (it said hatred). Examples are rewritten so each shows the dislike in action. Wrong answers come from look-alikes, adding apathy, the classic confusion; sympathy and empathy were dropped because they are close to antonyms. Added synonyms and antonyms. Second review round 1: plain line no longer follows Collins COBUILD; definition no longer claims the dislike is instinctive.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the new plain line is original. Weakest points: the definition's 'deep-rooted ... dislike' echoes Webster's New World on Collins ('strong or deep-rooted dislike; aversion'), but it is short shared phrasing; the apathy wrong answer still opens with Merriam-Webster's 'lack of interest or concern'.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the definition and the overstated plain one ("a total lack of feeling about anything"). Examples now show people not caring and not acting. Wrong answers come from look-alikes; the apostasy text was Oxford word for word and is rewritten, and antipathy is added. Dropped a near-copy other sense and the rare spiritlessness, and added antonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest points: the apogee wrong answer 'The highest or most successful point of something' rearranges Oxford Learner's 'the highest point of something, where it is greatest or most successful', and pathos 'The power of a story, speech or scene to stir pity and sadness' follows Cambridge's 'the power of a person, situation, piece of writing, or work of art to cause feelings of sadness'. Reword both. The definition's 'feels no urge to care' is awkward.

reviews.notes: The definition now says how one appeases (by giving in), and the plain one no longer follows Collins wording. Added a fourth example. Kept the look-alike set (appraise, apprehend, apprise, append, appeal) but wrote each meaning fresh. Rewrote "Overcome or allay." as a clear sense about hunger, dropped the near-copy "Make peace with.", and replaced the rare lenify. Second review round 1: reworded the append wrong answer (Cambridge) and widened the definition beyond granting part of a demand.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: no 3s. Weakest points, all shared phrasing: the definition's 'by giving them some or all of what they want' and the plain line 'calm an angry person by giving in to what they want' echo Collins COBUILD ('stop them from being angry by giving them what they want'); append 'to the end of a document' follows Oxford's 'add (something) to the end of a written document'.

reviews.notes: The definitions limited the word to physical effort; it covers mental work too, so both are rewritten and the two near-copy other senses are dropped. Examples now mix physical and mental tasks, and the fragment is gone. Wrong answers come from ar- look-alikes, replacing intrepid. The hook now uses the real Latin root. Removed the duplicate spelling gruelling and the loose heavy.
reviews.checker_notes: No problems found. Weakest point: the definition is a little long; 'so that it tires out whoever does it' could be cut.

reviews.notes: The first sense was the rare "provide with a joint"; changed it to putting thoughts into clear words, the meaning tests use, and kept the pronunciation and joint meanings as other senses. Rewrote the examples, wrong answers (new look-alikes such as gesticulate and speculate), hook and synonyms to match; removed joint and pronounce from the synonyms. Second review round 1: reworded the pronunciation sense, which followed Oxford.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the new pronunciation sense is original. Weakest points: the adjective is the meaning tests use most, and the essay example gives the weakest cloze clue.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 3 (other sense nearly repeated the first), examples 3 (two gave little clue), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes, absurd options), hook 2 (did not name the word), related 3 (eulogium and pean are rare). Kept WordNet definition and plain. Rewrote other sense, two examples, all wrong answers, hook and synonyms. Left out elegy as a wrong answer: it is the classic confusion but a mournful poem for the dead may read as too close.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: example 2 has a newspaper run a eulogy, where obituary is the natural word, so the cloze could be answered with obituary. The definition is WordNet's text, which is licensed. Synonyms encomium and panegyric fit praise in general more than funeral praise.

reviews.notes: Before: plain 3 (nearly the same as the definition), examples 3 (last one repeated diplomatic), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes, absurd options), hook 2 (did not name the word). Kept WordNet definition, synonyms and the antonym dysphemism. Rewrote plain, two examples, all wrong answers and the hook.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: embolism is a look-alike only through the -ism ending and would tempt few learners. The definition is WordNet's text (licensed), a little long. The only related word, dysphemism, is rare.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (WordNet's gloss is word for word the same as Merriam-Webster's), examples 3 (one fragment, one generic), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes, made-up region), hook 3 (the word does not contain vanish), related 3 (no synonyms). Rewrote definition, replaced two examples, all wrong answers, hook, synonyms and antonyms. Kept plain. Main session after second review: Reviewer scored definition 3 (followed Oxford clause by clause). Rewrote the definition and replaced example 4, which gave a weak clue.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the hook explains the root but gives no picture to remember; it could say directly that evanescent holds van, as in vanish. The new definition matched no dictionary in a search. The new example 4 (the firefly) gives a clear clue.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (Make worse. is too thin), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alike words, odd details like fishing trips), hook 2 (excess acrobatics is a stretch), related 3 (exasperate belongs to the other sense, no antonyms). Rewrote definition, other sense, all wrong answers, hook, synonyms and antonyms. Kept plain and examples. reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: example 3 uses the filler phrase 'served to'. With the exasperate sense gone, the entry is clean.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (WordNet's acquit gloss, the same text as exonerate's), examples 3 (exculpate of is unidiomatic), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes), hook 3 (clumsy), related 3 (assoil archaic, no antonyms). Rewrote definition, plain, one example, all wrong answers, hook and related words. Left out inculpate as an antonym because it is built on the same root and would give the answer away.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: extrapolate shares only ex- and -ate and is a weak look-alike. Examples 2 and 4 are generic ('worked tirelessly to', 'helped to'). Antonym convict is a court outcome, not the opposite of clearing blame; inculpate would be the exact opposite.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (Demanding attention. is thin), examples 3 (one fragment), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes), hook 1 (urgent exit is a false link), related 2 (beseeching is wrong, clamant rare, exacting from the other sense). Rewrote definition, plain, other sense, one example, all wrong answers, hook, synonyms and antonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: example 4 ('exigent family matters') gives little clue; personal or private would fit. Synonym insistent belongs to the other sense (demanding of others). Diligent is a weak look-alike (shares only -igent).

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (WordNet's acquit gloss, the same as exculpate's), examples 4, wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes), hook 3 (muddled), related 3 (assoil archaic, discharge off-sense, no antonyms). Rewrote definition, first example, all wrong answers, hook and related words. Kept plain. Main session after second review: Reviewer noted the hook said the word holds onus, but its letters are oner. Hook now gives the Latin stem oneris.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the definition requires an official finding (Oxford Learner's supports this), but example 4 has forensics, not an official body, doing the clearing, so the entry is slightly inconsistent. The new hook (ex plus onus, oneris) is accurate.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (thin, misses the not-principled shade), examples 3 (one fragment, the traffic route sentence uses the neutral sense), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes, made-up expando), hook 2 (confuses expedient with expeditious), related 2 (inexpedient is built on the word, no synonyms). Rewrote definition, two examples, all wrong answers, hook and related words. Kept plain and the WordNet other sense. Expeditious is a deliberate trap option: it means fast, not self-serving. Main session after second review: Reviewer scored definition 3 (speed belongs to expeditious, which is a wrong answer). Removed speed from the definition and replaced example 3, which read as merely prudent.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the definition shares its idea with American Heritage ('self-interest rather than principle') but not its wording, so it is fine. The new example 3 (painting over water stains) shows the meaning well. Obedient and explicit are weak look-alikes.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (WordNet gloss is clumsy), examples 2 (one had the ungrammatical and expunge from), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes; expiate also clashes with a sister entry), hook 3 (sponge is only a sound-alike), related 3 (strike and scratch are vague). Rewrote definition, one example, all wrong answers, hook and synonyms. Kept plain.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: example 1 (expunge errors from a manuscript) fits correct or remove just as well. Plunge is a rhyme rather than a real look-alike and is usually intransitive. No antonyms, which is fine.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (a bare list of verbs), examples 3 (one fragment), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes), hook 1 (X-ray image, does not name the word), related 3 (proclaim off-sense, no antonyms). Rewrote definition, one example, all wrong answers, hook and related words. Kept plain.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: all five examples share one pattern (subject + often/tend to + extol the virtues/benefits of X), and two use the stock phrase 'extol the virtues'. Vary the situations and sentence shapes. Exult is intransitive, so grammar weakly rules it out.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 3 (other sense from outside source was clunky), examples 3 (one fragment), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes), related 2 (orthogonal is jargon, impertinent misleads, purifying is junk). Kept WordNet definition, plain and hook. Rewrote other senses, one example, all wrong answers and related words.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: example 3 (clues that led away from the suspect) does not clearly show irrelevance. The plain line's 'completely unrelated' overstates; extraneous material is often loosely related but beside the point. The definition is WordNet's text (licensed).

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (WordNet's cleverly amusing misses the out-of-place shade tests use), plain 4, examples 3 (one fragment, one generic), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes), hook 3 (the vowel trick did not connect to the meaning), related 3. Rewrote definition, plain, one example, all wrong answers, hook and related words.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: example 2 (terrible cooking) and example 4 ('his facetious nature') give weak clues; sarcastic or witty fit. Facile's 'Glib' is close to facetious's flippant tone, though the meanings differ. The vowel note in the hook is a nice extra but not a meaning link; the Latin facetia part carries it.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 3 (second other sense repeated the first), definition 2 (circular, based on a fallacy), examples 3 (one fragment, one weak), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes), hook 3 (fall is only a sound-alike), related 3 (deceitful and fraudulent belong to the deception sense). Rewrote definition, other senses, two examples, all wrong answers, hook and related words. Kept plain. Left out fallible: too close a meaning to use as a wrong answer.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: gracious and audacious share only the -acious ending and tempt little. The definition's 'and so likely to mislead' blends in the other sense (intended to deceive), which is listed separately.

reviews.notes: Before: examples 2 (one fragment, one bureaucrat sentence with no clue), wrong answers 1 (no look-alikes, generic), hook 3 (office link true but unexplained), related 3 (busy, busybodied). Kept the WordNet definition and plain. Replaced the fragment and the weak example, wrote 5 look-alike wrong answers (official, efficacious, obsequious, facetious, auspicious), rewrote the hook on Latin officium, trimmed rare synonyms and replaced the antonym unintrusive with unobtrusive and discreet. Main session after second review: Reviewer scored wrongAnswers 3 (auspicious followed Oxford Learner's; obsequious echoed the plain text). Rewrote both.
reviews.checker_notes: Rescore after fixes. The new auspicious and obsequious meanings read as original (no dictionary match found). Weakest: the WordNet definition still leaves out the self-important, petty-authority side that examples 1 and 3 show; meddlesome and meddling are near duplicates.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (WordNet "Not easily borne; wearing." is thin and "wearing" is ambiguous), plain 3, examples 3 (one unpunctuated), wrong answers 1, hook 3 ("on us" sound-alike), related 4. Rewrote definition and plain in my own words, fixed the fragment and added a loan-terms example, wrote look-alike wrong answers (odorous, erroneous, numerous, oneiric, generous), hook now uses the true root Latin onus, added heavy, demanding, oppressive and undemanding.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: examples 1 and 2 fit heavy, harsh or difficult with no clue specific to burden; oneiric is rare and generous is a weak look-alike.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 3 (literal light-blocking sense first, while the synonyms and antonyms were for the figurative one; the figurative "hard to understand" sense is the one GRE texts use), examples 2 (two fragments, all literal), wrong answers 1 (no look-alikes; one was close to the literal meaning), hook 2 (only uses the word). Moved "hard to understand or see into" to the first sense and kept the literal meaning, reworded, as the other sense. Rewrote definition, plain, all examples, wrong answers (opulent, opportune, optimal, optical, operatic) and the hook (Latin opacus, "shaded"). Extended related words for the figurative sense. A reviewer may prefer the literal sense first; I chose the figurative one on purpose.
reviews.checker_notes: Figurative first sense is right for this audience: GRE texts use opaque for language, reasoning and institutions, adults already know the literal meaning, and it is kept as the other sense, which the hook connects. Weakest: "or see into" in the definition pulls the literal sense back in; synonym unintelligible is too strong (opaque is hard, not impossible, to understand); optical shares the light theme of the literal sense.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (WordNet "disgrace resulting from public abuse" misses the common use, harsh public criticism), examples 3 (one with no clue), wrong answers 1, hook 2 ("proper brium" means nothing), related 3. Rewrote the definition, replaced the weak example with a stadium scene, wrote look-alike wrong answers (oppression, delirium, equilibrium, emporium, moratorium; reworded three after a search found near-copies), hook on Latin probrum, added condemnation, censure, scorn and antonyms approbation, acclaim, praise. Kept the plain and the WordNet other sense. Main session after second review: Reviewer scored wrongAnswers 3 (emporium was Oxford with synonyms swapped). Rewrote it, replaced infamy (other sense) with vilification, and replaced a political example.
reviews.checker_notes: Rescore after fixes. The new emporium meaning matches no dictionary wording, and vilification fits public scorn. Weakest: "grand old shop where you could buy" makes emporium sound old and past tense, though the word is used for current shops too; 3 of 4 examples are still public figures caught in wrongdoing.

reviews.notes: Before: other sense 3 (formatted as "(of a display) ..."), examples 3 (one fragment, one weak), wrong answers 1, hook 2 ("on stage" is not a real sound-alike), related 2 (antonym unostentatious gives the answer away). Kept the WordNet definition and plain. Rewrote the other sense, two examples, wrong answers (ostensible, contentious, tendentious, osseous, conscientious), hook on Latin ostentare, and related words. Main session after second review: Reviewer scored sense 2 (the other sense repeated the first and matched stock gaudy/flashy wording). Dropped it.
reviews.checker_notes: Rescore after fixes: the near-duplicate other sense is gone. Weakest: the WordNet definition ("Intended to attract notice and impress others") leaves out the showy display that the plain text and examples carry.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (WordNet text is ungrammatical, "Lessen or to try to lessen"), examples 3 (palliate tensions belongs to the easing sense), wrong answers 1, hook 2 ("pale mate"), related 3 (relieve, alleviate, assuage belong to the other sense, physical relief). Rewrote the definition for the "make seem less serious" sense, replaced one example, wrote wrong answers (palpate, pollinate, collate, pall, populate), hook on Latin pallium "cloak", related words now extenuate, mitigate, excuse, gloss over, whitewash, downplay with antonyms aggravate, exaggerate. Main session after second review: Reviewer scored sense 3 (missed "without removing the cause"). Rewrote the definition and other sense, and reworded the pall meaning, which echoed Oxford Learner's.
reviews.checker_notes: Rescore after fixes. The new definition covers both the excuse and the medical use, and the other sense is a distinct medical meaning. Weakest: plain still lacks the "without dealing with the cause" part, so the new-word card shows only half the meaning; all examples are the excuse use; the other sense ends with "without curing it" as Oxford Learner's does (a common phrase, not a whole copied definition).

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (alchemy only, misses the figurative use), plain 4, examples 4, wrong answers 1, hook 1 ("allacea", "foracea" are not words), related 3 (catholicon is rare). Rewrote definition and plain, replaced one example with an exercise one, wrote wrong answers (pancreas, panorama, pandemic, placebo, pantheon), hook on Greek pan + akos, synonyms now cure-all, nostrum, elixir, magic bullet.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: placebo barely shares spelling with panacea and sits in the same medical domain, so it is a weak look-alike; examples 2 and 3 fit solution or cure with no extra clue.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 3 (other sense repeated the first), plain 3 ("how something should be done" is off), examples 3 (first was ungrammatical, little clue), wrong answers 1, hook 1 ("para gold" is a false root), related 3 (idol and saint are ambiguous). Dropped the duplicate other sense and kept the WordNet definition. Rewrote plain, examples, wrong answers (paradox, polygon, paramour, paragraph, paraffin), hook on Italian paragone (touchstone) and synonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: the WordNet definition is abstract ("a perfect embodiment of a concept"); polygon and paraffin are unlikely to tempt anyone.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 3 (other sense "Extreme stinginess." repeats the first), examples 4, wrong answers 1, hook 3 ("penny money"), related 2 (parsimoniousness gives the answer away; minginess rare). Replaced the other sense with the scientific "simplest explanation" sense, fixed "twenty five", wrote wrong answers (acrimony, matrimony, patrimony, parody, parsonage), hook on Latin parcere "to spare", new synonyms and antonyms.

reviews.notes: Before: wrong answers 1, hook 1 (nonsense text), related 3 (only dearth). Kept WordNet definition, plain and examples. Wrote wrong answers (pauper, audacity, veracity, capacity, paunch; reworded veracity and paunch after a search found near-copies), hook on Latin paucus "few", added synonyms and antonyms abundance, plenty, profusion.

reviews.notes: Before: examples 3 (missing apostrophe), wrong answers 1, hook 3 (implies ped means foot), related 3 (academic is ambiguous; unscholarly is a poor antonym). reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 ("A strong liking." is too thin), examples 3 (one unpunctuated stereotype), wrong answers 1, hook 2 ("plant" is not a sound-alike). Rewrote definition and plain, dropped the stereotype example, wrote wrong answers (pendant, pennant, penance, pension, chant; reworded pendant and penance after a search found Oxford wording), hook on French pencher "to lean", added synonyms and antonyms aversion, dislike. reviews.notes: Before: sense 4, definition 3 (opened with the circular 'Not tractable'), plain 4, examples 2 (two fragments, six examples), wrongAnswers 2 (no lookalikes), hook 3 ('tract' is not an English verb for pull; the real root is Latin tractare, to handle), related 3 (no synonyms; the antonym 'tractable' is the word minus its prefix and gives the answer away). reviews.notes: Before: sense 4, definition 3 (WordNet's list 'Impervious to pleas, persuasion, requests, reason.' is not a sentence and uses a hard word), plain 4, examples 3 (one fragment; generic union and board examples), wrongAnswers 2 (no lookalikes; several were near antonyms), hook 2 (does not name the word; 'in transit gent' is a made-up split), related 3 ('adamantine' is rare, 'inexorable' leans to another sense). Main session, round 4 (one wrong answer left, per the skill): residual followed Cambridge, so it is swapped for deciduous (shares -iduous, a classic mix-up); checked against downloaded pages first. FLAGGED after round 4: the fourth wrong-answer slot failed three times (insidious and residual copied a dictionary; deciduous is clean but describes trees, so it is the wrong kind of option and tempts nobody). Everything else scores 4 or more. Next run: replace deciduous with a look-alike that describes a person (the reviewer named perfidious or invidious), written from scratch and checked against downloaded pages.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 4. wrongAnswers 3: the deciduous option is original (Longman: 'deciduous trees lose their leaves in winter'; Oxford: 'that loses its leaves every year') and accurate enough. But it is the wrong kind of option. assiduous describes people and their effort, and the other three options (sedentary, audacious, assertive) describe people too. An option that opens 'Of trees and shrubs' is ruled out at a glance, which leaves only three real choices (trap: 'Wrong answers of the wrong kind'; I failed acupuncture under acumen for the same reason). The rhyme is strong, but the meaning cannot tempt anyone who half knows the word. Better: a person-describing look-alike, such as perfidious or invidious (they share -idious), or insidious again, written from a new angle. A word near 'care', such as fastidious, would be too close.

reviews.notes: New word: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook written from scratch. Before: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook were empty (score 1). Kept WordNet's group sense first and rewrote the definition and the plot sense in my own words. Examples are neutral (office managers, nobles, a board, company founders). Hook uses the true story of Charles II's CABAL ministry (around 1670), which popularized the word; it does not claim the acronym as the origin, and avoids the Hebrew etymology so the hook cannot be read as echoing conspiracy tropes. Look-alikes are all groups of people (cabinet, cadre, caucus, claque, cohort). Junto and camarilla are rare; kept junto, dropped camarilla. Note: cabal and coterie (also in this sheet) are near synonyms, so neither should ever be used as the other's wrong answer. Round 2: swapped the cadre option (followed AHD's frame) for cavalcade, written as a ceremonial ride; rewrote example 4 so caucus no longer fits; replaced the CABAL-ministry hook (it taught the acronym myth) with a spelling hook (starts with cab) that names no group. Main session, round 3: the round 2 hook linked cab by spelling only, but the first syllable is never said as cab, so it is replaced with the true route through French cabale (secret, hidden lore). Checked against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD, WordUp and YourDictionary pages: no shared run of 4 words.
reviews.checker_notes: hook 4: the etymology is true. Oxford Learner's, American Heritage, Longman, Dictionary.com and Wiktionary all trace cabal through French cabale and Medieval Latin cabala to the Hebrew word for the Kabbalah, a body of mystical teaching. 'A word for hidden knowledge' is a fair simplification: the Hebrew word literally means received tradition, and the secret sense came from the mystical teaching. Longman glosses the Latin form as 'secret knowledge', so the hook's two-word gloss is close to it, but that is a short, common gloss and not a copied definition. The rest of the hook copies nothing I could find in the nine dictionaries I checked, Wiktionary or Vocabulary.com's note. The hook is neutral: it does not repeat the acronym myth or play into conspiracy tropes, and the link from hidden knowledge to hidden plans is clear. Weakest point: it does not name the Kabbalah, so it is a little vague about what the French word referred to. wrongAnswers 4: cavalcade's option describes an event (a ceremonial ride) while the others describe groups of people, and the claque option shares the common phrase 'people hired to applaud' with WordUp, Wordsmyth and American Heritage. related 4: junto is rare, and conspiracy fits the plot sense more than the group.

reviews.checker_notes: wrongAnswers 4: dropping chivalrous fixes the clash with cavalier's own 'gallant gentleman' meaning. capricious is a good tempter for a learner who links cavalier with 'free and easy', and it does not overlap the meaning; its option is not copied. Weakest: cavernous and cadaverous describe spaces and looks, not attitudes, so a learner who knows cavalier describes how someone treats things can rule them out. Only 4 wrong answers. All 4 options match the definition's style and length. hook 4: unchanged; the picture of a rider looking down on people below matches Vocabulary.com's blurb for cavalier, although the wording differs. plain 4: unchanged; it drops the superior, disdainful part of the meaning.

reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The hook's etymology is true (Old French surmettre, from sur 'upon' + mettre 'put'). But the Old French verb meant 'to accuse' (put a charge upon someone), so the picture of laying a guess on top of the facts is a mnemonic, not the history. That is acceptable but worth knowing. Weakest wrong answer: the new sermonize option keeps the frame that Oxford and Longman share (moral advice given to people who do not want it), in new words. That is common phrasing, since it is what the word means, so it scores 4. Synonyms are better now that 'deduce' is gone. The definition's 'a likely idea of the facts' is still slightly stiff.

As a look-alike, untidy is fair, not strong. It shares 'unt-' and an un- sense of 'not as it should be', which can tempt a half-knower who links untoward with things being amiss. But it describes rooms and desks, while untoward describes events and behavior, so the kind of thing gives it away. The other four options also share only the un- prefix with untoward. Plain and examples are now clear (the added details in examples 1 and 4 give the cloze a real clue). The hook is true but its link to the meaning is still loose.

Main session, round 4 (one wrong answer left, per the skill): welterweight sat next to welter's informal boxing sense and its closing clause followed Longman, so it is swapped for weather (sounds close to welter, the state of things outdoors). shelter reworded so it no longer mirrors subterfuge's refuge option. reviews.checker_notes: Round 4. The weather option is acceptable. It sounds close to welter (/ˈwɛðɚ/ against /ˈwɛltɚ/), so a learner who half knows the word could mix them up by ear. It is also of a fitting kind: a state or condition, a mass noun like welter, unlike the dropped weld and welcome. Its wording follows the stock frame for weather: AHD has 'the state of the atmosphere at a given time and place, with respect to ... temperature, moisture, wind', Dictionary.com and Wordsmyth say much the same, and WordUp has 'what the air outside is like at a given place and time'. This text shares 'the state of the', 'a given' and the air-outdoors idea, but its list and its time phrase are its own, so it is common phrasing and scores 4 with this note. Random House also gives welter a sense of waves or wind tossing about. That is not close to weather in general, but it is worth knowing. shelter no longer mirrors subterfuge's refuge option. It shares 'covered place' and 'danger' with WordUp, Wordsmyth and AHD's usage note; that is common phrasing, so 4 with this note. welt is original. welfare's 'doing well' frame is shared with Webster's New World and Century, as noted in round 3; Merriam-Webster still could not be reached. No option fits 'a ___ of' in any example. Options are 11 to 16 words against a 12-word definition, so the weather option is the longest but not out of style. Wrong answers: sonorous had the "like a large bell" example (the listed problem) and Cambridge's "deep, pleasant sound"; sudorific followed AHD ("causing or increasing sweat"); superficial followed Dictionary.com/AHD; prolific combined Oxford's and AHD's "works ... results ... offspring"; all rewritten.
