Round 2: replaced the allergy-pill example (retold WordUp's don't-drive scene) with a bedtime routine; replaced prolific and superficial (shared only an ending) with honorific (rhymes, -orific) and sophistic (shares soph-), both checked in WordNet and the seven dictionaries first.
reviews.checker_notes: All 4 or more. The allergy-pill example is gone. The new bath-and-tax-law example is not a dictionary scene (WordUp's nearest is chamomile tea putting someone to sleep). honorific: it shares more than an ending, so it passes, though only just. It matches soporific's syllable count, stress and vowel pattern (ho-no-RIF-ic, so-po-RIF-ic), and it is built the same way (a Latin noun plus -fic, 'making'), which the hook itself teaches. A rhyme of this kind is weaker than a shared root, so it scores 4, not 5. sophistic: 'Built on clever-sounding reasoning meant to mislead.' is close to Cambridge's 'clever but untrue arguments... in order to deceive people'. Oxford and Longman define sophistry with the same 'clever... false... in order to deceive' frame, so it is shared and scores 4 with a note. plain 'makes you want to nap' is shared phrasing (Oxford, Cambridge), so it scores 4.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3, plain 3, examples 2, wrongAnswers 3. Definition and plain kept WordUp's frame ("seeming true, real, or well-supported at first, but actually false"); both rewritten. Examples: the ice cream link retold WordUp's "spurious link between ice cream and crime", the charity's spurious claims echoed Cambridge's "spurious claims", and the statistics example gave no clue; replaced with a forged certificate, an ad claim and a fortune teller. Wrong answers: sporadic combined AHD's "irregular intervals or ... scattered places; no pattern", usurious followed Dictionary.com ("illegal or exorbitant rates"), curious followed Dictionary.com's "eager to learn or know", spacious was close to WordUp; rewritten. curious shares mostly the ending with spurious, but it is the sound-alike learners mix up; kept with a note. Other sense "Born out of wedlock." is a common phrase; kept. Round 2: reworked the certificate and fortune-teller examples ("looked official, but", "exposed as") so curious in its strange sense no longer fits; replaced curious (shared mostly the ending) with spartan, which shares sp- and the stressed r syllable.
reviews.checker_notes: All 4 or more. The certificate and fortune-teller examples now give a clear clue ('looked official, but', 'exposed as'), and the wrong answers no longer include curious, so no wrong answer fits a blank. spartan, 'Stripped of every luxury, by choice or by hardship.', does not follow Oxford, Cambridge or WordUp's 'simple ... no comfort' frame. It shares only sp- and r with spurious, so it tempts only moderately. The definition's 'false though it seems real' frame and spacious's 'large ... room to move' wording are shared by three or more dictionaries, so each scores 4 with a note.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (kept Oxford's 'greater than is needed or can be used' frame), wrong answers 3 (pleurisy was WordUp's 'painful inflammation of the lining around the lungs' with one word changed; plight joined AHD's 'bad or unfortunate situation' to WordUp's 'not easy to get out of'), examples 3 (the jury sentence gave no sense of excess). Rewrote the definition, all four wrong answers from new angles, and replaced the jury example with one that shows too many settings. Plain is short shared phrasing (4). Hook root checked: Greek plethein, to be full; plenty is from Latin plenus, same Indo-European root. Round 2: the reviewer found the banquet and course-choice examples showed variety, not excess, and plectrum (an object) and plight (shares only pl) weak. Replaced both examples with scenes of too many soaps and too many cereals. Swapped plectrum for plenum (shares ple- and the Latin root for full, a kind of meeting) and plight for plateau (a level that stops changing, so a learner thinking about amounts could pick it); both written after reading their dictionary entries. Checked every example against plebiscite, pleurisy, plenum and plateau: none fits a blank.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The new examples fixed the clue problem: the hotel soaps ('far more than two guests could use in a week') and the cereal aisle both show excess, and neither retells an Oxford, Cambridge or WordUp scene. Wrong answers: plateau 'A point where a rising number stops climbing and holds steady for a while.' follows the meaning Oxford, Cambridge, Longman and Dictionary.com share, and it is a level of an amount, so it tempts. plenum 'A session of a council or party that every member is expected to attend.' follows the 'meeting with all members present' meaning that Oxford, Cambridge, American Heritage and WordUp share, so 4. Weakest: plebiscite and pleurisy are still not amounts. plenum's rare sense 'the condition of being full' (American Heritage) is near plethora, but the option uses the meeting sense, so it is safe.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (its list 'a belief, policy or person' followed Cambridge's and Longman's 'opinion, person, idea' frame), plain 3 (same frame), other senses 3 (WordNet glosses tracking Collins 'argument or controversy, esp over a doctrine, belief' and Dictionary.com 'a person who argues in opposition to another'), wrong answers 3 (policy had 'such as' and followed Longman's 'course of action officially agreed'; polish followed Longman's 'high level of skill or style in the way someone performs'; polity joined Oxford's two senses). Rewrote all of these, and moved the first example off a government measure (WordUp's scene) to factory farming. pomposity kept (no dictionary frame). Hook checked: Greek polemos, war.
reviews.checker_notes: sense 4: the other sense 'A heated public dispute, often over religious or political teaching.' keeps the frame of Collins 'an argument or controversy, esp over a doctrine, belief, etc' (WordNet's 'a controversy (especially over a belief or dogma)' tracks it too); Dictionary.com and American Heritage share it, so 4 with a note. Definition 'attack in words, usually in print' is near WordUp 'a strong verbal or written attack on someone or something' but keeps its own frame. Definition and plain give only the attacking side; Oxford, Cambridge and Longman also allow arguing for something. wrongAnswers: pomposity shares only 'po', and none of the four is a kind of speech or text.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (WordNet's 'Slow and laborious because of weight' is AHD's 'Slow and labored because of great bulk or weight' with words dropped), other sense 3 ('Labored and dull' is Dictionary.com's 'dull and labored' reversed), examples 3 (the bear's ponderous steps retold Longman's elephant and Oxford's cow walking), wrong answers 3 (pontifical followed Longman's 'speaking as if you think your judgment or opinion is always right', and its pompous-speech meaning sat next to the dull-speech other sense). Rewrote definition, plain and other sense; swapped the bear for an old elevator; pontifical now gives its papal meaning; porous reworded. Sense 4: the physical meaning leads, and the dull-writing meaning, just as common, is kept as the other sense. Round 2: the reviewer found pontifical kept Dictionary.com's 'relating to or proceeding from a pope' frame, and prosperous shared only p and -rous. Swapped pontifical for portentous (po-...-ous, a common mix-up), giving its omen meaning rather than its 'pretentiously weighty' one so it stays clear of the dull-speech other sense, and prosperous for preposterous (shares -pos- and -erous across four syllables). Neither option follows Oxford's, Longman's or WordUp's frame.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. pontifical and prosperous are gone. portentous 'Full of omens that make people brace for trouble.' follows the 'sign that something bad will happen' meaning shared by Oxford, Cambridge, Longman and WordUp. preposterous 'Too far-fetched or unreasonable for anyone to take seriously.' follows the 'completely unreasonable' meaning shared by Oxford, Cambridge and Longman; its 'take seriously' echoes a Cambridge example ('It was a preposterous idea, and no one took it seriously'), but this is not a definition copy, so 4. Weakest: portentous also means 'pretentiously weighty' (Oxford, Cambridge, American Heritage), which is near ponderous's other sense about plodding speech. The option uses the omen sense, so no option is marked wrong when it is right, but it is worth knowing.

reviews.notes: Before: examples 3 (the mayor taking a pragmatic approach retold WordUp's 'The mayor took a pragmatic approach'; the committee choosing steps over ideals followed WordUp's coach and farmers), wrong answers 3 (problematic was awkward; phlegmatic kept Cambridge's 'not easily excited or emotional; calm'). Replaced those two examples and reworded the two options. Definition kept: 'rather than theory or principle' is shared by Oxford, Cambridge, Longman and WordUp as the plain meaning, so 4 with this note. prismatic and pedantic checked against the dictionaries and kept. Round 2: the reviewer found the rival-party example also fit phlegmatic, phlegmatic's option kept AHD's 'calm, sluggish temperament; unemotional' frame, and pedantic shared only p and -tic. Replaced the example with one about not waiting for a perfect apartment (calm, prismatic or paradigmatic do not fit it). Rewrote phlegmatic from the angle of how the person meets news. Swapped pedantic for paradigmatic (p-a-r ... -matic), after reading its entries; written as 'textbook case', not WordUp's 'clear and representative example'. programmatic was considered but is not in WordNet.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The rival-party example is replaced by 'Too pragmatic to wait for the perfect apartment, she signed a lease on a decent one near the train.', which no wrong answer fits. phlegmatic 'Taking good news and bad news with the same unbothered face.' no longer follows American Heritage's frame. paradigmatic 'Serving as the textbook case that others of its type are measured against.' follows the 'typical or standard example' meaning that Oxford, Vocabulary.com and WordUp share, so 4. Weakest: the definition's 'rather than by theory or principle' is a frame that Oxford, Cambridge, Longman and WordUp all share, so 4.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (WordNet's 'Idle or foolish and irrelevant talk' follows AHD's 'Idle or meaningless chatter'), plain 3 (followed Longman's 'talk continuously about silly and unimportant things' and Vocabulary.com's 'go on and on'), wrong answers 3 (preamble was Longman's 'statement at the beginning of a ... document, or talk, explaining what it is about'; pratfall, a fall, is the wrong kind of thing for a kind of talk, the trap noted for prattle and paddle). Rewrote definition, plain and preamble; swapped pratfall for parable (also a kind of spoken text, shares p-a-r and the -le ending), written from the angle of a story used instead of an argument. prank is an act, not talk, but it shares pra- and the playful tone, so it still tempts. Examples checked against Cambridge's and Longman's; no scene retold.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: prank is an act, not talk (Collins: 'esp one in which something is done rather than said'), and pretext is a reason; the trap list asks for a kind of talk for a kind of talk. parable and preamble fit better. prank 'A playful trick meant to fool or tease someone.' is close to the 'trick ... as a joke' wording several dictionaries share, so not a copy. The hook uses rattle as a sound-alike only (prattle comes from prate); acceptable.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (kept WordUp's 'cause an event or change, often an unpleasant one, to begin at once or earlier than people expected'), examples 3 (the bank collapse 'precipitated a crisis' retold Oxford's and Cambridge's crisis examples; the angry post retold WordUp's 'One careless post online precipitated an argument'), wrong answers 3 (anticipate was Longman's 'expect that something will happen and be ready for it'; palpitate was Cambridge's and Longman's 'fast and irregular' frame). Rewrote definition and plain, replaced three examples with scenes that show an event arriving early, and reworded three options. participate kept (shared 'take part' phrasing). No other senses: the chemistry and weather senses are not needed here. Round 2: the reviewer found the definition followed WordUp clause by clause ('an event, often an unpleasant one, at once or earlier'). Rewrote it from the angle of a spark that makes a trouble already building break out early; 'sooner' alone is shared by Oxford, Cambridge, Longman and AHD. Replaced the heart-attack example, which had no timing clue, with one about heart failure doctors hoped to hold off for years.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The definition 'Be the spark that makes a looming trouble break out sooner than it otherwise would.' no longer follows WordUp's clause order. 'looming' is a little narrow: precipitate can also bring on a crisis nobody saw coming (Cambridge 'An invasion would certainly precipitate a war'). The new heart-failure example has a clear timing clue ('hoped to hold off for years'), and all four examples now show the 'sooner' part. Weakest: the plain 'To make something bad happen suddenly, before its time.' is still close to Oxford 'to make something, especially something bad, happen suddenly or sooner than it should', but Cambridge and Longman share 'make something happen suddenly', so 4.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (WordNet's 'make impossible' with 'keep from happening' is the Oxford, Cambridge, Longman frame almost word for word), examples 3 (the contract clause that precludes him retold Cambridge's 'His contract precludes him from discussing his work'), wrong answers 3 (conclude followed Cambridge and WordUp 'end a speech, meeting'; allude had an 'as by' example and was long; seclude was close to Dictionary.com's 'shut off; keep apart'). Rewrote the definition from the angle of closing off a possibility in advance, replaced the contract example, and rewrote three options; conclude now gives its reasoning meaning. Plain kept: 'prevent from happening' is shared by every dictionary. Hook: pre-close matches the real root, Latin praecludere, from claudere, to shut. Round 2: the reviewer noted that -clude and close do not sound alike. The hook now names the shared Latin root claudere, to shut (close comes from its past participle clausus), instead of a sound-alike.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The new hook is true: close and closet come through Old French from Latin claudere, and so does preclude. It does not name or describe conclude's option. Vocabulary.com uses a door picture for conclude ('pulling a door shut'), but the text differs. Weakest: the plain 'To prevent something from happening' matches Oxford's opening words, but Vocabulary.com and others share the phrase.

reviews.notes: Before: wrong answers 3 (precipitous had 'like a cliff'; precarious had an 'as if balanced' picture the definition does not have), examples 3 ('A precocious athlete, he was signed ... at fifteen' kept Cambridge's 'A precocious child, she went to university at the age of 15'; the poet's first collection followed Cambridge's first album at twelve and Oxford's 'precocious talent'). Replaced both examples and reworded both options plainly. Definition and plain checked: no dictionary uses the 'timetable' angle. Hook root checked: praecox, from prae and coquere. Round 2: the reviewer noted the options (7 to 9 words) were much shorter than the 15-word definition. Lengthened all four to 13 to 17 words, and reworded precise away from WordUp's 'exactly right' and Cambridge's 'small details'.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The wrong answers now run 14 to 17 words beside a 15-word definition, so length no longer gives the answer away. Weakest: precious 'Worth a great deal and treasured by its owner, often because it cannot be replaced.' uses the 'worth a lot, often because' frame of WordUp 'worth a lot, often because few exist, they cost much, or they matter deeply'. Cambridge ('of great value because of being rare') and Oxford ('rare and worth a lot of money') share the value-plus-rarity idea, so 4 with a note. Related: only 3 synonyms, and 'mature' is broad.

reviews.notes: Before: definition 3 (WordNet's 'A predisposition in favor of something' is thin and repeats Collins's 'a predisposition, preference, or bias'), plain 3 ('preference or bias toward' is Vocabulary.com's wording), examples 3 (the spicy-food example retold Cambridge's 'predilection for spicy food'; old films sat close to WordUp's old jazz records; two examples opened 'Given ...'), wrong answers 3 (prediction was Cambridge's 'statement about what you think will happen'; dereliction was AHD's 'neglect, as of duty'), hook 3 (its 'prae, before, and diligere, to choose or love' was Vocabulary.com's own breakdown). Rewrote all of these. New hook ties diligere (originally 'to single out') to diligent, which is a true link. predicament and predestination kept.
reviews.checker_notes: definition 4: 'A long-standing taste for a certain kind of thing' shares 'lasting', 'particular thing' and 'kind of' with WordUp 'a natural and lasting tendency to be drawn to a particular thing, activity, or kind of experience', but the frame differs; 'long-standing' is WordUp's emphasis, not in the other dictionaries. predestination 'The doctrine that every soul's fate was fixed by divine decree before birth.' uses American Heritage's 'doctrine' and 'souls', but the meaning is shared by Oxford, Cambridge and Longman.

reviews.notes: Before: plain 3 ('ability to know ... what will happen in the future' is Longman's 'able to imagine or know what will happen in the future'), examples 3 ('prescient warning' was Cambridge's one example; the novel example was generic). Rewrote plain and those two examples. Definition is WordNet's and no dictionary checked uses 'perceiving the significance'. Wrong answers checked against all four look-alikes' entries: prescriptive shares the 'rules for how things should be done' meaning that Oxford, Longman and Cambridge all give (4); presumptuous, pressing and present follow no dictionary's frame. Hook root checked: praescire, from scire, to know.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: the definition is WordNet's gloss (licensed); it is terse beside the other options but the options match its length. The rain-gear example ('the storm arrived a day earlier than forecast') is a weak case of foresight. pressing and present share only 'pres', and present's 'being in the same place' sense is far from anything a learner would confuse.

reviews.notes: Before: examples 2 (all four were generic: 'chose to prevaricate rather than give a direct answer', 'Politicians often prevaricate', and so on, with little to show the evasion), plain 3 (followed Oxford's 'avoid giving a direct answer ... to hide the truth'), wrong answers 3 (procrastinate was AHD's 'out of habitual carelessness' frame; prognosticate was AHD's and WordUp's 'according to present signs'; prefabricate followed Collins and WordUp 'sections ... in a factory ... assembled on site'). Wrote four new examples that show the dodging, rewrote plain, and reworded prevail, prognosticate, prefabricate and deprecate. Dropped procrastinate: AHD lists 'delay or procrastinate' as a disputed second sense of prevaricate and Collins includes avoiding a firm decision, so a learner could argue it is right. The four left share pre- or the -icate ending with the target. Definition is WordNet's and follows no dictionary checked.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: the definition is WordNet's gloss (licensed). prognosticate 'Read the clues of today and announce what tomorrow will bring.' follows the 'predict from present signs' frame shared by Dictionary.com, American Heritage and WordUp, and prefabricate follows the 'make building parts, ship them to the site, assemble' frame shared by Collins, American Heritage and WordUp; both 4 with a note. No antonyms; 'level with' or 'come clean' could be added only if WordNet has them.

reviews.notes: Before: examples 3 (the coral reef retold WordUp's 'Pristine coral reefs draw divers'; the clear mountain stream retold WordUp's mountain lake and AHD's 'a pristine stream'; the car in pristine condition retold Oxford's, Cambridge's and Longman's car), wrong answers 3 (prissy followed Oxford's and WordUp's 'easily shocked by rude' frame). Replaced three examples with scenes about being free of dirt or contamination, matching the definition, and reworded prissy. Definition is WordNet's; sense 4 because the common 'as good as new' and 'unspoiled by people' uses are only partly covered by 'free from dirt', with the original-state meaning kept as the other sense. prestigious, philistine and pricey checked and kept.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: the definition is WordNet's gloss (licensed) and covers only 'clean'; the common 'in original, like-new condition' and 'unspoiled by people' uses (Oxford, Longman, WordUp) are only partly covered. The hook's 'still as it first was' fits the other sense more than 'free from dirt'. pricey shares only 'pri'. In the surgeon example, sterile is the usual word.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 5, definition 3, plain 4, examples 3, wrongAnswers 3, hook 5, related 4. Definition was the stiff WordNet gloss ("as being wrong or evil or injurious") opening with the "deserving blame or censure" that Dictionary.com and AHD use; rewritten. Example 4 (court holds landlord culpable over smoke alarms) was close to Cambridge's landowner held culpable for a fire; replaced with a hospital dosing error. capable followed Oxford/Longman "able to do things well" plus Vocabulary.com's "handle whatever task"; palpable used the Cambridge/Longman "so strong that others notice it around them" frame; palatable copied WordUp's two-sense frame (food, then an idea people can "agree to or live with"). All three rewritten after reading the dictionaries.
reviews.checker_notes: All 4 or more. Definition: 'answerable ... justly earns blame' for 'a wrong' follows the responsible + deserving blame + wrong frame that Oxford ('responsible and deserving blame for having done something wrong'), Cambridge and Vocabulary.com share, so it scores 4 under the shared-frame line. Plain 'at fault for something bad' is close to Cambridge 'blamed ... for something bad' and WordUp 'at fault for causing it' (shared). Example 1 (an inquiry finds an organization culpable for a disaster) is the same kind of scene as WordUp's 'The court ruled that the factory was culpable for the chemical leak', with different details. Weakest look-alike: culinary shares only cul-.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 5, definition 3, plain 3, examples 3, wrongAnswers 3, hook 5, related 4. Definition was a terse WordNet gloss, much shorter than the wrong answers, so it stood out in the quiz; rewritten at their length. Plain ("more and more money and things, no matter how much you already have") followed WordUp's "money, property, or other valuable things, even after they have enough"; rewritten. Example 2 (heir selling grandmother's silver) retold WordUp's family-property scenes (mother's house, family farm); example 3 was a third rich-businessman scene. Replaced with a swindler and the gold rush. curiosity mixed Vocabulary.com's "urge... poke around" with WordUp's "ask questions or explore"; rewritten. acuity and capability shared only -ity and an a/c-p; swapped for timidity and lucidity, which rhyme with cupidity (dictionaries read first). Round 2: the reviewer found stupidity fits example 2 (the swindler scene), so it is replaced with a salary that never satisfies. Example 1 also read well with stupidity ("let his stupidity push him into shady deals"), so it now shows a tycoon who owns banks and an island still hunting for more. Example 3 now ends on "dreaming of sacks of gold" so curiosity does not fit. Each example checked against stupidity, curiosity, timidity and lucidity.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: all 4 or more. The new examples give clear clues to greed (already owning banks and an island, no salary ever enough, men who wanted only a good harvest dreaming of gold). None of stupidity, curiosity, timidity or lucidity fits a blank. They do not retell WordUp's or Longman's scenes. Example 2's anger at the boss's pay leans toward envy, but the first clause shows greed. Still weakest: timidity and lucidity share only the -idity ending. The definition's no-amount-is-enough idea is shared by Oxford, Vocabulary.com and WordUp.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 5, definition 4, plain 4, examples 3, wrongAnswers 3, hook 4, related 5. Example 3 (fishermen decry quotas at a noisy meeting) retold WordUp's residents decrying a bus cut at a hearing; replaced with a chef on television. descry ("far off or faint") was WordUp's "distant or unclear" with the two words swapped; decree ("an official order that others must obey") followed WordUp's "people must follow" and Cambridge's "officially order". Both rewritten. Definition is close in idea to Oxford's "criticize, especially publicly", which every dictionary shares; wording is its own.
reviews.checker_notes: All 4 or more. descry's option 'Make out with the eyes something that was barely visible' carries the unclear-or-distant idea that Dictionary.com, AHD and WordUp all give, and 'make out' is in Dictionary.com's Collins text ('discern or make out'); shared, so 4. Hook: strictly the source is Old French descrier (des- + crier); 'through French from crier' is a fair simplification. Plain 'loudly' adds a detail decry does not need.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 5, definition 4, plain 4, examples 3, wrongAnswers 3, hook 5, related 4. Example 4 (retired judge asked to run for mayor always demurs) was close to WordUp's "She demurred when asked to lead the project"; replaced with a striker asked to switch position. demote ("a less senior post") used Cambridge's "less senior job"; demarcate paired land with fields of work as Vocabulary.com does. Both rewritten. Example 2 (she demurs, then lets him pay) has the demur-then-agree shape of Oxford and Longman's examples, but that is the common use and the dinner scene is not theirs; kept. Round 2: the definition no longer says "giving polite reasons", which is not part of the meaning, and it now covers objecting to a claim as well as a request. Example 2 (she demurs, then lets him pay) now agrees with it. The hook no longer says "before saying yes", which suggested a demur always ends in agreement.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: all 4 or more. The new definition is accurate, now covers claims as well as requests, and fits example 2. Pairing hesitation with objecting matches WordUp ('show reluctance or hesitation, usually by objecting') and Vocabulary.com ('object ... or hesitate'), and Dictionary.com lists hesitate too, so this is a shared frame (4). Its 'proposal or claim' differs from Longman's 'plan or suggestion'. The new hook no longer implies a demur ends in yes, and 'hangs back' matches the Latin. The related word hesitate now fits the first sense.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 5, definition 3, plain 4, examples 3, wrongAnswers 3, hook 5, related 5. Definition ("describe as worthless or bad, usually unfairly") joined Oxford's "criticize unfairly; say it does not have any value"; rewritten. Example 1 (campaign ads denigrate a rival) retold WordUp's "denigrated his rival's achievements in the press"; replaced with tour guides and two capitals. delegate ("the staff below") followed Cambridge/Longman "someone in a lower position"; deteriorate's "age, wear or neglect" followed Vocabulary.com/AHD; negate ("wipe out the effect... or result") followed Oxford plus WordUp's "result or impact"; emigrate's "native land... abroad" was WordNet/Vocabulary.com. All four rewritten.
reviews.checker_notes: All 4 or more. Plain 'saying they are no good' is close to Cambridge 'to say that someone or something is not good or important', but Oxford and Longman frame it the same way, so shared. Definition's 'without fair grounds' matches Oxford and WordUp 'criticize unfairly' (shared). delegate's option 'Entrust part of one's own job to an assistant or deputy' keeps Longman's 'part of your power or work' detail with Dictionary.com's 'deputy'; it reads as the shared meaning but is the option nearest a single source. emigrate shares mainly the -igrate sound.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 4, definition 2, plain 4, examples 3, wrongAnswers 3, hook 4, related 4. Definition "Express strong disapproval of; deplore." was AHD's "To express disapproval of; deplore." with one word added (and Oxford's "strong disapproval"); rewritten. Other sense ("outdated and likely to be removed") followed AHD's "obsolete... phased out"; rewritten. Example 1 (report deprecates hiring relatives) was close to Cambridge's "We deprecate this use of company funds"; replaced with a club dress rule. desecrate used Longman's "spoil... holy" and Vocabulary.com's vandals; depress listed WordUp's "button, lever, pedal" and was a weak tempter, so swapped for deprive (dictionaries read first); dedicate listed Oxford/Cambridge's "book, music, performance" frame; all rewritten. depreciate kept (its money sense is not the belittle sense deprecate shares).
reviews.checker_notes: All 4 or more. Sense: the belittle sense (as in self-deprecating, given by Cambridge, Dictionary.com, AHD, WordUp) is common and missing from otherSenses; worth adding. Definition 'firmly objects' tracks the strong-disapproval wording Oxford, Longman and Dictionary.com share. deprive's option 'something they had or were owed' parallels Vocabulary.com's 'something that someone already had, or feels they deserve to have'; the take-away-or-withhold pair is also in Dictionary.com, AHD and WordUp, so shared, but it is the closest option to one source.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 5, definition 3, plain 4, examples 2, wrongAnswers 3, hook 5, related 4. Definition was WordNet's gloss, which Vocabulary.com repeats ("an amateur... who pretends to be very knowledgeable"); rewritten. Examples: painters regarding him as a mere dilettante retold Cambridge's "To serious artists, he was merely a dilettante"; the wine expert retold Cambridge's wine example; the six careers and the chapter-here-page-there reader retold WordUp's "started five different courses but finished none". All four replaced. delegate ("sends to a conference") followed WordUp's "sent by an organisation" to a conference; rewritten. litigant is the weakest look-alike (shares lit- and -ant) but is the right kind (a person).
reviews.checker_notes: All 4 or more. Definition 'a casual follower of an art or field' keeps the two-item 'an art or a field of knowledge' list of AHD ('One who dabbles in an art or a field of knowledge'); Merriam-Webster uses the same pair ('an art or a branch of knowledge') and Dictionary.com 'an art, activity, or subject', so it is a shared frame and scores 4, but it is the weakest point. Example 3 (an expert scorning amateurs who claim expertise) is the same kind of scene as WordUp's gallery owner dismissing a dilettante, in a different field. litigant shares only the -ant ending.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 5, definition 3, plain 4, examples 3, wrongAnswers 3, hook 4, related 5. Definition was WordNet's terse "Cause to lose one's composure" (Vocabulary.com shows it), much shorter than the wrong answers; rewritten. Example 4 (a surprise question discomfits a speaker) retold WordUp's "His unexpected question discomfited her"; example 2 (her steady stare) was close to Longman's "discomfited by her silence". Both replaced. discount ("a rumor or warning") took AHD's "discount a rumor"; rewritten. Look-alikes share only dis-, but discount and discover also share the disco- sound.
reviews.checker_notes: All 4 or more. Definition adds 'fumble', which discomfit does not require. Sense: Dictionary.com still gives 'to frustrate the plans of; thwart' as a live sense, which could be an other sense. discover's option 'a fact or place that was unknown until then' echoes Longman's 'new place, fact' and Cambridge's 'information, a place ... not known before'; shared, but the nearest to a source. Watch-out: Wiktionary lists the reveal/show use as "perhaps nonstandard", so the note calls it disputed, not wrong. Pairings: appearance belies 4.0, exterior belies 3.4, smile belied 7.5 per billion. Showing the contradict sense (the numbers belie the claim), a current meaning. Hook (contains lie, from an Old English word for deceiving) is true; unchanged. Round 2: register set to null on both senses, since formal now needs all three dictionaries and Longman gives no label (no other label has two of three). Watch-out now calls the reveal use a common mistake, as no dictionary gives that sense.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. Weakest point: the origin's gloss "to deceive with lies" is very close to Wiktionary's and Oxford's "deceive by lying", but it is a short shared fact. Both registers are now null, which is right because Longman has no label. The watch-out is now true: no dictionary gives a "reveal" sense, and calling that use a common mistake matches usage guides. The origin, hook, pairings and Also means sense are unchanged and sound.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary beneficent (Latin *beneficens, from bene, well, + -ficens from facere, to make or do). Roots: facere (bene is on the affix stoplist). Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman agree. Pairings for the agent sense: beneficent god 9.4, beneficent creator 5.5, beneficent ruler 2.0 per billion; beneficent influence (10.5) left out because it is the other sense. Showing the helpful-effect sense: AHD and Longman give it and it is the most common use (beneficent influence, beneficent effects). No watch-out: beneficent and benevolent are near synonyms, not a common misreading. Hook (bene well, -ficent from facere) is true; unchanged. Round 2: pairing beneficent ruler (2.0 per billion, not in the tool's lists) and beneficent creator (same point as god) swapped for beneficent power (7.0) and beneficent rule (4.1), both in the tool's lists. The effect sense's register set to null: Oxford and Cambridge do not give that sense, so formal (now all three) is not met for it. The first sense stays formal: all three mark it.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. Weakest point: "beneficent power" can also be read in the effect sense (Oxford's example is "the beneficent powers of Nature"), though it fits the first sense as well. All three pairings are now in the tool's list of nouns (beneficent God 5.8, power 6.4, rule 4.1 per billion). Formal on the first sense is marked by all three dictionaries. A null register on the effect sense fits the all-three rule, since only Longman's definition covers that sense.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary bolster (Old English bolster, pillow; Proto-Germanic *bulstraz, pillow, cushion; noun and verb share one etymology). No root. Tone null: no label in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman. Pairings: bolster confidence 7.6, bolster morale 4.5, bolster the economy 4.5 per billion. The two other senses (propping someone up in bed, padding) are rare and not shown. Hook makes no claim beyond the pillow noun; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: "a pillow or cushion" merges the Old English gloss (pillow) with the Proto-Germanic one (pillow, cushion), which is harmless. The origin and the hook match Wiktionary. No dictionary labels the word. The pairings are in the tool's top lists. The two hidden senses (propping someone up in bed, padding) are rare and rightly hidden.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary bombastic (bombast + -ic) and bombast (Old French bombace, cotton wadding; Late Latin bombax, cotton; senses: cotton used to stuff garments, then high-sounding words). Wiktionary says the sense was possibly influenced by bomb and bombard; I left that hedge out rather than state it. No root. Tone null: Oxford says formal, Cambridge mainly disapproving, Longman nothing, so no two agree (disapproving would be defensible). Watch-out: the bomb sound-alike leads learners to read it as explosive; the note is true per Wiktionary (bomb is unrelated). Pairings: bombastic style 4.9, rhetoric 3.8, language 2.4 per billion. Hook (bombast, cotton stuffing to pad out clothes) matches Wiktionary sense 2 of bombast; unchanged. Round 2: watch-out rewritten: Wiktionary lists a colloquial loud, aggressive, explosive sense and Cambridge starts its definition with forceful, so the note now calls that use common but disputed and no longer says the word has nothing to do with bomb (Wiktionary says the sense was possibly influenced by bomb and bombard). It keeps the cotton-padding origin.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. Weakest point: the watch-out leads with the origin rather than with what the word does not mean, but it is one true sentence. It now describes the loud or aggressive use as common but disputed, which matches Wiktionary's colloquial sense and Cambridge's "forceful". It also no longer says flatly that the word is not from bomb, which Wiktionary hedges on. The origin, hook, tone and pairings are unchanged and sound.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary boorish (boor + -ish) and boor (from Dutch boer, peasant; senses peasant, yokel or country bumpkin, uncultured person). No root. Tone null: no label in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman. Pairings: boorish behavior 12.8, boorish manners 1.7 per billion. Hook: Dutch boer, a farmer, is true (Wiktionary glosses peasant); "city snobs once used boor for anyone they thought had rough country manners" goes beyond Wiktionary, which shows only the peasant to bumpkin to rude-person shift. Not false, so unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: hook 4 (weakest point): "city snobs once used boor for anyone..." is a colorful detail that Wiktionary does not give. Wiktionary says only that boor comes from Dutch boer, peasant, and compares the change of sense with pagan. The detail is not false, so no change is needed. The origin matches Wiktionary's entries for boorish and boor. No dictionary labels the word. The pairings are the tool's top two.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary burgeon: verb from Middle English burjounen, Old French borjoner; noun from Old French burjon, a bud. Wiktionary gives two accounts of where burjon itself comes from (Frankish or Latin burra), so the origin stops at Old French. No root. Tone formal: Oxford and Longman (Cambridge says literary). Pairings: burgeoning field 52.3, population 29.8, market 12.9 per billion. The plant sense is marked archaic in Wiktionary and is not shown. Hook (from an old French word for a bud) is true; unchanged. Round 2: register set to null: Oxford and Longman say formal but Cambridge says literary, and formal now needs all three.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The register is now null, which is right because Cambridge marks the word literary while Oxford and Longman mark it formal. Weakest point: the hook's "an old French word for a bud" skips the verb borjoner, but it is not false. Everything else is unchanged and sound.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary buttress (Old French ars bouterez, supporting arcs, from bouteret, from Frankish *botan, Proto-Germanic *bautana, to push). No root. Tone formal: Oxford (buttress verb page, fetched separately) and Longman mark the verb formal; Cambridge has no label. Pairings: buttress the argument 2.2, buttress the case 1.7 per billion (buttress his argument 3.0). Hook: "an old French word meaning to push against" is loose but not false: Wiktionary's chain goes from bouterez straight to Frankish, and the French entry bouter shows Old French bouter, to strike or push, from the same Frankish verb. Unchanged. Round 2: register set to null: Oxford (verb page) and Longman say formal, Cambridge gives the verb no label, and formal now needs all three.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The register is now null, which is right because Cambridge's verb senses have no label. Weakest point: the pairings are the most common figurative uses in the tool's data but are not frequent (about 2 per billion). The origin and hook are unchanged and match Wiktionary and Oxford's boter (to strike or thrust).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary cacophony (French cacophonie, Ancient Greek kakophonia, kakos bad + phone sound). Root phone (telephone, symphony, euphony); kakos left out because it shows only in rare words. Tone null: only Oxford marks it formal. Pairings: cacophony of voices 38.1, of sounds 17.9, deafening cacophony 5.6 per billion. The poetry sense is a specialist term, labeled technical and not shown. Hook (kakos bad, phone sound) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the origin is a bare chain in Wiktionary's order with no closing clause, though the meaning (bad sound) is plain from it. The root phone is in the linking form (telephone, symphony). Only Oxford marks the word formal, so null is right. The pairings are common (cacophony of voices 38 per billion). The poetry sense is technical and rightly hidden.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary cajole (French cajoler, probably a blend of Middle French cageoler, chatter like a jay, and Old French gaioler, entice into a cage); the hedge is kept with "probably". No root: Latin cavea, cage, sits behind only the hedged half. Tone null: no label in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman (Cambridge's labels are on synonyms in its thesaurus box). Pairings: cajoled into 33.9, cajoling tone 5.4, coax and cajole 2.3 per billion. Hook is a sound-alike (cajole rhymes with goal: kuh-JOLE, gole); it does rhyme, and it makes no origin claim. Unchanged. Round 2: origin reworded so it no longer uses Wiktionary's gloss word for word, and it now ties the jay and the cage to coaxing. The probably hedge stays.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The origin keeps Wiktionary's hedge (probably) and now describes the two verbs in its own words (a jay's chattering, luring into a cage). It also ties them to today's sense. Weakest point: "which together suggest coaxing talk" is the writer's reading rather than a sense history from a source, though it is fairly framed as a suggestion. The hook and pairings are unchanged and sound.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary callous (Latin callosus, hard-skinned, from callum, hardened skin) and callus (from Latin callum). Root callum (callus). Tone null: no label in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman. Watch-out: callous and callus are often mixed up in spelling; Wiktionary also lists callous as a noun form, so the note says "usually". Pairings: callous disregard 35.9, indifference 22.3, attitude 12.8 per billion. The hardened-skin sense is uncommon (calloused is the usual word) and not shown. Hook (shares callum with callus) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the root callum shows up in English mainly through callus, the noun the watch-out names. The origin and the hook match Wiktionary (callosus, hard-skinned, from callum). The watch-out is about a real, common spelling mix-up and is true (Wiktionary also gives callous as a noun spelling, which "usually" allows for). The pairings are the tool's top three. The skin sense is rightly hidden.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary candor (Latin candor, brightness, whiteness, from candeo, to shine), candle (Latin candela, from candeo) and candid (Latin candidus, white). Root candere. Tone null: no label in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman. Pairings: refreshing candor 2.4, disarming candor 2.0, brutal candor 1.7 per billion. The impartiality sense is old and rare, not shown. Hook (shares candere with candid and candle) is true; unchanged. Round 2: origin now gives the step to today's meaning: Wiktionary's Latin candor already had a sense of frankness, openness and purity of character, and its English entry dates the obsolete whiteness sense from about 1500 and the frank-speech sense from about 1600. Pairing brutal candor swapped for complete candor (6.3 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. origin 4 (weakest point): the facts are right. Wiktionary's Latin candor has the sense "of mind or character: frankness, openness", and its English entry dates the whiteness sense to c. 1500 and the frank sense to c. 1600. But "a word Latin also used for an open, honest character" comes right after "candere, to shine", so it reads as if the verb had that sense; it was the noun candor. Moving that clause next to candor would fix it. The pairings are now the tool's own list (complete 6.3, refreshing 2.4, disarming 2.0 per billion).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary capricious (Middle French capricieux, Italian capriccioso, from capriccio), caprice (Italian capriccio, from caporiccio) and the Italian entry capriccio (from earlier caporiccio, capo + riccio, literally curly head). English and Italian Wiktionary gloss caporiccio differently (fright, sudden start; curly head), so the origin names its parts and does not explain how they led to whim. The goat (capra) story is not in Wiktionary and is left out. No root. Tone null: Oxford says formal, Cambridge literary, Longman nothing on this sense. Pairings: capricious gods 3.7, behavior 3.1, weather 2.6 per billion. The other sense (decided on a whim) is close to the first and not shown; its old plain definition named the word, so it is rewritten. Hook makes no origin claim; unchanged. Round 2: origin now gives both accounts of caporiccio, hedged: Wiktionary's Italian capriccio (capo + riccio, curly head, curls taken as a sign of an unruly character) and its English caprice (fright, sudden start).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. origin 4 (weakest point): it now gives the missing step with a fair hedge. It covers both of Wiktionary's explanations (curly hair thought a sign of an unruly character; caporiccio as a fright or sudden start). But the second sentence is long and hard to follow, and "taken as a sign of an unruly nature" and "a fright or sudden start" stay close to Wiktionary's own wording. These are short facts, so this is not a copy. Tone null, the pairings and the hidden arbitrary-decision sense are unchanged and sound.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary castigate (Latin castigatus, from castigo, to reprove, from castus, pure; doublet of chastise and chasten) and the Latin entry castigo, which is more careful: from an unattested noun *castis, purity, with the same root as castus. The origin follows the Latin entry. Root castus (chaste, chastity). Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman agree. Pairings: publicly castigated 2.3, roundly castigated 1.4 per billion. The punish sense is old and not shown; its old plain definition named the word, so it is rewritten. Hook (Latin castigare, to correct or punish) matches the Latin entry; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: origin 4 (weakest point): it matches Wiktionary's Latin entry (castīgō from an unattested *castis, purity, with the same root as castus; chastise and chasten are doublets). But "formed on a stem meaning purity that is related to castus" reads awkwardly, and it drops the -igō (make) part that turns purity into correcting. The root castus can be spotted only through chaste and caste. All three dictionaries mark the word formal. The pairings are in the tool's data.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary catalyst (catalysis + -ist) and catalysis (Ancient Greek katalysis, dissolution, from katalyo, from kata, down, + lyo, to loose). Root lyein, the dictionary form of lyo (analysis, paralysis). Tone null for the first sense; the chemistry sense is technical (Oxford chemistry, Cambridge specialized, Longman technical). Showing the chemistry sense: it is the base meaning and the commonest use in the data (acid catalyst, catalyst surface). Pairings: catalyst for change 83.9, act as a catalyst 76.8, catalyst for reform 3.2 per billion. Hook (Greek katalysis, dissolving) is true through catalysis; unchanged. Round 2: origin now gives the step to today's meaning: catalysis is a chemistry term for speeding up a reaction (Wiktionary's only sense for it), and the general sense of setting off change grew from the chemical one.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The origin now gives the chemistry step (catalysis, speeding up a reaction, Wiktionary's only sense for it) and says the general sense grew from it. Every claim matches Wiktionary and Oxford's word origin. Weakest point: at 210 characters it is close to the limit. The root lyein, the technical chemistry sense and the pairings are unchanged and sound.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary caustic (Latin causticus, Ancient Greek kaustikos, burning, from kaustos, burnt). Root kaustos (holocaust). Tone null: no register label in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman for either sense. Showing the chemical sense: current and common (caustic soda, caustic cleaners). Pairings: caustic remarks 11.9, wit 11.0, criticism 4.0 per billion. Hook (Greek kaustikos, burning) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: alsoMeans 4 (weakest point): in the plain definition, "as a chemical" sits awkwardly in the middle of "Harsh enough as a chemical to injure skin". Lead with the chemical. The chemical sense is current (caustic soda) and rightly shown, with no label, as in the dictionaries. The origin and the hook match Wiktionary (causticus, kaustikos, kaustos). The root kaustos shows in holocaust.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary chicanery (French chicanerie, trickery, from chicaner) and the French entry chicaner (to quibble, squabble; from Middle Low German schicken, to arrange). The deeper Germanic source is left out. No root. Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman agree. Pairings: political chicanery 8.0, financial 3.7, legal 3.0 per billion. Hook (French chicaner, to quibble) matches the French entry; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the origin is a short chain that Oxford's word origin also gives (chicanerie, from chicaner, to quibble). These are shared facts, and they match Wiktionary's French chicaner (quibble, squabble). All three dictionaries mark the word formal. The pairings are the tool's top three.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary coagulate (Latin coagulatus, from coagulo, to curdle, from coagulum, rennet, from cogo, bring together, from co- + ago, drive). Roots cogere (shared with cogent) and agere (agent, act). Tone null: no label in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman. Pairings: coagulated blood 28.4, blood coagulates 3.9, proteins coagulate 2.0 per billion. Hook (Latin coagulum, rennet) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: a four-step chain is long for a card, though every step matches Wiktionary (coāgulō, to curdle; coāgulum, rennet; cōgō, to bring together; co- + agō, to drive). The roots cogere and agere are spelled the same way as on cogent. The pairings are common in the tool's data.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary coalesce (Latin coalesco, from co- + alesco, grow up) and the Latin entries coalesco and alesco (derived terms include adolesco and adulescens). Root alescere (adolescent). Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman agree. Pairings: coalesce into 140.6, coalesce around 62.8, droplets coalesce 2.6 per billion. Hook (co-, together, and alescere, to grow) is true; unchanged. Round 2: origin reworded so its glosses no longer follow Oxford's word-origin note; alescere is glossed from Wiktionary's Latin alesco (grow, increase).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The origin now uses Wiktionary's glosses in its own words (alēscō, to grow, to increase) instead of following Oxford's word origin. The adolescent link is supported by Wiktionary's adolescent entry (ad- + alēscere). Weakest point: it opens with "Latin coalescere joined..." without saying that English took the word from Latin, and the root alescere shows in adolescent only as -olesc-. Formal is marked by all three dictionaries.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary cogent (French cogent, Latin cogens, present participle of cogo, drive together, compel, from co + ago, drive). Hook (Latin cogere, to drive together or compel) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: none of substance. The origin matches Wiktionary (French cogent; Latin cōgēns, from cōgō, co- + agō), and the roots match coagulate's. All three dictionaries mark the word formal. The pairings are the tool's top nouns.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary commensurate (Late Latin commensuratus, com- + mensuratus, from mensuro, to measure, from Latin mensura, measure; first attested 1641).
