Round 2: register set to null: Oxford and Cambridge say formal, Longman gives no label, and formal now needs all three.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The register is now null, which is right because Longman gives no label. Weakest point: the root mensura shows in English mostly through measure and mensuration. The origin, hook and pairings are unchanged and sound.

reviews.notes: The English entry conciliatory has no etymology; checked against Wiktionary conciliate (Latin conciliatus, from concilio, to unite, from concilium, council, meeting), the Latin entry concilio (unite, bring together, win over) and the Latin entry reconcilio (re- + concilio). Root conciliare (conciliate, reconcile). Tone null: only Oxford marks it formal. Pairings: conciliatory tone 59.4, approach 30.8, gesture 24.7 per billion. The concessions sense is a near-repeat of the first and is not shown. Hook (Latin conciliare, to bring together or win over, root of reconcile) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: Wiktionary gives conciliatory itself no etymology. The origin rightly says "Goes back to", and its glosses match the entries for conciliate and Latin conciliō (unite, bring together, win over; concilium, council or meeting). Only Oxford marks the word formal, so null is right. The concessions sense is a near-repeat of the first and rightly hidden.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary condone (learned borrowing from Latin condonare, to forgive) and the Latin entry condono (con- + dono; senses give, surrender, forgive, permit). Root donare (donate, donor). Tone null: only Cambridge (its American entry) marks it disapproving. Pairings: condone violence 12.6, tacitly condoned 3.5, condone such behavior 2.2 per billion. Hook (shares donare, to give, with donate) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: none of substance. Wiktionary's Latin condōnō supports "give up" (surrender) and "forgive", and the con- + dōnō formation. The root donare (donate, donor) and the hook match. Only Cambridge marks the word disapproving, so null is right. The pairings are in the tool's data.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary conflagration (Latin conflagratio) and the Latin pages conflagratio (conflagro + -tio), conflagro (con- + flagro, burn) and flagro (to burn, blaze); Middle French step left out. Hook claims (conflagrare, flagrare) match; unchanged. Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark the fire sense formal. Other sense (war) shown, a common use (world, general, nuclear conflagration); Oxford has no war sense, so no formal label there.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin facts check against Wiktionary (conflagratio from conflagro, con- + flagro 'burn, blaze'); weakest point there is 'a great burning', which adds 'great' to a gloss that is just 'a burning', and the Middle French step is skipped. formal is right: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it. Pairings: 'great' and 'major' are generic size words; only 'conflagration spread' shows the sense. Also means: the war sense is current and worth showing (general, European and nuclear conflagration are top collocates), but 'spreads across many places at once' is slightly off, since the sense is a war that spreads widely, not one that breaks out everywhere at the same moment.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary connoisseur (French, 1705 to 1715, from connoître, old spelling of connaître) and French connaître (Old French conoistre, from Latin cognoscere). Hook (old French word for to know, related to recognize) is true; unchanged. No tone label in any learner's dictionary. Pairings: true connoisseur is a little generic. Round 2: origin rewritten so it no longer walks through Wiktionary's sentence or keeps the old-spelling aside; it now explains the word as 'a knower' from connaître, from Latin cognoscere (facts as before).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the new origin checks against Wiktionary (French connoisseur from connoître, the old spelling of connaître; Latin cognoscere via Old French conoistre) and no longer follows Wiktionary's sentence; 'knower' is a one-word gloss (Dictionary.com glosses Latin cognoscitor the same way), not copying. Weakest point: 'true connoisseur' is a generic pairing beside 'wine' and 'art'.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary contrite (contritus, past participle of conterere, from con- + terere, rub) and trite (also from terere, so the root links). Hook (contritus, crushed) matches; unchanged. Formal in all three learner's dictionaries. Pairings from Datamuse and Ngram (contrite heart 66, looked contrite 17, truly contrite 6 per billion); truly is generic.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin checks (contritus, past participle of contero 'grind, crush', con- + tero 'rub'); terere is a good root (trite, attrition). formal is marked by all three learner's dictionaries. Weakest point: 'truly contrite' uses an intensifier that fits any adjective.

reviews.notes: Wiktionary calls the origin unknown and says it spread as a mock scholastic Latin word; the origin keeps the hedge and leaves out the Coimbra theory. Hook is a sound-alike with no origin claim. Pairings: moral and philosophical conundrum about 6 per billion, poses a conundrum 2.5. Round 2: dropped the mock-Latin sentence that paraphrased Wiktionary; kept the unknown-origin hedge and added the Coimbra theory Wiktionary credits to Anatoly Liberman, worded as one etymologist's best guess.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the Coimbra theory is the one Wiktionary credits to Anatoly Liberman (the Conimbricenses, 16th-century Jesuit commentaries on Aristotle that lean on words with several meanings), and 'best guess' after 'Of unknown origin' keeps it a guess. Weakest point: the second sentence follows Wiktionary's clause in order and in most of its nouns (largely unavoidable proper nouns), and it drops Wiktionary's condition that the theory applies only if the word is more than a nonce coinage, along with the better-supported point that it caught on as mock scholastic Latin.

reviews.notes: Wiktionary convoluted has no etymology; checked convolute (from Latin convolutum, past participle of convolvere, to roll together; lists convoluted as derived) and convolve (con- + volvo, roll; compare revolve, involve). Hook matches; unchanged. First sense has no tone label; the coiled sense is formal only in Oxford and Longman, so null. Shown under Also means because Oxford and Longman list it as a general sense (brain folds, coiled shells); Wiktionary marks it chiefly anatomy, so a reviewer may judge it technical. Round 2: coiled-sense plain rewritten to drop WordUp's twists, curves and folds trio; it now says looped back on itself, like a coil of rope or the ridges of a brain.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the new plain definition for the coiled sense, 'Looped back on itself again and again, like a coil of rope or the ridges of a brain', follows no dictionary's wording or examples (WordUp's are pipes, rivers, blood vessels and wires). Weakest point: a brain's ridges are folded more than looped; minor.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary copious (copiosus, from copia, from co- + ops) and Latin cornucopia (cornu + copia), which supports the hook; hook unchanged. No tone labels. Pairings: copious amounts is the most common but a little generic.
reviews.checker_notes: All claims check. Weakest point: 'built from ops' leaves out the co- that Wiktionary gives (copia is co- + ops); harmless.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary corroborate (corroboro, from con- + roboro, from robur, strength), Latin robur (oak tree, hardness, strength; earlier robus) and robustus (from robus, oak). The hook says corroborate and robust share robur; robust comes from robus, the earlier form of the same word, so it holds; unchanged. Formal in all three. Watch-out on the common collaborate mix-up.
reviews.checker_notes: robur 'hard oak wood and so strength' checks against the Latin entry (tough-wooded oak, hardness, strength), and robust comes from robustus, from robur. formal is marked by all three. Weakest point: the watch-out is a real sound-alike slip (collaborate) but less of a classic misreading than the usual watch-outs; it is true and brief.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary credulous (credulus, from credo, infinitive credere). Hook (credere, like credit and creed) matches; unchanged. Formal in all three. Watch-out: credulous and credible are a classic test pair. Only two pairings are common enough (credulous people 7, credulous public 3 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: All claims check (credulus from credo). formal is marked by all three. The watch-out on credible is a classic mix-up. Weakest point: 'credulous people' is a plain noun, though it is the top collocate.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary cursory (Middle French cursoire, Latin cursorius) and Latin cursorius (from cursor) and cursor (from curro, run). Hook says cursory comes from cursor, runner, which holds through cursorius; unchanged. Tone null: only Oxford labels it (often disapproving).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the origin skips Wiktionary's Middle French step (cursoire), and its glosses 'of running' and 'runner' match AHD's; these are short shared facts. Null tone is right (only Oxford labels it, 'often disapproving').

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary dearth (Middle English derthe, corresponding to dear + -th; first sense a time when food is scarce and dear). The Old English step is hedged (probably), so the origin leaves it out. Hook matches; unchanged. Tone null: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal but Longman does not, so the all-three rule leaves it unlabelled. Round 2: origin no longer rewords Wiktionary's sense line; it now gives the Proto-Germanic meaning (costliness) from the Wiktionary etymology and links scarcity to high cost; 'which matches' replaced.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the new origin checks (Proto-Germanic *diuriþō 'costliness, preciousness', corresponding to dear + -th); 'Its Germanic source' stays clear of the 'probably' that Wiktionary puts on the Old English step, and the scarcity-makes-dear link is in the writer's own words (Vocabulary.com argues the other direction). Weakest point: 'relative dearth' is a generic pairing.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary debacle (French debacle, from debacler, de- + bacler; the bacler step is hedged with perhaps and left out) and French debacle (geology: break-up of ice dam; figurative: fiasco), which also supports the hook; unchanged. Other sense (ice-dam flood) is geology: labelled technical and not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: All claims check: French débâcle has both the ice-breakup and the figurative fiasco senses on Wiktionary, so 'in both languages' holds. Weakest point: none of substance; the ice-flood other sense is rightly hidden.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary debunk (de- + bunk, from bunkum, from Buncombe County, 1923) and bunkum (Felix Walker's 1820 speech he said was for Buncombe). Hook matches; unchanged. Cambridge alone marks it informal, so null. Pairings: debunk the notion is about 3 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: The Buncombe story matches Wiktionary's bunkum entry (Felix Walker, 1820, speaking 'to Buncombe'), and bunk is a clipping of bunkum. Weakest point: 'thoroughly debunked' uses a generic intensifier.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary decorum (neuter of decorus) and the Latin pages decorus (from decor) and decor (from decet). No root: nothing in common English shows decorus clearly. Hook matches; unchanged. Formal in all three.
reviews.checker_notes: All claims check (decorum is the neuter of decorus, which the Latin entry derives from decor). formal is marked by all three. Weakest point: none of substance.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary deference (French deference; defer + -ence), defer etymology 2 (Middle French deferer, from Latin defero; the yielding sense; lists deference as derived), French deferer and Latin defero (de- + fero; carry down, hand over). Hook (from defer, to yield) matches; unchanged. Tone null: Oxford gives no label. Other sense (courteous regard) not shown: learner's dictionaries treat respect and yielding as one sense, so it reads as a near-repeat.
reviews.checker_notes: All claims check (French déférence; Latin dēferō; ferre is a good root). Null tone is right (Oxford has no label). Weakest point: the hook's 'comes from defer' compresses the route through French déférence, but Wiktionary calls it morphologically defer + -ence, so it holds.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary deleterious (Greek deleterios, from deleter, destroyer, from deleomai, hurt, spoil; not related to delete). Hook matches; unchanged. Formal in all three. Pairings: effects and consequences are common but broad; substances shows the health sense.
reviews.checker_notes: All claims check, including 'not related to delete'. formal is marked by all three. Weakest point: 'Greek' could be 'Ancient Greek'.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary deride (Latin derideo, de- + rideo; the PIE step for rideo is hedged and left out). Hook (ridere, root of ridicule) matches; unchanged. Formal in all three. Pairings: derided as is common but loose.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin checks; Wiktionary's hedge covers only the Indo-European root, which is left out. formal is marked by all three. Weakest point: the pairings are all adverb or preposition frames ('widely derided', 'openly derided', 'derided as'); a subject such as 'critics derided' (3.7 per billion) would show the meaning better.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary derivative (Middle French derivatif, Latin derivatus, derivo) and the Latin pages derivo (de- + rivo, to draw off) and rivo (from rivus, brook, channel). No root: rivus is not visible in common English words. Hook has no origin claim beyond derived; unchanged. Disapproving: Cambridge and Longman (used to show disapproval). Pairings are all adverbs; noun pairings are rare or belong to other senses (derivative work is legal, derivative plot is calculus).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin checks (derivo 'draw off', from rivus 'brook, channel'); Wiktionary says Middle French rather than French. disapproving matches Cambridge and Longman. Weakest point: all three pairings are degree adverbs that fit any adjective; noun pairings for this sense are rare in the data ('derivative style' 0.88 per billion), so this is acceptable.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary desiccate (desicco, de- completely + sicco, from siccus, dry). No root: siccus shows only in desiccant and rare siccative. Hook matches; unchanged. No tone labels. Other sense (wither the spirit) is rare as a verb: not shown, plain written. Round 2: hidden figurative sense rewritten after reading dictionary-defs output (WordUp script text included): no drain, life and feeling, or dull and empty result; it now speaks of killing off warmth and spark.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the hidden figurative sense's new plain definition, 'To kill off the warmth and spark in a person, a group or a piece of work', no longer follows WordUp's 'drain ... of its liveliness, emotion ... flat, empty' frame or any other dictionary's definition. Weakest point: its person, group and work loosely echo the kinds of thing in WordUp's examples (a person's spirit, an art scene, a director's films), though not their wording; hiding the sense is right.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary diaphanous (Medieval Latin diaphanus, Greek diaphanes, dia- + phaino) and Greek phaino (to show, bring to light; to shine), which supports the hook's to show; unchanged. Root phainein, in the infinitive form other worksheets use for Greek verbs (graphein, lyein); it also links sycophant. Literary: Cambridge and Longman.
reviews.checker_notes: All claims check (diaphanes from dia- + phaino). Weakest point: none of substance; literary matches Cambridge and Longman (Oxford says formal).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary diatribe (French, Latin diatriba, learned discourse, Greek diatribe, way of spending time, lecture, from dia + tribo) and Greek tribo (rub; rub away, wear away), which supports the hook; unchanged. Formal in all three. Round 2: origin now links wearing away to a pastime (wearing away time), using tribo's 'to waste, wear away' gloss; dropped the English-sense clause to keep it short.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the facts check (Greek diatribe 'a way of spending time; pastime; lecture', from tribo 'rub, wear away'; Latin diatriba 'learned discourse'), and 'wearing away time, so a pastime' now links the steps. Weakest point: the origin stops at Latin's 'learned discourse' and no longer says that English uses the word for a bitter attack, so the move to today's meaning is left out; the glosses (pastime, lecture, rub, wear away) are shared by Wiktionary, AHD and Vocabulary.com, so they count as facts, not copying.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary didactic (French didactique, Greek didaktikos, from didaktos, from didasko). Root didaskein also in autodidact. Hook matches; unchanged. Tone: Oxford (usually disapproving, on its lecturing sense) and Cambridge (mainly disapproving) agree, and the definition carries that lecturing sense; formal was also possible (Oxford headword, Cambridge US).
reviews.checker_notes: All claims check. Weakest point: didaskein shows in English mainly as didact- (autodidact), and disapproving matches Oxford ('usually') and Cambridge ('mainly') although common genre uses such as 'didactic poetry' and the pairing 'didactic purpose' are neutral.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary diffident (Latin diffidere; archaic sense distrustful of others), Latin diffido (dis- + fido) and fido (to trust), and confident (from confidere). Hook matches; unchanged. No tone labels. Watch-out on reading diffident as indifferent; judgment call on how common that is.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin checks (diffido is dis- + fido; the archaic 'distrustful' sense is on Wiktionary). Weakest point: diffident read as indifferent is a real mix-up (Vocabulary.com warns the manner can be taken for aloofness) but less established than the classic watch-outs; the note is true.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary dirge (Latin dirige, steer, direct, first word of the antiphon in matins for the dead). Hook matches; unchanged. Oxford's informal, disapproving label is for a slow, dull song, a sense not in the record, so null.
reviews.checker_notes: All claims check against Wiktionary (dirige, opening the first antiphon of matins for the dead). Weakest point: the record lacks the 'any too slow, dreary song' sense that Oxford (informal, disapproving) and Longman give, a main-worksheet matter.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary disabuse (dis- + abuse; compare French desabuser) and abuse (obsolete verb sense: to deceive, impose on), which supports the hook; unchanged. Formal in all three. Watch-out on the classic misreading as stopping abuse.
reviews.checker_notes: 'abuse' in its obsolete sense 'to deceive' is on Wiktionary (late 15th to early 19th century), and formal is marked by all three. Weakest point: 'quickly disabused' uses a generic adverb.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary discordant (Anglo-Norman, Middle and Old French discordant, Latin discordare, from discors, from dis- apart + cor heart). Hook matches; unchanged. Tone null: Oxford and Longman mark the disagreement sense formal, Cambridge does not. Sound sense shown: it is the most common use (discordant note, sounds). Round 2: sound-sense plain rewritten after reading dictionary-defs output: no 'because the sounds ... blend' frame; it now describes the sound through an out-of-tune piano and clashing keys.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the new plain definition for the sound sense, 'Grating to listen to, like an out-of-tune piano or instruments playing in different keys', no longer follows WordUp's 'because the sounds do not blend' frame, and its examples differ from every dictionary's (WordUp's trumpet, buzzing speaker, voices and guitar chord; Vocabulary.com's traffic horns). Weakest point: 'Grating to listen to' alone could fit any harsh noise, though the examples make the clash of tones clear.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary discrepancy (Latin discrepantia, from discrepo, from crepo) and the Latin pages discrepo (dis- + crepo; "to disagree, differ") and crepo ("to rattle, creak"). Root crepare: English decrepit comes from Latin decrepitus, from crepo (Wiktionary decrepit). Hook kept, scored 4: "to sound different" is the literal reading of dis- + crepare, though Wiktionary glosses discrepo only as "to differ". Tone null: only Cambridge marks it formal. Pairings from Ngram: apparent discrepancy 49, explain the discrepancy 27, slight discrepancy 14 per billion. Round 2: hook gloss of discrepare changed from "to sound different" to "to differ or disagree", to match the origin and Wiktionary's Latin discrepo.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the hook now glosses discrepare "to differ or disagree", which matches Wiktionary's discrepo and the origin; "do not sound the same" is now only an image, not a claim about the Latin. Weakest point: none of note.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary disparage (Old French desparagier, des- + parage "equal rank, rank"; obsolete English senses "to match unequally; to degrade", "marriage with an inferior"), English parage (from Old French pair "equal" + -age) and French pair (from Latin par "equal"). The Old French desparagier page does not exist. No root: par is under 3 letters. Hook kept: the par in disparage does go back to Latin par through pair and parage. Tone formal: Oxford and Longman. Pairings: Ngram disparaging remarks 62, disparaging comments 33, disparage others 16. Round 2: register null (Cambridge gives no label). Origin no longer says the obsolete senses came first and drops "in marriage" (that detail is in the obsolete noun sense); it now gives the obsolete verb sense as Wiktionary does.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: register null is right (Cambridge has no label). Origin 4: the facts are right (Wiktionary's obsolete "to match unequally; to degrade or dishonor"; Oxford's word origin also bases desparagier on Latin par), but "English once also used it to mean to match unequally" is stiff, and "match unequally" says nothing to a learner without "in marriage", which Oxford Learner's word origin ("marry someone of unequal rank") does support. Weakest pairing point: disparaging remarks and comments are near repeats.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary disparate (Latin disparatus, from disparo "to divide", dis- "apart" + paro "to arrange"; either through Middle French desparat or directly, so "perhaps by way of") and the Latin page separo (se- + paro), which backs the hook. Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman. Pairings: Ngram disparate elements 80, seemingly disparate 76, disparate sources 40. Left out disparate impact (a legal term).
reviews.checker_notes: All good. The origin keeps Wiktionary's either/or (Middle French desparat or Latin disparatus) as "perhaps by way of Middle French", and parare does sit inside separate (and prepare). formal is marked by all three learner's dictionaries. Weakest point: none of note; seemingly disparate, disparate elements and disparate sources are top Datamuse partners.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary dissemble (Old French dessembler, from Latin dissimulo, reshaped after sembler, semblance; doublet of dissimulate) and the Latin pages dissimulo (from dissimilis "unlike"), dissimilis (dis- + similis) and simulo (from similis), which back the hook. Root similis also fits semblance. Tone formal: Oxford and Cambridge (Longman says literary). Watch-out: the common mix-up with disassemble; Wiktionary gives dissemble no "take apart" sense. No pairings: nothing is common (dissemble his 4.2 per billion; the rest are function words). Round 2: register set to null under the new rule (formal only when Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark the sense formal); Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal and Longman marks it literary, so neither label has the support it needs.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: register null is right (formal in Oxford Learner's and Cambridge, literary in Longman). Weakest point: none of note.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary disseminate (Latin dissemino "to broadcast", dis- "in all directions" + semino "to sow", from semen "seed"). Hook kept: Wiktionary seminar goes back through German Seminar to Latin seminarium, from semen, and seminal is from the same noun. Tone formal: all three learner's dictionaries. Pairings: Ngram disseminate information 204, widely disseminated 164, disseminate knowledge 48; left out the medical disseminated disease.
reviews.checker_notes: All good. Origin and hook match Wiktionary (dis- in all directions, seminare to sow, semen seed; seminar and seminal share semen). formal is in all three dictionaries; the pairings are the top Datamuse partners. Weakest point: the origin's glosses follow Wiktionary's closely, acceptable for short shared facts.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary dissonance (Middle French dissonance, Latin dissonantia) and the Latin pages dissonantia and dissono (dis- + sono "to sound"; "to disagree in sound"). Hook kept. Tone formal on the first sense (all three mark the "disagreement" sense formal); the music sense is technical (Cambridge specialized, Longman technical). Music sense shown although it is technical: it is the literal sense most readers meet in reviews and concert notes. Pairings: Ngram cognitive dissonance 468, cultural dissonance 15, reduce dissonance 10.
reviews.checker_notes: All good. Latin dissono (dis- + sono; "to disagree in sound", "to disagree, differ") supports the origin and hook. formal on the disagreement sense is in all three dictionaries, and the music sense is labelled music, specialized and technical by them, the case the skill says to show. Weakest point: cultural dissonance shows the meaning less than cognitive dissonance or reduce dissonance.

reviews.notes: Wiktionary distend shows only a template, so the origin was checked against the Latin page distendo (dis- "asunder, apart" + tendo "stretch"; "to stretch out, swell"). Hook kept: extend and tension also come from tendere. Root tendere also fits portend. Tone formal: Oxford (formal or medical) and Longman. Pairings: Ngram distended abdomen 33, belly 19, stomach 17. Round 2: register set to null under the new rule (formal only when Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark the sense formal); Cambridge gives no label. Pairings: distended belly and stomach swapped for distended bladder (top Datamuse partner, Ngram 31 per billion) and distended veins (8), so the three do not name the same body part.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: register null is right (Cambridge has no label). The pairings now cover abdomen, bladder (the top Datamuse partner) and veins, all in the tool's lists. Weakest point: the hook still pictures a belly, which is fine.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary dogmatic (Middle French dogmatique and Late Latin dogmaticus, from Greek dogmatikos "didactic", from dogma) and the Greek page dogma ("opinion, belief; decision, decree"). No root: dogma is itself the English word and no other word in the list shares it. Hook kept. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge. Other sense shown: dogmatic theology is the most frequent pairing in Datamuse, and a reader who knows only the first sense would misread it. Pairings: Ngram dogmatic approach 15, dogmatic assertion 9, dogmatic attitude 6.
reviews.checker_notes: Also means 4: the doctrinal sense is current (AHD sense 1; dogmatic theology is the top Datamuse partner), but a general reader meets it mostly in theology, so showing it is a judgment call. Origin matches Wiktionary and the Greek dogma page (opinion, belief; decree). disapproving is marked by Oxford Learner's and Cambridge.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary dubious (Latin dubius; like doubt, from duo) and the Latin page dubius, which calls the link to "two" somewhat uncertain but likely (through PIE *dwi-), so the origin hedges and does not name duo. Hook kept. Tone null: only Oxford marks the "not honest" sense disapproving. Shown: the "unsure, doubting" sense, which all three learner's dictionaries have; not shown: "of uncertain outcome", which is rare. Pairings: Ngram dubious distinction 56, morally dubious 33, dubious reputation 23, dubious claims 15. Round 2: dubious distinction (an ironic set phrase, not the first sense) replaced by dubious practices (Datamuse noun list, Ngram 11 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: dubious practices (11 per billion, in the Datamuse noun list) replaces the ironic dubious distinction; all four pairings now show the first sense. Weakest point: none of note.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary ebullient (Latin ebulliens, from ebullio, from bullio "to bubble up", English boil) and the Latin page ebullio (ex- + bullio; "to boil or bubble up"). Hook changed: "to boil over" became "to boil up", since ebullio means to boil or bubble up, not to boil over. Tone formal: Oxford and Longman. Pairings: ebullient mood 6.9 and ebullient personality 3.4 per billion (top Datamuse nouns); nothing else is common (ebullient optimism 0.8). Round 2: register set to null under the new rule (formal only when Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark the sense formal); Cambridge gives no label.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: register null is right (Cambridge has no label). Weakest point: none of note.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary eclectic (French eclectique, from Greek eklektikos "selective", from eklego "to pick, choose", from ek "out" + lego "to choose, count"; cognate to elect). Hook kept. No root: legein is not a stem a learner would spot in other words. Tone formal: Oxford and Cambridge. Pairings: Ngram eclectic mix 115, eclectic approach 56, eclectic collection 42. Round 2: register set to null under the new rule (formal only when Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark the sense formal); Longman's formal label is on the noun, not the adjective.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: register null is right (Longman's adjective has no label). Weakest point: none of note.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary efficacy (Old French efficace, Late Latin efficacia, from efficax) and the Latin pages efficax (efficio + -ax) and efficio (ex- "out of" + facio "to do, to make"; "to bring about"). The hook makes no origin claim (a sound-alike; effect does come from the same verb). Tone formal: all three. Watch-out: efficacy and efficiency are often mixed up. Pairings: Ngram clinical efficacy 268, therapeutic efficacy 238, proven efficacy 40.
reviews.checker_notes: All good. Origin checked against efficacy and efficacious (efficax from efficere); formal in all three dictionaries; the efficiency watch-out is a real mix-up stated correctly; proven efficacy is 40 per billion. Weakest point: two of the three pairings are medical.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary elegy (Middle French elegie, Latin elegia, Greek elegeia, short for elegeia ode "an elegiac song") and the Greek page elegeia (from elegeios, from elegos "poem or song of lament", perhaps from Phrygian, kept as "may"). Hook kept: elegos is the source. Tone null: no label in the three. Watch-out: the elegy and eulogy mix-up. Pairings: Ngram an elegy for 27, pastoral elegy 14, funeral elegy 8; an elegy for has a generic partner.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings 4: "an elegy for" is a frame that fits many nouns and shows no partner; funeral elegy and pastoral elegy are fine. Origin: elegeia as an ellipsis of "elegiac song", elegos "song of lament", and the Phrygian hedge are all on Wiktionary's Greek pages. The eulogy watch-out is a classic mix-up.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary eloquent (Old French eloquent, Latin eloquens, present participle of eloquor "to speak out", from e "out" + loquor "to speak"). Hook kept. Root loqui also fits loquacious, grandiloquent and interlocutor. Tone null: no label in the three. Shown: the sense of a look or silence that says something (Oxford, Longman). Pairings: Ngram eloquent speech 34, eloquent speaker 21, waxed eloquent 16, eloquent plea 10.
reviews.checker_notes: All good. Origin matches Wiktionary (eloquor from e out + loquor speak). The wordless sense is current and its plain definition is clear. Weakest point: none of note.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary embellish (Middle English embelishen, Old French embellir, from em- + bel) and Old French bel (from Latin bellus; "graceful, beautiful"). Hook kept. Tone null: only Oxford marks it formal. Shown: the "decorate" sense, which the learner's dictionaries list first. Pairings: Ngram embellished version 5.3, embellish the story 5.1, embellish the truth 3.8.
reviews.checker_notes: All good. Old French bel from Latin bellus is on Wiktionary's Old French page; null tone is right (only Oxford Learner's marks formal); the decorate sense is current and well defined. Weakest point: embellish the truth (3.8 per billion) and embellish the story (5.1) are only moderately common, though they show the first sense.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary empirical (empiric + -al) and English empiric (Latin empiricus, from Greek empeirikos "experienced", from empeiria "experience", from empeiros, from en + peira "a trial, experiment, attempt"; "Not related to empire"). Hook kept. No root: peira shows in no common English word. Tone null: only Oxford marks it formal. Pairings: Ngram empirical evidence 2136, empirical research 1461, empirical data 891. Round 2: origin reworded so it no longer follows the empiric entry clause by clause or repeats its "Not related to empire" aside.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the origin is now in its own words. Every step is supported by Wiktionary's empiric entry (Latin empiricus, Greek empeiria "experience", from empeiros, en + peira "a trial"); skipping empeirikos and empeiros is fine, and "knowledge won by trying things" is a fair reading of peira. The empire note is reworded. Weakest point: "goes back through" compresses two Greek steps.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary emulate (Latin aemulatus, from aemulor "to rival, emulate") and the Latin page aemulor (from aemulus "rival, emulator"; "to try to equal or excel, rival"). Hook kept. Tone formal: Oxford and Cambridge. Computing sense not shown (a specialist sense), labeled technical as Oxford does. Pairings: Ngram worth emulating 18, emulate the success 7. Round 2: register set to null under the new rule (formal only when Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark the sense formal); Longman gives no label.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: register null is right (Longman has no label). Also means 4 stays: the computing sense (Oxford Learner's sense 2, technical) is hidden, which is defensible though readers meet emulators fairly often.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary engender, etymology 1 (Middle English engendren, Old French engendrer, Latin ingenero), and the Latin pages ingenero (in- + genero; "to implant") and genero (from genus "descent, origin, birth"; "to beget, produce"). Hook kept. Tone formal: all three. The "father offspring" sense is not shown: Wiktionary marks it obsolete and the learner's dictionaries leave it out. Pairings: Ngram engender trust 17, engender confidence 5, engender fear 5.
reviews.checker_notes: All good. Latin ingenero (in- + genero, "to implant") and genero from genus (descent, origin, birth) support the origin and hook; formal in all three dictionaries. Weakest point: none of note; the hidden "father offspring" sense is rightly not shown.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary ephemeral (New Latin ephemerus, from Greek ephemeros, from epi "on" + hemera "day"). Hook kept. No root: hemera shows in no common English word. Tone null: only Oxford marks it formal. Pairings: Ngram ephemeral nature 58, ephemeral existence 7, proved ephemeral 6.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings 4: ephemeral nature is common (58 per billion) but generic; ephemeral existence and proved ephemeral show the sense better. Origin matches Wiktionary; null tone is right (only Oxford Learner's marks formal).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary epigram (Middle French epigramme, Latin epigramma, Greek epigramma "inscription") and the Greek pages epigramma (from epigrapho + -ma) and epigrapho (epi- + grapho; "to write upon, inscribe"). Root graphein (graph, paragraph, autograph). Hook kept, scored 4: the gram of epigram is graph- plus -ma, the same pieces as gramma, so "Greek for something written" holds, though Wiktionary derives epigramma from the verb. Watch-out: the classic epigram, epigraph, epitaph mix-up. No pairings: famous epigram is 4.1 per billion and witty epigram 0.7; Greek and Latin epigram name the genre.
reviews.checker_notes: All good. Greek epigramma from epigrapho (epi + grapho) is on Wiktionary's Greek page; the epigraph/epitaph watch-out is a real mix-up. Empty pairings are right: witty epigrams is only 1.6 per billion. Weakest point: none of note.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary equivocate (Medieval Latin aequivocatus, from aequivoco "to be called by the same name", from Late Latin aequivocus "ambiguous") and the Latin pages aequivocus (aequus "equal" + -vocus), -vocus (from voco "to name, designate") and voco (from vox "voice, speech"). Hook changed: it said the word joins aequus and vox; the second part is vocare, which comes from vox, so it now reads "and vocare, to call (from vox, voice)". Roots aequus (equanimity) and vocare (irrevocable). Tone formal: all three. No pairings: only prepositions follow it (equivocate on 4.2 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Watch-out 4: null is acceptable, but equivocate used for equate ("equivocate X with Y") is a misuse a note could catch. Origin: Wiktionary has aequivocus from aequus + -vocus (from voco) and voco formed from the stem of vox, so "made of aequus and vocare" is a fair simplification; the corrected hook is accurate, and "two equal voices" is an image, not an origin claim.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary erudite (Latin eruditus, from erudio "educate, train", from e- "out of" + rudis "rude, unskilled") and the Latin page rudis ("rough, raw, uncultivated; unskilled"; derived terms rudimentum, erudio; English rude comes from it), which backs the hook. Tone formal: Oxford (formal, approving) and Cambridge. Pairings: Ngram erudite scholar 9.6, erudite work 3.6; only two are common. Round 2: register set to null under the new rule (formal only when Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark the sense formal); Longman gives no label.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary impassive (im- + passive in its old sense, able to suffer), passive (Latin passivus from passus, past participle of pati, to suffer; compare patient) and passion. reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary imperious (Latin imperiosus from imperium, command, power) and empire. Root imperium (empire, imperial). Hook true. reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary impertinent (Latin impertinens, im- + pertinent; its usage note says "not pertinent" was the original meaning and "rude" came later), pertinent (Latin pertinens) and Latin pertineo (per- + teneo, to hold; to concern, belong). reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: two roots where pertinere already contains tenere; both are real stems (pertinent, pertain; tenacious, tenant). 'First meant irrelevant, later rude' matches Oxford's word origin and Wiktionary's im- plus pertinent. The watch-out is true (the not-pertinent sense survives in legal writing) and covers the sense left out of Also means. No labels. Pairings are common (impertinent questions, curiosity, remarks).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary impervious (Latin impervius, in- + pervius) and Latin pervius (per + via; having a passage through). Pairings for the first sense: impervious to pain 9.4, to reason 4.5, to criticism 4.1 per billion. Checked against Oxford, Cambridge, Longman and WordUp wording for that sense.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: none of substance. The new plain definition of the material sense ('Letting no water or gas seep into it or through it') matches how dictionaries describe impervious rock and surfaces. The technical label matches Oxford (specialist), Cambridge (specialized) and Longman (technical). The origin is true: per plus via is the standard analysis of pervius. Pairings are common (impervious to pain 9.4, to reason 4.5, to criticism 4.1 per billion).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary impute (Middle French imputer, Latin imputo, to bring into the reckoning, charge), Latin imputo (in- + puto) and putative (puto, to think, consider, reckon); hook's compute checked against Latin computo. Pairings: impute motives 1.9 and impute blame 1.4 per billion, the top Datamuse objects, but not frequent, so 4. The headword pages in .cache/dict only link to the phrasal verb, so I saved the three phrasal-verb pages and their label lines with URLs in the scratch folder: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-little-lexicon/c5359333-97c3-58b7-a63d-3a586fd02c78/scratchpad/extras-f/impute-formal-labels.txt (pages in impute-pages/ beside it). reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: Also means. The estimating sense is frequent in the data (imputed income, rent, value; impute missing values) and could be shown as technical, but leaving it out is defensible. I checked the formal label against the saved pages: Oxford's impute-to entry has (formal), Longman's 'impute something to somebody' has REGISTERLAB formal, and Cambridge's 'impute something to someone' has formal in its header, so all three mark the sense and formal is right. The origin is true (imputare from in- plus putare; root putare shows in compute and dispute). Pairings are common enough (impute motives 1.9, impute blame 1.4 per billion).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary indigent (Old French, Latin indigens, present participle of indigeo, from indu, within, + egeo, to be in need). Roots empty: egere shows in no other English word a learner would know. Hook true. Tone formal: all three learner's dictionaries. Watch out: indigent, indigenous and indignant are a well-known look-alike trio. Pairings: indigent defendants 34, patients 15, families 6 per billion. Round 2: watch-out reworded; the old glosses matched WordUp's usage note ("native to a place", "angry at unfairness", "means very poor").
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: in the reworded watch-out, 'feeling wronged' for indignant leaves out the anger that is the core of the word; 'angry at being treated unfairly' would be exact. The mix-ups are real, the note is true, and it no longer echoes WordUp's note. The origin matches Wiktionary (indigens, indigere, indu plus egere, via Old French) in the writer's own order. Formal in all three dictionaries. Pairings are top items in the data.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary indolent (French indolent or Late Latin indolens, in- + dolens, hurting, from doleo; the lazy sense "perhaps" developed in French, hedge kept). Root dolere (doleful, condolence). Hook kept: in- + dolere is right and the tumor sense is real; "the indolent avoid the pain of hard work" reads as a memory aid, not a claim about how the sense arose, 4. Tone null under the updated rule: Oxford and Longman say formal, but Cambridge's main entry says literary (formal only in its American dictionary). Pairings: indolent life 3.4, habits 2.3 per billion. Also means: the medical sense is technical, so not shown. Round 2: origin rewritten in a new order and wording (it had kept Wiktionary's two sentences); same facts, hedge kept with "Perhaps".
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the hook. 'The indolent avoid the pain of hard work' implies a path from painless to lazy that Wiktionary does not give, though it reads as a memory picture. The rewritten origin is now in the writer's own words and order, keeps Wiktionary's 'perhaps', and gives the step (painless, then easygoing, then lazy) that matches Wiktionary's 'living easily, slothful'. Tone (4): Oxford and Longman mark it formal, Cambridge Advanced says literary (its American edition says fml), so null fits the all-three rule but is borderline. Also means (4): the medical sense is frequent in the data (indolent course, ulcers, lymphomas), and the hook already mentions it, so showing it as technical is defensible.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary ineffable (from Middle French), Latin ineffabilis (in- + effabilis, utterable), Latin effor (ex- + for; to speak out, utter) and affable (for, to speak). reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: none of substance. The chain (ineffabilis, effabilis, effari, fari) is standard and matches the full Wiktionary page; root fari shows in fable, affable and infant. Formal in all three. 'Ineffable name' is the most frequent pairing in the data, so showing the holy-name sense is right, and its plain definition is clear.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary inexorable (Latin inexorabilis, in- + exorabilis, from exoro, ex- + oro, to beg, plead, pray). Root orare (oration, orator). Hook true. reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: none. Origin and hook match Wiktionary (inexorabilis, exorabilis, exorare, orare). Formal in all three. Pairings are in the data (logic, march, decline). Leaving the person sense out of Also means is right: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman give only the process sense.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary inimical (Late Latin inimicalis from inimicus, in- + amicus) and amicable (Late Latin amicabilis, friendly). Root amicus (amicable, amity). Hook true. Tone formal on the first sense (all three); null on the unfriendly sense, which only Oxford lists. Watch out: inimical and inimitable are a classic look-alike pair. Pairings: inimical to the interests 8.5, to democracy 2.3, to freedom 2.0 per billion; "the interests" is a little generic, so 4. Also means: the unfriendly sense, listed by Oxford and Wiktionary.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: 'inimical to the interests' is a fragment (the interests of what?); a complete phrase such as 'inimical to growth' would read better. The inimitable watch-out names a look-alike Vocabulary.com warns about, real but not one of the classic mix-ups. The ill-will sense is current (inimical forces, attitude), but its plain 'Acting like an enemy toward someone' overstates 'unfriendly' a little. Origin and hook match Wiktionary. Formal in all three.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary iniquity (Old French, Latin iniquitas from iniquus, in- + aequus, equal, fair), equanimity (aequus) and equal (Latin aequalis). reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary nadir (Medieval Latin, from Arabic naẓīr as-samt, naẓīr "counterpart", as-samt "the zenith") and AHD (Arabic naẓīr, "opposite (the zenith)"). No root: nothing else in English shows naẓīr. Hook unchanged: its gloss of nazir as "opposite" is AHD's, and Wiktionary's "counterpart" means the same point here. Tone null: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal, Longman marks it "written", so the all-three rule for formal is not met. Pairings: "reached its nadir" 16.9 per billion, "absolute nadir" 2.6 (the tool's top adjective). The astronomy sense is shown as technical (Cambridge marks it specialized); it explains the zenith contrast the hook relies on.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (Medieval Latin from Arabic nazir as-samt, 'counterpart of the zenith'); AHD, Oxford and Dictionary.com gloss nazir as 'opposite', so the hook holds. Tone null is right: Oxford and Cambridge say formal, Longman only 'written'. Weakest points: 'absolute nadir' (2.6 per billion) is an intensifier pairing, where 'at its nadir' (9.2) or 'reached a nadir' (8.9) show use better; the astronomy sense is borderline as one a general reader often meets, though the origin leans on it, and its plain shares the standard 'point directly below the observer, opposite the zenith' frame (AHD, Cambridge, WordUp).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary nascent (Latin nāscēns, present participle of nāscor, "to be born") and AHD (present participle of nāscī). Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it formal. Pairings from Google Books 2010 to 2022: nascent democracy 10.2, industry 9.5, movement 8.4 per billion. No other senses.
reviews.checker_notes: All checks pass. Formal is marked by all three (Oxford, Cambridge at the headword, Longman). Pairings are common (democracy 10.2, industry 9.5, movement 8.4). Weakest point: 'a form of nasci' is vague for a present participle, and natal and native show the nat- stem rather than nasc-, which the origin handles by calling nasci 'the verb behind' them.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary nebulous (Middle English, from Middle French nebuleus, from Latin nebulōsus "full of mist", from nebula "mist, vapour, cloud") and AHD. The tool's "obscure" hedge note comes from a gloss of the Old English cognate, not from a doubt about the origin, which I leave out. Root nebula (nebula, nebulizer). Hook (Latin nebula, mist) true; unchanged. Tone null: Oxford and Longman mark it formal, Cambridge does not. Pairings: nebulous concept 17.4, term 7.2, idea 5.0 per billion. The astronomy sense (of nebulae) is not shown: learner's dictionaries leave it out and its corpus hits are mostly old astronomy books ("nebulous matter"). Round 2: the closing clause followed Longman's "an idea that is nebulous is ... no definite edges" frame; rewritten as a plan seen as if through fog.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the new step to today's meaning ('a nebulous plan is one you can only make out as if through fog') no longer follows Longman's frame or its 'no definite edges', and no cached dictionary uses it ('nebulous plan' is only a WordUp example phrase, and a common pairing). The facts are unchanged and right (Latin nebulosus from nebula, via Middle French). Weakest point: none of note; the rest stands as in round 1.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary nefarious (Latin nefārius, from nefās "contrary to divine law", from ne- "not" + fās "divine law") and AHD (fās, divine law). reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (nefarius from nefas, ne- plus fas). Formal is marked by all three. Pairings are strong (activities 36.7, purposes 33.8, schemes 7.7). Weakest point: the hook glosses fas as 'what is right' where Wiktionary gives 'divine law'; Lewis and Short allow it, so it stays true.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary neophyte (Latin neophytus, from Ancient Greek neophytos "newly planted", from neos "new" + phyton "plant") and AHD (-phutos, "planted"). Pairings: political neophyte 3.8, young neophyte 1.8 per billion (young is generic; the tool's top two adjectives). The plant sense is rare and stays hidden. Round 2: hook changed from "phytos, planted" to "phyton, plant" so it names the same form and gloss as the origin; the rest of the hook is unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the hook now names phyton, 'plant', as the origin does, and the claim is true (Wiktionary: neos plus phyton, 'newly planted'). Pairings 4: 'young neophyte' (1.8) is generic. Also means 4: the religious sense is current and its plain is accurate for the record's Christian definition, though learner's dictionaries give it for any religion.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary obfuscate (either from Middle French obfusquer or directly from Late Latin obfuscātus, from ob- + fuscō "to darken"), the Latin page fuscō (from fuscus "dark, dusky"), and AHD. reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary obsequious (Latin obsequiōsus, from obsequium "compliance", from obsequor "comply with, yield to", from ob "towards" + sequor "follow", cf. sequel) and AHD (obsequī, to comply; ob-, to; sequī, to follow). Pairings: smile 5.6, manner 4.0, servant 1.5 per billion. No other senses. reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary obstinate (Latin obstinātus, participle of obstinō "set one's mind firmly upon, resolve", from ob + *stinare, from stare "to stand") and AHD (obstināre, to persist). The reconstructed *stinare step is left out. Root stare (stable, station, statue). Hook (obstinare to persist, a relative of stare) matches AHD and Wiktionary; unchanged. Tone disapproving: Oxford "often disapproving", Cambridge "usually disapproving". Pairings: refusal 15.3, resistance 15.2, silence 8.8 per billion. reviews.checker_notes: Origin 4: the gloss 'to set one's mind firmly on' is Wiktionary's 'set one's mind firmly upon' almost word for word. It is a short gloss, so a nit, but rewording it would be safer. 'built on stare' skips Wiktionary's *stinare step, which is fine for learners. Hook, tone (disapproving in Oxford and Cambridge), pairings (refusal 15.3, resistance 15.2, silence 8.8) and the persistent-problem sense are all good.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary obtuse (Latin obtūsus "blunt, dull", participle of obtundō "to beat; to blunt", from ob- "against" + tundō "to beat") and AHD. No root: tundere shows in no common English word. Hook (obtusus, blunted) true; unchanged. Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark the slow-witted sense formal (only Oxford adds disapproving). Watch out: AHD reports its Usage Panel split on obtuse meaning "hard to understand", so the note calls it disputed. Pairings: deliberately obtuse 15.4, being obtuse 14.1 per billion. The angle sense is shown as technical (Oxford geometry, Cambridge specialized); the blunt-tip sense is botanical and hidden. Round 2: the angle sense's plain followed WordUp's "wider than a right angle but not as wide as a straight line"; rewritten by degrees in my own words, avoiding Cambridge's "more than ... less than" and Oxford's "between".
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the angle plain ('measuring somewhere from just over 90 degrees up to just under 180') is accurate and drops WordUp's right-angle and straight-line frame. Its 90-to-180 range is the plain geometric fact that Oxford, Cambridge, Collins and Vocabulary.com all give, so that is not copying. Also means 4: 'somewhere from just over ... up to just under' is wordy, and 'just over 90' can read as 'close to 90' until the second half. Pairings 4: 'being obtuse' (14.1) is generic, though mostly the understanding sense.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary officious (Middle English, from Latin officiōsus "kindly", from officium "service") and AHD (officiōsus obliging, dutiful; officium duty). Root officium (office, official, officiate). Hook (officium duty, root of office) true; unchanged. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge label it, Longman says it shows disapproval. Watch out: learners take it for a formal word for official (WordUp lists this as a common mistake). Pairings: manner 3.7, interference 1.8 per billion. No other senses. Round 2: the watch-out note's "help, advice or orders" followed Dictionary.com's list; rewritten without a list, and without WordUp's "nobody asked" or Cambridge and Longman's "too eager to".
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the watch-out note drops Dictionary.com's 'services, help, or advice' list and is not copied. The officious/official mix-up is real and the note is true in substance. Watch-out 4: 'takes over matters' is a little stronger than the dictionaries' sense: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman centre on being too eager to tell people what to do, AHD on pushing unwanted help or advice. An officious person interferes and gives orders without necessarily taking control. Pairings 4: both are low (manner 3.7, interference 1.8) and 'manner' is generic.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary onerous (inherited from Middle English; compare exonerate), Wiktionary onus (Latin onus, "burden") and exonerate (onus, oner-, "a burden, load"), and AHD (Old French onereus, from Latin onerōsus, from onus). Root onus, spelled as on exonerate. Hook (Latin onus, burden) true; unchanged. Tone formal: all three mark it formal. Pairings: task 49.9, burden 15.2, duties 13.2, conditions 13.2 per billion. No other senses.
reviews.checker_notes: All checks pass. The rendered Wiktionary etymology (Middle English from Middle French onereux, Old French onereus, Latin onerosus from onus) supports the origin; root onus links to exonerate. Formal is marked by all three. Pairings are strong (task 49.9). Weakest point: 'Through Old French' skips the Middle French step, which is harmless.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary opaque (Middle English opake, from Latin opācus "shaded, shady, dark", of unknown origin, later reinforced from Middle French) and AHD; the unknown source of opacus is kept. reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary opprobrium (Latin opprobrium "a reproach; disgrace", from opprobrō "to reproach, taunt", from ob- "towards" + probrum "disgrace, shame; abuse, insult") and AHD. reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary palliate (Middle English palliaten, from Middle French pallier or directly from Latin palliātus, of palliō "to cover with a cloak", from pallium "a cloak") and AHD. reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary pedantic (pedant + -ic) and the page pedant (from Middle French pedant, pedante, from Italian pedante "a teacher, schoolmaster, pedant"; archaic English sense "a teacher or schoolmaster"). reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the copied 'points of learning' is gone, and 'a stickler for petty rules' is not dictionary wording. But it leaves out the small points of fact and the show of learning, which the first-sense definition names ('minor points of rule or fact ... to display one's learning'). Alone, it could describe a rule-enforcing official as well as a pedant. Pairings 4: all three partners are generic, though the data offers no common partner that shows the meaning.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary penury (Late Middle English, from Latin pēnūria "need, scarcity, want"; further origin uncertain, possibly related to paene "almost") and AHD; the hedge is kept, and no root is given because the paene link is only possible. reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary perfidious (Latin perfidiōsus "treacherous", from perfidia), perfidy (perfidia, from perfidus "faithless, treacherous", from fides "faith"; related to fidelity) and the Latin page perfidus (per "through" + fidēs "faith", from the phrase per fidem dēcipere, "to deceive through faith"). reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary perfunctory (Late Latin perfunctōrius "careless, negligent", from perfungor "perform, carry through", from per- + fungor), the Latin pages perfungor ("to fulfil, perform, discharge") and fungor ("to perform"; derived terms dēfungor, fūnctiō), and AHD (perfungī, to get through with). reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the origin now gives the step to today's meaning ('a perfunctory act is aimed only at getting the duty over') in its own words; no cached dictionary uses it. The glosses match Wiktionary (perfungor 'perform, carry through', from per- plus fungor 'perform') and Lewis and Short ('fulfil'), and function is a true relative. Pairings 4: 'perfunctory manner' is generic; nod (9.1) and kiss (10.2) are good. Weakest point otherwise: 'fulfil' is the British spelling.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (abate: Anglo-Norman/Old French abatre "to demolish, knock down", Late Latin abbattere, Latin ab- + battere from older battuere) and the Wiktionary pages for Latin battuo and English debate (from Latin battuo). reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (either Middle French abscondre or directly Latin abscondo "hide", abs "away" + condo "put together, store"; the either/or is kept as "perhaps by way of Middle French") and the etymology of recondite (re- + condo "to put away, store"), which is in the list. reviews.notes:
Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English absteinen, Old French abstenir, Latin abstineo "to hold oneself back", abs- "from" + teneo "to hold"). tenere also links untenable, impertinent and retinue in the list. The voting sense is current (abstain from voting 22.2), so it is shown under Also means.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin admoneo "to remind, warn", ad- + moneo "to warn, advise") and the Wiktionary page for monitor (from monere "to warn"). reviews.checker_notes: Origin leaves out the Old French step Wiktionary hedges with 'perhaps', which is allowed; monitor from monere checks out. formal: all three dictionaries mark sense 1, and the other sense rightly stays null (Longman lacks it). pairings 4: 'gently admonished' (5.4) and 'sternly admonished' (3.4) are common, but their adverbs fit any verb of telling; 'an admonishing finger' is the one that shows the word. alsoMeans 4: the sense is current (Oxford and Cambridge sense 2), but the plain 'firmly urge someone to do something, or warn them not to' follows the do-or-not-do frame that Dictionary.com ('advise to do or against doing something'), Cambridge's American entry and Oxford ('strongly advise somebody to do something') share. Shared by three, so a note only.

Weakest point: the glosses 'to' and 'the other' are Wiktionary's own, but they are short shared facts.

reviews.notes:
Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (German Asthetik or French esthetique, New Latin aestheticus, Greek aisthetikos "of sense perception", from aisthanomai "to feel"; analysable as aesthe(sis) + -tic) and the Wiktionary pages for Greek aisthesis (from aisthanomai "to perceive") and English anesthesia (an- + aisthesis "sensation"). Root aisthesis is a judgment call: it is the stem learners see in anesthesia and synesthesia, though aesthetic itself comes from the verb. Hook claim (aisthanesthai, the infinitive of aisthanomai; anesthetic from the same root) is true. Tone null: no label in the three. The "stylish, beautiful" sense is current (Oxford and Cambridge list it), so it is shown.
Round 2: origin rewritten to add the step to beauty (the beauty sense arose in German in the mid 1700s and reached English in the early 1800s, per Oxford's word origin) and to drop the anesthesia aside; aisthesis stays named, as a relative of aisthetikos (both from aisthanomai, per Wiktionary). Round 3 (main session): second sentence recast so it no longer follows the shape of Oxford's word-origin note; same facts.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 3: the origin now explains the beauty sense in its own shape. Wiktionary's English entry does not give the German step, but Oxford's word origin (beauty sense first used in German in the mid 18th century, adopted into English in the early 19th) and Vocabulary.com (German philosophers used it for a theory of the beautiful) both support it, and the sentence follows neither: 'named the study of taste after the senses' is the writer's own angle. Weakest point: 'after the senses' simplifies 'after the Greek word for perception', and the first sentence keeps Wiktionary's gloss 'of sense perception' (a short shared fact). Other fields unchanged: the other sense's plain opens with 'Pleasing to look at', which WordUp also uses.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (French agrandir; surface ag- + grand + -ize), the Wiktionary French page for agrandir (a- + grand + -ir, "to enlarge"), English grand (from Latin grandis) and grandiloquent (Latin grandis "great, full"), which is in the list. The watch-out is now one tight, true clause. Weakest point: 'psychiatrist' is not in Wiktionary, though Bleuler was one (Dictionary.com says psychologist).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against the Wiktionary page for ameliorate (alteration of meliorate after French ameliorer; the tool could not read the "from" template, so I read the page) and for meliorate (Late Latin melioratus, meliorare, from Latin melior "better"). Hook claim (contains Latin melior, better) is true. Tone formal: all three mark it formal. Pairings: ameliorate the effects 19.9, the situation 15.8, conditions 4.7 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin checks out against Wiktionary (alteration of meliorate after French améliorer; meliorate from Late Latin melioro, from melior). origin 4: the root melior appears only in rare words (meliorate, meliorism), so a learner will not spot it elsewhere, and 'after French améliorer' is Wiktionary's own phrase. formal: all three dictionaries mark it.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (French anachronisme or New Latin anachronismus, Greek anachronismos, from anachronizomai "referring to the wrong time", ana "up against" + chronizo, from chronos "time"). Hook claim (contains chronos, time) is true. Tone null: no label in the three. The "out of date" sense is current and common, so it is shown. Pairings: historical anachronism 5.8, deliberate anachronism 2.2 per billion; glaring anachronism (1.0) was too rare.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Greek anachronismos, anachronizomai, ana + chronos), skipping French and New Latin, which is fine; chronos is a good root. The out-of-date sense is current (Oxford's sense 1) with a clear plain definition. Weakest point: 'deliberate anachronism' is the less common pairing (2.2 per billion), though Datamuse lists it.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin analogus, Greek analogos), the Wiktionary Greek pages for analogos (ana- + -logos, "proportionate") and analogia (analogos + -ia), and English analogy (Greek ana- + logos "speech, reckoning"). Root logos is broad (it also links eulogy, where Wiktionary hedges the step), hence 4. Hook claim (analogos, in due proportion, the source of analogy) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Longman mark formal, Cambridge does not. The biology sense is technical and not often met by general readers, so it is not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Checked Wiktionary's Greek pages: analogos is ana- + -logos, 'proportionate', and analogia is analogos + -ia, so the origin's analogy link and the hook's 'source of analogy too' hold. Tone null is right (Oxford and Longman say formal, Cambridge does not). pairings 4: 'closely' and 'directly' are degree adverbs that fit any comparison word and 'analogous situation' is generic, though the data's nouns for analogous are all generic. The biology sense is rightly hidden with the technical label.

reviews.notes:
Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin anomalia, Greek anomalia, from anomalos "irregular, uneven", negating homalos "even", from homos "same") and the Wiktionary Greek page for homalos, which derives it from a PIE root and says the link to homos is only "often thought"; so the origin stops at homalos and homos is not used as a root. Hook claim (an- not, homalos even or regular) is true. Tone null: Cambridge and Longman mark formal, Oxford does not. The astronomy sense is rare and technical, so it is not shown.
Round 2: origin recast in my own order; homalos glossed "level" from the Wiktionary Greek page (even, level). Facts unchanged (Wiktionary and Oxford: via Latin from Greek anomalia, from anomalos, an- + homalos).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the recast origin has its own shape and checks out against Wiktionary and Oxford (an- + homalos, anomalos 'uneven', anomalia into English through Latin); Wiktionary's homalos page gives 'even, level', so 'level' holds. pairings 4 (unchanged from round 1): 'strange anomaly' (11.1 per billion) is generic; 'statistical anomaly' and 'apparent anomaly' are good.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle French antipathie and Latin antipathia, from Greek antipatheia, from antipathes, anti- "against" + pathos "suffering, strong feeling"). Wiktionary hedges only the further origin of pathos, which the origin does not mention. pathos links apathy and pathos in the list. Hook claim (pathos with syn- and anti-) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Longman mark formal, Cambridge does not. Watch-out: antipathy and apathy are a listed confusable pair; how often learners mix them is less certain, hence 4. The object-of-dislike sense is rare, so it is not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (French and Latin, Greek antipatheia, anti- + pathos); the hedge on pathos's deeper origin is rightly left out. Tone null is right (Oxford and Longman say formal, Cambridge does not). watchOut 4: antipathy and apathy are a real pair on confused-word lists and the note is true and brief, but it is a less common mix-up than the classic misreadings. pairings 4: 'strong antipathy' is common, but 'strong' fits any feeling.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (French apathie, Latin apathia, Greek apatheia "freedom from emotion", from apathes, a- "not" + pathos "emotion, passion"). Hook claim (a-, without, plus pathos, feeling) is true. Tone null: no label in the three. The antipathy/apathy note sits on antipathy. Pairings: political apathy 38.5, public apathy 16.4, voter apathy 14.3 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary and Oxford (French apathie, Latin apathia, Greek apatheia, a- + pathos). Pairings political, public and voter apathy are the top three in the data. Weakest point: the gloss 'freedom from emotion' is one of Wiktionary's own, but short.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English apesen, Old French apeser "to pacify, bring to peace"); Wiktionary has no page for apeser, so I checked Old French apaisier (a + pais + -ier), French apaiser (from apaisier, from pais "peace") and Old French pais (from Latin pax). Hook claim (peace inside it, from Old French pais) is true. Tone disapproving: Oxford "formal, usually disapproving", Cambridge "often disapproving"; formal is not set because Cambridge does not mark it. The hunger sense is shown (appease his hunger 3.0, appease the hunger 2.4 per billion); it is current but literary, the weakest point. Pairings: appease the gods 22.2, the public 3.8, critics 2.3.
reviews.checker_notes: Wiktionary's English page stops at Old French apeser; its Old French apaisier is a + pais + -ier, Oxford and Longman agree, and its peace entry has Old French pais from Latin pax, so the origin and the pax root hold. disapproving: Oxford ('usually disapproving') and Cambridge mark it. alsoMeans 4: the hunger sense is real (Dictionary.com, AHD, Vocabulary.com; 'appease his hunger' 3.0 per billion) but less common, and Oxford and Longman leave it out; defensible to show.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin arduus "lofty, high, steep, hard to reach, difficult"). No root: arduus shows in no other English word. Hook claim (arduus, steep) is true. Tone null: no label in the three. Pairings: arduous task 150.9, arduous journey 105.9, arduous process 66.3 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (arduus 'lofty, high, steep, hard to reach') and adds its own link to today's meaning. Roots left empty is right. Weakest point: the glosses are a subset of Wiktionary's list; short shared facts.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin articulatus, participle of articulo) and the Wiktionary Latin pages for articulo (from articulus; "to divide into joints", figuratively "to utter distinctly") and articulus (diminutive of artus "joint"), and English article (from Latin articulus). Hook claim (articulus, small joint) is true. Tone formal for the "express" sense: Oxford, Cambridge (verb entry) and Longman all mark it formal; the pronounce sense has no formal label in Oxford or Longman, so null. Pairings: clearly articulated 251.6, articulate a vision 20.8, articulate their needs 10.3 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Checked Wiktionary's Latin articulo (articulus 'joint' + -o; 'divide into joints', figuratively 'utter distinctly') and article from articulus. formal: all three dictionaries mark the express sense; the pronounce sense rightly stays null. Weakest point: the origin's gloss pair and pointer to article sit close to Longman's word origin ('to divide into joints, speak clearly', see ARTICLE), though Oxford and Wiktionary give the same facts.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Medieval Latin asceticus, Greek asketikos, from asketes "monk, hermit", from askeo "to exercise") and the Wiktionary Greek pages for asketes (from askeo) and askesis (also from askeo, "exercise, training"). Hook changed: askesis ("exercise") became askeo ("to exercise"), because askesis is a sister noun of the same verb, not the source of ascetic. No root: askeo shows in no other English word. Tone null: no label in the three. Watch-out: ascetic/aesthetic is a classic sound-alike mix-up.
reviews.checker_notes: Checked Wiktionary's Ancient Greek askeo: its senses include 'practise, exercise, train', so the gloss holds (Wiktionary calls askeo itself of unknown origin, which the origin does not need to cover). The hook change from askesis to askeo is right: the word comes through asketes from askeo, and askesis is a sister noun. The watch-out on aesthetic is the classic mix-up, true and brief. Weakest point: 'monk, hermit' is Wiktionary's gloss word for word, but short.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English aswagen, Old French asuagier "to appease, to calm", Vulgar Latin *assuavio, Latin ad- + suavis "sweet") and the Wiktionary page for suave (from Latin suavis). Hook claim (suavis, sweet, root of suave) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Cambridge mark formal, Longman marks literary, so neither rule is met. The thirst/hunger sense is shown (assuages thirst and assuage hunger appear in Datamuse). Sense 580 ("cause to be more favorably inclined; gain the good will of") is WordNet's sense of conciliate or propitiate and rare for assuage; it is hidden, and it is worth reviewing on a main worksheet.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Old French asuagier, Vulgar Latin *assuavio, ad- + suavis; suave from suavis). Tone null is right: Oxford and Cambridge say formal, Longman says literary. alsoMeans 4: the hunger and thirst sense is in Dictionary.com and AHD but not in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman, and it is uncommon ('assuage thirst' 0.5, 'assuage hunger' 1.3 per billion); defensible to show. The goodwill sense is rightly hidden.

reviews.notes:
Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin audacia "boldness" + -ious, from audax "bold", from audeo "to be bold, to dare"). No root: audere shows only in audacity, the same word family. Hook claim (audere, to dare, not audire) is true. Tone null: only Oxford marks formal. The existing plain for the impudent sense is kept and shown: it is a current meaning (an audacious lie). Pairings: audacious plan 15.3, audacious move 8.0, audacious attempt 6.8 per billion.
Round 2: origin recast so it starts from the verb and ends with the English word; facts unchanged (Wiktionary: audacia + -ious, from audax, from audeo; Oxford: audax from audere).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the recast origin has its own shape and checks out against Wiktionary (audeo 'to dare', audax 'bold', audacia, + -ious). Weakest point: Longman routes the word through French audacieux, which Wiktionary does not mention, so leaving it out is fine; the other sense's plain sits near Dictionary.com's 'recklessly bold in defiance of convention, propriety', though it follows the record's own definition.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary pernicious (Old French pernicios, Latin perniciosus, pernicies, per + nex) and Latin pernicies (ruin, destruction; from perneco). Hook checked: internecine goes back through internecio and interneco to inter + neco, and Latin neco is formed from nex, so "the same root found in internecine" holds; hook kept. Roots left empty: nex shows only faintly in internecine, through necare. Etymology 2 (pernix, swift) is an obsolete adjective and is left out. Tone: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it formal. No common mix-up. Pairings from Datamuse (influence, effects, habit); pernicious anemia left out as a medical term.
reviews.checker_notes: All claims check out against Wiktionary (perniciosus, pernicies, per + nex), and nex does sit behind internecine (via necare). Formal is marked by Oxford, Cambridge and Longman. Weakest point: roots is empty although the hook links nex to internecine; fine while internecine is not in the list.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary perspicacious (Late Latin perspicacitas, Latin perspicax, perspicio, per- + specio) and perspective (from perspicere, per- + specere). Hook (perspicere, the same root as perspective) agrees; kept. Root specere is shared by circumspect and specious in the list, so their writers should use the same form. Tone: all three learner dictionaries mark it formal (Cambridge also approving, alone). Watch-out: perspicuous is the classic confusion and is already a look-alike in the quiz; the note is written in my own words, away from that option and from Cambridge. Pairings from Datamuse (reader, observer, critic).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (perspicax, perspicere, per + specere) in the writer's own words; specere is a good linking root (spectator, inspect). Formal on all three learner's dictionaries. Weakest point: skips the Late Latin perspicacitas step Wiktionary gives, which a learner does not need.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary pervasive (pervasus, pervado, per + vado) and invade, with Latin invado (in- + vado, to go). Hook (per and vadere, as in invade) agrees; kept. Tone: only Cambridge marks it formal, so null. No common mix-up. Pairings from Datamuse (influence, problem, theme).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (pervadere, per + vadere); vadere links invade and evade. Null tone is right (only Cambridge marks it formal). Weakest point: English pervasive is formed from the participle pervasus or from pervade, not straight from the verb, a nit.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary petulant (Middle French, Latin petulans, "akin to" peto) and Latin petulans (pert, saucy, impudent; from an unattested *petulo, from peto, to aim at, ask). Because the step runs through an unattested form and the English page says only "akin to", the origin says "is traced to" rather than "comes from"; origin 4 for that softness. Root petere would also link impetuous (impetus, from impetere) if that writer uses the same form. Hook is a sound-alike (starts with pet, said PET-) and makes no origin claim; kept. Tone: only Cambridge marks it disapproving, and the meaning already carries it, so null. Pairings from Datamuse (child, tone, voice).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin: Wiktionary says petulans is only akin to peto; 'traced to petere' is a little firmer than that (the Latin page could not be fetched; Wiktionary rate-limited it), and the origin stops at 'saucy, impudent' without the shift to today's childish sulkiness (English first meant pert or insolent, now obsolete). Null tone is right (only Cambridge marks it disapproving).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary pithy (pith + -y) and pith (Middle English pith, Old English pitha, Proto-Germanic; "further etymology unknown", a hedge the origin keeps).
