Hook (pith, the soft core of a plant stem) agrees; kept. No roots: an English word with no Latin or Greek stem. Tone: only Oxford marks it approving, so null. Pairings from Datamuse (sayings, remark, phrase).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin: Wiktionary takes pith back past Old English to Proto-Germanic (with Dutch pit as a cognate) before 'further etymology unknown', so 'where it came from before that is unknown' puts the unknown one step too early. Tone null is right (only Oxford marks it approving).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary placate (Latin placatus, placo, related to placeo; "more at please") and placid (French placide, Latin placidus, from placeo). The literal "smooth" sense and the Proto-Indo-European root are hedged ("thought to be") on Wiktionary, so they are left out. Root placare matches implacable on worksheet f. Hook (placare, a cousin of placid) agrees; kept. Tone: only Longman marks it formal, so null. Pairings: placating gesture (20 per billion) and placating tone (10) in Google Books; easily placated (3.8) is the top Datamuse partner but fits many verbs, so pairings 4. Placate critics (1.2) was too rare.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (placo, related to placeo; placid from placeo); placare matches implacable's root in the record. Tone null is right (only Longman marks formal). Pairings: all three use participle forms and 'easily placated' (3.8 per billion) is a generic partner; the base verb with an object would show the meaning better.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary platitude (French platitude, from plat) and the French entry on the same page (flatness; figuratively blandness, triteness). Root plat is the French stem also seen in plateau and platform; origin 4 because a reviewer may prefer no root for a French stem. Hook (French plat, flat) agrees; kept. Tone: Oxford and Cambridge mark it disapproving and Longman says it is used to show disapproval. Pairings from Datamuse (pious, empty, mouthing).
reviews.checker_notes: French platitude 'flatness' and figurative 'blandness, triteness' is on Wiktionary's French entry, so the step to today's meaning is supported. Disapproving is marked by all three learner's dictionaries. Weakest point: plat is a French stem; it is visible in plateau and platform, so it is acceptable.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary plethora (Late Latin plethora, Greek plethora, from pletho, to be full), Greek pletho (from Proto-Indo-European *pleh1-) and plenty (Latin plenus, from *pl.h1-nos). Hook ("a distant cousin of plenty") agrees with that shared root; kept. No roots: plethein shows in no other common English word. Tone: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman (a plethora of something) all mark it formal. Watch-out: Wiktionary gives "an excessive amount or number; an abundance" and Cambridge "especially a larger amount than you need", so the note describes the excess-versus-abundance use as a dispute. Pairings from Google Books: a plethora of information (19 per billion), studies (14), options (7).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin: fullness to oversupply skips the medical history (Wiktionary keeps a medical sense, an excess of blood) that explains the 'too much' meaning. Tone: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal; Longman's cached page only cross-refers to 'a plethora of something', so the third formal mark is unverified. Watch-out describes the excess/large-amount dispute as a dispute, good.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary polemic (French polemique, Greek polemikos, of war, from polemos, war). Hook (Greek polemos, war) agrees; kept. No roots: polemos shows only in polemic's own derivatives (polemical, polemicist). Tone: all three learner dictionaries mark it formal. Pairings from Datamuse (bitter, political, religious). Other senses not shown: 1330 (a heated public dispute) is close to the uncountable "polemics" sense and rare as a countable noun in English; 1331 (a person) is rare, polemicist being the usual word.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (French polemique, Greek polemikos, polemos 'war'). Formal on all three. Weakest point: polemikos is glossed 'warlike' where Wiktionary has 'of war', a nit. Hiding the dispute and polemicist senses is right.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary ponderous (Latin ponderosus), Latin ponderosus (pondus + -osus), ponder (Latin ponderare, from pondus) and pound (borrowed early from Latin pondo, ablative of pondus). Hook (pondus, the same root as pound and ponder) agrees; kept. Tone: first (physical) sense null, since only Cambridge marks the whole entry; the writing sense is disapproving in Oxford and Cambridge. Formal is in Oxford and Cambridge only. Pairings from Datamuse for the physical sense (mass, weight, machinery); all are 1 to 6 per billion in Google Books, so pairings 4. Ponderous tomes left out as it leans to the writing sense. Other sense 1332 (ponderous prose) is a common current meaning, shown with a plain definition written away from Oxford, Cambridge and Longman.
reviews.checker_notes: Wiktionary supports pound via Latin pondo, the ablative of pondus, and ponder via ponderare. First-sense null is right (Longman has no label; Oxford and Cambridge mark formal), and the writing sense's disapproving has Oxford and Cambridge. Weakest point: 'ponderous weight' is a little redundant.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary pragmatic (Middle French pragmatique, Late Latin pragmaticus, Greek pragmatikos, active, versed in affairs, from pragma, a thing done, from prasso, to do, "whence English practical"). Root prassein chosen over pragma because practical and practice show it, while pragma shows only in pragmatic's own family; origin 4 because the stem is spelled prag- and prac- in English. Hook (Greek pragma, a deed or thing done) agrees; kept. Tone: no label in any of the three. Pairings from Datamuse and Google Books (approach, reasons, considerations 58 per billion). Other senses (philosophy, linguistics) labeled technical and not shown: a general reader rarely meets the adjective in these senses.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (pragmatikos, pragma, prasso, whence practical). Hiding the philosophy and linguistics senses is right. Weakest point: roots prassein is a stem few learners will see in practical; acceptable.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary prattle (prate + -le, early modern English frequentative suffix; compare Dutch pruttelen) and prate (Middle English praten, either inherited from Old English or borrowed from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German); the either-or is kept. Hook is a sound-alike (rattle) with no origin claim; kept. No roots. Tone: only Oxford labels it (old-fashioned, often disapproving), so null. Pairings from Datamuse (childish, idle, endless).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin keeps Wiktionary's hedge on prate (Old English or Middle Dutch/Middle Low German) and explains the frequentative -le. Tone null is right (only Oxford labels it). Weakest point: the second clause on prate's source is more detail than a learner needs.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary precipitate (praecipitatus, praecipito, throw headlong, from praeceps, prae + -ceps, headed), Latin praeceps (headfirst, headlong) and Latin -ceps (from the same root as caput). Root caput would also link capitulate (worksheet m) if that writer uses the same form. Hook (Latin praeceps, headlong) agrees; kept. Tone: the verb sense is formal in Oxford, Cambridge and Longman. No watch-out: the precipitate/precipitous mix-up concerns the adjective, not this verb. Pairings from Google Books: precipitating event (56 per billion), precipitating factor (49), precipitate a crisis (9).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin facts match Wiktionary (praecipitare, praeceps, prae + -ceps from caput), but it stops at 'headlong' and does not say how flinging headlong became bringing something on suddenly; only the hook makes that step. Formal on all three. Pairings checked: 'precipitate a crisis' 9.4 per billion.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary preclude (learned borrowing from Latin praecludere; read from the ety template), Latin praecludo (prae- + claudo; to close or block) and close (Old French clos, Latin clausus, from claudo). Hook (close and closet, Latin claudere) agrees: closet is Old French closet, from clos, from Latin clausum. Kept. Tone: formal in all three. Pairings from Google Books: preclude the possibility (109 per billion), preclude the use (64).
reviews.checker_notes: Wiktionary has only 'learned borrowing from praecludere'; prae + claudere and close from claudere (close and closet pages) check out. Formal on all three. Weakest point: two pairings only, though both are common ('preclude the possibility' 109 per billion).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary precocious (Latin praecox, from praecoquo, prae + coquo; doublet of apricot), Latin praecox (praecoquo + -s), and apricot (from Late Latin praecoquum, "which ripens early", through Greek, Arabic and Catalan). Hook (praecox, prae and coquere) agrees; kept. Tone: Oxford "sometimes disapproving", Cambridge marks a separate UK sense disapproving, and Longman says sometimes disapproving in British English. Left null because the first sense as defined (talent, knowledge) is neutral and the label would mislead on precocious talent. Pairings from Datamuse (child, talent, genius); precocious puberty left out as medical. The botanical other sense is labeled technical and not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (praecox, praecoquo, prae + coquo; apricot from Late Latin praecoquum, 'which ripens early'). Null tone right (Oxford 'sometimes disapproving', Cambridge only on a UK sub-sense). Weakest point: coquere is a stem learners see only in concoct and cook.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary predilection (borrowed from Medieval Latin praedilectio; read from the ety template), Latin praedilectio (praediligo, to prefer or love greatly, + -tio), Latin diligo (to esteem, love; to set apart by choosing, single out) and diligent (from diligens, of diligo). Latin legere is left out: Wiktionary gives two possible sources for diligo (dis- + lego, to choose, or a Proto-Italic *lego, to care). Hook (diligere, to single out and love, the root of diligent) agrees; kept. Tone: formal in all three. Pairings from Datamuse (strong, personal, natural).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin: Medieval Latin praedilectio agrees with Wiktionary; diligere ('to love, esteem', literally 'to choose') behind diligent checks out. Formal on all three. Pairings: common, but 'strong' and 'personal' fit any noun; 'a predilection for' is the pattern that shows the meaning.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary prescient (Latin praesciens, praescio, prae- + scio) and science (Latin scientia, from sciens, of scire). Root scire would also link unconscionable (worksheet x) if that writer uses the same form. Hook (prae and scire, the root of science) agrees; kept. Tone: formal in all three. Pairings from Datamuse (warning, observation, proved prescient).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (praesciens, praescire, prae + scire). Formal on all three. Weakest point: none of note; 'proved prescient' is a good pick from the data.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary prevaricate (Latin praevaricatus, praevaricor, to walk crookedly, to play a double part, from prae- + varico, to straddle, from varicus) and Latin praevaricor (also: to collude; in law, to be a false advocate colluding with the opposing party). Hook (praevaricari, to walk crookedly) agrees; kept. No roots: varicare shows in no common English word. Tone: formal in all three. Watch-out: the procrastinate mix-up is the one usage guides name; watchOut 4 because Collins also allows "avoid making a firm decision", which sits near delay. Pairings left empty: every candidate is rare in Google Books (stop prevaricating 1.2 per billion, prevaricate about 1.2).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (praevaricor 'walk crookedly; play a double part', varico 'straddle'), and English Wiktionary's legal sense (collusion in a sham prosecution) backs the lawyer example. Formal on all three. Watch-out is a real, common confusion and true. Weakest point: empty pairings, rightly.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary pristine (Middle French pristin, Latin pristinus) and Latin pristinus (former, old; early, original). Etymology 2 (Greek pristis, sawfish) is a separate zoological adjective and is left out. Hook (pristinus, former or original) agrees; kept. Tone: only Cambridge labels it (formal, approving), so null. Pairings from Datamuse (condition, beaches, white). Other sense 648 (original, unchanged) is current and common (pristine wilderness), so it is shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Middle French pristin, Latin pristinus) and gives the step to 'unspoiled'. Null tone right (only Cambridge labels it). The shown 'original state' sense is current (Oxford and Longman list it). Weakest point: 'pristine condition' fits both senses.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary probity (Middle English probyte, Middle French probite, Latin probitas, from probus; "see probe, prove") and prove (Latin probo, from probus; doublet of probe). Hook (probus, which also gave us prove) agrees, since prove comes through probare from probus; kept. Root probus: reprobate (worksheet j) and approbation (worksheet m) come from probare, which comes from probus, so naming probus there too would link all three. Opprobrium is unrelated (probrum). Tone: formal in all three. Pairings from Datamuse (moral, financial, personal).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (probitas, probus; see probe, prove). Formal on all three. Pairings: common, but 'personal' is a partner that fits any noun; moral and financial probity show the meaning.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary proclivity (Latin proclivitas, from proclivis, prone to), Latin proclivis (pro- + clivus; sloping downward, prone to) and Latin clivus (slope, hill). Hook (pro, forward, and clivus, a slope) agrees; kept. Its downhill picture no longer points at a look-alike: the current wrong answers are proclamation, productivity, proficiency and profundity. Roots left empty: clivus shows only in rare declivity and acclivity. Tone: formal in all three. Pairings from Datamuse (natural, strong, political).
reviews.checker_notes: Latin proclivis (pro + clivus; 'downward, downhill; prone to') checks out on Wiktionary's Latin entry. Formal on all three. Pairings: common, but 'strong' fits any noun; 'a proclivity for' would show the meaning.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary prodigal (Middle French prodigal, Late Latin prodigalis, Latin prodigus, prodigo, to consume, squander, drive forth, prod- + ago, to drive; unrelated to prodigy). Root agere matches the form on other worksheets. Hook (prodigere, to drive away or squander; the parable son squandered his inheritance) agrees; kept. Tone: formal in all three (Oxford also disapproving, alone). Watch-out: Wiktionary and Cambridge record the "returning" use, so the note does not call it an error; it says where it comes from and what the word means. Pairings: prodigal son (431 per billion) uses the wasteful sense of the parable; prodigal expenditure is in Datamuse's list but only 1.3 per billion in Google Books, so pairings 4.
reviews.checker_notes: Watch-out: true and a real mix-up, but Cambridge and Vocabulary.com now record the noun 'a prodigal' for someone who returns, so 'many take it to mean' reads as a plain misreading where it is an allusive extension. Pairings: 'prodigal expenditure' is only 1.3 per billion (2010 to 2022), and 'prodigal son' is now mostly used for a returnee. Formal on all three.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary profligate (Latin profligatus, of profligo, to strike down, cast down, pro- + fligo, to strike), Latin profligatus (profligate; depraved, wanton), Latin profligo (to strike to the ground; overthrow; dishearten, debase) and inflict (Latin infligo, in- + fligo). Hook ("to strike down or ruin") is close: Wiktionary gives strike down, overthrow and debase rather than ruin; hook 4, kept as not false. Tone: formal in all three on the wasteful sense; the immoral other sense is not in Oxford, so it stays null. Pairings from Datamuse (spending, use, expenditure). Other sense 396 (dissolute) is current and shown; its existing plain definition was kept.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin: profligatus 'depraved' explains the immoral sense (the shown other sense) but not how the word came to mean wasteful, today's main sense; that step is missing. Facts check out (profligo 'strike down', fligo 'strike', inflict from infligo); the hook's 'ruin' is backed by Wiktionary's participial sense 'overthrown, ruined'. Formal on all three; the shown immoral sense is current.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary prolific (French prolifique and Latin prolificus, from proles, offspring, + -ficus, making; -ficus is the combining form of facere). Hook (proles shared with proliferate) agrees: proliferate is a back-formation from proliferation, which also goes back to proles. Kept. Tone: no label in any of the three. Pairings from Datamuse (writer, author, composer). Other sense 1305 (breeding fast) is current and shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (prolificus, proles + -ficus from facere; proliferate shares proles). Roots match the record (facere). Weakest point: the origin is close to the skill's own model sentence, which is fine.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (French sardonique, Latin sardonius, Ancient Greek sardonios, a form of sardanios "bitter or scornful laughter"; the link to a Sardinian plant that twisted the eater's face is given as "often cited", the plant species and a link to sairo "to grin" are hedged). The origin keeps the hedge ("often linked", "said to") and leaves out the plant species and sairo; its wording differs from Longman's and Dictionary.com's plant clauses. Hook unchanged: it calls the plant story a tale, which fits the hedge, but "goes back to" states the link a little more firmly than Wiktionary, so 4. No root: nothing else in English shows sardonios. Tone null: Oxford marks disapproving, Cambridge has no label, Longman marks only "written". Pairings: sardonic smile 88.9, sardonic laugh 18.5, sardonic humor 10.7 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the hook says sardonic 'goes back to a Greek tale' of the Sardinian plant, while Wiktionary says the Greek word is only often cited as coming from that plant (and may instead be related to sairo, 'to grin'). Calling it a tale keeps it a story, so it stands. Origin keeps the hedge ('often linked'); null tone is right (only Oxford says disapproving, Longman says written); smile, laugh and humor top the tool's list.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin satiatus, participle of satio "to fill full, satiate, satisfy", from satis "sufficient"), the Latin page for satio (satis + -o) and the page for satisfy (Latin satisfacere, from satis + facio). Hook claim (satis, the same root as satisfy) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Cambridge mark formal, Longman marks literary, so neither rule is met. Pairings: fully satiated 4.3, satiate their hunger 1.6 per billion; both modest, the weakest point. The other sense (eat far more than one needs) is a rare use and is not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings 4: 'fully satiated' pairs the word with an adverb that fits almost any participle, and 'satiate their hunger' is real but modest (1.6 per billion). Origin and hook match Wiktionary (satio, from satis). Null tone is right: Oxford and Cambridge say formal, Longman literary. The hidden overeat sense is rightly not shown.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English saturnine, from Old French saturnin or directly Medieval Latin Saturninus, from Saturnus + -inus; the gloomy sense comes from the astrological belief about people born under Saturn). The either/or is kept. Hook claim (astrologers held people born under Saturn were gloomy) matches Wiktionary's sense note. No root: Saturn is a proper name and no list word shares it. Tone literary: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it literary. Pairings: saturnine face 5.8, saturnine features 2.5, saturnine expression 1.0 per billion (saturnine gout, also common, is the lead-poisoning sense and is left out). The other sense (bitter or scornful) is near the first and close to sardonic's meaning, so it is not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the three pairings (face, features, expression) all describe a look, so they repeat one idea; all are top of the tool's list. Origin matches Wiktionary (Old French saturnin or Medieval Latin Saturninus; the gloomy sense from astrology). Literary is marked by Oxford, Cambridge and Longman.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (French savant, from Latin sapio; sense 3 is a clipping of idiot savant), the French section of the savant page (old present participle of savoir) and the Latin page for sapio ("to be wise", "to taste"). The origin avoids Wiktionary's and Dictionary.com's "old present participle" wording. sapere also links insipid. Hook claim (from French savoir, to know) is true. Tone formal on both senses: Oxford and Longman label the whole entry formal, and Cambridge labels its one sense, which covers both meanings, formal. Pairings empty: the first-sense phrases are rare (French savants 3.2, great savant 1.8, distinguished savant 0.6 per billion); idiot savant, autistic savant and savant syndrome belong to the other sense. That sense is shown: it is the meaning most readers meet today.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the shown plain definition limits savant syndrome to autism or a brain injury; it also occurs with other developmental disabilities. The other sense's formal label rests on the entry-level labels in Oxford and Longman and Cambridge's single combined definition, so it follows the three-of-three rule, though that sense is mostly a clinical term. Origin checked against Wiktionary's French savant (old present participle of savoir) and Latin sapio; empty pairings are right (no common first-sense partner in the tool's data).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Old French servil, Latin servilis, from servus "slave") and the page for serve (Old French servir, Latin servio, from servus). Hook claim (shares its Latin root with servant and serve) is true. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge label it, and Longman adds "used to show disapproval". Pairings: servile obedience 4.2, servile attitude 3.6, servile flattery 2.2 per billion. The slave sense is shown: servile war, servile labor, servile condition and servile status lead the collocation lists, and Longman lists it as sense 2.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings 4: 'servile attitude' (3.6 per billion, not in the tool's lists) uses a partner that fits any adjective; 'servile imitation' (top of the tool's first-sense partners, 7.5) would show the slavish sense better. Disapproving is marked by all three dictionaries. The Also means sense (slaves, servile labor and status) is common in the tool's data and its plain definition is right.

reviews.notes: The English entry gives only a template (borrowed from French soporifique; sopor + -ific), so the origin was checked against the Wiktionary pages for French soporifique (Latin sopor "deep sleep" + -ficus), Latin sopor and Latin -ficus (forms adjectives of making, related to Proto-Italic *fakio, the source of facio). facere also links beneficent and efficacy. Hook claim (Latin sopor, deep sleep, plus -fic, making) is true; the word came through French. Tone null: Oxford and Longman mark formal, Cambridge does not. Pairings: soporific effect 11.4 per billion; soporific drugs is high in Datamuse but 1.0 in Google Books, the weakest point.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: 'soporific drugs' is in the tool's list but only 1.0 per billion in Google Books. Origin matches Wiktionary's French soporifique (Latin sopor 'deep sleep' + -ficus). Null tone is right (Cambridge has no formal label).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Late Latin spurius "illegitimate, bastardly", possibly related to sperno or from Etruscan) and the Latin page for spurius (adjective: of illegitimate birth; false). The hedge on the Latin word's source is kept; the origin avoids Oxford's "born out of wedlock" gloss. Hook unchanged: it glosses spurius as "illegitimate child"; Wiktionary gives the adjective, and Longman gives the Latin noun "child of unmarried parents", so the claim holds. Tone null: no label in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman. watchOut null: specious is a known neighbour, but Oxford's own spurious sense ("apparently but not actually valid") overlaps it, so a sharp contrast would overstate the difference (Dictionary.com lists specious vs. spurious as a common comparison; a reviewer may want a note). Pairings: spurious correlation 22.4, spurious claims 13.4, spurious grounds 6.9 per billion. The born-out-of-wedlock sense is archaic and not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Watch-out 4: no note, though spurious and specious are a well-known confusable pair (fake versus plausible but wrong); null is defensible. Origin matches Wiktionary: Latin spurius had both the illegitimate-birth and the 'false' senses, and its source is hedged there (perhaps Indo-European, or Etruscan), which 'uncertain' keeps. Born-out-of-wedlock sense rightly hidden.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (earliest uses late 16th century, also "to scatter"; of unknown origin, perhaps a blend of scatter and wander). Both hedges are kept. Hook makes no origin claim: squander and wander rhyme when said aloud. Tone null: only Cambridge marks disapproving. Pairings: squander money 6.5, squander time 5.6, squander the opportunity 4.5 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: none of substance. Origin keeps Wiktionary's hedges (unknown, perhaps a blend of scatter and wander) and its early 'scatter' sense; the hook is a true rhyme with wander and makes no origin claim.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (an obsolete spelling of stayed, past participle of stay, used as an adjective); worded differently from Wiktionary's sentence. Hook claim (began as an old spelling of stayed) is true. No root. Tone null: no label in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman. Pairings: Datamuse's noun list for staid is mostly the old past tense (staid three days), so phrases were checked: staid and conservative 2.1, staid and respectable 1.8 per billion; two-word partners are rarer (staid British 1.4, staid image 1.0). Modest, the weakest point. Round 2: origin recast so it no longer follows Wiktionary's sentence order or keeps "used as an adjective"; same facts (an old spelling of stayed, the past participle of stay).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. Origin 5: own wording and order now, facts match Wiktionary, AHD and Oxford (an old spelling of stayed, the past participle of stay), and 'settled' gives the step to the meaning. Pairings 4 (unchanged): 'staid and respectable' (1.8 per billion) and 'staid and conservative' (2.1) are real but are binomials, not a noun partner. The tool's list for staid is mostly the old spelling of stayed, so it offers nothing better.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (French strident, Latin stridens, participle of strido) and the Latin page for strido (to make a shrill or harsh sound: creak, screech, hiss; from an imitative root). Hook claim (stridere, to creak or screech) is true. No root: stridere shows only in rare words such as stridor. Tone null: no label in the three. Pairings: strident voice 35.1, strident tone 15.0, strident criticism 5.6, strident rhetoric 4.1 per billion, covering both the sound and the argument halves of the definition. strident progress (for great strides) is 0.09, so no watch-out.
reviews.checker_notes: Watch-out 4: no note, though Wiktionary records a nonstandard use meaning vigorous or making strides (forceful in a positive way); null is defensible. Origin checked against Wiktionary's Latin strido page, which calls the verb imitative, so 'a verb whose sound imitates the noise it names' is supported. Pairings all top the tool's list.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (from the golf meaning, a ball blocking another from the hole; perhaps from Scots stymie "person with poor eyesight", or from Scots styme "glimmer"). The hedge is kept. Hook unchanged: "began as a golf word" holds for English, but if the Scots source is right the word existed before golf, so 4. Tone informal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it informal. Pairings: stymie efforts 1.7, stymie progress 1.1 per billion (efforts and progress lead Datamuse's list); stymied by is common (129.8) but generic. Modest, the weakest point.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the origin gives only one of Wiktionary's two Scots guesses (a person with poor eyesight; or styme, a glimmer), but under 'uncertain, perhaps', so it is fine. Informal is marked by Oxford, Cambridge and Longman.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (adjective from Middle French sublime and Latin sublimis "elevated, raised; exalted"). Wiktionary hedges the Latin word's further source (sub- plus possibly a root behind limen), so the origin stops at sublimis. sublimis also shows in sublimate. Hook claim (sublimis, raised high) is true. Tone null: the first sense has no label; Oxford's "formal, often disapproving" is on the extreme sense (sublime indifference). Pairings: sublime beauty 18.5, sublime spectacle 6.9, sublime scenery 4.5 per billion. The other sense (worthy of adoration) is rare and close to the first, so not shown. For a main worksheet: the record lacks the common "extreme" sense (sublime confidence, sublime indifference).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the root sublimis links only to sublime's own family (sublimate, sublimation), and a learner may wrongly connect subliminal (from limen). For a main worksheet: the record lacks Oxford's and Longman's current sense 'extreme, without noticing' (sublime indifference), so it cannot be shown under Also means; the hidden 'worthy of adoration' sense is a near-repeat and rightly hidden.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Medieval Latin substantiatus "given substance", from substantiare) and the Latin page for substantia (substo + -ia; sub- "under" + sto "to stand"). substantia also shows in substance and substantive. Hook claim (contains substance) is true. Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it formal. Pairings: substantiate the claim 23.7, substantiating evidence 7.8, substantiate the allegations 2.2 per billion. The other sense (represent in bodily form) is rare and not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: 'substantiate the allegations' is the least common pairing (2.2 per billion, against 23.7 for 'substantiate the claim'). Origin matches Wiktionary (Medieval Latin substantiare; Latin substantia from substo, sub + sto). Formal is marked by all three dictionaries.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin superfluus, from superfluo "overflow", super "over" + fluo "flow"; compare fluid) and the Latin page for fluo (infinitive fluere). Hook claim (super, over, and fluere, to flow) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Longman mark formal, Cambridge does not. Pairings: superfluous words 14.1, superfluous information 9.6, superfluous details 5.0 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: none of substance. Origin matches Wiktionary (superfluus, from superfluo, super + fluo; fluid is in its compare list). Null tone is right (Cambridge has no formal label).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English surfeite, from Anglo-Norman surfet, surfeit and Old French sorfet, sorfait, past participle of surfaire "to augment, exaggerate, exceed", sur- + faire "to do") and the page for French faire (from Latin facio, facere). Hook claim (Old French surfait, overdone: sur plus fait) is true: Wiktionary spells the Old French form sorfait and the Anglo-Norman surfet, surfeit, and AHD and Dictionary.com give surfait. Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it formal. Pairings: a surfeit of information 2.0, a surfeit of food 1.3 per billion (high for four-word phrases). The other sense (overeating) is dated and not shown. Round 2: the origin now spells the Old French form surfait, as the hook does (AHD and Dictionary.com give surfait; Wiktionary lists sorfait and Anglo-Norman surfet, surfeit), and drops the Anglo-Norman form and surfaire so a learner meets fewer foreign forms. Hook unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. Origin 5: the origin is now short and plain and matches the hook's spelling. The facts are right (surfaire from sur plus faire, from Latin facere). Weakest point: Wiktionary spells the Old French forms sorfet and sorfait, while surfait is the spelling in AHD and Dictionary.com (the latter as Middle French). Also 'formed from sur and faire' compresses the step through the past participle fait, which the hook gives.

reviews.notes: Wiktionary disagrees with itself here. tools/etymology.py gives Latin surrepticius from surrepo "to creep along"; the Latin page for surrepticius builds it on surreptus, and the page for surreptus gives it as the participle of both surripio (sub- + rapio, "to snatch away; to steal") and surrepo ("to creep under"). Oxford, AHD and Dictionary.com all derive it from surripere (sub- + rapere "to seize"). The origin leads with surripere ("usually traced") and keeps the creep-under account as the alternative. Hook claim (surripere, to snatch from under) matches the Latin pages and the three dictionaries. rapere also links rapacious; a reviewer who reads only the English entry may question it. Tone null: no label in the three. Pairings: surreptitious glance 26.1, surreptitious entry 4.4, surreptitious recording 2.6 per billion. Round 2: hook changed from "comes from Latin surripere" to "is usually traced to Latin surripere", the same hedge the origin uses, since Wiktionary's English entry gives surrepere instead.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. Origin 4 (unchanged): Wiktionary's English entry derives the word from surrepo ('to creep along'), and the origin calls that the minority view ('Some trace it instead'). 'usually traced to surripere' rests on AHD, Dictionary.com and Oxford, which all say surripere, so the claim holds and both accounts are kept. Hook 5: 'is usually traced to' now matches the origin's hedge.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (first attested 1537; Latin sycophanta "informer, trickster", Ancient Greek sykophantes, from sykon "fig" + phaino "to show"; Wiktionary tells the showing-the-fig gesture and the politicians' story as a story). The origin says only that stories explain the sense. phainein also links diaphanous. Hook claim (literally fig-shower) is true; the basket of figs is framed as a picture, not as history. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge label it, Longman adds "used to show disapproval"; all three also mark it formal, but only one label fits and disapproving matters more for using it. Pairings: surrounded by sycophants 4.1, fawning sycophants 1.1 per billion; the second is modest. Round 2: the origin now gives the step to today's meaning (in English first an informer, Wiktionary's obsolete sense, then a flatterer of the powerful); the Latin step and its gloss were cut to fit, and the fig-shower link keeps its hedge ("for reasons now unclear"). The Greek gloss "informer" follows Oxford, AHD and Dictionary.com. Hook score lowered to 4 after the reviewer's point that the courtier picture could be remembered as the origin; hook unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. Origin 5: the informer-to-flatterer step is now given and is supported (Wiktionary's obsolete 'informer, talebearer' sense; Oxford's 'mid 16th cent., denoting an informer'). 'for reasons now unclear' keeps the hedge on the fig stories. Dropping the Latin step is fine. The sykon 'fig' and phainein 'to show' glosses are the short facts every dictionary shares. Hook 4 (unchanged, weakest point): the courtier-with-figs picture is invented. It is framed as 'Picture', but a learner may remember it as the origin.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (back-formation from taciturnity, from Latin taciturnitas; or from French taciturne reinforced by Latin taciturnus, from tacitus), the Latin page for tacitus (participle of taceo) and the page for tacit (Latin tacitus, from tacere "to be silent"). The either/or is kept. tacere also links tacit. Hook claim (tacere, to be silent, the same root as tacit) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Longman mark formal, Cambridge does not. Pairings: taciturn man 18.2, taciturn nature 3.4, taciturn disposition 1.5 per billion. Round 2: "back-formation" replaced with plain words ("made by shortening taciturnity") and the two accounts put in a different order from Wiktionary's; both are still given.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. Origin 5: 'made by shortening taciturnity' replaces the jargon, and both of Wiktionary's accounts are kept. Both lead back to tacitus and tacere, so 'either way' is right. Pairings 4 (unchanged): man, nature and disposition are real and top the tool's list, but they are generic nouns for a personality adjective.

reviews.notes: The English entry gives only a template (tangent + -ial), so the origin was checked against the Wiktionary page for tangent (Latin tangentem, from tangens "touching", in linea tangens "a touching line", participle of tango "touch"). Hook claim (from tangent, a line touching a circle at one point) is true. Tone null on the first sense: Oxford and Longman mark formal, Cambridge does not; technical on the geometry sense, which Oxford labels geometry. Pairings: tangential connection 4.4, tangential relevance 1.7, tangential issue 1.6 per billion; Datamuse's lists are all physics (tangential velocity, force), so these are modest. The geometry sense is shown because it is common in school maths and physics and explains the first sense; a reviewer may judge it too technical.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings 4: 'tangential issue' (1.6 per billion), 'tangential connection' (4.4) and 'tangential relevance' (1.7) are real but modest, and none is in the tool's lists, which show only the geometry sense. Also means 4: the plain definition's 'a line that just touches a curve at one point' is close to WordUp's 'a straight line that just touches the edge of a curve at a single point'; touching a curve at one point is every dictionary's meaning, but 'just touches' is WordUp's. Origin checked against Wiktionary's tangent (linea tangens, from tango).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (irregularly formed from Latin tenuis "thin, slight" + -ous) and the page for attenuate (ad- + tenuo, from tenuis), which is in the list; worded differently from Wiktionary's sentence. Hook claim (tenuis, thin) is true. Tone null on the first sense (no label in the three); literary on the thin sense, which Cambridge and Longman mark literary. Pairings: tenuous connection 35.9, tenuous hold 33.0, tenuous link 24.4, tenuous grip 16.0 per billion. The thin sense is shown with a new plain definition (the old one, "Extremely thin ...", opened like Oxford's); the thin-gas sense is rare and not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the shown literary sense (very thin) is less common than the first; Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all list it and Cambridge and Longman mark it literary, so showing it with that label is fine. Origin matches Wiktionary (tenuis + -ous); attenuate is from the same adjective.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin tersus "clean, wiped off; neat", participle of tergeo, tergo "to clean, rub, wipe"), the senses on the terse page (obsolete "polished; neat, spruce" from the early 1600s, then "brief, concise" by extension) and the page for detergent (Latin detergeo, de + tergeo "wipe"). The gloss avoids Longman's "clean, neat". Hook claim (tersus, wiped clean) is true. Tone null: no label in the three. Pairings: terse reply 22.3, terse statement 10.5, terse note 9.3 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: none of substance. 'In English it first meant polished or neat' is supported by Wiktionary's obsolete sense (burnished, polished, neat, spruce, from the early 17th century), and detergent is from tergere.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Old French tortuos, Latin tortuosus, from tortus "a twisting, winding"), the Latin page for tortus (participle of torqueo) and the pages for torque (Latin torqueo "to twist") and contort (contorqueo, com- + torqueo). Hook claim (torquere, the root of contort and torque) is true. Tone null: only Oxford marks formal. watchOut: tortuous and torturous are a well-known pair of look-alikes (both go back to torquere); Google Books has torturous path 4.2, torturous road 1.7 and tortuous pain 1.0 per billion, so the mix-up is in print. Pairings: tortuous process 12.9, tortuous history 5.7, tortuous negotiations 4.4 per billion; tortuous path (34.5) fits both senses and is left out. The road and river sense is shown: Oxford and Longman list it and tortuous course, road and streets are common. Round 2: the watch-out was reworded in a new frame, since its opening followed Vocabulary.com's usage note; it also avoids Dictionary.com's second-r tip and AHD's road example.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. Watch-out 5: the mix-up is real, the note is true and short, and it no longer shares wording with Vocabulary.com's or Dictionary.com's usage notes (no three-word run in common with any cached page). Weakest point: Dictionary.com notes that some contexts could take either word; the note is still right as a general rule.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin tractabilis "that may be touched, handled, or managed", from tracto "handle, manage", frequentative of traho "draw") and the Latin pages for tracto (traho + frequentative -to) and traho (infinitive trahere). trahere also links intractable. Hook claim (tractare, to handle) is true. Tone formal on both senses: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman each give one formal sense that covers people and problems ("easy to deal with or control"). Pairings empty: first-sense phrases are rare (docile and tractable 1.3, tractable disposition 1.0, tractable people 0.6 per billion); tractable problem and computationally tractable belong to the other sense, which is shown because it is the commonest use.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: empty pairings; 'tractable disposition' is in the tool's list for the first sense but only 1.0 per billion, so empty is defensible. Formal on both senses follows the entry-level labels in all three dictionaries. Origin matches Wiktionary (tractabilis, from tracto, frequentative of traho).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Old French trenchant, present participle of trenchier "to cut") and the pages for English trench (from Old French trenche) and Old French trenche (from the verb trenchier); worded differently from Wiktionary's sentence. trenchier's own source is uncertain and is left out. The root trenchier also shows in trench and retrench. Hook claim (trenchier, to cut, the same source as trench) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Cambridge mark formal, Longman marks only "written". Pairings: trenchant critique 23.9, trenchant criticism 15.6, trenchant analysis 7.8, trenchant critic 6.2 per billion. trenchant supporter (an entrenched misuse) is 0.08, so no watch-out. The clear-cut sense is rare and not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings 4: three of the four (criticism, critique, critic) are the same idea; all top the tool's list, but one could give way to another partner from it (style, observations, wit). Null tone is right: Longman says written, not formal. Origin matches Wiktionary (trenchier, present participle trenchant); trench comes from Old French trenche, from the same verb.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (New Latin propensitas; surface propense + -ity) and the Wiktionary pages for English propense (from Latin propensus, participle of propendeo) and Latin propendeo (pro- + pendeo "to hang"; "to hang forward", figuratively "to be inclined"). Hook claim (propendere, to hang or lean forward) is true. Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it formal. Pairings from Ngram: natural propensity 35.7, propensity for violence 26.7, strong propensity 20.3 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: All claims check out against Wiktionary (propensity; Latin propendeo, propensus): New Latin propensitas, propensus 'inclined' as the participle of propendere, pro- + pendere 'hang'. formal: OALD, Cambridge and Longman all mark it. Pairings are in the tool, and 'propensity for violence' is 26.7 per billion. Weakest point: the origin is one chain of four 'from' steps. It reads clearly, but it is long.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle French prosaique, Medieval Latin prosaicus "in prose", Latin prosa "prose"); the second sentence explains the move from "in prose" to "dull", matching the Wiktionary senses. The deeper steps (prorsus, vertere) are left out, so no root: only prose itself shows prosa. Hook claim (grows from prose) is true. Tone null: Oxford says usually disapproving, Cambridge formal, Longman nothing, so no two agree. Pairings from Ngram: prosaic reality 5.5, prosaic explanation 5.4, prosaic details 2.9 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Latin prosa, Medieval Latin prosaicus, Middle French). The step from prose to dull is an inference, but a sound one. Null tone is right (OALD 'usually disapproving', Cambridge formal, Longman none). Weakest point: AHD and Longman call prosaicus Late Latin. The origin follows Wiktionary's Medieval Latin, which is fine.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Proteus + -an, the shape-changing Greek sea god) and the Wiktionary page for Proteus (from Ancient Greek, a sea god who could change his shape). No root, as it is a name. Hook claim is true. Tone literary: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it literary. Pairings from Ngram: protean nature 14.1, protean career 12.6, protean forms 3.8 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Hook: 'so that no one could hold him' goes past Wiktionary, which says only that Proteus could change his shape at will. In the Odyssey, Menelaus does hold him through the changes, so the clause is a little off (he changed shape to escape whoever seized him). Origin is right and in its own words. literary: all three dictionaries agree.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Old French prudent, Latin prudens, contracted from providens, participle of provideo; unrelated to prude) and the Wiktionary page for Latin provideo (pro- "fore-" + video "to see"). Root videre is shown in provide, video and evident. Hook says prudent is a shortened form of providens: true in substance, though it skips the Latin form prudens, so 4 and left as it is. Tone null: only Oxford marks it formal. Pairings from Ngram: prudent management 37.8, prudent course 37.6, prudent investor 37.2 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Hook: 'Prudent is a shortened form of Latin providens' skips a step. Per Wiktionary, English prudent comes from Latin prudens, and prudens is the contraction of providens. Smallest fix: make it 'comes from Latin prudens, a shortened form of providens'. Origin is right, and its note that prude is unrelated matches Wiktionary. Null tone is right (only OALD marks it formal).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin puerilis "childish", from puer "child, boy"). No root: puer shows only in rare words such as puerperal. Hook claim (Latin puer, boy) is true. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge mark it disapproving (Longman marks formal only). Pairings: the word is rare, and its most common content partners in Ngram are puerile jokes 0.66 and puerile nonsense 0.58 per billion (nonsense is also in the Datamuse list); low counts are the weakest point. Other sense (relating to children) is old and rare, so it is not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (puerilis from puer). Empty roots are right, since puer shows only in puerile and puerility. disapproving: OALD and Cambridge (Longman says formal). Hiding 'relating to children' is right. Weakest point: both pairings are rare in absolute terms (puerile jokes 0.66 and puerile nonsense 0.58 per billion), though they are among the word's most common partners.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin pugnax, from pugno "to fight", from pugnus "fist") and the Wiktionary pages for Latin pugno and pugnax. Root pugnare links impugn (Latin impugno, im- + pugno). Hook claim (pugnare, to fight, from pugnus, fist) is true. Tone formal: all three mark it formal. Pairings from Ngram: pugnacious face 2.5, pugnacious attitude 1.8, pugnacious spirit 1.1 per billion; all low because the word is rare, the weakest point.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (pugnax from pugno, from pugnus 'fist'). pugnare is a good root (repugnant, impugn). formal: all three. Weakest point: 'pugnacious face' describes a look rather than behavior; 'pugnacious disposition' (top in the tool) shows the meaning better.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin pungens, participle of pungo "to sting"; doublet of poignant) and the Wiktionary page for Latin pungo ("to prick, to puncture, to sting"). Root pungere matches expunge on worksheet e. Poignant is left out of the origin on purpose: it is one of this word's wrong answers. Hook claim (pungere, to prick, root of puncture) is true. Tone null on both senses: no label on the first; on the critical sense Cambridge says literary and Longman formal, which do not agree. Pairings from Ngram: pungent smell 135.3, pungent odor 78.2, pungent aroma 42.7 per billion. The stinging-criticism sense is current (pungent wit and satire are in the Datamuse list), so it is shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings: smell, odor and aroma are the same partner three times. The definition also covers flavor, and 'pungent taste' (34482 in the tool) or 'pungent flavor' would show that half. Origin facts match Wiktionary (pungo 'prick, sting'; puncture comes from the same verb). Its first clause runs close to Dictionary.com's line (pungens 'pricking', present participle of pungere 'to prick'), but these are standard short facts. Also means: the stinging, witty sense is current (pungent wit, pungent satire) and the plain definition is clear. Null tone is right for both senses.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (learned borrowing from Latin quiescens) and the Wiktionary page for Latin quiesco (quies "rest" + -sco; "to rest, keep still"). Root quiescere links acquiesce (Latin acquiesco, ad + quiesco). Acquiesce is not named in the origin because acquiescent is one of this word's wrong answers. Hook claim (quiescere, to rest, same root as quiet) is true. Tone formal: all three mark it formal. Pairings from Ngram: quiescent state 50.2, remain quiescent 13.3, quiescent period 10.4 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (quiesco from quies + -sco: rest, be still). The hook's 'same root as quiet' is true, since quietus is the participle of quiesco. quiescere links to acquiesce. formal: all three. Weakest point: 'quiescent state' and 'quiescent period' lean technical, though they are the top partners in the data.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (from Spanish Quixote, the title character of the novel by Miguel de Cervantes, + -ic); the windmill episode is from the novel and matches the hook. No root, as it is a name. Tone null: Oxford says formal, Cambridge literary, Longman nothing. Pairings from Ngram: quixotic quest 8.8, quixotic attempt 3.4, quixotic gesture 2.1 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary and the novel. Null tone is right (OALD formal, Cambridge literary, Longman none). Weakest point: the origin is one long sentence, but it gives the step to today's meaning through the windmills.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Anglo-Norman and Middle French cotidien and their source Latin quotidianus "daily", from quotidie "every day", from an unattested adjective from quot + the locative of dies); "a form of dies" covers that step. No root: dies is not plain to see in other English words. Hook claim (quotidie, every day, built from dies) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Cambridge say formal, Longman literary. Pairings from Ngram: quotidian life 23.1, quotidian reality 7.7, quotidian existence 7.0 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary: it came by way of Anglo-Norman and Middle French, and quotidie comes from quot plus a form of dies. 'A form of' fairly covers the locative and the unattested middle step. Null tone is right (formal in OALD and Cambridge only, literary in Longman). Weakest point: life, reality and existence are near-synonyms. 'quotidian details' or 'quotidian concerns' would vary them.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (rancor + -ous) and the Wiktionary page for English rancor (Old French rancor, Latin rancor "rancidity, grudge", from ranceo "to be rotten"; rancid is a cognate). The rotten-smell root and rancid are left out on purpose: rancid is one of this word's wrong answers ("too far gone to eat"), and the trap list warns against pointing at a wrong answer. Hook claim (built on rancor) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal, but Longman has no entry, so the all-three rule is not met. Pairings from Ngram: rancorous debate 5.9, rancorous dispute 1.2 per billion; the second is less common. Main session, after review 1: dropped "also" (reviewer: it implied an unstated other meaning).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the dangling 'also' is gone, and the origin is now true and complete. Wiktionary's Latin rancor meant rancidity and a grudge, so 'could mean' is accurate, and leaving out the rot meaning keeps the card away from the rancid wrong answer. Weakest point: the second sentence repeats the grudge gloss from the first, so the origin adds little beyond the route through Old French. Null tone is right (Longman has no entry; OALD and Cambridge mark it formal).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English rarefien, Old French rarefier, Latin rarefacere "make rare") and the Wiktionary pages for Latin rarefacio (rare + facio) and Latin rare (adverb of rarus "thin, loose"). Roots rarus (rare, rarity) and facere. Hook says rarus plus facere: the Latin verb uses the adverb rare, from rarus, so the claim is loose but true; 4 and left as it is. Tone null: Cambridge has no label and Oxford and Longman have no entry. Pairings use the participle: rarefied air 29.8, rarefied gas 28.0 per billion (rarefy the air only 0.4), the weakest point. The figurative sense is shown because readers often meet it in rarefied world and rarefied atmosphere.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin facts match Wiktionary (Old French rarefier, Latin rarefacere from rare + facio; rarus 'thin, loose'). The clause 'rarus ..., in its adverb form rārē,' is awkward, and it holds the only macrons on the card. Also means: the figurative sense is real, but learners mostly meet it as the adjective 'rarefied' (rarefied world, rarefied heights). The plain definition's 'few people can relate to it' adds an idea the definition does not have. Roots rarus (rare) and facere are fine.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (French recalcitrant, Latin recalcitro "be disobedient, kick back [as a horse]", from calx "heel"). No root: calx "heel" shows in no common English word, and calcium comes from a different calx. Hook claim (kick back with the heels, calx heel) is true. Tone formal: all three mark it formal. Pairings from Ngram: recalcitrant child 13.4, recalcitrant states 6.8, recalcitrant members 5.5 per billion. Main session, after review 1: set root calx (already named in the origin) so it links with inculcate.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the root calx ('heel') is right. Wiktionary derives recalcitro from re- + calcitro, from calx, and derives inculcate through calco ('tread') from calx 'heel' (its Etymology 2 entry). Worksheet s gives inculcate the same root, so the link is real, and calx is the correct nominative linking form, named in the origin. formal: all three dictionaries. Weakest point: the stem is hard to see in inculcate's spelling (culc), and Latin has a separate calx, 'limestone' (calcium, chalk), which must never get this root id.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin refractarius "obstinate", from refractus, participle of refringere "to break up") and the Wiktionary page for Latin refringo (re- + frango; "to break up or open"). Root frangere matches fractious on worksheet e. Hook changed: "to break back" became "to break up", the gloss Wiktionary gives; the rest (same root as fracture) is true. Tone formal on the first sense: all three mark it formal; the illness, nerve and brick senses are technical (all three mark the illness sense medical). Pairings left empty: the first sense has no common partner (refractory child 1.3, refractory priests 4.8 is a historical term), and the common ones (refractory period, refractory materials) belong to other senses. Shown: the illness and nerve senses, which general readers meet (refractory period is the most common pairing in Datamuse); the furnace-brick sense is hidden.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings: the list is empty, but 'refractory child' (1.25 per billion) and 'refractory children' (0.92) are attested for the first sense, about as often as pairings accepted elsewhere on this sheet. Origin matches Wiktionary (refractarius from refractus; refringere is re- + frango). Longman derives it from refragari instead, but Wiktionary and Dictionary.com agree with the origin. formal: all three. technical on the illness and nerve senses matches OALD and Longman 'medical' and Cambridge 'specialized'. The furnace-brick sense is about as common in the data as the nerve sense, so either choice for Also means is defensible.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin refuto) and the Wiktionary page for Latin refuto ("to check, repress; restrain, oppose; refute"; from re- + an unattested *futo "to beat", left out). Hook claim (refutare, to drive back) matches the Latin "check, repress". Tone formal: all three mark it formal. Watch-out: Oxford and Longman list "say something is not true" as a second sense while usage guides object, so it is stated as a dispute. Pairings from Ngram: refute the claim 14.8, refute the argument 8.7 per billion (refute the charges 6.2 and refute the allegations 3.8 are left out because they usually mean deny).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary's Latin refuto ('check, repress; oppose; refute'). The watch-out calls the 'deny' sense disputed, as Wiktionary's usage note does, and it is a classic mix-up. formal: all three. Weakest point: the hook's 'drive back' paraphrases 'check, repress' rather than using Wiktionary's own gloss, but it agrees with the origin's 'push back'.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin relegatus, participle of relego "to dispatch, banish") and the Wiktionary pages for Latin relego (relego from re- "back" + lego "send, dispatch"; figuratively "to put aside, remove") and Latin delego (de- + lego "send"). Root legare is shown in delegate and legate. Hook claim (relegare, to send away) is true. Tone null: only Longman marks it formal. No watch-out. Pairings from Ngram: relegated to the background 33.9, relegated to the margins 29.2, relegated to a footnote 5.5 per billion. Other senses hidden: "hand a matter over to someone else to settle" is rare and sits next to the meaning of delegate, so it could teach that mix-up (consider dropping it on a main worksheet); "order someone to leave the country" is historical. The common British sports sense (a team moved down a division) is missing from the record; add it on a main worksheet. That gap is why alsoMeans is 4.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary's Latin relego (re- + lego 'send'; 'send away, banish', and figuratively 'put aside'). legare is the right linking form (delegate, legate, legacy). Null tone is right (only Longman marks it formal). Hiding the 'refer' and 'exile' senses is right. Weakest point: the record has no British sports sense (a team moved down a division); that would be a main-worksheet change, not an extras one.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Late Latin remonstro, from re- + monstro) and the Wiktionary pages for Latin remonstro (re- glossed "against" + monstro "to show") and monstro ("to show, point out"); the English page lists both "to point out" and "to object". Root monstrare. Demonstrate is not named in the origin because it is one of this word's wrong answers. Hook changed: "re-, again" became "re-", because Wiktionary glosses this re- as "against", not "again"; the rest is true. Tone formal: all three mark it formal. Pairings from Ngram: remonstrate with 54.9 (the usual pattern, remonstrate with someone), gently remonstrated 1.2 per billion; the second is less common, the weakest point. The hook's "point by point" sits near the demonstrate option ("step by step"); not an origin claim, so left alone.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings: 'remonstrate with' (54.9 per billion) is a grammar pattern, not a partner that shows the meaning, and 'gently remonstrated' is uncommon (1.15). The tool's top partner is 'strongly remonstrated'. Origin matches Wiktionary (re- + monstro 'show'), and the English entry keeps a 'point out, show' sense, which supports the stated shift. Wiktionary's Latin page says Medieval Latin while its English page says Late Latin; either is fine. formal: all three.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English reprobat "condemned, damned", Latin reprobatus, participle of reprobo) and the Wiktionary pages for Latin reprobo (re- + probo, "to disapprove, reject, condemn") and probo ("to approve; to test"; equivalent to probus "good" + -o). Roots probare (approbation) and probus (probity), as the main session asked. Hook changed: "to reject after testing" became "to reject or condemn", since reprobare means to reject or condemn and "after testing" is not in any source; the rest is a metaphor. Tone humorous: Cambridge marks the noun formal and humorous, Longman formal and "often used humorously"; Oxford has only the adjective, so formal is not met by all three. Pairings from Ngram: old reprobate 15.7, young reprobate 1.9 per billion; both partners are generic adjectives, the weakest point.
reviews.checker_notes: Tone: humorous rests on Cambridge ('formal or humorous') and Longman ('formal', 'often used humorously'). Both pair it with formal, and next to a serious definition, 'humorous' alone may suggest the word is only ever a joke. It is defensible. Origin matches Wiktionary (reprobo from re- + probo; probo from probus 'good'; Middle English 'condemned, damned'). probare and probus both show in English words (prove, probation, probity).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin repudiatus, participle of repudio "to cast off, reject", from repudium "rejection, repudiation, divorce"). The Wiktionary page for Latin repudium gives re- + pudeo "to feel ashamed", but the English entry does not, so no root. Hook claim (repudium, a divorce) is true. Tone formal: all three mark it formal. Pairings from Ngram: publicly repudiated 5.0, openly repudiated 2.4 per billion. The debt-and-contract sense is legal (Oxford and Longman mark it law, Cambridge law and finance), so technical and hidden.
reviews.checker_notes: Hook: 'repudium, a formal divorce' is narrower than the source. Wiktionary gives repudium as repudiation, rejection and divorce, and 'formal' is extra. It is not false, but the origin's 'a rejection and also a divorce' is the checked version. Pairings: 'publicly repudiated' and 'openly repudiated' say the same thing twice; 'explicitly' or 'emphatically' (both in the tool) would vary them. formal: all three. Hiding the debt and contract sense is defensible.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin rescindo "to cut back", from re- "back" + scindo "to cut") and the Wiktionary page for Latin rescindo ("to cut off"; figuratively "to annul, revoke"). No root: scindere shows only in rare words such as scission. Hook claim (rescindere, to cut off) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal, Longman does not. Pairings from Ngram: rescind the order 7.3, rescind the offer 3.9 per billion (rescind the decision 1.5 and rescind the ban 1.5 are rarer).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (rescindo: re- 'back' + scindo; 'cut off', and figuratively 'annul'). Empty roots are right. Null tone is right (OALD and Cambridge formal, Longman none). Weakest point: 'rescind the offer' (3.9 per billion) is the weaker pairing; the tool's top partner is 'contract'.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin reticens, participle of reticeo "to keep silence") and the Wiktionary page for Latin reticeo (re- + taceo "to be silent"); tacit comes from tacitus, from tacere, and taciturn from tacitus. Root tacere links tacit and taciturn. Hook claim (reticere, built on tacere, root of tacit) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal, Longman does not. Watch-out: Wiktionary marks the "reluctant" sense proscribed and AHD calls it a usage problem, so it is stated as a dispute. Both other senses are close to the first ("cool and formal in manner", "reluctant to draw attention to yourself") and are hidden; their old plain text named the word, so it was rewritten. Consider dropping them on a main worksheet. Pairings from Ngram: reticent about 90.5, naturally reticent 2.6 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Watch-out: the dispute over 'reluctant' is real and is rightly called disputed, but 'unwilling to talk about yourself' is narrower than the definition (private matters, or a subject such as a deal). Pairings: 'reticent about' (90 per billion) is a grammar pattern; 'naturally reticent' is fine, and a noun partner (reticent man, reticent nature) would show the meaning. Origin facts match Wiktionary (reticeo is re- + taceo). Its clause order is close to AHD's line, but these are standard short facts. Null tone is right (Longman has no label).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English and Middle French reverent and Latin reverens; surface revere + -ent) and the Wiktionary pages for Latin reverens (participle of revereor) and revereor (re- + vereor; "to stand in awe of, respect"). Root revereri is shown in revere, reverence and irreverent. Hook claim (revereri, to stand in awe) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Longman mark it formal, Cambridge does not. Watch-out: reverent and reverend are a common mix-up in writing. Pairings from Ngram: reverent silence 17.1, reverent awe 12.6, reverent hush 4.3 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (Middle French and Latin reverens; revereor 'stand in awe of'; revere comes from the same verb). The watch-out names a real, common mix-up (reverent and Reverend), and what it says is true. Null tone is right (Cambridge has no label). Weakest point: 'reverent hush' (4.3 per billion) is the least common of the three; 'reverent attitude' is in the tool.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle French sanction, Latin sanctio) and the Wiktionary pages for Latin sanctio (sancio + -tio; "law, decree; penalty") and sancio ("to make sacred; to forbid under pain of punishment; to decree, ratify"). Root sancire links sanctimonious, which is on this sheet. Hook claim (sancire, to make sacred or decree) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Longman mark approval formal, but Cambridge British does not. Watch-out: the word has nearly opposite senses. Pairings from Ngram, all in the approval sense: official sanction 55.3, divine sanction 48.9, royal sanction 8.6 per billion (legal sanction 54.7 is left out because it often means a penalty). The penalty sense is very common (economic sanctions leads the Datamuse list), so it is shown. Main session, after review 1: added the confirm/ratify sense of sancire, which links the approval meaning.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the origin now matches Wiktionary in full. sanctio meant a decree or a penalty, and sancio meant 'make sacred' and also 'confirm, ratify', which gives the step to both of today's meanings. It is in its own words, not AHD's or Dictionary.com's. The watch-out is unchanged: a real mix-up, stated correctly, but its example 'the sanction of the court' is Oxford Learner's own example ('These changes will require the sanction of the court'), so use another. Null tone is right. The penalty sense under Also means is right, and its plain definition is clear.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (sanctimony + -ous) and the Wiktionary pages for English sanctimony (Middle French sanctimonie, Latin sanctimonia, from sanctus "holy" + -monia; obsolete sense "a state of holiness") and Latin sanctus (participle of sancio). Root sancire links sanction. Hook claim (sanctus, holy, as in saint and sanctuary) is true. Tone disapproving: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it disapproving. Pairings from Ngram: sanctimonious tone 2.0, sanctimonious attitude 1.6, sanctimonious hypocrite 1.3 per billion; low because the word is rare, the weakest point.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary: sanctimony from Latin sanctimonia, from sanctus, which is sancio's participle, and sanctimony's obsolete 'state of holiness' sense. sancire links it with sanction. disapproving: all three dictionaries. Weakest point: the hook says it comes from sanctus, skipping sanctimonia, which is fine as ancestry.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary accolade: English section (French accolade, via Occitan acolada, from Vulgar Latin *accollo, ad- + collum "neck", English collar) and French section (Old French acolee, verb acoler). The knighting embrace is Wiktionary's historical sense; the praise sense dates from 1852. Tone from the cached Oxford Learner's, Cambridge and Longman pages: Oxford and Cambridge formal, Longman none, so null. Other sense (knighting rite) is historical, not shown. Hook says "comes from French accoler": loose, since the noun is French accolade formed on Old French acoler (modern accoler), but not false; left unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the hook says French accoler while the origin says French accolade. Both hold: Wiktionary's French entry traces accolade to Old French acoler (ad + collum), and the English entry backs the knighting embrace and the later sense of praise.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary acerbic (17th century, Latin acerbus) and the Latin acerbus page fetched through the API (senses: of taste harsh, unripe, sour; of a person rough, severe, bitter; from Proto-Italic *akris, the source of acer, which supports the hook's "related to acer"). Root acerbus also links exacerbate (Latin acerbo, from acerbus). Tone from the cached Oxford Learner's, Cambridge and Longman pages: Oxford and Cambridge formal, Longman none, so null. Taste sense is rare, not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the unripe-fruit and harsh-person claims go past the English entry, but the Latin acerbus page supports them (of taste: unripe, sour; of a person: harsh, bitter), and it backs the hook's link to acer (both from Proto-Italic *akris).

Pairings: "complete" and "direct" from the tool list (15, 8), "very antithesis" 55.
reviews.checker_notes: Also means (4): the rhetorical-device sense is hidden; Oxford calls it the earliest current sense and a learner may meet it in literature classes, so showing it with technical is worth considering. Origin follows Wiktionary's surface analysis (anti- + thesis); dictionaries derive it from antitithenai, which agrees. Tone null right: Oxford and Longman formal, Cambridge not.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English gainsayen, gain- + say) and the Wiktionary page gain- (Old English gean-, 'against'; 'More at again'), which also supports the hook's 'as in against'; Oxford, Longman and AHD agree. No root: gain- is a prefix and say is English. Hook true, unchanged. Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it formal. Pairings: gainsay the fact 1.94 (the top object in 'gainsay the *'), dare gainsay 1.23 per billion (Datamuse 'dare'); the verb is rare, hence 4.
reviews.checker_notes: All claims match Wiktionary (Middle English gainsayen, gain- + say; the gain- page gives 'against'). Formal in Oxford, Cambridge and Longman. Weakest point: only two pairings, and 'dare gainsay' (1.23 per billion) shows the usual negative frame rather than the meaning; 'gainsay the fact' (1.94) is the one that shows it. The hook's "'against' (as in against)" reads awkwardly but is true.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py, which hedges every step ('Unknown, possibly from obsolete Middle English gawren, to stare'); Oxford and AHD also say origin unknown, so the origin says unknown and keeps the 'may' on gawren and leaves out the Old Norse steps. Hook is a sound-alike (glare) with no origin claim. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge. Pairings: garish colors 10.88, light 7.86, neon 5.27 per billion, all top Datamuse nouns.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin keeps Wiktionary's hedge (unknown, possibly Middle English gawren 'to stare'). Disapproving in Oxford and Cambridge, Longman unlabelled. Pairings are top Datamuse partners (garish light 7.9, garish neon 5.3 per billion). Weakest point: 'garish light' leans on glare rather than the color-and-taste definition, though Cambridge's 'unpleasantly bright' covers it.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (variant of german, 'having the same parents; related', its current sense from allusions to Shakespeare's Hamlet) and the Wiktionary page german (Old French germain, Latin germanus, senses 'same parents' and obsolete 'closely related, akin'); Oxford's word origin agrees. Hook (Latin germanus, having the same parents) true, unchanged. No root: germanus shows in no common English word. Tone formal: all three learner's dictionaries. Pairings: germane to the discussion 3.59, germane to the question 2.73 (Datamuse 'question'), directly germane 5.35 per billion; particularly germane (22.2) is commoner but fits any adjective.
reviews.checker_notes: Checked against Wiktionary germane (variant of german; this sense from allusions to its use in Hamlet) and german (from Latin germanus; obsolete 'closely related, akin'). Formal in all three. Pairings: directly germane 5.4, germane to the discussion 3.6, to the question 2.7 per billion. Weakest point: the opening 'A form of the old word german' stays close to Wiktionary's 'A variant form of german', though it is a bare fact.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle French grandiloquent, Latin grandiloquus, grandis 'great' + loquens, from loquor 'to speak'; compare eloquent); Oxford, Longman and AHD agree. Roots grandis (as on aggrandize) and loqui (as on eloquent and loquacious). Hook true, unchanged. Tone: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal and disapproving, Longman formal; as on intransigent, disapproving (two of three) is set because it is the label that matters for use. Pairings: style 1.68, language 1.43, title 1.07 per billion, the top Datamuse nouns, but rare.
reviews.checker_notes: Matches Wiktionary (Middle French, Latin grandiloquus, grandis + loquens from loquor; compare eloquent); loquacious is also from loqui. Roots grandis and loqui are spelled as on aggrandize and eloquent. Pairings style, title, language are the top partners. Weakest point: all three dictionaries also mark it formal, so either label fits; disapproving (Oxford, Cambridge) is the more useful one.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin gratuitus 'free', from gratia 'favor', gratus), the Latin page gratuitus (from the root of gratia and gratus; senses 'freely given', 'vain, futile') and the English page's sense order (given freely, then unjustified), which supports the step from free to uncalled for. Root gratia (gratis, ingratiate on worksheet s). Hook (shares its root with gratis) true: Wiktionary gratis is from Latin gratis and lists gratuitous as related. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge. Pairings: violence 28.38, cruelty 5.85, insult 5.33 per billion. Also means: the 'free' sense is shown; it is the top Datamuse use (services, advice, instruction, relief) and Longman Business has it under LAW, but Oxford and Cambridge omit it, hence 4.
reviews.checker_notes: Checked against Wiktionary gratuitous (Latin gratuitus, from gratia), Latin gratuitus ('freely given', from the root of gratia) and gratis (from Latin gratis), so the hook's shared root holds. Disapproving in Oxford and Cambridge. Also means: 'given freely' is Wiktionary's sense 1 and common in the data (gratuitous services, advice). Weakest point: 'given for nothing came to mean done for no good reason' is a fair reading of the two senses, not a step Wiktionary states.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Old French herbergeor, from herbergier 'to shelter', Germanic 'army camp, shelter'; originally a person sent ahead to arrange lodgings) and the English page's obsolete sense (the officer of the English royal household who went before the court to prepare lodgings), which supports the hook; unchanged. No root. Tone literary: Cambridge and Longman mark it literary, Oxford 'formal or literary'; formal is not set because Cambridge does not mark it. Pairings: harbinger of doom 12.76, of spring 8.45 (both in Wiktionary's collocations), early harbinger 2.91 per billion (Datamuse 'early').
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary: herbergeor from herbergier 'to shelter', 'originally a person sent in advance to arrange lodgings', and the obsolete sense of the royal-household officer who went ahead of the travelling court. Literary in all three (Oxford 'formal or literary'). Pairings: harbinger of doom 12.8, of spring 8.5, early harbinger 2.9 per billion. Weakest point: the hook's 'you knew the king himself was coming' is an inference, though a fair one.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (learned borrowing from Ancient Greek hubris, 'pride, insolence, outrage') and the English sense ('originally, in Greek mythology, toward the gods'). No root. Hook (Greek word for insolent, outrageous behavior) true, unchanged; its proverb is a memory aid, not an origin claim. Tone literary: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it literary. Pairings: human 12.05, imperial 7.94, intellectual 2.72 per billion, all from Datamuse.
