reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary: borrowed from Greek hubris ('pride, insolence, outrage'), and its definition, 'originally (Greek mythology) toward the gods', backs the second clause. Literary in all three. Pairings (4): human 12.1, imperial 7.9, intellectual 2.7 per billion are common, but they are classifying adjectives that do not show the meaning, and 'imperial hubris' is partly the title of a 2004 book; 'act of hubris' (7.7) would show it.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Greek idiosynkrasia, 'one's own temperament', from idios + syn + krasis) and the Greek page krasis ('mixture; temperament'), which supports the hook's 'a blend'; Oxford and AHD agree. Root idios (idiom, idiot). Hook true, unchanged. Tone null: no label in any of the three. Watch out: a spelling note, as on callous; the Wiktionary page idiosyncracy says that spelling is commonly considered a misspelling while Webster's Third gives both, so the note says 'widely treated as a mistake' rather than calling it wrong. Pairings: personal 13.54, individual 8.52, little 6.94 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (idiosynkrasia, idios + syn + krasis) and the Greek krasis page ('mixture', 'temperament'), so 'a mixing' and the hook's 'a blend' hold. Root idios is right. No label in any of the three. Watch out (4): true, and hedged as Wiktionary's idiosyncracy usage note is ('commonly considered a misspelling'), and the -cracy slip is common, but it is a spelling note rather than the meaning mix-up the field is for, and it repeats the origin's 'from Greek krasis, a mixing'.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin ignominiosus, from ignominia, from ig- for in- 'not' + nomen 'name; good name, reputation') and Oxford's word origin. Root nomen (nominate, nominal, misnomer on worksheet w). Hook (nomen, name, as in nominate) true, unchanged. Tone null: Oxford and Longman say formal but Cambridge literary, so neither label has the agreement it needs. Pairings: end 22.49, defeat 16.74, retreat 7.30 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Matches Wiktionary (ignominiosus, from ignominia, from ig-, a variant of in- 'not', + nomen 'name, good name'). Root nomen is right. Oxford and Longman formal, Cambridge literary, so null is right. Pairings end, defeat, retreat are top partners. Weakest point: the origin skips the Middle French route Wiktionary gives as an alternative, which is fine for one line.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Old French impetueux, Late Latin impetuosus 'violent', Latin impetus 'attack, violence') and the Latin pages impetus (from impeto, 'to rush upon, attack'; an intermediate form is hedged, so it is left out) and impeto (in- + peto). Root petere, the form petulant uses (coordinator's note). Hook (impetus, a rush or attack) true: the Latin page gives 'an attack, a charge' and 'a rapid motion'. Tone null: no label in any of the three. Pairings: nature 9.30, youth 5.33, temper 2.71 per billion; impetuous torrent is left out as the other sense. Other sense (surging like floodwater) kept hidden: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman omit it, and dictionary.com (poetic) and WordUp (literary) label it, so it is set literary.
reviews.checker_notes: Checked against Wiktionary impetuous, Latin impetus ('attack', from impeto), impeto ('to rush upon, assail', in- + peto) and peto ('seek', 'attack'). Root petere matches petulant. Null tone is right; the hidden sense's literary label matches Collins's 'poetic' (the learner's dictionaries lack that sense), and hiding it is right. Weakest point: that hidden sense's plain ('Rushing along with violent force') sits near Collins ('rushing') and AHD ('violent force').

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle French importuner, Medieval Latin importunor, Latin importunus 'unfit, troublesome', originally 'having no harbor') and the Latin page importunus (in- + portus + -nus; antonym opportunus), which supports the hook's 'opposite of opportunus'; unchanged. Root portus (port, opportune). Tone formal: all three learner's dictionaries. Pairings left empty: the Datamuse partners are rare in Ngram (constantly importuned 0.41, repeatedly 0.28, earnestly 0.40 per billion) and the common ones are generic (importuned by 8.30, importuned him 5.21).
reviews.checker_notes: Matches Wiktionary importune and Latin importunus (in- + portus; 'inconvenient, unsuitable', 'annoying'; originally 'having no harbor'; antonym opportunus, which backs the hook). Formal in all three. Empty pairings are right: nothing with a meaning partner is common (importuned by 8.3 per billion is generic, importune him for 0.43). Weakest point: Cambridge's legal sense (soliciting for sex) is not in the record; rare for a general reader.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin incorrigibilis, in- + corrigere 'to correct' + -ibilis); Oxford, Longman and AHD agree. Root corrigere: it shows in corrigible and, less visibly, in correct, so origin 4. Hook true, unchanged. Tone humorous: Cambridge labels it humorous, Oxford 'disapproving or humorous', and Longman's definition says it is often used humorously; 4 because serious uses (incorrigible offenders) remain. Pairings: rogue 2.36, optimist 1.93, offenders 1.32 per billion, the top Datamuse nouns but not frequent.
reviews.checker_notes: Matches Wiktionary (incorrigibilis, in- + corrigere + -ibilis). Humorous: Oxford 'disapproving or humorous', Cambridge 'mainly humorous', Longman 'often used humorously'. Pairings optimist, rogue, offenders are top partners. Weakest point: the root corrigere shows in English mostly through correct (from its participle) and corrigendum, so the link is less visible than for most roots.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin indefatigabilis 'untiring', in- + defatigo 'to tire out') and the Latin page defatigo (de- + fatigo; 'to tire out or exhaust'); Longman and Oxford tie it to fatigue through fatigare. Root fatigare (fatigue). Hook (fatigue hidden inside it) true, unchanged. Tone formal: Oxford (formal, approving), Cambridge and Longman. Pairings: energy 7.37, efforts 6.45, worker 6.20 per billion; indefatigable industry is left out because it uses industry in its old sense of hard work.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin (4): the facts match Wiktionary (indefatigabilis, in- + defatigo 'to tire out'; defatigo is de- + fatigo), but 'defatigare, a form of fatigare' is loose: it is fatigare with the prefix de-. Root fatigare (fatigue) is right. Formal in all three. Pairings energy, efforts, worker are top partners.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (French insouciant, in- 'not' + souciant 'worrying', 1828) and AHD (souciant, present participle of soucier). No root. Hook (in- plus soucier, to worry; souci, worry) true, unchanged. Tone null: Oxford formal, Cambridge literary, and Longman has only insouciance (formal), fetched to scratch since Longman has no insouciant page. Pairings: smile 1.89, attitude 1.79, shrug 1.68 per billion, the top Datamuse nouns but rare.
reviews.checker_notes: Matches Wiktionary (French insouciant, in- + souciant 'worrying', 1828). Oxford and Longman (insouciance) formal, Cambridge literary, so null is right. Pairings attitude 1.8, shrug 1.7 per billion and smile are top partners. Weakest point: the hook says in- plus soucier, where the word is in- plus its participle souciant; harmless.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English inuren, in- + ure 'practise, exercise') and the Wiktionary page ure (obsolete, only in 'in ure' and 'out of ure': use, practice), which supports the hook's 'in ure, in use'; Oxford and AHD agree. No root. Tone null: Oxford (inure to) and Cambridge mark it formal, Longman (inure to, fetched to scratch) has no label. Pairings: become inured 26.28, inured to hardship 3.22, inured to violence 1.99 per billion. Also means 4: the record has only one sense, but the legal sense (to take effect, as in 'inure to the benefit of') is in Wiktionary and dominates Datamuse (earnings inures, benefit inuring); consider adding it as an other sense on a main worksheet.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (inuren, in- + ure; ure 'use, practice', obsolete, only in 'in ure' and 'out of ure'). Oxford and Cambridge formal, Longman unlabelled, so null is right. Pairings: become inured 26.3, inured to hardship 3.2, to violence 2.0 per billion. Also means (4): the record lacks Wiktionary's chiefly legal sense 'to take effect' ('inures to the benefit of'), which dominates inure and inures in the collocation data; it is technical, so leaving it out is defensible, but it is a main-worksheet decision.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle French invective, Medieval Latin invectiva 'abusive speech', Latin invectivus, invectus, inveho 'bring in', in- + veho 'carry'; see vehicle) and the Latin page inveho (senses 'carry into', 'attack', passive 'attack with words, inveigh against'). Root vehere (vehicle, inveigh). Hook changed: it said invehi is literally 'to be carried against', but Wiktionary glosses the in- as 'in' and the verb as 'carry into', and Oxford gives 'be carried into', so 'against' became 'into'. Tone formal: all three. Pairings: stream of invective 8.29, personal 5.16, bitter 4.33 per billion (personal and bitter top Datamuse).
reviews.checker_notes: Matches Wiktionary invective (Medieval Latin invectiva 'abusive speech', from invectus, inveho, in- + veho; see vehicle) and Latin inveho (passive: 'to attack with words'). The hook fix ('carried into' for 'carried against') follows inveho's literal sense. Formal in all three. Pairings: stream of invective 8.3, personal 5.2, bitter 4.3 per billion. Weakest point: 'a tirade' for invectiva drops the 'abusive' part.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin iocularis, from ioculus 'a little jest', diminutive of iocus 'a jest') and the Wiktionary pages iocus and joke (joke from Latin iocus), which support the hook; unchanged. Spelled with j as in the hook, Oxford and Longman. Root jocus (joke, jocose). Tone formal: all three. Pairings: tone 10.73, manner 5.32, remark 2.65 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Matches Wiktionary jocular (iocularis, ioculus 'a little jest', iocus 'a jest'), joke (from Latin iocus) and iocus. Root jocus is right. Formal in all three. Pairings tone, manner, remark are top partners. Weakest point: the hook repeats the origin almost word for word, which the owner allows.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (French judicieux, ultimately from Latin iudico; related to judge, judicial) and the Latin page iudicium (from iudico 'to judge' + -ium, alternative form judicium); Oxford, Longman and AHD give Latin judicium. Root judicare, in the j spelling English dictionaries use, so adjudicate (worksheet t) can share it. Hook (judicium, judgment) true, unchanged. Tone null: Oxford and Longman say formal, Cambridge has no label. Watch out: judicial and judicious are a known confusable pair (Cambridge's entry says 'Compare judicial' and dictionary.com has a usage note on the two); 4 because I have no count of how often they are confused. Pairings: use 208.36, choice 34.49, selection 26.98 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Wiktionary says only 'from French judicieux, ultimately derived from Latin iudico' (its French judicieux page, fetched today, says the same), and Latin iudicium is iudico + -ium. The step 'French built judicieux on judicium' (origin and hook) is not stated there but agrees with it and with standard sources, so it stands; that is the weakest point. Watch out: judicial/judicious is a classic confusable, stated briefly and correctly. Oxford and Longman formal, Cambridge none, so null is right.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin lachrymosus, lacrimosus, from lacrima 'tear' + -osus; from Old Latin dacrima, Proto-Indo-European *dakru-, cognate with English tear) and Oxford and AHD. No root: lacrima shows only in rare words such as lacrimal. Hook (lacrima, a tear) true, unchanged. Tone null on both senses: Oxford and Longman formal, Cambridge literary. Pairings left empty: the first-sense partners are rare (lachrymose voice 0.43, tone 0.26 per billion) and the others (sentimentality, drama) belong to the second sense. Also means: the 'making people cry' sense is shown; Oxford ('making you cry'), AHD and dictionary.com list it, and vocabulary.com notes its use for sentimental books and films.
reviews.checker_notes: Matches Wiktionary (lacrimosus, lacrima 'tear', cognate with English tear). Oxford and Longman formal, Cambridge literary, so null is right. Empty pairings are right (lachrymose voice 0.43 per billion; 'lachrymose conception' is a term from Jewish historiography). Also means (4): the tear-jerker sense is current (Oxford 'making you cry'), but 'Meant to make an audience cry' adds intent where the sense is about the effect.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (first attested 1637, probably lam 'beat' + baste 'beat'), the Wiktionary pages lam ('to beat or thrash', listing lambaste) and baste (etymology 3, 'to beat with a stick', listing lambaste); AHD also says perhaps. The origin keeps 'probably'. Hook changed: 'begins with lam, an old verb meaning to beat hard' stated the hedged step as fact; it now says 'probably the old verb'. Tone null: Oxford and Longman have the entry only as lambast (both formal, fetched to scratch), Cambridge has no label. Pairings: critics lambasted 2.14, publicly lambasted 1.35 per billion (Datamuse 'critics', 'publicly'). The thrash sense stays hidden: Wiktionary calls it dated in British English and the learner's dictionaries omit it.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin (4): facts and hedge match Wiktionary (first attested 1637; probably lam 'beat' + baste 'beat'; the lam and baste pages confirm both), but it opens with Dictionary.com's stock 'First recorded in' + date and keeps the date-then-probably-lam-plus-baste order that Dictionary.com and Wiktionary share; with so few facts that comes close to a shared frame. The hook fix (adding 'probably') keeps the hedge. Oxford and Longman (lambast) formal, Cambridge none, so null is right. Pairings: critics lambasted 2.1, publicly lambasted 1.4 per billion.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle French languide or Latin languidus, from langueo 'to be faint or weak'; see languish) and the Latin page langueo (derived terms include languor). Root languere (languish, languor). Hook 4: Latin languere is right, but Wiktionary glosses it 'to be faint, weak' and 'listless', not 'droop'; the hook's 'lack strength' matches, so it is left as is. Tone literary: Cambridge and Longman. Pairings: voice 6.37, air 6.36, grace 6.13 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Matches Wiktionary languid (Middle French languide or Latin languidus, from langueo; see languish) and Latin langueo ('to be faint, weak'; 'listless'). Root languere is right. Cambridge and Longman literary. Pairings: languid air 6.4, grace 6.1 per billion, and voice. Weakest point: 'From Latin languidus' drops the Middle French route Wiktionary gives as an alternative; fine for one line.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English largesse, Old French largesce 'generosity', from large 'big, generous, wide') and the Latin page largus ('abundant, plentiful', 'bountiful, liberal'), which supports the hook's 'generous as well as abundant'; Oxford, Longman and AHD agree. Root largus (large, enlarge). Tone formal on both senses: Oxford ('formal or humorous'), Cambridge and Longman mark the entry formal, covering the giving and the money given. Pairings: government 11.01, federal 5.29, royal 2.79 per billion. The other sense (the gifts themselves) stays hidden: Oxford folds it into one sense with the first.
reviews.checker_notes: Matches Wiktionary largesse (Old French largesce, from large 'generous, wide') and Latin largus ('abundant, plentiful'; 'bountiful, liberal', so the hook's 'generous as well as abundant' holds). Cambridge and Longman formal and Oxford 'formal or humorous', so formal is in all three, on the hidden sense too; hiding the near-repeat sense is right. Weakest point: Oxford's 'or humorous' is lost with formal alone.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (lion + -ize) and the Wiktionary page lion (sense 'a famous person regarded with interest and curiosity', quoted from the 1800s), which supports the hook's 'old use of lion for a celebrity'; the Tower of London story is not in Wiktionary and is not used. No root. Tone null: Oxford formal, Longman written, Cambridge none. Pairings left empty: lionized by 10.77 is generic and lionized by the press is 0.34 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Wiktionary gives only lion + -ize; its lion page has 'a famous person regarded with interest and curiosity', which supports the origin and hook. Origin (4): 'a famous person whom everyone is curious to see' stays close to that gloss (famous person, curiosity); say it from another angle. Oxford formal, Cambridge none, Longman 'written', so null is right. Empty pairings are right: only 'lionized by' and 'was lionized' are common, and they do not show the meaning.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin lugubris 'mournful; gloomy' + -ious) and the Latin page lugubris (from the root of lugeo 'mourn, lament'); Oxford, Longman and AHD agree. No root: lugere shows in no common English word. Hook (lugere, to mourn) true, unchanged. Tone literary: Cambridge and Longman (Longman adds 'sometimes used humorously'). Pairings: face 3.63, expression 2.74, voice 2.09 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Matches Wiktionary lugubrious (Latin lugubris 'mournful; gloomy', with -ious) and Latin lugubris ('from the root of lugeo, mourn'), so the hedge 'from the root of lugere' is right. Cambridge and Longman literary (Longman: 'sometimes used humorously', which backs the closing clause). Pairings face, expression, voice are top partners. Weakest point: 'from the root of lugere' echoes the Latin page's own phrase, though it is a short fact.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary malevolent (Latin malevolens from male "badly" + volens "wishing", from velle "to wish") and volition (Latin volo, velle), so velle links it with volition. Hook matches; unchanged. Tone null: Oxford and Longman say formal, Cambridge literary, so formal is not on all three and literary on only one. No common mix-up. Pairings from the collocations lists (intent, spirit, eyes; 10.6, 19.4 and 9.8 per billion); I left out "malevolent forces" because forces belong to the other sense. The other sense (of forces rather than people) is a near-repeat of the first, so not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: All claims check out against Wiktionary (male, volens, velle) and volition's entry (from volo, velle). Null tone is right: Oxford and Longman mark it formal, Cambridge literary. Weakest point: 'malevolent spirit' (19.4 per billion) leans on supernatural beings; 'malevolent intent' and 'malevolent eyes' show the first sense more directly. Hiding the forces sense is right, as a near repeat.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary mawkish (mawk + -ish; archaic senses "feeling sick, queasy" and "sickening or insipid in taste or smell") and mawk (obsolete or dialect "a maggot", from Middle English mawke, from Old Norse). Hook change: "first described food" became "once described food". Wiktionary gives both archaic senses without an order, and the queasy (person) sense may be the older one, so "first" claimed more than the sources show. No root. Tone null: only Oxford marks it disapproving. Pairings: the two sentiment nouns at the top of the collocations list (3.2 and 1.7 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and the changed hook match Wiktionary (mawk, maggot, from Old Norse; archaic senses 'queasy' and 'sickening or insipid in taste or smell'). Null tone is right (only Oxford marks it disapproving). Weakest point: the two pairings are near repeats ('mawkish sentimentality' 3.16, 'mawkish sentiment' 1.70); a second partner from the tool's list would add more.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary misanthrope (Ancient Greek miseo "I hate" + anthropos "man; human"); misein is the infinitive, the linking form for Greek verbs. Both roots show in other English words (misogyny, anthropology). Hook matches; unchanged. Tone null: only Oxford says formal, Cambridge has no label, and Longman has no entry. Pairings empty: the best in the collocations list, "confirmed misanthrope", is 0.56 per billion and the rest are lower, so nothing is common enough.
reviews.checker_notes: misein and anthropos match Wiktionary and are good linking roots (misogyny, philanthropy, anthropology). Null tone is right (only Oxford marks it formal). Empty pairings are right: 'confirmed misanthrope' is 0.56 per billion. Weakest point: none of note.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary modicum (Latin modicum "a little", neuter of modicus "moderate", from modus "a measure") and modus. Hook matches; unchanged. Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman (at its entry "a modicum of something") all mark it formal. Pairings from the "modicum of *" slot (privacy 17.0, respect 13.0, success 12.6 per billion; "a modicum of" is 489).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (noun use of modicus, from modus); modus is a good root (mode, moderate, modest). formal is right: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman ('a modicum of something') all mark it. All three pairings are the top fillers of 'a modicum of *'. Weakest point: the hook says 'comes from modus' and skips modicus, which is fine for a hook.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary mordant (French mordant, from Latin mordeo), mordeo ("to bite; to sting") and remorse (Latin remordeo, literally "to bite back", from re- + mordeo); Longman gives French mordant as the present participle of mordre "to bite". Hook matches; unchanged. Tone formal: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal, and so does Longman at its entry "mordant wit/satire/humour". Pairings: the top nouns in the collocations list (wit 5.7, humor 2.6, satire 1.3 per billion); the dye nouns belong to the noun sense.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (French mordant from Latin mordeo) and remorse's entry (remordeo, from mordeo). formal is right: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman ('mordant wit/satire/humour') all mark it. Pairings are the tool's top three. Weakest point: mordere shows in English mainly through remorse, a thin but real link.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary obviate (Latin obviatus, from obvio), obvio ("to meet; to prevent, hinder", from obvius), obvius (ob- + via) and obvious (Latin obvius, from ob- + via). Hook ("shares Latin via with obvious") matches; unchanged. Tone formal: all three learner's dictionaries. No watch-out: Wiktionary notes that some call "obviate the need" redundant and that the objection is groundless, which is not a misreading. Pairings: "obviate the need" (129.7 per billion; "need" is the top word after obviates) and "obviate the necessity" (13.5).
reviews.checker_notes: Facts check out against Wiktionary's obvio ('to meet', 'to prevent', post-classical), obvius ('in the way', from ob and via) and obvious. Weakest point: the closing 'to obviate a need is to meet it early' can read as the English idiom 'meet a need' (satisfy it), the opposite of making it unneeded. Pairings: 'obviate the necessity' (13.5) repeats 'obviate the need' (129); 'obviate the risk' or 'the problem' would show more. formal is right on all three dictionaries.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary odious (Middle English, from Old French odieus, from Latin odiosus, from odium "hate") and odium. Hook matches; unchanged. Tone formal: all three learner's dictionaries. Pairings from the collocations list (task 4.4, crime 2.8, comparisons 2.5 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Old French odieus, Latin odiosus, odium) and English odium's entry. formal is right on all three dictionaries. Weakest point: the root odium links only to the uncommon English word odium, and 'odious comparisons' (2.47) is the proverb's set phrase rather than a plain use of the first sense.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary panegyric (French panegyrique, from Ancient Greek panegyrikos), panegyrikos (from panegyris "festival, assembly"; "of or for a public festival or assembly", by extension "flattering") and panegyris (pan- + agyris, the Aeolic form of agora; "a general or national assembly; festival"). No root: pan is a bare prefix, and agora would need more words than the origin can carry. Hook ("panegyris, a gathering of all the people") matches; unchanged. Tone formal: all three (Longman "old-fashioned formal"). Pairings: adjectives from the collocations list that show praise (glowing 0.58, fulsome 0.54, funeral 0.78 per billion); the word is rare, so all its pairings are, hence 4.
reviews.checker_notes: Facts check out against Wiktionary's panegyrikos ('of or for a public festival or assembly', 'by extension flattering') and panegyris (pan- plus agyris, 'assembly'). Origin (4): the step from a festival assembly to a speech of praise is left to 'could also mean flattering'; it never says that festival speeches praised. Hook (4): 'it was praise spoken before the whole crowd' simplifies a festival oration, loose but not false. formal is right on all three dictionaries.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary pariah (Tamil paraiyar, from paraiyan "drummer", from parai "drum", or the Malayalam equivalent; the drummers were in the lower strata of the caste system; alternatively from Sanskrit para "distant; outsider"). Oxford and Longman give the Tamil account. I kept Wiktionary's alternative. Hook gives the Tamil account Oxford and Longman give; unchanged. Tone null: Oxford's "sometimes offensive" and Cambridge's "old-fashioned offensive" (on the caste sense) are not labels the app uses. Pairings from the collocations list (social pariah 17.4, pariah status 17.2, become a pariah 8.5 per billion); "pariah state" is about countries.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary and keeps its Sanskrit alternative; it leaves out the Malayalam source Wiktionary also names, which a learner does not need. Hook (4): gives the Tamil account as the whole story, without the alternative the origin keeps; Oxford, AHD and Dictionary.com all give Tamil, so no change is required. Null tone is right (Oxford's 'sometimes offensive' is not one of our labels).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary pejorative (Late Latin peioratus, past participle of peiorare "worsen", from Latin peior "worse", + -ive). No root: peior shows in no common English word. Hook ("Latin pejor, worse") matches; pejor is the usual variant spelling. Tone formal: all three learner's dictionaries. Pairings: the top nouns in the collocations list (term 68.3, sense 53.9, connotations 22.3 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Late Latin peiorare, from peior). formal is right on all three dictionaries. Pairings are the tool's top nouns. Weakest point: the gloss 'to make worse' is Longman's and Oxford's, a short shared fact.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary peripatetic (French peripatetique, from Latin peripateticus, from Ancient Greek peripatetikos "given to walking around", from peripateo "to walk around", from peri + pateo) and Peripatetic (Aristotle's school was named either for his supposed habit of teaching while walking the walkways of the Lyceum or for the walkways themselves); peripatos also glossed "a covered walk". Hook change: Wiktionary gives two explanations, so "Aristotle's pupils got the name from the covered walk" became "Aristotle's pupils perhaps got the name from the covered walk". No root: peri is a bare prefix and pateo shows in no common English word. Tone formal: all three. Pairings from the collocations list (life 11.1, existence 6.1, teacher 2.0 per billion). The Aristotle sense is shown with technical: "peripatetic school" and "peripatetic philosophy" lead the collocation data (13.3 and 9.1 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and the changed hook match Wiktionary's Peripatetic entry (named for Aristotle's supposed teaching while walking the Lyceum's walkways, or for the walkways), and the hedge is kept in both. formal is right on all three dictionaries. Also means (4): showing the Aristotle sense is right ('peripatetic school', 'philosophy', 'philosopher' are the word's top collocates), but its plain follows the frame Dictionary.com, AHD and Wiktionary share ('of or relating to Aristotle ... school of philosophy ... followers'), and it does not say the sense is usually capitalized.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary plaudit (for earlier plaudite, from Latin plaudite, plural imperative of plaudere), plaudo ("to strike, clap; to applaud"), applaud (ad + plaudere) and plausible (plausibilis, from plaudere). Tone formal: Cambridge, and Oxford and Longman at their entries for plaudits. Pairings from the collocations list (won 8.0, earned 2.3, critical 2.2 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (earlier plaudite, plural imperative of plaudere) and the applaud and plausible entries. The hook's 'cue that closed a Roman comedy' is supported by Wiktionary's plaudo entry (Plaudite! is the last word of Terence's Andria) and by AHD. formal is right: Cambridge, Oxford ('plaudits') and Longman ('plaudits') all mark it. Weakest point: none of note.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary proscribe (Middle English, from Latin proscribo "to proclaim, forbid, banish") and proscribo (pro- + scribo "write"; "to advertise, proclaim; to publish; to proscribe, ban; to outlaw, banish"). Hook matches; unchanged. Tone formal: all three learner's dictionaries. Watch-out: proscribe and prescribe are a classic confusion with nearly opposite meanings. Pairings from the collocations list (proscribed conduct 8.4, proscribed by law 6.2, law proscribes 3.0 per billion). The other sense (outlawing and banishing a person) is mainly historical, so not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin (4): 'to publish in writing' is Dictionary.com's (Random House) gloss of proscribere word for word; Wiktionary's Latin entry gives 'to advertise, proclaim', 'to publish', 'to outlaw, banish'. The posting of outlaws' names goes past Wiktionary but AHD supports it ('to put up someone's name as outlawed'). The watch-out is a real, common mix-up (Oxford has a prescribe/proscribe note) and is stated in the writer's own words. formal is right on all three dictionaries.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary querulous (Old French querelos, from Late Latin querulosus, from Latin querulus, from queror "to complain") and quarrel (Latin querela, from queri "to complain"). Hook matches; unchanged. Tone formal: all three (Oxford adds disapproving, only one source). Pairings: the top nouns in the collocations list (voice 15.8, tone 5.1, note 2.4 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Old French querelos, Late Latin querulosus, queror) and quarrel's entry (querela, from queri). formal is right on all three dictionaries. Watch out (4): no note, though Vocabulary.com and Dictionary.com both warn that querulous is not related to query, a misreading learners make; null is defensible since it is not a classic like enervate.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary rapacious ("perhaps from rapacity", ultimately from Latin rapax "grasping, greedy"), rapax (from rapio "to grab" + -ax) and rapio ("to snatch, grab, carry off"); I kept the "perhaps". Hook ("rapere, to seize") matches; unchanged. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal and disapproving, Longman formal. Pairings from the collocations list (appetite 3.2, greed 3.0, landlords 1.9 per billion). The animal sense is not shown: Wiktionary calls it dated except of birds, and no learner's dictionary lists it.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin keeps Wiktionary's 'perhaps' on rapacity; rapax and rapere ('to snatch, carry off') match the Latin entries; rapere is a good root (rapt, rapture, rapid). disapproving is right (Oxford, Cambridge). Hiding the animal sense is right. Weakest point: 'rapacious greed' (3.01) is redundant; 'rapacious landlords' and 'rapacious appetite' carry the meaning.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary recant (Latin recantare "to sing back, re-echo ... recant, recall, revoke", from re- "back" + canto "to chant, to sing"). cantare is the linking form for chant and incantation. Hook matches; unchanged. Tone formal: all three learner's dictionaries. Pairings from the collocations list (later recanted 13.0, recanted his testimony 1.8, publicly recant 1.6 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (recantare, re- and canto; the Latin already meant recall and revoke), and cantare is a good root (chant, enchant, incantation). formal is right on all three dictionaries. Weakest point: 'later recanted' (13.0) is common but generic, an adverb that fits any verb.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary sanguine (Old French sanguin, ultimately Latin sanguineus "of blood", from sanguis "blood"; the humour sense: a constitution with more blood than the other humours, linked with cheerfulness and confidence). I left out the hedged older origin of sanguis. Hook ("medieval doctors") matches; unchanged. Tone formal: all three learner's dictionaries. Watch-out: Wiktionary's usage note says not to confuse it with sanguinary. Pairings from the collocations list (expectations 16.8, view 16.2, hopes 14.3 per billion). The colour and complexion senses are not shown: they are literary or dated, and only Cambridge lists the colour.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (sanguineus, sanguis, Old French; the humor blood linked with cheerfulness). formal is right on all three dictionaries. The watch-out is true: the bloody sense of sanguine is obsolete (Collins), and sanguine/sanguinary is a known pair. Weakest point: 'It means hopeful and confident' is stated flatly though the record keeps a blood-red sense; hiding that rare sense is still the right call.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary specious (Middle English, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French, from Latin speciosus "good-looking"; an obsolete sense "beautiful"), speciosus ("good-looking, handsome; showy, specious"; from species), species ("from specio, to see"; "external appearance; semblance") and specio ("to look at"). Hook matches; unchanged. Tone formal: all three (Cambridge adds disapproving, only one). Pairings from the collocations list (argument 11.8, reasoning 6.2, pretext 3.6 per billion). The other sense (showy but hollow) is close to the first, so not shown.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (speciosus 'good-looking'; obsolete English sense 'beautiful') and the species and specio entries; specere is a good root. formal is right on all three dictionaries. Watch out (4): no note, though specious and spurious are a recognized confusion (Dictionary.com lists the pair as commonly confused, and Wiktionary's entry points to spurious); null is defensible.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary supercilious (learned borrowing from Latin superciliosus "haughty") and supercilium (super- + cilium "eyelid"; senses "the eyebrow" and "pride, haughtiness, arrogance"). No root: cilium shows only in the technical word cilia. Hook matches; unchanged. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge; Longman says formal and "used to show disapproval". Pairings from the collocations list (look 12.1, smile 9.3, tone 4.1 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary's superciliosus ('haughty') and Latin supercilium ('eyebrow'; 'pride, haughtiness'), and gives the step to today's meaning. disapproving is right (Oxford, Cambridge, and Longman's 'used to show disapproval'). Empty roots are right. Weakest point: none of note.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary tacit ("borrowed from late Middle French tacite, or from Latin tacitus", from tacere "to be silent"), tacitus (participle of taceo) and taciturn (from tacitus); I kept the either-or. tacere matches reticent on worksheet j. Hook matches; unchanged. Tone null: no learner's dictionary labels it. Pairings: four of the top nouns in the collocations list (understanding 137, agreement 115, approval 79, consent 62 per billion); "tacit knowledge" is a technical term.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin keeps Wiktionary's either/or (French tacite or Latin tacitus) and matches taciturn's entry (from tacitus). Null tone is right (no dictionary labels it). Pairings are four of the tool's top nouns. Weakest point: 'tacere to be silent' is the same short gloss Longman and Wiktionary give, a shared fact.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary temerity (Old French temerite, from Latin temeritas "chance, accident, rashness", from temere "by chance, casually, rashly") and temere (from Proto-Italic *temezi "in darkness, blindly"; senses "by chance, at random", "rashly, heedlessly"). Hook ("temere, blindly or rashly"): "rashly" is the Latin sense and "blindly" the older one Wiktionary gives, so I left it; scored 4 for that. Tone formal: all three (Cambridge adds disapproving). Pairings: "had the temerity to" (97 per billion for "had the temerity") and "his own temerity" ("own" tops the collocations list).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary's temeritas and temere entries, including the older form meaning 'in darkness, blindly'. Hook (4): glosses Latin temere as 'blindly', which is the sense of its reconstructed ancestor; Latin temere itself means 'by chance, rashly'. Pairings (4): 'had the temerity to' (99.7) is right; 'his own temerity' (4.53) rests on a generic 'own'. formal is right on all three dictionaries.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (incongruous; Latin congruus and congruo, which gives "come together, meet" and "agree, fit"). Root congruere also shows in congruent. Tone null: no label in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman. No common mix-up. Pairings from the collocation lists, all checked in Google Books. Hook claims are true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (incongruus, in- + congruus); the gloss of congruere ('come together, agree') matches Wiktionary's Latin congruo page. Null tone is right (no label in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman). Pairings are all in the tool's lists (incongruous sight 8.1, mixture 3.2, strangely incongruous 3.9 per billion). Weakest point: congruere links no other word in the list yet.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (inculcate: inculco from in- and calco, from calx "heel", the heel sense, not the lime sense). Root calx links with recalcitrant, whose origin on worksheet j names calx but sets no root. Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it formal. No common mix-up. Pairings from the collocation lists. Hook (press in with the heel) agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (inculcatus, in- + calco 'tread upon', from calx 'heel') and AHD ('to force upon', calcare 'to trample'). The Latin inculco page would not load (429), so the literal gloss 'press in by treading' was judged against those two. calx links correctly to recalcitrant (heel). formal: all three dictionaries. Pairings in the tool's lists (values 6.0, habits 2.3, respect 1.9). Weakest point: no note on the criticized 'inculcate someone with' construction; null is defensible, since it is not a misreading of the meaning.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (ingratiate: Italian ingraziare or Medieval Latin, from in gratiam), which gives the two sources as alternatives, so the origin names both. Root gratia also links with gratuitous (Latin gratuitus, from gratia). Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge label it disapproving and Longman says it is used to show disapproval. Hook changed: it called gratia "the root of gratitude and grace", but Wiktionary derives gratitude from gratus, the adjective behind gratia, so "the root of" became "related to". Pairings from the collocation lists (the verb is nearly always reflexive).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin: Wiktionary has Italian ingraziare or Medieval Latin *ingratiatus, the asterisk marking an unattested form, and 'a Medieval Latin verb' states it as a real word (small nit). 'into favor' for in gratiam matches AHD. Hook: the change to 'related to gratitude and grace' is right (gratitude comes from gratus, not gratia). Tone: disapproving in Oxford, Cambridge and Longman ('used to show disapproval'). Pairings: 'tried to ingratiate' (6.4) is generic; 'ingratiate himself with' (60.4) and 'ingratiating smile' (23.8) are strong.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (inscrutable: Late Latin inscrutabilis, from in- and scruto "to examine"; scrutari is the usual deponent form, as in Oxford's note). Root scrutari shows in scrutiny and scrutinize. Tone null: no label in any of the three. No common mix-up. Pairings from the collocation lists. Hook agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (Late Latin inscrutabilis, in- + scruto); scrutari is the usual deponent form, and scrutiny does come from it. No tone label in any of the three. Pairings all in the tool's lists (expression 22.1, face 12.1, smile 11.1). Weakest point: scrutari links no other word in the list yet.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (interlocutor etymology 1: Medieval Latin interlocutor, from interloquor, from inter- and loquor). Root loqui matches eloquent and loquacious. Tone formal: all three dictionaries mark it formal. Also Means shows the go-between sense, which Oxford and Cambridge give (news writing uses it for a party speaking for one side in talks); register null because Longman lacks the sense. Pairings from the collocation lists. Hook agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (Medieval Latin interlocutor, from interloquor, inter- + loquor); loqui joins eloquent, loquacious and grandiloquent. formal: all three for the first sense; null on the go-between sense is right under the all-three rule (Longman lacks that sense). Pairings: 'my interlocutor' (26.9) is a generic possessive; 'imaginary' (6.4) and 'principal' (2.8) are in the tool's list. Also means: the sense is current (diplomatic go-betweens), but 'carries talks' is unidiomatic and a careful editor would reword it.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (lampoon: French lampon, built on lampons "let us drink", a refrain for scurrilous songs, from lamper; Littre quotes such a song mocking James II). Wiktionary states it plainly, but Oxford ("said to be") and Longman ("probably") hedge the lampons step, so the origin says probably, as the hook says may. No roots: nothing in English shows lamper. Tone null. No common mix-up. Pairings from the collocation lists; none is very frequent in Google Books (1 to 2 per billion), so pairings get 4.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (lampon, built on lampons 'let us drink', from lamper) and AHD; 'probably' sits between Wiktionary (no hedge) and AHD ('perhaps'), which is fine, and songs mocking public figures are supported by Littre's song against James II. Hook keeps 'may'. No tone label (Cambridge's 'informal' belongs to a word in its Compare list). Pairings: all in the tool's lists, but 'often lampooned' (1.7) is generic and all three sit at 1.0 to 1.7 per billion.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (litany: Old French letanie, Latin litania, Greek litaneia "prayer", from lite). No root a learner could spot elsewhere. Tone null: only Oxford marks the list sense formal and only Longman marks disapproval. No common mix-up. Also Means shows the church prayer, which all three learner's dictionaries give and which explains the list sense. Pairings checked in Google Books (litany of complaints 24 per billion). Hook agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (Old French letanie, Latin litania, Greek litaneia 'prayer', from lite 'prayer, entreaty'), with the step to a tiresome list given. Null tone is right: only Longman marks disapproval and only Oxford marks formal. Pairings strong (of complaints 24.3, long 14.2, familiar 8.5). Also means: the church sense is current and the plain is clear, but 'the same answer to each one' overstates; the dictionaries say set responses, and some litanies change the reply from section to section.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (loath: Middle English loth, from Old English lath or Old Norse leid, from Proto-Germanic laithaz; its obsolete senses "hostile" and "loathsome" show the shift). Wiktionary gives Old English or Old Norse, so the origin names both. Tone formal: Oxford and Cambridge mark loath formal and Longman marks "be loath to do something" formal. Watch-out: Wiktionary's usage note warns against confusing it with loathe. Pairings checked in Google Books. Hook makes no origin claim; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Middle English loth, from Old English lath or Old Norse leid, either/or kept); 'hateful, hostile' is a fair gloss of the Old English word (Wiktionary has 'evil; loathsome', with 'hostile' at the Proto-Germanic step). formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman (its 'be loath to do something' page). Watch-out is the classic loath/loathe mix-up, stated correctly. 'loath to part with' checked at 8.2 per billion. Weakest point: the watch-out repeats the hook, which is allowed.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (pastiche: French pastiche, Italian pasticcio "pie, something blended", Late Latin pasta). Root pasta shows in paste and pastry. Tone null: no label in any of the three. No common mix-up. The other sense (a musical medley by several composers) is rare, so it is not shown. Pairings from the collocation lists. Hook agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (French pastiche, Italian pasticcio 'pie, something blended', Late Latin pasta); pasta shows in paste and pastry. No tone label in any of the three. The musical-medley sense is rightly hidden. Pairings are the tool's top three adjectives, but 'mere pastiche' (1.6) leans on a generic modifier and 'literary pastiche' is low (1.2).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (pathos: Ancient Greek pathos "suffering"; the Greek entry also gives "any strong feeling, passion, emotion"). Root pathos matches antipathy and apathy. Tone null: only Cambridge marks it literary. No common mix-up. Also Means shows the rhetoric sense with technical, since students meet ethos, pathos and logos in school. Pairings from the collocation lists. Hook agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (Greek pathos 'suffering'; its Greek page also gives 'any strong feeling'); sympathy, empathy and pathetic share the root, and pathos joins antipathy and apathy. Null tone is right (only Cambridge marks literary). The rhetoric sense with the technical label is one students meet in writing classes; the plain is clear (19 words). Weakest point: the plain leans on ethos and logos, which a learner may not know.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (peruse: either Medieval Latin peruto, perusito "wear out" or Anglo-Norman peruser "use up", by surface analysis per- + use; only the "examine" line survives) and Oxford's note (perhaps per- + use). No roots. Tone formal: Oxford (formal or humorous), Cambridge and Longman all mark it formal. Watch-out: Wiktionary's usage note says the skimming sense is proscribed by some authorities and Cambridge's American dictionary gives both, so it is stated as a dispute. Hook says "probably built from per- and use" and "first meant to use something up"; Longman says probably per- + use and Oxford dates the use-up sense first, so it stands, scored 4 because Wiktionary treats per- + use only as surface analysis. Pairings: carefully perused is on the collocation lists; the other two come from the tool's check of "peruse the *" (about 2 per billion each), skipping peruse the menu, which is the disputed browsing sense.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin: facts match Wiktionary (Anglo-Norman peruser or Medieval Latin perusito; per- + use; the using-up sense died out), but 'in form per- ("thoroughly") and use' is awkward, and 'Of uncertain origin' is strong when both candidates are per- + use (AHD gives Middle English perusen 'to use up' with no hedge). Hook: 'first meant to use something up' agrees with AHD. formal: all three (Oxford 'formal or humorous'). Watch-out calls the skim sense disputed, which matches AHD's usage note, in own words. Pairings: carefully perused 5.5 (tool list), peruse the contents 2.4 and the pages 2.2 (checked); the two object pairings are generic and fit the disputed browse sense as well.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (philistine: from Philistine via German Philister, used at German universities for people outside the university and then for people indifferent to culture; brought into English by Thomas Carlyle and popularized by Matthew Arnold). The 1693 Jena sermon story is left out: Wiktionary says it is often told but the OED finds the word in that sense in 1687. Hook changed: it said Matthew Arnold "brought the insult into English", but Wiktionary credits Carlyle with introducing it and Arnold with popularizing it, so it now says Arnold "popularized the insult in English". Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge. Also Means shows the ancient people, the sense most of the word's uses in books refer to (Philistine cities, army, giant). Pairings from the collocation lists (adjectives used with it); only two fit the first sense.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (from Philistine, influenced by German Philister, the students' word for townspeople outside the university; Carlyle introduced it to English); 'through German' is a little stronger than 'influenced by' but right for the cultural sense. Hook: changing Arnold from 'brought' to 'popularized' is the right fix. disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge. Pairings: both are in the tool's lists but are the rarest in this sheet (bourgeois 1.0, cultural 0.8 per billion). Also means: fine to show, but 'in Bible stories' can read as if the people were only legendary; 'in the Bible' is safer.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (pique etymology 1: the noun from Middle French pique "a quarrel; resentment", from piquer "to prick, sting"). The deeper source of piquer (imitative or Frankish) is hedged there, so it is left out. No roots. Tone null: only Oxford marks it formal. Watch-out: Wiktionary's usage note says the verb is often confused with peek and peak. The other sense (a ribbed cotton cloth) is a variant of the separate word pique with an accent, said differently, so it is not shown. Pairings from the collocation lists. Hook agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (noun from Middle French pique 'a quarrel; resentment', from piquer 'to prick, sting'). Null tone is right (only Oxford marks formal). Cloth sense rightly hidden. Pairings strong (fit of pique 41.8, personal 6.7). Watch-out: the peak/peek misspelling is real, common and stated correctly, but it concerns the verb ('piqued my curiosity'), a sense this noun entry does not show.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (plebeian: Latin plebeius, from plebes, plus -an; a possible Middle French influence is hedged there and left out). Root plebs shows in plebiscite. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge label it and Longman says it is used to show disapproval; only Cambridge adds formal. Also Means shows the ancient Roman sense, which most book uses refer to (plebeian tribunes, assembly). Pairings: plebeian culture and plebeian origins come from the collocation lists, which are dominated by the Roman sense; plebeian tastes was dropped as rare (0.85 per billion). Two pairings, the second modest, so 4.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (plebeius, from plebes; the 'possibly' Middle French influence is left out, which is allowed); plebs is the usual nominative. disapproving: Cambridge, Longman ('used to show disapproval') and Oxford's no-culture sense. The Roman sense is current (plebeian tribunes, assembly) and its plain is accurate. Pairings: plebeian culture (6.8) and origins (1.7) fit the 'ordinary people' half of the sense but show none of the snobbish shade, and 'plebeian culture' is mostly historians' neutral term.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (pontificate etymology 2: Medieval Latin pontifico, from pontifex "high priest", from pons and facere). Roots pontifex (pontiff, pontifical) and facere. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge. No common mix-up. The other sense (leading a service as a bishop) is rare, so it is not shown. Pairings: the collocation lists mostly show the noun (a pope's reign), so the pairings are the verb's usual patterns, pontificate about and pontificate on (Longman gives both; about 11 and 12 per billion in Google Books). Prepositions only, so 4.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (Medieval Latin pontifico, from pontifex 'high priest', pons + facere); pontifex shows in pontiff, and facere joins prolific and efficacy. disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge. Officiating sense rightly hidden. Pairings: both are bare prepositions (about 10.6, on 12.2), common but neither shows the meaning; the tool's lists offer little else (most hits are the noun).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (portend: Latin portendere, from por- and tendere). Root tendere matches distend. Tone null: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal but Longman marks it literary, so neither label has the agreement it needs. No common mix-up. Pairings from the collocation lists. Hook agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (portendere 'to foretell', por- + tendere); tendere joins distend. Hook: 'portendere, to stretch forward' gives the literal makeup as if it were the Latin verb's meaning, which was 'to foretell'; adding 'literally' would fix it. Null tone is right: Oxford and Cambridge mark formal, Longman literary. Pairings in the tool's lists (disaster 1.1, trouble 1.1).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (posit: Latin positus, perfect participle of pono "put, place"). Root ponere links with expound (Latin exponere), which is on worksheet u. Tone formal: all three mark it formal. No common mix-up. The other sense (to place something firmly) is rare, so it is not shown. Pairings from the collocation lists. Hook agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (positus, perfect participle of pono); position and deposit do come from ponere. formal: all three. Physical-placing sense rightly hidden. Pairings strong (theory posits 76.5, posit the existence 24.0, theorists posit 5.6). Weakest point: ponere links no other word yet (expound has no roots set).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (precept: Late Latin praeceptum, from praecipio, from prae and capio; the Latin praecipio entry gives both "take beforehand, anticipate" and "teach, instruct"). Root capere matches incipient. Tone formal: all three mark it formal. No common mix-up. The other sense (a court's written order) is rare, so it is not shown. Pairings from the collocation lists. Hook agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (praeceptum, from praecipio, prae + capio) and its Latin page ('take beforehand', 'teach, instruct'); capere joins incipient. Hook: the parts are right, but 'lessons you take in before life tests you' reads as the meaning of prae + capere from the learner's side, while the Latin verb went from taking beforehand to instructing (the teacher's act); a memory picture, so loose rather than false. formal: all three. Pairings strong (moral precepts 82.4).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (promulgate: Latin promulgo, either from provulgo or from mulgeo "to milk, bring forth"; the Latin entry is marked for etymology review), so the origin says the source is uncertain and sets no root. Tone formal: all three mark the entry formal. Also Means shows the law sense with formal: it is the sense most uses in books have (promulgate regulations, rules, laws), and all three dictionaries give it. Pairings: the collocation lists are all for the law sense, so the two first-sense pairings come from the tool's check (promulgated the idea 3.4 per billion, the doctrine 1.1); scored 4. Hook says Roman officials made new laws known this way. That matches Roman practice and the word's law sense, but Wiktionary's Latin entries (promulgo, promulgatio) only say "publish, proclaim", so hook gets 4; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin: facts match Wiktionary (promulgo, from pro + vulgo or from mulgeo; its Latin page flags the etymology, so 'uncertain' is right), but it keeps Wiktionary's gloss and either/or order, and 'either pro- with vulgare or mulgere' reads as if the second option had no pro-. Hook: the Roman-laws claim goes past Wiktionary but is right (Lewis and Short: used especially of laws). formal: all three, on both senses. Pairings: first-sense pairings are moderate (the idea 3.4, the doctrine 1.1); the word's commonest use is the legal sense, shown under Also means.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (putative: Middle French putatif, Latin putativus, from putatus, from puto "to think, reckon"). Root putare matches impute. Tone formal: Oxford (formal or law), Cambridge and Longman. No common mix-up. Pairings from the collocation lists. Hook agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (Middle French putatif, Latin putativus, from puto); reputation and compute share putare, which joins impute. formal: all three (Oxford 'formal or law'). Pairings strong (father 51.7, author 7.7). Weakest point: only two pairings, which is fine.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (qualm: perhaps Old English cwealm, or Dutch kwalm or German Qualm "vapor", earlier "daze"; faintness from 1530, doubt from 1553, scruple of conscience from 1649) and Oxford's note (perhaps related to cwealm); the hedge is kept. No roots. Tone null: no labels. No common mix-up. The other sense (a spell of nausea) is rare today, so it is not shown. Pairings: moral qualms and few qualms are on the collocation lists; no qualms about is very common in Google Books (280 per billion). Hook is a rhyme with no origin claim (qualm and calm do rhyme); unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin keeps Wiktionary's hedge ('perhaps' Old English cwealm, or Dutch/German Qualm 'vapor', earlier 'daze') and gives the sense history (faintness, then doubt, then conscience) in own words; AHD says origin unknown. Hook is a true rhyme with no origin claim. No tone label in any of the three. Nausea sense rightly hidden. Pairings strong (no qualms about 279.6, moral 21.5, few 19.5).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (regale: French regaler, from Old French regale, from gale "merriment", probably Germanic; influenced by se rigoler, of unknown origin, left out) and Oxford's and Longman's notes. No roots. Tone null: only Longman marks it (written). No common mix-up. Also Means shows the food-and-drink sense: Wiktionary dates it from the 17th century alongside the story sense, and the collocation lists show it is common in books (regaled themselves). Learner's dictionaries omit it, so alsoMeans gets 4. Pairings checked in Google Books (regaled us with 21 per billion, regaled with stories 3); the collocation lists show mostly the reflexive feasting use, so pairings get 4. Hook says regale contains gale as in a gale of laughter, a sound-alike with no origin claim; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary and AHD (French regaler, from Old French gale 'merriment', 'probably' Germanic, hedge kept). Hook: no false claim, but the gale of 'a gale of laughter' is the wind word, not the Old French gale the origin names, so the two lines invite a learner to merge them. Null tone is right (only Longman marks 'written'). Pairings: 'regaled us with' (21.1) is the bare frame and fits the feast sense too; 'regaled with stories' (3.1) is good. Also means: the feast sense is in AHD and common in older books ('regaled themselves with'), but none of the three learner's dictionaries lists it; acceptable.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (remiss: Latin remissus "languid, negligent", from remitto; the Latin remitto entry gives re- + mitto and the senses "send back", "relax, diminish"). Root mittere shows in remit, mission, transmit. Tone formal: all three mark it formal. No common mix-up. Pairings checked in Google Books (would be remiss 176 per billion; the other two about 1 to 2). Hook says remiss contains miss, a spelling hook with no origin claim; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Middle English remisse, Latin remissus, from remitto) and its Latin page (send back, relax); mittere joins surmise. Hook is a sound-alike with no origin claim. formal: all three. Pairings: 'would be remiss' (176.3) is the stock frame and shows no meaning; 'remiss in failing to' (1.9) and 'in his duty' (1.0) are low but fit.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (borrowed from French coterie), the French section of the same Wiktionary page (learned borrowing of Medieval Latin coteria, from Old English cot; historical sense "feudal community of peasants", figurative sense "clique") and the Wiktionary pages cot (Old English cot "cottage"; "more distantly related to cottage") and cottage (from Anglo-Norman cot, Old French cote "cottage, hut"). No root: nothing else in the list shares cot. Hook changed: it said coterie "goes back to French cote", but Wiktionary traces coterie to Old English cot, not French cote; the smallest fix names cot, "an old word for a hut, kin to cottage". Tone null: Oxford "formal, often disapproving", Longman formal, Cambridge nothing, so neither label meets its rule. Pairings: small coterie 25.0, coterie of friends 6.2, literary coterie 5.1 per billion (small and literary top the Datamuse list); small is the generic one.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point (origin): it says flatly that Medieval Latin coteria goes back to Old English cot. Wiktionary's French entry supports that, but Oxford Learner's traces the French word to Middle Low German kote, so the sources differ; "from a Germanic word for a hut, kin to English cot" would hold under both. The peasant-community sense matches Wiktionary's French entry (marked historical) and Oxford ("an association of tenants"). Tone null is right: Oxford formal and often disapproving, Cambridge none, Longman formal. Pairings pass --check: small coterie 25.0, coterie of friends 6.2, literary coterie 5.1 per billion. Hook change checked: the record's "French cote, a hut, the root of cottage" had no source; the new "cot, an old word for a hut, kin to cottage" fits Wiktionary (cot: archaic, a cottage; cottage listed as related).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English contenaunce, Anglo-Norman and Old French contenance, from the present participle of contenir, or from Late Latin continentia; doublet of continence), the Wiktionary Latin page contineo (con- "together" + teneo "to hold"; "to hold or keep together") and the Wiktionary noun senses (face and expression; "favour, support, encouragement") against the verb sense (to tolerate, support, approve). Both of Wiktionary's routes go back to continere, so the origin says "goes back to" and skips the either/or. Root tenere links abstain, impertinent, untenable and retinue. Hook (countenance is also a word for a face) is true and makes no false origin claim. Tone formal: the Oxford verb entry (countenance_2), Cambridge and Longman all mark the verb formal. Pairings from the Ngram wildcard lists: refused to countenance 25.7, willing to countenance 14.6, countenance the idea 8.6 per billion; Datamuse's lists for this word are mostly the noun.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point (origin): it goes from continere "to hold together" straight to "a face" without the middle step (Oxford: Old French contenance meant bearing or demeanour, then facial expression, then the face). The noun sense "favour, support" is on Wiktionary, so the link to the verb holds, and tenere is a good root. formal is right: Oxford's verb page (saved by the writer), Cambridge and Longman all mark the verb formal. Pairings pass --check: refused to countenance 25.7, willing to countenance 14.6, countenance the idea 8.6.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English cravant, either from Old French cravanté "defeated", past participle of cravanter, ultimately from Latin crepare, or a modification of creaunt "defeated" after craven "to crave"). The either/or is kept as "Of uncertain origin". No root: crepare sits only in one branch of the hedge, so it is left out. Hook is a sound-alike (craven, cave in) and makes no origin claim. Tone: Oxford "formal, disapproving", Cambridge "formal, disapproving", Longman formal; formal and disapproving both qualify, and disapproving is set, as on intransigent and sycophant, because it is the label that matters for use. Pairings from the Datamuse noun list: craven fear 5.6, craven coward 3.2, craven submission 0.84 per billion; submission is the weak one.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest points: the origin's first sentence tracks Wiktionary's single sentence closely (same either/or order, both "defeated" glosses, its "a modification of creaunt after craven" reworded as "reshaped to look like crave"); it is facts only, but recast it if the entry is touched again. "Of uncertain origin" is a fair hedge (Oxford also says "perhaps"). "craven submission" is only 0.84 per billion for 2010 to 2022, the weakest pairing; craven fear 5.6 and craven coward 3.2 are fine. Tone: disapproving on Oxford and Cambridge (all three also mark it formal; one label only).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English deinen, Old French daigner, from Latin dignare, of digno "to deem fitting, suitable or worthy; to condescend", from dignus "worthy") and the Wiktionary page dignity (Latin dignitas, from dignus; "cognate to deign"). Root dignus (dignity, indignant, dignitary). Hook kept: it gives the Latin as dignari, the deponent form of the same verb (Wiktionary cites the active dignare); "to think worthy" and dignus, root of dignity, are true. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge both label the verb disapproving (Longman gives the phrase only). Pairings: did not deign 30.5, deign to answer 11.5, scarcely deigned 2.4 per billion (scarcely, even and hardly lead the Datamuse lists).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the hook names Latin dignari while the origin (and Wiktionary) say dignare. Oxford gives both forms, so neither is wrong, but the card will show two spellings. disapproving matches Oxford and Cambridge (Longman's cached page is a stub). Pairings pass --check: did not deign 30.5, deign to answer 11.5, scarcely deigned 2.4.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle French démagogue, from Ancient Greek demagogos "popular leader, mob leader", from demos "people" + agogos "guide") and the Wiktionary senses (pejorative political sense first; "a leader of the people" marked historical). Roots: demos (democracy, demography, epidemic) and agogos, which the Wiktionary pedagogue page also gives (paidagogos, from pais "child" + agogos "guide"). Hook (demos, the people, and agogos, leader) is true. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge label it, and Longman says it is used to show disapproval. Pairings from the Datamuse lists: populist demagogue 2.0, dangerous demagogue 1.7, political demagogue 1.4 per billion; all modest, the weakest point.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point (pairings): all three are in the tool's lists but modest and partly generic: populist demagogue 2.0, dangerous demagogue 1.7 (dangerous fits any noun), political demagogue 1.4. Origin matches Wiktionary and Oxford; agogos also shows in pedagogue (Wiktionary). disapproving on all three.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English denisein, Old French denzein, from deinz "within" + -ein, from Late Latin de intus "from within"). No root: intus is not a stem a learner would spot. Hook (Old French deinz, inside) is true. Tone literary: Cambridge and Longman mark it literary; Oxford says "formal or humorous". Pairings: denizens of the deep 7.9, denizens of the forest 5.0, local denizens 2.4 per billion (local and forest are in the Datamuse list). The other sense, a plant or animal naturalized in a new region, is a biology term a general reader seldom meets, so it is not shown and is marked technical.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: nothing of substance. Origin matches Wiktionary and Oxford (Old French deinz, Late Latin de intus). literary matches Cambridge and Longman (Oxford: formal or humorous). Sense 997 (a naturalized species) is rightly hidden and labelled technical. Pairings pass --check: denizens of the deep 7.9, denizens of the forest 5.0, local denizens 2.4.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (from disinterest, verb, "to cause to be impartial", + -ed, or from dis- "not" + interested "having a stake in"); both routes are kept. No root. Hook (dis- plus interest in its older stake sense, as in conflict of interest) agrees with the second route. Tone null: no label on the impartial sense in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman. Watch out: Wiktionary's usage note calls the "uninterested" use disputed, Longman says many teachers think it is not correct, and Oxford marks it informal, so the note describes a dispute. Pairings: disinterested observer 14.9, disinterested party 11.1, disinterested third party 7.5 per billion (observer and party lead the Datamuse noun list).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point (pairings): "disinterested party" (11.1) and "disinterested third party" (7.5) repeat one pattern; a different partner from the tool's list (motives, service), checked with --check, would teach more. Origin keeps both of Wiktionary's derivations. The watch-out rightly calls the "not interested" use disputed (Oxford labels it informal, Longman says many teachers reject it).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (French drôle "comical, odd, funny", from drôle "buffoon", Middle French drolle "a merry fellow, pleasant rascal", Old French drolle, from Middle Dutch drol "fat little man, goblin", from Old Norse troll). The troll link is left out to keep it short. No root. Hook (French drôle, funny or odd) is true. Tone null: only Oxford labels it ("old-fashioned or ironic"). Pairings: droll stories 5.7, droll smile 4.8, droll humor 3.4 per billion (stories, humor and smile are in the Datamuse noun list).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the origin states the Middle Dutch drol link flatly; Wiktionary does too, though Oxford hedges it with "perhaps". Tone null is right (only Oxford labels it: old-fashioned or ironic). Pairings pass --check: droll stories 5.7 (partly Balzac's title), droll smile 4.8, droll humor 3.4.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against the Wiktionary page (the tool could not read its ety template; the template gives erst "first, formerly" + while). No root. Hook (erst, an old word for formerly, with while) is true. Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it formal. No watch-out: Wiktionary lists a proscribed sense "respected", but none of the learner's dictionaries mentions a common mix-up. Pairings: erstwhile friend 14.5, erstwhile allies 14.3, erstwhile colleagues 7.1 per billion (the top of the Datamuse noun list).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the origin is one short sentence, which is enough here since "formerly" makes the link plain (Wiktionary: erst, "first, formerly", plus while). formal on all three. Pairings pass --check: erstwhile allies 14.3, erstwhile friend 14.5, erstwhile colleagues 7.1.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle French évincer, from Latin evinco "conquer entirely, prevail over; prove exhaustively", from e- intensive + vinco "conquer"; doublet of evict). Root vincere (victory, invincible, convince). Hook (Latin evincere, to prove) is true. Tone formal: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it formal. Pairings from the Datamuse lists (interest, little, great): evinced little interest 3.3, evince interest 1.8 per billion; evinced great interest is only 1.0, so it is left out. Both are modest, the weakest point.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point (pairings): the two pairings are one pattern, "evinced little interest" (3.3) and "evince interest" (1.8). evince is rare in any pairing, so this is acceptable, but a second, different partner would teach more. Origin matches Wiktionary and Oxford (Oxford gives "prove by argument or evidence" as the first English sense). formal on all three.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Latin extans, present participle of exto "to stand out, exist, be extant", from ex- "out" + sto "stand"). Root stare links obstinate. Hook (Latin exstare, to stand out or exist) is true; exstare is the other spelling of the same verb. Tone formal: Oxford and Longman mark it formal, and Cambridge marks the headword formal. Pairings: still extant 122, earliest extant 94, extant manuscripts 50 per billion (still, earliest and manuscripts lead the Datamuse lists).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the hook spells the Latin verb exstare and the origin extare; both are real spellings (Oxford uses exstare), but the card will show both. No watch-out is fine, since the hook already sets extant against extinct. formal on all three. Pairings very common (still extant 122, earliest extant 94, extant manuscripts 50).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle French facile, from Latin facilis "easy to do", from facere "to do, make") and the dates on the Wiktionary senses (easy from the 15th century, effortless from the 17th, simplistic and superficial from the 19th). Root facere links beneficent, efficacy and prolific. Hook (Latin facilis, easy, as in facility) is true. Tone null: Oxford marks this sense disapproving, but Cambridge and Longman give no label. The effortless sense is current and distinct, so it is shown; the fluent-speaker sense repeats it and is not shown. Pairings from the Datamuse noun list for the shallow sense: facile solution 4.0, facile optimism 3.6, facile assumption 3.5 per billion; facile pen (4.0) belongs to the fluent sense and is left out.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: nothing of substance. The 1800s date for the shallow sense matches Wiktionary's sense dates (from the 19th century; "easy" from the 15th). Tone null is right (disapproving only on Oxford). Showing sense 999 (effortless, practised) is right: "facile pen" is the top pairing in the data. Pairings pass --check (solution 4.0, optimism 3.6, assumption 3.5).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle English feaute, Anglo-Norman feauté, from Latin fidelitas "faithfulness", "homage, fealty" in Medieval Latin, from fidelis + -tas; doublet of fidelity) and the Wiktionary Latin page fidelis (fides "faith, trust" + -elis). Root fides links perfidious. Hook (through Old French from Latin fidelitas, the root of fidelity) is true; Anglo-Norman is the Old French of England. Tone old-fashioned: Oxford and Cambridge say "old use" and Longman "old-fashioned". Pairings: swear fealty 28.7, oath of fealty 28.5, pledged fealty 3.3 per billion (swear and pledged lead the Datamuse list).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the hook says "through Old French" where the origin says Anglo-Norman; Oxford says Old French, so both hold. fides is supported (Wiktionary fidelis entry, Oxford). old-fashioned matches Oxford and Cambridge (old use) and Longman (old-fashioned). Pairings: swear fealty 28.7, oath of fealty 28.5, pledged fealty 3.3.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Middle French furtif, from Latin furtivus "clandestine, secret; hidden; stolen", from furtum "theft", from fur "thief"). No root: fur shows up in no other common English word. Hook (Latin fur, thief) is true. Tone null: only Oxford marks it disapproving. Pairings: furtive glance 81.9, furtive look 29.4, furtive movements 8.2 per billion (the top of the Datamuse noun list).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: nothing. furtivus from furtum from fur matches Wiktionary and Oxford. Tone null is right (disapproving only on Oxford). Pairings very common: furtive glance 81.9, furtive look 29.4, furtive movements 8.2.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (French gauche "left, awkward", from gauchir "to veer, turn", from Old French gaucher "to trample, walk clumsily", Frankish *walkan) and the French sections of the Wiktionary pages gauche (from gauchir "to bend, dodge, warp"; gauche replaced senestre as the word for "left" in the sixteenth century; senses "left" and "awkward, clumsy") and gauchir. Hook changed: it said a prejudice against left-handers made gauche come to mean awkward, but the word comes from a verb for bending and warping and became the word for left later, so that story runs the wrong way. The fix keeps "French for left", adds "and also for awkward", and turns the rest into a picture with no origin claim. Tone null: no label in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman. Pairings left empty: Datamuse's lists are French text and chemistry (gauche conformation), and the English phrases are rare (rather gauche 2.2, gauche and awkward 1.3, socially gauche 0.52 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: nothing of substance. gauchir "to bend, warp" and the 16th-century replacement of the older word for "left" are both in Wiktionary's French entries, retold in the writer's own words. Empty pairings are right: the data is French and chemistry, and the English candidates are rare (socially gauche 0.52, gauche manners 0.32, gauche remark 0.19). Hook change checked: the record's story that a prejudice against left-handers made gauche mean awkward runs against Wiktionary's French entry (awkward came first; "left" replaced senestre in the 1500s), and the new hook only states the two current meanings.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (blend of Gerry + salamander, after Elbridge Gerry, then governor of Massachusetts; coined by the editors of the Boston Gazette in a 26 March 1812 article comparing a district he signed into law to a salamander). No root. Hook (Gerry, the governor who signed an 1812 map, and salamander) is true. Tone disapproving: Oxford and Cambridge label it disapproving (Longman has no entry). Pairings from the Datamuse lists: partisan gerrymandering 25.7, gerrymandered districts 3.9, racially gerrymandered 1.2 per billion; the last is modest.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point (origin and hook): both say Gerry signed a map. Wiktionary says the district boundary was signed into law by him, and Oxford says the map was drawn while he was in office. "a district he signed into law" would be exact.
