The date, the Boston Gazette and the salamander blend are right. disapproving on Oxford and Cambridge.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (a shortening of obsolete English glibbery "slippery" or of its source, Low German or Dutch glibberig "slippery"; archaic literal sense "smooth or slippery"). No root. Hook kept, scored 4: "related to old Dutch and German words for slippery" is loose (Wiktionary says shortened from glibbery or its Low German or Dutch source) but not false. Tone disapproving: Oxford labels it and Longman says it is used to show disapproval; Cambridge gives no label. Pairings: glib tongue 18.4, glib answer 5.7, glib talk 3.2 per billion (the top of the Datamuse noun list).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest points: the origin follows Wiktionary's sentence closely (same either/or order, keeps "its source"), and "an old English word" can be read as Old English; Wiktionary calls glibbery obsolete English. The hook calls the Dutch and German words "old", but Dutch and Low German glibberig are current words; dropping "old" fixes it. disapproving on Oxford and Longman. Pairings pass --check: glib tongue 18.4, glib answer 5.7, glib talk 3.2.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (from about 1400, from hap "luck" + -less) and the Wiktionary page hap (derived terms include happen, mishap, perhaps and haphazard). Root hap (happen, mishap, perhaps, haphazard). Hook (hap, still heard in happen and mishap) is true. Tone null: Oxford and Cambridge say formal, Longman literary, so neither label meets its rule. Pairings: hapless victim 24.3, hapless creature 4.6 per billion (both in the Datamuse noun list).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (borrowed from Latin impingo "dash against"; compare impact, from its perfect passive participle), the Wiktionary Latin page impingo (in- + pango "fasten, drive in"; "to push, strike, dash against; to drive, thrust") and the English senses (physical impact first, the others marked figurative). No root: pangere is not a stem a learner would spot. Hook (impingere, to drive or push into) matches the Latin page. Tone null: only Oxford marks it formal. Sense 988 (light or a jet striking a surface) is hidden, though it is the most frequent use in the tool's data (light, beam, waves, jets); hiding it as technical is defensible, and showing it would be too. Origin matches Wiktionary and Oxford (literal sense first, "encroach" later). Tone null is right (formal only on Oxford).

reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: nothing. impugnare from pugnare from pugnus matches Wiktionary; pugnare is a good root (pugnacious, repugnant). formal on all three. Pairings pass --check: impugn the integrity 2.7, the motives 2.6, the character 1.7.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against tools/etymology.py (Medieval Latin incisivus, from incido "to cut in, cut through" + -ivus) and the Wiktionary Latin page incido, etymology 2 (in- + caedo "to cut"; derived Latin incisio and incisor). Root caedere (incision, concise, decide). Hook (incidere, to cut into, root of incision and incisor) is true. Tone null: only Oxford labels it (approving). The cutting sense belongs to anatomy (incisive teeth, incisive canal), so it is not shown and is marked technical. Tone null is right (approving only on Oxford). Sense 1026 (cutting teeth) is rightly hidden. Pairings common: incisive analysis 20.9, comments 15.8, mind 6.4.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary clandestine and the Latin page clandestinus (from an earlier adverb built on clam, 'secretly'); Oxford Learner's and Longman origin notes agree. Weakest point: the origin says 'formed from clam' where Wiktionary has an intermediate adverb, a fair simplification.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary conflate (conflatus, participle of conflo, 'fuse, kindle, blow together') and the Latin page conflo; Oxford's note gives con- plus flare, 'to blow'. Hook (conflare, 'to blow together', used for fusing metals) agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (conflo 'fuse, kindle, blow together') and Oxford's note that the English word first meant fusing metal; the step to today's meaning is given. Root flare is the right linking form (inflate, deflate). Tone null is right (Oxford and Longman formal, Cambridge not). Weakest point: pairings. 'conflate the two' is common (18.3 per billion in Google Books 2010 to 2022), but 'mistakenly conflate' is thin there (0.8) though Datamuse lists it.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary consternation and the Latin page consterno (sense 'to alarm, shock, throw into confusion'). Wiktionary ties it to sternere, 'to strew', but calls the derivation of the ending disputed, so the origin stops at consternare and no root is given. Tone: only Oxford marks it formal, so null. Pairings from the collocations list (caused, utter, great before consternation); 'great' is generic, so pairings 4. Hook is a sound-alike picture (stern in the middle) and makes no origin claim; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (French consternation, Latin consternatio); the gloss of consternare goes past the English page (the Latin page consterno would not load under rate limits) and agrees with Oxford ('lay prostrate, terrify') and Longman ('to frighten'). Hook is a spelling picture with no origin claim. Tone null is right (only Oxford marks it formal). Pairings: 'great consternation' (41 per billion) and 'utter consternation' (6.9) are intensifiers that fit any noun; only 'caused consternation' (31) shows the word at work.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary culpable (Old French culpable, Latin culpabilis, culpo, culpa 'fault'). Root culpa matches exculpate in the record. Tone: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it formal. Pairings from the collocations lists (morally, held before; negligence after). Hook (culpa, fault, as in mea culpa) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (culpabilis, from culpo, from culpa 'fault'); exculpate and mea culpa are true relatives, and culpa is spelled as on exculpate. Formal in Oxford, Cambridge and Longman. Pairings are all high in the tool's lists. Weakest point: 'culpable negligence' leans toward the legal use Longman lists separately, though it fits the first sense.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary cupidity (French cupidite, Latin cupiditas 'strong desire', cupidus; compare Cupid) ; Oxford and Longman origin notes give cupidus from cupere, 'to desire' (Wiktionary's cupidus page could not be fetched, rate limit). Root cupere also shows in Cupid and concupiscence. Tone: all three mark it formal. Watch-out: the Cupid link tempts learners to read it as love, a classic test trap. Pairings from the collocations list (insatiable, human, selfish). Hook is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (French cupidite, Latin cupiditas, cupidus) and Oxford and AHD for cupidus from cupere; Cupid is a true relative and the step to 'greed for money' is given. Formal in all three dictionaries. The Cupid watch-out is a real trap for this word. Weakest point: pairings. 'selfish cupidity' is thin (0.22 per billion against 0.89 for 'insatiable' and 1.23 for 'human') and says little, since cupidity is selfish by definition. Root cupere shows in few English words besides cupid.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary decry (Middle French decrier, Old French descrier 'to shout'; the run-down sense and the currency sense were in French by the 13th century, 'presumably' from reading de- as 'down', a hedge kept as 'probably'). Oxford's note also gives the coin sense. No root. Tone: all three mark it formal. Pairings from the collocations lists (critics before decry; widely, publicly before decried). Hook (through French from crier, to cry out) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Middle French decrier, Old French descrier 'to shout') and keeps its hedge on de- read as 'down' ('presumably' becomes 'probably'); the coin sense is in Wiktionary and Oxford. Hook's 'from crier' agrees with AHD (des- + crier). Formal in all three. Pairings all in the tool's lists. Weakest point: the coin sentence is a side fact that a learner does not need.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary demur (Middle English demuren, Old French demorer 'to remain, stay', Latin demorari, from de- and moror 'to delay'); the Indo-European step Wiktionary hedges is left out. Root morari also shows in moratorium. Tone: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal, Longman does not, so null. Watch-out: demur and demure are a common look-alike pair. Pairings: 'politely' is in the collocations list before demurs, and Google Books gives 'politely demurred' 2.2 and 'demurred at' 12 per billion ('demurred at' shows the construction but is generic, so pairings 4); 'little demur' and 'without demur' use the noun and were left out. Hook (demorari, to linger or delay) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (Old French demorer, Latin demorari, moror 'to delay') and leave out its hedged PIE part; morari shows in moratorium. Tone null is right (Oxford and Cambridge formal, Longman not). The demure watch-out is the classic mix-up and is true. Weakest point: pairings. 'politely demurred' is good (2.2 per billion), but 'demurred at' (12.1) is only a preposition and does not show the meaning.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary denigrate (denigratus, from de- and nigro 'to blacken'; it keeps the literal 'to blacken' as a rare sense) ; Oxford's note agrees. Pairings from the collocations lists (remarks, comments after denigrating; systematically before denigrated). Hook (denigrare, to blacken) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (denigro 'to blacken', from nigro). Tone null is right (only Oxford marks it formal). Pairings are in the tool's lists ('denigrating remarks' 13602, 'denigrating comments' 10839, 'systematically denigrated' 7600). Weakest point: two of the three pairings use the -ing adjective rather than the verb.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary deprecate (deprecatus, from deprecor 'to pray against', from de- and precor 'to pray'); Oxford's note gives the early 17th-century sense 'pray against'. Root precari also shows in imprecation and precarious. Tone: all three mark it formal. Watch-out follows Wiktionary's usage note: the 'belittle' sense is sometimes condemned as a confusion with depreciate, but AHD reports it as widespread, so it is stated as an objection, not an error. Pairings from the collocations lists (strongly, earnestly before deprecate). Software sense shown: Oxford Learner's lists it (computing) and 'deprecated features' is common; labelled technical. Hook is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (deprecor 'to pray against', from precor) and give the step to disapproval. Formal in all three; technical on the software sense matches Oxford's computing label. Watch-out is a real mix-up and frames the 'belittle' use as a dispute, but the sentence is crowded and AHD treats that use as a development rather than a mix-up. Pairings: 'earnestly deprecate' is dated (0.74 per billion in 2010 to 2022). Also means: 'flag a feature as old' is loose; deprecation marks it as discouraged or superseded.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary dilettante (present participle of Italian dilettare, from Latin delectare; related terms delectable, delight). Root delectare also shows in delectable. Tone: Oxford (noun entry dilettante_2, fetched) marks it disapproving and Cambridge 'usually disapproving'; Longman has no label. Pairings from the collocations list (mere, wealthy, literary). Hook (dilettare, to delight) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (Italian present participle of dilettare, from Latin delectare); delectable is a true relative and the step to dabbling for pleasure is given. Disapproving matches Oxford and Cambridge ('usually disapproving'); Longman has no label. Pairings are the tool's top adjectives. Weakest point: 'literary dilettante' is the thinnest pairing (0.64 per billion).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary discomfit (Old French desconfit, desconfire 'to undo, to destroy', confire, Latin conficio from com- and facio; the later sense 'to embarrass, disconcert' from confusion with the unrelated discomfort). Oxford's note gives the first sense 'defeat in battle'. Root facere is spelled as in the record. Tone: Oxford literary, Cambridge and Longman formal; no label reaches the rule, so null. Watch-out follows Wiktionary's usage note (prescriptive guides call the 'embarrass' sense a mistake; Merriam-Webster calls it established), stated as a dispute. Pairings from the collocations lists (questions after discomfiting; looked before discomfited); the 'utterly discomfited army' pairings belong to the old 'defeat' sense and were left out. Hook (sounds like discomfort, though the roots differ) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary, including the later sense from confusion with discomfort, and Oxford's 'defeat in battle'; facere is the right root. Hook's 'the roots differ' is true. Tone null is right (Oxford literary, Cambridge and Longman formal). Watch-out: the discomfort mix-up is real (Vocabulary.com lists the pair), but the note packs two points into one long sentence, and 'some usage guides still limit it to defeat' could not be checked in the cached pages.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary disingenuous (dis- plus ingenuous), ingenuous and the Latin page ingenuus. Root ingenuus links to ingenuous in the list. Tone: all three mark it formal. Pairings from the collocations list (argument, claim, attempt). Hook (dis- plus ingenuous) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (dis- + ingenuous; ingenuous is a learned borrowing of Latin ingenuus 'of noble character, frank'); 'freeborn' goes past that page and agrees with Vocabulary.com's note. Weakest point: root ingenuus links mostly to ingenuous, the same word without dis-; ingenue is the only other English word that shows it.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary dissolute (Middle English, Latin dissolutus), the Latin pages dissolutus (adjective 'loose, lax, negligent'; participle of dissolvo) and dissolvo (dis- and solvo). reviews.checker_notes: Wiktionary's English page stops at Latin dissolutus; the dissolvere and solvere steps agree with Oxford, Longman and AHD, and the wording is not theirs. Tone null follows the rule (Oxford formal and disapproving, Cambridge literary, Longman none). Pairings are the tool's top nouns. Weakest point: the origin's 'loose, lax' gloss of dissolutus is not on Wiktionary's English page, though Oxford gives 'disconnected, loose'.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary duplicity (from Latin duplicare, equivalent to duplex plus -ity) (Wiktionary has no Latin page duplicitas); Oxford and Longman notes give French duplicite from Latin duplex. Root duplex also shows in duplicate and duplex. Tone: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal; Longman's main entry does not (only its business dictionary does), so null. Pairings from the collocations list (political, moral). Hook (duplex, double) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin is true but loose: 'Built on Latin duplex' names no source for the word itself (Late Latin duplicitas, through French, per Oxford, Longman and AHD; Wiktionary has only 'from duplicare, equivalent to duplex + -ity'). Tone null is right (Oxford and Cambridge formal, Longman's main dictionary not). Pairings 'political duplicity' (1.69 per billion) and 'moral duplicity' (1.33) are common but are classifiers that show little of the deceit.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary egregious (Latin egregius from e- and grex 'flock'; usage note: the negative meaning arose in the late 16th century, 'probably' from irony, and before that it meant outstanding in a good way). The hedge is kept as 'probably'. Root grex is spelled as on gregarious. Tone: all three mark it formal (Cambridge also disapproving, only one source). Pairings from the collocations list (error, blunder, violations). Hook (e- and grex, stands out from the herd) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (egregius, e- + grex), and its usage note supports the late-16th-century bad sense 'probably' from irony, hedge kept; the wording is not Wiktionary's or Oxford's. grex is spelled as on gregarious. Formal in all three. Pairings are the tool's top nouns. Weakest point: none of substance; 'herd' in the origin against 'flock' in the gloss is a small inconsistency.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary eschew (Middle English eschewen, Anglo-Norman eschiver, Frankish *skiuhijan 'to dread, shun, avoid'; a doublet of skew; the page lists shy under See also); Oxford Learner's origin note says the French word is of Germanic origin and related to shy. Pairings from the collocations lists (violence, politics after eschew; deliberately before eschewed). Hook (an Old French word related to English shy) agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Anglo-Norman eschiver, from Frankish *skiuhijan 'to dread, shun'; a doublet of skew, whose form comes through Old Northern French eskiver). Pairings are in the tool's lists ('eschew violence' 4.1 per billion, 'deliberately eschewed' 4.2, 'eschew politics' 2.2). Weakest point: the origin follows Wiktionary's order of steps and packs three languages into two sentences; it is reworded, but dense for a learner.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary exhort (Middle English exorten, Old French exhorter, Latin exhortari 'to encourage', from ex- and hortari 'to incite, spur'). Hook (hortari, to urge, as in hortatory) is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (Old French exhorter, Latin exhortari, hortari 'to incite, spur'); hortatory is a true relative. Formal in all three. Weakest point: pairings. 'exhorting people' (6.5 per billion) has a generic object; 'earnestly exhort' (1.9) and 'exhorts believers' (5.6) are fine.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary expiate (expiatus, participle of expio 'atone for'), the Latin pages expio (ex- and pio 'appease; expiate; avenge'), pio and pius; Oxford and Longman notes give piare from pius. Root pius also shows in pious and piety. Tone: all three mark it formal. Pairings from the collocations lists (sin, guilt after expiate). Hook changed: it named piare as the shared root of pious and glossed it 'to make holy', which Wiktionary's pio does not support (it gives 'to appease, propitiate; to purify, expiate', from pius). Smallest fix: the gloss is now 'to purify or appease' and the hook adds 'from pius', so the root pious shares is named correctly.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and the changed hook match Wiktionary: expio 'atone for', and the Latin page pio gives 'to appease, propitiate; to purify, expiate', formed from pius; Oxford and AHD agree, and pious is a true relative. The hook change ('make holy' to 'purify', adding 'from pius') makes it closer to the source. Formal in all three. Weakest point: pairings 'expiate sin' (2.2 per billion) and 'expiate guilt' (1.1) are right, but the bare 'expiate sin' reads less naturally than 'expiate his sins' (2.2).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary fastidious (Latin fastidiosus, from fastidium 'loathing, aversion, disgust, niceness of taste, daintiness'); the further step Wiktionary hedges ('perhaps' from fastus and taedium) is left out. No root. Tone: only Oxford labels it ('sometimes disapproving', on the cleanliness sense), so null. Pairings from the collocations list (taste, attention, care); 'fastidious organisms' belongs to the biology sense and was left out. Biology sense not shown: a general reader rarely meets it. Hook (fastidium, 'disgust') is true; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin and hook match Wiktionary (fastidiosus, from fastidium 'loathing, niceness of taste') and leave out its hedged fastus + taedium split; the step to 'hard to please' is given. Tone null is right (Oxford's 'sometimes disapproving' is on its second sense only). Hiding the biology sense is right. Pairings are in the tool's lists ('fastidious taste' 7.4 per billion). Weakest point: 'Someone easily put off is hard to please' is a little abstract for the step.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary feckless (Scots feckless, variant of fectless, an aphetic form of effectless) ; Oxford and Longman origin notes give Scots feck as a form of effect. No root. Tone: Oxford disapproving, Cambridge formal, Longman none, so null. Pairings from the collocations list (husband, father, youth). Hook (Scots feck, a shortened form of effect) agrees; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Scots feckless, variant of fectless, a shortened effectless); the hook's 'Scots feck, a shortened form of effect' goes past that page and agrees with Oxford, AHD and Dictionary.com. reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary fecund (Middle French fecond, Latin fecundus 'fertile', related to fetus and femina 'woman'). No root: the shared fe- is too short to spot. Pairings from the collocations lists (soil, earth); 'fecund imagination' belongs to the other sense. Hook (shares fe- with fetus) agrees with Wiktionary's 'related to fetus'; unchanged.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin matches Wiktionary (Middle French fecond, Latin fecundus, related to fetus and femina) in new words; the hook's shared fe- agrees with Dictionary.com's fe- (see fetus). Formal in all three; null on the creative sense is right since Longman lacks it. The creative sense is current ('fecund imagination' is high in the tool) and its plain definition is clear. Weakest point: pairings 'fecund soil' (1.5 per billion) and 'fecund earth' (2.5) are fine but only two.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary florid (French floride, Latin floridus 'flowery, blooming') ; flos is from the Oxford and Longman origin notes (Wiktionary's floridus page could not be fetched, rate limit). reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (feinte from feindre, from Latin fingere "to fashion, shape; to feign, pretend"; feign, fiction, figment listed as related) and AHD. reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (probably from archaic Dutch vuisten "to take into one's hand", from vuyst "fist"; hedge kept), AHD (probably Dutch dialectal vuisten) and Oxford Learner's word origin, which gives the first English sense as hiding a die in the hand to bring it out at the right moment. Wiktionary gives no sense history, so the dice step rests on Oxford (and Etymonline, "palm a false die"). Hook change: added "probably" before "goes back", since Wiktionary and AHD hedge the Dutch source; the dice story itself is supported by Oxford and Etymonline. No labels in Oxford, Cambridge or Longman (their pages are the phrasal verb foist on/upon). Other sense (insert slyly into a text) is dated and in no learner's dictionary, so not shown. Pairings from --check "foisted on the *" and "foisted upon *" (on the public 1.8, upon them 10.3 per billion).
reviews.checker_notes: Origin 4: Wiktionary gives only the probable Dutch vuisten < vuyst, fist (hedge kept); the dice sense is not in Wiktionary but Oxford's Word Origin supports it ('hide a dice in one's hand'). 'Palming a die to sneak it into a game' is close to Vocabulary.com's 'palming a loaded die into a game'; reword. Pairings 4: both common ('foisted upon them' 10.3, 'foisted on the public' 1.8, the top fill of its slot) but 'foisted upon them' has only a pronoun partner.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (forbearance = forbear + -ance; forbear from Old English forberan "abstain from, refrain; suffer, endure, tolerate", equivalent to for- + bear). Hook true: the bear in forbear is the endure sense. Tone: Oxford, Cambridge and Longman all mark it formal. Other sense: the lending sense (AHD and Collins label it law) is shown with technical, since mortgage and student-loan forbearance is common in US news; a reviewer may judge it too specialist. Pairings checked: mutual 13.6, patient 4.0, exercise forbearance 2.5 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: pairings, 'exercise forbearance' (2.5 per billion) is also used of lenders and regulators (the other sense). Origin matches Wiktionary forbearance (forbear + -ance) and forbear (Old English forberan, for- + bear). Formal is marked by Oxford, Cambridge and Longman; technical fits the lending sense.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (adjective from Middle English fraught "burdened, loaded", past participle of fraughten "to load a ship with cargo", from Middle Dutch vrachten, from vracht "cargo"; noun fraught is a doublet of freight) and AHD. Hook true ("old cousin of freight", ships once fraught with cargo). No register labels (Oxford marks the tense sense especially British, which is not a tone label). Pairings from --check "fraught with *" (danger 104.8, difficulties 78.5, peril 31.0 per billion). The tense sense is shown: common (fraught relationship 38 per billion) and in Oxford and Longman.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: origin compresses the chain (the Middle English verb came from Middle Dutch vrachten, from vracht), which is acceptable. Pairings are common (fraught with danger 106, difficulties 79, peril 32 per billion); the tense sense is current and well defined.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (Old French frenetike, Latin phreneticus, Greek phrenetikos "delirious", from phrenitis "delirium", from phren "mind"; doublet of frantic; frenzy listed as related; obsolete senses "insane" and "delirium") and Oxford word origin (first English sense insane). Hook true: frenzy shares phren. No labels. Pairings are the tool's top nouns. Checked: pace 44.5, activity 31.5, energy 18.9 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: 'frenzy shares the root' goes past the frenetic entry. Wiktionary's frenzy page would not load (429s), so I judged it on Wiktionary frenetic (phrenetikos < phrenitis, delirium < phren, mind) and Oxford and AHD, which trace frenetic to phrenitis; frenzy also comes from phrenitis via Latin phrenesis. 'Once used of the insane' matches Wiktionary's obsolete sense and Oxford.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (gall + -ing; the adjective follows from the verb), dictionary.com (gall 2 + -ing) and the gall entries quoted in vocabulary.com and WordUp (gall: to chafe or rub sore; a raw spot on a working horse from saddle or harness). Wiktionary's gall page could not be fetched (rate limit), so the sore sense is checked against those dictionaries only. Hook: "comes from gall, a sore" is slightly loose (galling comes from the verb, which comes from the noun) but not false; left unchanged. No labels. Pairings: galling has few noun partners in its main sense (the tool's yoke, fetters and fire are the old chafing and harassing senses), so two are adverb frames; "particularly galling" is generic. Checked: particularly galling 23.9, all the more galling 6.7, galling to see 1.8 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings 4: 'particularly galling' (24 per billion) and 'all the more galling' (6.7) are degree phrases that fit any adjective of annoyance, and 'galling to see' is only 1.8; 'galling for' (13) is more common. Origin checked against Wiktionary gall (fetched): Old English gealla, a saddle sore on a horse; verb to chafe, figuratively to exasperate.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (Middle English glenen "to gather heads of grain left by reapers", Old French glener, Late Latin glen(n)are "to make a collection"; further origin uncertain, possibly Celtic: hedge kept), AHD and Oxford (probably Celtic). Hook true: the harvest sense is the first sense in Wiktionary and the Middle English gloss. No labels. The harvest sense is shown: Longman lists it, and gleaning is still practiced (food-bank gleaning, the Book of Ruth). Pairings checked: glean information 30.4, glean insights 8.3, information gleaned from 85.1 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: alsoMeans, the harvest sense is now met mostly in history, the Bible and food-rescue gleaning, but it is the literal meaning and worth showing. Wiktionary's hedge on glennare (uncertain, possibly Celtic) is kept.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (Latin imbuo "wet, moisten"), AHD ("to moisten, stain") and Longman ("to make wet, stain"). Hook true: "to wet or soak" fits. Tone: Oxford and Cambridge mark it formal, and Longman marks the entry imbue somebody/something with something formal (the main Longman page has no definition). No root: imbuere appears in no other English word (imbibe is from bibere). Other sense (soak with dye) is rare today and in no learner's dictionary, so not shown. Pairings checked: deeply imbued 31.1, thoroughly imbued 17.5, imbued with a sense 26.8 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings 4: 'deeply imbued' (31 per billion) and 'thoroughly imbued' (17) are both intensifying adverbs; 'imbued with meaning' (16) would show the sense better. Formal is marked by Oxford, Cambridge and Longman (imbue with).

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (Middle English inordinat, Latin inordinatus "not arranged, disordered, irregular", from in- + ordinatus, past participle of ordinare "to arrange, order"), AHD and Oxford. reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (Latin insinuo "to push in, creep in, steal in", from in- + sinus "a winding, bend, fold"), AHD (sinuare, to curve, from sinus) and Oxford. I did not claim an English sense history: Oxford gives the first English sense as entering a document on a register. Hook true. Tone of the first sense null: only Oxford marks it (usually disapproving). Other sense shown (insinuate oneself is very common in the tool data); Oxford and Cambridge (phrasal entry insinuate yourself into) mark it formal and disapproving, Longman formal. Both labels qualify; I chose disapproving as the one that matters for use. Pairings checked: are you insinuating 28.1, insinuated that 84.6, insinuating tone 4.6 per billion.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings 4: 'insinuated that' (85 per billion) is a bare clause pattern that fits any verb of saying; 'are you insinuating' (28) and 'insinuating tone' (4.6) are good. Disapproving on the other sense matches Oxford and Cambridge.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (Anglo-Norman getteson, Old French getaison, from geter/jeter, possibly from Vulgar Latin *iectatio from Latin iacto; noun sense "the act of throwing goods overboard to lighten a ship"), AHD and Oxford (jactare, frequentative of jacere). Wiktionary hedges only the step through a Vulgar Latin noun *iectatio; the origin leaves that step out and says only that jeter comes from Latin iactare, which Oxford and AHD give plainly (Wiktionary's jeter page could not be fetched because of the rate limit). Hook true on the same basis. Root iacere (eject, reject, project); Wiktionary itself does not name iacere, Oxford does. The literal sense is shown (planes jettison fuel). Pairings checked: jettison the idea 1.8, jettison everything 1.4, jettisoned altogether 1.2 per billion (all low; the word is uncommon), so scored 4.
reviews.checker_notes: Pairings 4: all three are under 2 per billion; 'jettisoned altogether' is a generic adverb and 'jettison everything' also fits the cargo sense, while 'jettison the idea' (1.8) is the top fill of its slot. Wiktionary hedges getaison < Vulgar Latin (possibly); the origin avoids that step, and Oxford and AHD give the Latin iactare link unhedged.

reviews.notes: Origin checked against Wiktionary (figurative use of metal since the 16th century; the two spellings interchangeable at first, split by sense in the 18th century; mettle also listed as an obsolete spelling of metal) and Oxford. Written in a different order from Wiktionary's note, and reworded to stay clear of vocabulary.com's note (metal and mettle once used interchangeably). Hook true. No labels. No watch-out: mettle spelled metal is rare in print (test their metal 0.32 against test their mettle 8.18 per billion). Pairings checked: prove their mettle 8.3, test their mettle 8.2, true mettle 5.0.
reviews.checker_notes: Origin 4: it follows the sequence of Wiktionary's two sentences and AHD's word history closely (variant of metal, figurative from the 1500s, spelling fixed by sense in the 1700s), and it does not say why metal came to mean spirit (the stuff a person is made of). Recast in your own order and add that step.
